#5556. A Halloween tale: Spooky events and a haunted house sale

Author and trainer Bernice Ross shares a spooky tale of unusual home happenings and a sale process plagued by tragedy.

When you’re in the real estate business, sooner or later there will be a house that someone says is haunted. The story below is true. Were these events just coincidence, or were they something else?

When I was working on my doctorate, my closest friend and study partner was living in a new house in Orange County. She was in the antique business. Her home was like a showcase, every last inch of it beautifully decorated. When I met her, she was in the process of getting a divorce.

Although her house was a little over a year old, it already had the makings of a strange history. While the house was being built, a little girl was sexually assaulted in it. A few months after she and her husband moved in, he became manic-depressive.

Over the next few months, he had numerous confrontations with the police. He refused to take his meds. Unbeknownst to his wife, he placed a warranty deed on the property to access part of the equity. He then took off to Hawaii, where he was reportedly living in the bush outside the Honolulu airport.

We would normally study together at her house about twice per month. The lights would flicker periodically. If we went out for dinner, it was common for pieces of the furniture to be moved away from the wall.

Since my friend had changed the locks and placed a security system on the house, there was no one who had access to move the furniture. There was also a window in the family room overlooking the canyon that would vibrate for no apparent reason. You could put your hand on the window and tell it to stop vibrating, and it did.

After spending the afternoon preparing for our upcoming qualifying exams, we decided to go out to dinner to take a break. When we returned, the lights were flickering, and a number of pieces of furniture were moved again.

As we sat back down to hit the books again, there was a loud rustling in the garage where she refinished her antiques. Her German shepherd, a very mellow dog who never barked, started barking and scratching crazily at the door to the garage.

Although this didn’t disturb my friend, I made sure the dog was between me and whatever was in the garage. As soon as she opened the door, the dog broke away from me and raced into the garage. The dog raced to the other side of the garage, sat down and acted as if nothing had happened.

After consuming a carton of chocolate ice cream to soothe our jangled nerves, we decided to watch a movie — The Ghost of Flight 401. This probably wasn’t the smartest movie choice, but that was the best of the evening’s shows back in the days of seven TV channels and no cable.

As I was getting ready to leave, we were standing by the front door adjacent to the stairway. Her stairs had beautiful wrought iron work topped with a heavy oak banister.

As we were standing there talking, the banister and the wrought iron started to vibrate. Everything else in the house was still. I turned and asked her, “Do you see what I see?” She did.

We were both mesmerized because nothing else was moving. This went on for about five minutes, and then it stopped. At that point, I was out of there, and there was no way I was going back.

My friend wanted out of the house. Needless to say, there were numerous challenges that had to be addressed before she could legally sell the property. California law allowed her to list the property, but both she and her husband had to sign the grant deed to close the transaction.

The lender who held the warranty deed was demanding payment as per the terms of the note. Normally, their option would have been to foreclose. The challenge was that the police reports documented the fact that the husband was probably not legally competent at the time he signed the deed.

Since he was nowhere to be found, my friend and the lender petitioned the court to order the sale as part of the divorce proceedings. The court granted her request.

The house was listed and finally went under contract. The buyer was a deputy sheriff. Two days after opening escrow on the property, the escrow officer had a heart attack and died. The title officer handling the file also had a heart attack but recovered.

About four weeks into the transaction, the deputy sheriff’s right arm became mysteriously paralyzed. He saw several specialists, but no one could find a cause for the problem. He was forced to take disability leave from his job. This meant he didn’t have sufficient income to qualify for the loan. The transaction was canceled. Within a few days after he canceled, the paralysis disappeared.

After almost a year, the house finally sold. The buyer was a psychiatrist.

Fortunately, this transaction took place prior to California passing its disclosure laws. I have to wonder how you would make those disclosures today. Much of what happened could be coincidence. I still don’t have an explanation for the moved furniture, the strange window and, most of all, the vibrating staircase. Perhaps it’s just as well that I don’t.

Bernice Ross is president and CEO of BrokerageUP and RealEstateCoach.com, the founder of Profit.RealEstate and a national speaker, author and trainer with over 1,500 published articles.

#5555. Did Mark Zuckerberg’s Meta AI Just Expose Real Bitcoin Bottom in January 2027?

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

Bitcoin’s cycle bottom is likely already in or very close, as a Mark Zuckerberg Meta AI Bitcoin bottom prediction highlights a final low expected in the $60,000–$68,000 zone by late December 2026 or early January 2027 at the latest. As of November 11, 2026, Bitcoin trades near $73,700–$73,900, roughly 41% below its October 2025 all-time high around $126,000.

The market has been grinding lower after a failed recovery attempt into the low $80,000s, with recent sessions testing the psychologically important $73,000 level. While the short-term trend remains soft, longer-term structure and historical cycle patterns suggest the deepest part of the correction is largely complete.

Bitcoin is consolidating in a tight range after a multi-week decline. Immediate support sits at the $73,000 round number, which coincides with recent daily lows, the approximate 200-day moving average, and prior structural levels from earlier in the year.

A daily close below $73,000 would open the door to the next support cluster near $71,500 (prior swing area) and then the 50-day moving average zone around $68,500. Deeper support resides in the $62,000–$65,000 region, with the July 2026 low near $57,700–$58,000 acting as the major cycle floor.

On the upside, resistance is layered at $75,000, followed by the more significant $80,000 area. Momentum indicators such as the RSI have cooled into neutral-to-oversold territory on daily timeframes, leaving room for either a relief bounce or one final liquidity sweep lower before a more durable base forms.

Volume has been elevated on down days, consistent with distribution by short-term holders, but longer-term holder metrics and the 200-week moving average (historically a strong demand zone) continue to provide a structural floor.

Bitcoin | Net shorts just hit an ATH.The last 4 times we saw these levels, they marked a major bottom. pic.twitter.com/n9DkeYEYqy

My base-case view is that the primary cycle low was printed in July 2026 near $58,000. That level marked a roughly 54% drawdown from the prior peak, shallower than the 70–80%+ declines of previous bear markets, reflecting Bitcoin’s growing institutional base and ETF demand.

The current pullback into the low $70,000s looks more like a higher-low retest or secondary correction within a broader bottoming process rather than the start of a new leg down. If $73,000 fails, a final flush into the $62,000–$68,000 zone remains the most probable destination.

This area aligns with Fibonacci retracements of the 2025–2026 rally, prior demand zones, and the upper end of the July low region. I expect any such move to occur relatively quickly, within the next four to eight weeks, driven by residual profit-taking, macro uncertainty, or year-end positioning.

By late December 2026 or the first half of January 2027 at the latest, this process should be complete. A sustained defense of the $68,000–$70,000 area (or a higher low above $70,000) would strongly support the thesis that the bottom is in.

Conversely, a decisive break below the July low near $58,000 would invalidate the constructive view and open a path toward $50,000–$55,000, though that outcome currently carries lower probability given the maturity of the correction and the strength of long-term holder support.

In short, Bitcoin appears to be in the late stages of its post-2025 correction. The most likely final low sits in the $60,000–$68,000 range, timed for the remainder of Q4 2026 into very early 2027. Once that floor is confirmed with a higher low and a reclaim of $80,000, the stage would be set for a more meaningful recovery phase.

#5554. 3 ways AI is changing the healthcare revenue cycle

The healthcare revenue cycle depends on teams investigating denied claims, checking payer rules and deciding which problems need a human’s attention. AI agents could take on some of that work, but the harder question is how to fit them into the way health systems operate.

For Mount Sinai Health System Inc., that starts with clear workflows and accountability when automation encounters an exception, according to Salonia Brown, system vice president of revenue cycle at Mount Sinai. Without those foundations, adding AI could make existing problems harder to manage.

“If you don’t have your workflows down pat, if you don’t have operational owners, when something kicks out, when you use AI, if there’s no ownership over that or accountability, then what you’re in essence doing is kind of digitizing dysfunction,” Brown said in an interview with theCUBE. “It’s very simple and easy to inject AI, but to do it the right way, making sure there’s governance [and] that the economics make sense? That takes a little bit of time.”

Brown and Akash Magoon, co-founder and chief executive officer of Adonis Technology Inc., along with other industry experts, spoke with theCUBE’s host Gemma Allen for the Adonis Reimagining Claim to Cash interview series on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how AI agents can handle claims work, how health systems govern exceptions and where human judgment remains essential. (* Disclosure below.)

Here are three insights from this exclusive interview series:

Adonis is building agents to investigate denied claims and reduce the manual work involved in pursuing payment, according to Magoon. The company uses voice AI to call insurers for claims information and makes tens of thousands of those calls each week on behalf of its partners.

At Mount Sinai, Brown’s team helps determine which tasks can be automated and which require critical judgment. Employees need to trust the technology and know who is responsible when an exception arises, he noted. The goal is to free staff from repetitive administrative work so they can focus on more complex cases.

Adonis distinguishes between frequent, repetitive tasks suited to automation and complex work that calls for better information and decisions, according to David Unger, managing director of health system sales at Adonis. For a high-value appeal, that can mean helping a team decide whether to pursue it and what evidence may improve its chances.

At Rush University System for Health, frontline employees help identify time-consuming steps that add little value, according to Blake Evans, system vice president of revenue cycle at Rush. Their firsthand knowledge helps the company decide where to automate and has made staff advocates for further changes.

Adonis aims to identify revenue-cycle issues as they emerge and recommend a response, according to Doug Pickett, chief revenue officer of Adonis. An issue might call for automation, or it might reveal an upstream coding or provider-credentialing problem that a health system needs to fix before it grows.

Clinicians and operating teams are increasingly asking for AI tools that could reduce administrative burdens, according to Sap Sinha, chief executive officer of Panoramic Health. Yet rules governing billing, documentation and interactions with insurers have not kept pace with the technology. How those rules evolve could shape whether and how providers and insurers can use AI agents to interact over claims.

#5553. ‘Haunted as a matter of law’: How real estate agents handle stigmatized listings in 2026

Stigmatized homes have long sold at a steep discount. Agents and attorneys say an unaffordable, low-inventory 2026 market may be shrinking it.

Many may assume that the rule of thumb on stigmatized homes is simple: A murder, suicide or infamous ghost story knocks a big chunk off the price. Real estate agents who’ve sold these homes say it’s more complicated, and today’s unaffordable, short-on-inventory market may be shrinking the discount.

A “stigmatized” property can mean many things. It can be a home tied to a violent crime, a suicide, a notorious former owner or an alleged haunting.

Would you live in the Amityville Horror house, where Ronald DeFeo Jr. killed six members of his family in 1974?

Or what about the Menendez mansion in Beverly Hills, where Lyle and Erik Menendez killed their parents, José and Kitty, in 1989, a case that has stayed in the headlines for more than three decades?

These gruesome crimes may not always change the bedroom count or the square footage. But they can change who’s willing to buy, and for how much.

Ahead of Halloween, Inman asked real estate agents and attorneys how they handle stigmatized listings in 2026.

Their answers suggest the discount is real but uneven. It often depends less on the stigma itself than on how many buyers it drives away. And in a market with increasingly few affordable options, fewer buyers may be walking away.

The best-known estimate for stigmatized listings comes from real estate economist Randall Bell, who has put the typical “murder-house” discount at 10 to 25 percent. Bell has also said he’s seen some stigmatized homes sell at full value — usually smaller, more affordable homes — while others sit unsold for a long time.

Bell is an expert on real estate damage, earning the nickname “Master of Disaster,” and he runs the advisory firm Landmark Research. He has consulted on some of the most notorious crime-linked properties in history, from the Rancho Santa Fe mansions where the bodies of 39 Heaven’s Gate cult members were found to the home of Sandy Hook shooter Adam Lanza.

While Bell’s estimates are frequently cited, academic research suggests the price discount effect on stigmatized properties may fade over time.

A 2020 study of Tokyo apartment buildings by economist Taisuke Sadayuki found that a homicide in one unit initially cut rents on other units in the same building by about 10 percent, with the effect disappearing after roughly seven to eight years.

Survey data suggests buyers may also be less squeamish than agents assume. In a 2023 Zillow survey, 67 percent of prospective buyers said they could be persuaded to buy a “haunted” house with the right features, location or price.

When Inman covered stigmatized homes more than a decade ago, we framed them as bargains. The market has changed a lot since then.

Rebecca Chambliss, an agent with Carmody Real Estate in the Santa Monica, California, area, recently sold a home in a gated community where the previous owner had died by suicide only a few months before it was listed. All of the neighbors knew.

Chambliss disclosed the death to serious buyers who were discussing an offer. In her experience, buyers don’t spread out along a spectrum of tolerance. They split into two groups.

“Some people will never buy a home where a suicide or other non-natural death occurred no matter what, and then there are people who it doesn’t bother,” Chambliss told Inman. “There aren’t people in between.”

One interested buyer made an unexpected offer. When Chambliss disclosed the death, he demanded to know exactly where in the house it happened and how. Chambliss had chosen not to learn those details herself and told him as much. He wouldn’t move forward without them and withdrew the offer.

The home did eventually sell at a discount because of the suicide, Chambliss said. The buyer understood that he’d have to disclose the death if he ever sold. He relisted it about a year later, asking $1 million more than he paid, and the home still hasn’t sold.

Chambliss also brought in an energy clearer before marketing the home. It’s a reminder that for some agents, handling a stigmatized listing takes more than paperwork.

The discount doesn’t always stay with the property. Sometimes a savvy investor who knows about it collects it.

Jonathan Carcone, principal of 4 Brothers Buy Houses and a licensed agent in Washington state, bought a home in Poulsbo, Washington, with local ghost stories attached.

He said the home was listed at $640,000, while comparable homes were selling for about $650,000. Carcone said the listing didn’t mention ghost stories, but neighbors told him about them.

Carcone used the ghost stories in negotiations and bought the house for $585,000, about 9 percent below list and roughly 10 percent below comps.

Carcone’s company buys, renovates and sells dozens of houses every year, including “challenging properties.” After renovating the house in Poulsbo, he sold it for $660,000 about two months later.

“The ghost stories had no influence on the sale, and we made a good profit,” Carcone told Inman.

He said Washington law doesn’t require agents to disclose a home’s reputation, including ghost stories, so he didn’t. No buyer asked about it during showings, either. So, in this case, Carcone used the stigma to his advantage.

Because the resale price reflects a renovation, it isn’t a clean before-and-after comparison. Still, the pattern is worth noting. The seller absorbed a 10 percent discount for the stigma, and the next buyer paid none.

What agents must disclose for stigmatized properties varies widely by state.

California sets a three-year line. Under California Civil Code Section 1710.2, sellers and agents aren’t required to disclose a death that occurred on the property more than three years before a buyer’s offer. They also can’t be sued for staying silent. Whether it must be disclosed depends on whether it’s material, and the common practice is to disclose to be safe.

Answering a direct question is a separate matter. The law doesn’t protect anyone who lies when asked.

“The main point of contention between sellers and buyers is whether answering questions truthfully violates the seller’s wishes,” Nick Heimlich, founder and attorney of San Jose, California-based Nick Heimlich Law, told Inman. “Under California Civil Code, a seller’s agent cannot refuse to answer questions about the property’s history.”

Texas Property Code Section 5.008(c) says a seller or seller’s agent has no duty to disclose a death on the property from natural causes, suicide or an accident unrelated to the property’s condition. But not homicide, which may still be a material fact that must be disclosed.

Tennessee goes further. Tenn. Code Ann. § 66-5-207 lists a homicide, felony or suicide on the property among the things sellers don’t have to disclose. It also covers any act or occurrence that didn’t affect the property’s physical structure.

Ghost stories bring their own risk. In the famous case of Stambovsky v. Ackley (1991), a New York appellate court let a buyer back out of buying an allegedly haunted home in Nyack, New York.

The seller had publicized the ghost stories herself in Reader’s Digest and the local press, then didn’t tell the out-of-town buyer. In effect, the court held that because she’d told everyone else the house was haunted, it was haunted as a matter of law.

Donald Leeth, managing partner at Leeth & Gaglione, has spent 27 years as a criminal defense attorney and former prosecutor in Monroe County, Pennsylvania, and the Poconos. During that time, he’s encountered many homes where crimes took place. He advises disclosing rather than gambling on the legal minimum.

“It’s always best to be honest up front so you’re not dealing with misrepresentation claims once your transaction has closed,” Leeth said.

The more interesting question for 2026 is whether affordability is eroding the discount stigmatized listings usually have.

Median prices for new and existing homes now both top $400,000, according to Harvard University’s Joint Center for Housing Studies. Existing-home prices have climbed 54 percent nationwide since 2020 and sit at nearly five times median income, well above the 3-to-1 ratio that held in the 1990s.

Leeth thinks the affordability crisis is negating the discount effect on stigmatized listings.

“Many buyers won’t care if there’s an infamous story behind a house because they simply don’t have other options,” he said. “Stigma isn’t as much of a factor as it once was because the price will determine what someone buys.”

That fits with Chambliss’s two-camp theory. If the buyers who’ll never consider a stigmatized home stay out no matter what, the discount depends on how many buyers are left in the other camp. In a tight, low-inventory market, more buyers are in that camp, and they may have fewer alternatives.

Heimlich said the type of event still matters. Buyers might shrug at a home that sat empty for a long time, he said, but something like a murder “can severely influence the property value.”

Still, he added, it likely depends on the market. And if stigma leads to a bargain, that helps, too.

“Some buyers may be willing to invest in stigmatized real estate if it falls within an affordable price range,” Heimlich said.

For agents, the practical takeaway is that a stigmatized listing’s real challenge is finding the buyers who don’t care, not pricing in a fixed discount, and disclosing in a way that doesn’t create legal exposure after closing.

Sometimes the stigma bothers the buyer’s friends and family more than the buyer themselves.

Years ago, Chambliss, the California-based agent, sold a home where a murder had taken place in the front yard. The buyer was a young single father whose Italian immigrant parents were involved in the buying process and may have been helping with the purchase. Chambliss took him outside and told him what had happened there.

He became very concerned, then immediately asked, “Do you have to tell my parents?”

His whole body relaxed, and he laughed. Then he said, “OK, I have no issue with it. But my parents would never let me buy this house if they knew.”

He bought the house, and Chambliss assumed he never told them.

#5552. Commission settlement accounts hold $711M as claim payouts await (EXCLUSIVE)

New disclosures show that the settlement fund accounts received about $17.7 million in interest during the first nine months of 2026.

That’s how much money was held in accounts associated with the sweeping real estate commission antitrust settlements as of Sept. 30, according to newly filed federal court documents offering a fresh look at the money from the nationwide agreements.

The disclosures, filed Thursday in federal court in Missouri, show that the accounts received about $17.7 million in interest during the first nine months of 2026, while roughly $5.8 million was transferred out during the same period.

The filings also come amid an ongoing court-ordered audit of settlement administrator JND Legal Administration, which reported earlier this year that it had received and processed more than 2.7 million claim submissions.

The financial accounting follows a series of appellate rulings upholding the commission settlements, although questions remain about when eligible homesellers will receive payments.

According to a declaration signed Oct. 13 by Isaac Lim, a senior vice president and senior risk officer at Morgan Stanley Smith Barney, and filed by plaintiffs Oct. 29, the settlement accounts had a combined balance of $711,251,720.86 as of Sept. 30.

The funds were transferred from Huntington Bank to Morgan Stanley on Oct. 23, 2025, at class counsel’s direction.

Lim reported that $17,705,101.82 in interest was paid into the accounts between January and September 2026, while $5,780,467.43 was transferred out during the same period. The declaration does not identify the purpose of those transfers or establish whether any money has been distributed directly to eligible homesellers.

According to the filing, the money is invested in a BlackRock institutional money market fund yielding about 3.63 percent annually, Morgan Stanley’s preferred savings program paying 4 percent or a combination of both. The yields are estimates and subject to change.

The reported balance represents funds held in the identified Morgan Stanley accounts, rather than necessarily the full amount collected through the broader commission settlements. The declaration does not provide a complete accounting of earlier distributions, expenses or outstanding settlement contributions.

In a June declaration, Jennifer Keough, CEO of JND Legal Administration, said the company had received and processed more than 2.7 million claim submissions. In June 2025, more than 2.5 million claims had already been submitted, while JND had invoiced approximately $32.8 million for its administrative work.

Keough said JND’s original assignment expanded into six separate notification campaigns involving more than 138 million emails and 44 million postcards. Four of those direct-mail campaigns cost about $18.7 million in postage alone, which JND characterized as a pass-through expense.

In May, Missouri-based U.S. District Judge Stephen Bough ordered JND to stop receiving payments while the court considered appointing a special master to audit the company’s past and future bills.

On July 27, the judge appointed Chris Hellums and Randall Sansom as special masters.

Hellums was tasked with overseeing the audit and helping establish future administration arrangements, while Sansom, a certified public accountant, was directed to audit JND’s billing and expenses dating back to the beginning of its work.

The order requires JND to provide detailed financial records, including employee timesheets, vendor invoices, billing records and information about rebates, credits or other financial incentives.

JND opposed the need for an independent audit, arguing in a June filing that the process would be expensive and burdensome and that its work had been performed appropriately. The company said it would cooperate if the audit proceeded, but requested confidentiality protections for commercially sensitive pricing information.

JND also said its responsibilities had expanded substantially at class counsel’s direction and that it had advanced nearly $3 million in out-of-pocket costs on behalf of the class.

The dispute escalated in August when JND sought to disqualify Hellums, alleging he had demonstrated bias against the company through his involvement in a separate antitrust settlement proceeding.

Bough denied the motion Aug. 26, finding that JND, as a nonparty, could not seek disqualification under the applicable rules. He added that even if JND could bring the challenge, it had failed to establish sufficient grounds to question Hellums’ impartiality.

The ruling also examined a question Hellums had raised in the Blue Cross Blue Shield case about potential vendor rebates and credits, which Bough said JND never answered in its email exchange with him and only partly addressed at the Aug. 20 hearing. Keough acknowledged at the hearing that separate vendor agreements govern how rebates and credits are calculated.

JND has maintained in sworn declarations that it has received no rebates, credits or other financial benefits from banks or vendors in connection with the commission settlements.

In its latest accounting, JND reported $155,932 in additional administrative invoices covering July through September, bringing the outstanding balance shown on its October invoice to $494,249.

Keough said JND continues submitting invoices and performing administrative work despite not currently receiving payments.

JND did not respond to Inman’s request for comment by the time of publication.

Despite a series of appellate rulings upholding the real estate commission settlements, it remains unclear when eligible homesellers can expect to receive payments.

On Aug. 19, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 8th Circuit unanimously upheld the landmark Sitzer | Burnett settlement, rejecting seven appeals challenging its scope, fairness and accompanying industry practice changes.

The court subsequently affirmed another $110.6 million in brokerage settlements in the related Gibson litigation on Sept. 1, bringing the total collected for the class to about $1.02 billion, according to the appellate opinion.

After rejecting three additional objector appeals on Sept. 15 and denying rehearing petitions from objectors Robert Friedman and Monty March on Sept. 24, the 8th Circuit issued its mandate in the main Sitzer | Burnett appeals Oct. 2, concluding those proceedings before the appeals court. Objectors may still seek review from the U.S. Supreme Court.

The 8th Circuit issued its mandate in the Gibson appeals Oct. 14.

Despite those developments, the latest financial disclosures do not establish when eligible homesellers will receive distributions or precisely how much of the $711 million held in Morgan Stanley accounts is available for payment.

Eric Dirks, an attorney with the Kansas City-based Williams Dirks Dameron, one of the plaintiffs’ co-lead counsel firms, did not respond to Inman’s request for comment regarding the account balance, interest earnings and anticipated distribution timeline.

#5551. Housing on the ballot: What to watch in the Nov. 3 midterms

Realtor associations in Florida, California and Massachusetts have lined up behind statewide housing measures on the Nov. 3 ballot, led by $18 million from Florida Realtors for a property tax cut.

Those are among six midterm housing ballot measures at the state level in four U.S. states, the most in a single election year since at least 2006, according to Ballotpedia, not counting property tax measures like Florida’s.

Thirty-six states will also elect governors, and candidates in California, Texas and Florida have released housing plans that range from a statewide housing emergency to ending school property taxes on homesteads.

In federal races, housing has surfaced as part of a broader argument about cost of living. Among Americans who plan to vote, 85 percent say housing affordability is at least somewhat important in choosing candidates, but 64 percent don’t know where their congressional candidates stand on housing, according to a Clever Real Estate survey.

Inman’s editorial staff will be watching California, Texas and Florida most closely next Tuesday. Each has a large real estate market and pairs a governor’s race with policy that would affect transactions, property taxes or construction.

In California, Democrat Xavier Becerra would declare a housing state of emergency on his first day, penalize cities that ignore housing element commitments, back local rent control within the statewide framework and seek disclosure of bulk investor purchases. Republican Steve Hilton would cap government fees and mandates on a new home at $50,000 and freeze new housing rules for five years.

In Texas, Republican Gov. Greg Abbott says his plan would cut the cost of a new home by more than $16,000 through faster inspections and pre-approved designs, and he wants to end school property taxes on homesteads. Democratic state Rep. Gina Hinojosa would restrict corporate purchases of single-family homes and pursue an end to residential property taxes.

In Florida, Republican Byron Donalds wants local governments to remove zoning restraints and supports Amendment 3. Democrat David Jolly opposes the amendment and says the state’s Live Local Act has not delivered affordable housing.

Housing is also a campaign issue in governor races in Colorado, Michigan, Massachusetts and Rhode Island. In Colorado, Democrat Phil Weiser has proposed 40,000 more owner-occupied homes by 2035, and Republican Victor Marx would cut state regulations and red tape. In Michigan, Democrat Jocelyn Benson has pitched affordability proposals, and Republican John James says local codes add more than $100,000 to developers’ costs.

Massachusetts Gov. Maura Healey, a Democrat seeking a second term, supports Question 7, a zoning change that could lead to the construction of more single-family homes. In Rhode Island, Democrat Helena Foulkes proposes a $1 billion plan for 20,000 homes over eight years, funded by a millionaire tax; independent Ken Block says the fund would produce no more than 375 units.

Florida Realtors had contributed $18 million to the Vote Yes on 3 committee as of late September, funding the campaign in full, WLRN reported. Amendment 3 would raise the state’s homestead property tax exemption.

“Affordability is on the forefront for every Floridian, and they need meaningful relief,” Florida Realtors President Chuck Bonfiglio Jr. said in a statement.

The California Association of Realtors supports Prop. 37, which would fund second mortgages for buyers of newly built homes, and Prop. 45, which would speed permitting and shorten environmental review. The Massachusetts Association of Realtors supports Question 7.

At the federal level, NAR’s political action committee directed more candidate contributions and independent expenditures to Texas than to any other state through February, according to FEC filings Inman reporters reviewed. NAHB’s BUILD-PAC backs what the group calls pro-housing, pro-business candidates for Congress.

The National Association of Hispanic Real Estate Professionals backed the ROAD to Housing Act in a March letter to Senate leaders, citing its provisions on zoning reform and by-right development.

Florida’s Amendment 3 would raise the homestead exemption on non-school property taxes from about $50,000 to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028, and lower the cap on annual assessment increases for non-homestead properties from 10 percent to 5 percent. It needs 60 percent of the vote.

California voters will decide Prop. 1, an $11.25 billion housing bond; Prop. 37, up to $25 billion in revenue bonds for second mortgages covering up to 17 percent of a new home’s price; and Prop. 45, which would set permitting deadlines and shorten environmental review.

In Massachusetts, Question 7 would require cities and towns to allow a single-family home on residentially zoned lots of at least 5,000 square feet with 50 feet of street frontage and public water and sewer.

Below the statewide level, voters will weigh more than 50 housing-related measures, according to a Shelterforce scan. Inman reporters will track the local questions most likely to touch agents’ markets, including property tax relief for older homeowners, transfer tax changes in San Francisco and Oakland and housing bonds in Charlotte and Raleigh.

Congress passed the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act in July. None of the 12 housing bills Inman reporter AJ LaTrace is tracking have advanced since September, including a bipartisan proposal to double the capital gains exclusion on home sales.

Bills that don’t pass before the current Congressional session ends in January would need to be reintroduced. When lawmakers return after the election, they face a Dec. 11 deadline to fund federal agencies, including HUD, and to reauthorize the National Flood Insurance Program.

Inman reporters will follow how the results shape development, including data center development, which has become a campaign issue in Tennessee. The state has about 60 operating data centers and 15 to 20 more proposed, according to WSMV, and the major-party nominees for governor differ on how to handle them. Republican nominee Sen. Marsha Blackburn has said local communities should decide, and Democrat Jerri Green has called for a moratorium.

Most governors elected Nov. 3 will take office in January as state legislatures convene. That same month, the ROAD to Housing Act’s limits on large investors buying additional single-family homes take effect, and Florida’s higher homestead exemption would follow in 2027 if voters approve it.

#5549. SDI Presence CEO Hardik Bhatt Named Chicago Titan 100 Honoree for Second Consecutive Year

Recognition celebrates Bhatt's visionary leadership, commitment to innovation, and continued growth of SDI Presence

CHICAGO, Nov. 12, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- SDI Presence LLC (SDI), a leading IT consultancy and managed services provider, announces that Chief Executive Officer Hardik Bhatt has been named a Chicago Titan 100 honoree for the second consecutive year. The prestigious recognition celebrates the region's most accomplished CEOs and C-level executives who demonstrate exceptional leadership, vision, and influence.

Under Bhatt's leadership, SDI has continued to strengthen its position as a trusted technology partner to organizations managing complex, mission-critical operations. Bhatt's strategic vision has helped advance the firm's growth, expand its capabilities in emerging technologies, and deepen its commitment to delivering meaningful outcomes for clients across the public and private sectors.

The recognition comes as SDI celebrates its 30th anniversary, marking three decades of helping organizations navigate technological complexity and change. With a growing national presence and nearly 450 technical professionals, the firm continues to build on its established strengths in IT managed services, ServiceNow, technology consulting and advisory services, and emerging technologies, including data and artificial intelligence.

"Being recognized for a second consecutive year is a tremendous honor, particularly among so many accomplished leaders in Chicago's business community," said Bhatt. "At SDI, our success is driven by the talented people who bring expertise, dedication, and fresh thinking to our clients every day. As we celebrate 30 years in business, I'm proud of what we've built together and even more excited about the opportunities ahead."

Beyond SDI's business growth, Bhatt has championed initiatives that connect technology innovation with economic opportunity. His leadership has helped advance Xchange Chicago, an innovative workforce development and onshore IT delivery initiative launching technology careers while helping organizations access emerging talent. The initiative reflects SDI's broader commitment to investing in people, strengthening communities, and building a more inclusive workforce.

The Titan 100 program recognizes 100 distinguished CEOs and C-level executives in the Chicago region annually. Honorees are selected for their leadership, vision, passion, and contributions to their organizations and communities. A second-year recognition reflects continued distinction among the region's leading executives.

As SDI enters its fourth decade, Bhatt remains focused on accelerating innovation, strengthening strategic partnerships, and positioning the firm for sustained growth while preserving the client-focused culture that has defined its success.

SDI Presence LLC is a leading IT consultancy and managed services provider helping organizations modernize, manage, and optimize the technology that powers their most critical operations. From technology strategy and enterprise platforms to managed services and emerging technologies, SDI delivers solutions that strengthen resilience, accelerate innovation, and create lasting value.

#5547. The Slowest Contracts Spend over 40% of their Time Waiting On Signers, ContractSafe Data Shows

ContractSafe's 2026 Contract Lifecycle Report is built on timestamp analysis from more than 55,000 contracts. For contracts that take more than three weeks from start to finish, the longest period is waiting for signatures â more than during approval and negotiation combined.

MALIBU, Calif., Nov. 12, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Among companies that use contract lifecycle management (CLM) software, half of contracts are signed within 2.8 days of being added, but the slowest 10% take 24 days or more. For the slowest contracts, 40% of that time passes after they've been sent to be signed, according to ContractSafe's 2026 Contract Lifecycle Report.

ContractSafe's 2026 Contract Lifecycle Report is built on timestamp analysis from more than 55,000 contracts.

For those slowest contracts, the biggest wait comes at the last step. Of the time they spent in the four steps the report tracks (waiting to start, in progress, approval, and signature), 44% went to waiting for signatures, more than twice the 19% that went to approval. That means most of the delay comes after the contract has already gone out. It's sitting with someone who only has to sign it.

"Everyone has a theory about why contracts are slow, and most of those theories come from surveys," said Randy Bishop, CEO and co-founder of ContractSafe. "We looked at what contracts actually did. Most are signed in days. The ones that get stuck are often waiting on one person, an approver who hasn't answered or a signer who hasn't signed. And these are teams that have visibility into their contracts. Teams working out of email and shared drives usually can't tell which contracts are waiting, or who they're waiting on."

The report, "Where Contracts Get Stuck (...and How to Fix It)," is ContractSafe's 2026 proprietary data white paper. It isn't survey results. It's built on real-world anonymized timestamps showing how contracts actually moved at companies that use ContractSafe, from August 2025 to September 2026, including more than 15,000 approval requests and 48,000 e-signature requests.

The report advises seven moves a team can make this quarter, including naming an owner the day a contract is added, reminding the one approver who hasn't answered, and using an intake form so new requests arrive with the key facts.

"Small and midsize teams don't need a six-month project to speed up contracts," said Ken Button, co-founder of ContractSafe. "They need to see which contracts are stuck and whose turn it is. Once you can see that, the fix is usually one reminder or one setting."

The full report is available free at https://www.contractsafe.com/2026-contract-data-white-paper. All data is anonymized and aggregated, and no company, contract, or person can be identified.

ContractSafe is a contract lifecycle management (CLM) platform built for small and midsize organizations. Refreshingly simple and surprisingly affordable, it helps legal, finance, procurement, and operations teams manage the full contract lifecycle, from intake through renewal, with practical AI built in. ContractSafe was founded in 2015 and is backed by Five Elms Capital. Learn more at https://www.contractsafe.com.

#5546. What real estate agents should watch on Election Day, per NAHB

NAHB’s Ken Wingert on housing and the midterms, from state ballot measures and the ROAD to Housing Act to tariffs, labor and mortgage rates.

Housing may not be on many ballots by name on Nov. 3, but it’s running through nearly every race.

With the midterms set for Tuesday, candidates from both parties are pitching voters on affordability. Lawmakers are campaigning on the recently passed 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, states from California to Massachusetts are voting on measures meant to make building easier, and homebuilders are grappling with tariffs and immigration enforcement that have driven up costs and thinned out job-site crews.

Inman spoke with Ken Wingert, chief advocacy officer at the National Association of Home Builders, about the races and ballot measures NAHB is watching, whether data centers are really competing with housing for land, and what agents should keep an eye on as votes are counted.

Inman: What are two or three outcomes to the midterms you think matter most for housing — on the federal- level and state-level?

Ken Wingert: The overall theme is that this is turning out to be, once again, an affordability election, and housing is at the top of that pain point … because we don’t have enough of it. So regardless of who controls Congress or who wins the governor’s race in any given state, I think housing will be near or at the top of the agenda going into 2027. That gives us, and other groups you’re probably talking to, a lot of opportunity to advocate for more housing supply.

On specific issues, people are starting to understand that supply matters. You’re seeing ballot initiatives in a number of states aimed at making it easier for builders to build and cutting some of that red tape. Members of Congress are running on the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act. Congress is still debating permitting reform that may pass in the lame-duck session or get kicked to the next Congress.

From a congressional standpoint, if Democrats win at least one chamber, there will probably be more pushback and oversight on issues like tariffs and immigration, which have made it harder for builders to build more housing, or at least more expensive.

Are there specific races that NAHB is watching closely, at the state, federal or local level?

We’re not quite NAR size, but we’re involved in a lot. At the federal level, I think we’ll see how big a wave is, if one materializes, and whether it takes out some folks who have been very helpful on housing over the years.

Financial Services Chairman French Hill will be fine, I think, but he’s in a tighter race than expected. Mike Hill, chairman of the House Financial Services Subcommittee on Housing and Insurance, faces the same challenge. In Michigan, Bill Huizenga is a former Realtor and builder. Sherrod Brown, former chair of the Banking Committee, is potentially coming back to the Senate from Ohio. A lot of folks are watching that race.

But really, at the state level: California has a couple of ballot initiatives, one in particular we’ve been involved with on changes to CEQA, the California Environmental Quality Act. The legislature had made some changes, and this would codify them in state law. In Massachusetts, we’re supporting a ballot initiative that would reduce minimum lot sizes, meaning how big your lot has to be to build on it. And there are a bunch of funding ballot initiatives around the country. All of those aim to increase supply, so we’re keyed in on those state-level races.

I’ve seen candidates from both parties campaigning on the recently passed ROAD to Housing Act. Does that kind of policy achievement resonate with voters, or does a general affordability pitch resonate more?

Both parties are campaigning on the fact that Congress passed major housing legislation with overwhelming bipartisan support. Beyond affordability, another theme in this election is that people want less divisiveness and more collaboration to solve problems. ROAD to Housing was a great example of both parties giving up a few things to get a bill they wanted.

I don’t know that the average voter is digging into a bill with 60 titles, but they understand that Congress recognized a housing supply problem and is at least trying to fix it. If I’m running for Congress, that’s something I’m going to go out and tell people.

Have you noticed more local candidates running explicitly on pro-housing or YIMBY platforms? Any examples?

Our state and local associations make their own endorsements and funding decisions, so, honestly, I’m too far removed to say whether a certain state rep in Texas is doing X.

One interesting part of this election is that the NIMBY focus has shifted from housing to data centers. The recognition that we need more housing has shifted more in the YIMBY direction. That’s a dynamic we’re not encouraging, because data centers are a separate issue, but it’s been interesting.

Talking to our locals, more folks at the city council and county level, where the rubber really meets the road on development, are talking about the need to build more affordable and workforce housing.

We’ve seen in our own polling a real desire, and real angst, from younger voters who feel they can’t afford a home, and from their parents, who are also worried their kids can’t afford a home, may be living with them for a long time, and want them to stay in their state and area and raise their families there. That underlying affordability challenge is driving a lot of the rhetoric and, quite frankly, a lot of the ads. They may not mention housing specifically, but it’s embedded in broader affordability concerns.

You mentioned data centers. I’ve written a couple of stories about data centers competing with housing development for the same land. Is that something NAHB has seen? Is it a real phenomenon?

I think it’s a little overblown, at least right now. A lot of the areas where they’re looking to build data centers aren’t necessarily areas where you would build housing. So there may be some competition over land, but it’s not as big an issue as people may think.

The larger issue is competition for labor. Residential construction always competes with commercial construction for talent and labor, whether it’s somebody building an office building or a house. That competition is real, but it also means more investment in workforce training and more attention to the trades.

We’ve seen many large tech companies announce they’ll fund apprenticeship and training programs because they also need those workers. So there may be some trickle-down help for homebuilding. But it’s still too soon to see real impact, beyond utilities and similar things.

Speaking of labor, I’ve seen quite a few stories about how immigration policy and enforcement have affected construction labor. Has NAHB seen that, what’s your stance, and how have you worked with lawmakers on it?

We’ve definitely heard a lot about it, especially in the last few months. It’s been primarily in Southern states, but not exclusively.

The big concern from members is that the way enforcement is being carried out, whether at the local level, by ICE or some combination, is scaring off all Hispanic workers, regardless of immigration status or citizenship. They’re coming onto job sites, rounding everyone up and detaining folks for hours, repeatedly showing up or pulling people over in a van on the way to a job site. That’s made it very hard to retain workers or get them to show up, because there’s a fear factor in the Hispanic community about even U.S. citizens and green card holders getting roped in with folks who may not be here legally.

That’s caused delays on job sites and made it hard to find labor, period, because there’s no immediate replacement. That’s why we’re so focused on workforce training.

I think it’ll be a factor in places like Texas and Florida, and in the electoral outcome. You’re already seeing Hispanic turnout larger than historic levels. Some polling shows that even folks who supported the president on immigration, who maybe voted for him based on closing the border and enforcement, feel the enforcement has gone too far. It’ll be interesting to see what the exit polls show.

Inman’s core audience is real estate agents. What should agents pay the most attention to in these midterms? Does it depend on their local market, or is there something general to watch?

Disclosure: I used to work for NAR, too, so I understand where they’re coming from. I don’t know if there’s one particular issue, or whether it’s about the House or Senate flipping. It’s the overall voter mindset. If Congress changes control, or a governorship flips one way or the other, does it have an immediate impact? Does it change the [Trump] administration’s course? Those are all open questions.

Ultimately, voters hope inflation can be tamed, and interest rates obviously drive much of this for agents. Resolving the situation in Iran, and maybe dialing back some tariff policies, could affect the inflation numbers driving interest rates. If we can get rates back down, certainly below 7 percent and into the mid-6s, that will unlock a lot of demand that’s still out there but has moved to the sidelines over the last six months.

It’s hard to see how those things will change, no matter the outcome. They all feel very up in the air.

Yeah, but there’s a certain psyche to it. We saw this after the 2024 election. Everyone’s so wrapped up in politics now that people go into a weird holding pattern for the last month or two before an election. They say, “I’m going to wait until after the election and see, and then make a major decision.”

Uncertainty is a factor, and depending on your political outlook, you may be much happier on Nov. 4, or you may not be. But at least it resolves one more question mark for the next two years before we start a presidential cycle.

I hope that, whatever the outcome, having the election behind us will ease angst for potential buyers and sellers, calm the overall market, and get it moving again.

#5545. Reconciling the OCC’s Final Stablecoin Reserve Floors Against the Fed’s Proposal

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

The OCC's final GENIUS Act rule sets a 5% cash floor and a 40% cap on any one counterparty. The Fed's open proposal uses neither figure, and its comment window runs until November 30.

Issuers now face two sets of reserve rules that share a redemption deadline and differ on almost everything else.

Ask a stablecoin issuer what its reserves must look like in 2027, and the honest answer is now: it depends which regulator you ask.

The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) gave its answer on October 21, the final rule implementing the GENIUS Act. Our October 19 piece on staggered agency filings expected that rule "before the end of October," and it came two days later. The rule sets specific numbers: at least 5% of reserves in demand deposits or similar instant-access funds, and no more than 40% of reserves with a single counterparty.

The Federal Reserve's answer is still a proposal. Its GENIUS Act rulemaking remains open for comment until November 30, and it contains neither of those numbers. Until the Fed finalizes its rule, any company planning to issue under both agencies' rules, or deciding which one to apply to, is working with one fixed set of numbers and one open-ended set of principles.

The OCC's final rule was published in the Federal Register on October 23 and takes effect on January 18, 2027, the same day as the GENIUS Act itself. Comptroller Jonathan V. Gould called it "a clear, practical framework for payment stablecoin innovation, with strong standards for reserve backing, redemption, and risk management."

The reserve rules are looser than the March proposal in several places:

The OCC also removed the rebuttable presumption that some affiliate yield arrangements break the GENIUS Act's ban on paying interest, though it kept its broader anti-evasion powers. The agency received about 328 comments.

For existing issuers, the timeline is short. Under OCC Bulletin 2026-51, firms already operating in the United States that file a "substantially complete" application by January 18 can generally expect a waiver of the prior-approval requirement.

The Fed released its two proposals on September 24. They were published in the Federal Register on September 29 under Docket No. R-1899, and comments are due November 30.

The main requirements proposal would require Board-supervised issuers to "fully back their stablecoins with certain permissible reserve assets". The reserves' fair value would have to equal or exceed the stablecoins' outstanding value at all times. Permissible assets include:

On diversification, however, the Fed sets no numbers. Reserves must be "sufficiently diverse" to keep one-to-one backing at all times, and issuers must manage concentration in uninsured deposits and repo counterparties. The Board says it generally expects reserves to be mostly Treasuries, but it sets no cash floor and no counterparty percentage.

Redemption is where the two agencies agree most closely. Both define timely redemption as no later than two business days after a request. The difference lies in what happens under stress.

The FDIC, in its own proposal, uses a third approach: issuers would report on their own when redemption requests exceed 10% of issuance within 24 hours.

The clearest conflict is not about how much cash an issuer must hold, but how each agency treats bank deposits.

Under the OCC rule, at least 5% of reserves must be held in demand deposits or similar balances. That is a direct requirement to hold bank money.

The Fed proposal has no deposit floor. Instead, it would charge 2% capital against reserves held as uninsured deposits at an insured bank, and the same charge applies to undercollateralized reverse repo. One agency requires a minimum amount in deposits, and the other makes issuers hold extra capital against the deposits they choose to keep.

Concentration works the same way. An issuer with 60% of its deposit reserves at one bank would breach the OCC's 40% cap, unless one of the custodian or government exemptions applies. Under the Fed's current text, that issuer would face only a judgment by its supervisor about whether it has managed concentration risk properly.

The rules for a reserve shortfall also differ:

The difference is largest on capital. The OCC sets an individualized capital requirement measured in GAAP tangible equity. It has a $5 million floor that now lasts for the issuer's whole life, plus an operational backstop equal to 12 months of total expenses, up to half of which can be funded with qualifying subordinated debt.

The Fed proposes a fixed formula. On top of the 2% charges on deposits and repo, it adds an operational-risk charge on outstanding issuance:

It also adds 25% of three-year average revenue from sources other than reserves, adjusted by a loss scalar.

For an issuer with $50 billion in circulation, the issuance charge alone works out to $850 million under the Fed's proposal, before the revenue add-on. The OCC rule has no comparable fixed figure. Its capital depends on the issuer's own risk profile, with the $5 million floor as the only set minimum.

For now, the OCC's figures are final and the Fed's are not. Issuers and banks that hold reserves can still argue for changes until the Fed's comment period closes on November 30, and the Fed has asked 277 questions.

The decisions that matter most are clear from the comparison above:

Both sets of rules apply from the same date, January 18, 2027. If the Fed's final rule keeps its current approach, the United States will begin regulating stablecoins with a common redemption deadline and two different reserve rulebooks, decided by which agency charters the issuer.

#5544. What to expect during SC26: Join theCUBE Nov. 17–19

High-performance computing and artificial intelligence are converging, driven by advances in exascale computing, accelerated systems, data storage and high-speed networking.

The convergence of these technologies is a prime topic for discussion during SC26 in Chicago this month. Major industry players, such as Dell Technologies Inc., Google LLC and Nvidia Corp., have pursued a set of initiatives in the HPC arena, and SC26 will be an occasion to learn more about how AI and HPC workloads are evolving to write supercomputing’s next chapter.

“SC26 provides an important opportunity to examine how the convergence of AI, high-performance computing and application development are reshaping enterprise infrastructure priorities,” said theCUBE Research’s Paul Nashawaty. “Organizations must connect high-performance infrastructure, accessible data and modern application development to move beyond experimentation and accelerate production-ready AI deployments. For Dell and the broader HPC ecosystem, SC26 offers a platform to demonstrate how integrated compute, storage and AI infrastructure can address these challenges.”

TheCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio, will be covering the latest HPC news and announcements from SC26 in Chicago, Nov. 17–19. Coverage will feature on-site reporting and exclusive interviews with industry leaders and analysts as theCUBE explores how supercomputing’s future is being shaped at the intersection of exascale systems and AI infrastructure. Discussion will focus on ways that accelerated computing is transforming research environments, while quantum-HPC integration and agentic AI push scientific discovery toward greater autonomy. (* Disclosure below.)

Dell’s ongoing collaboration with Nvidia and other organizations has yielded several new developments in the HPC arena over the past year, particularly in the area of quantum computing.

The two companies have been working with the U.S. Department of Energy to build and deliver the Doudna supercomputer at Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory. The system will use Nvidia’s Vera Rubin CPU-GPU platform and Quantum-X800 InfiniBand networking inside Dell’s integrated rack systems and PowerEdge servers to support large-scale scientific computing and data-intensive research.

In September, Dell announced a collaboration with silicon-spin qubit developer Diraq to integrate quantum processing units with HPC and AI server infrastructure. The joint effort is designed to integrate quantum processors with classical computing infrastructure in commercial data centers.

Moves such as these point toward a convergence of AI and quantum technologies, which will likely propel both forward as new platforms are built and deployed.

“The market for high-performance computing is meeting the AI factory at the point of innovation,” said theCUBE Research’s Dave Vellante. “HPC has always led the most challenging data problems, so this trend makes perfect sense. Quantum will be the next big inflection point and we’re seeing that new technologies are often complementary to existing infrastructure. We expect that to be the case between accelerated computing and quantum, particularly in the area of error correction.”

Hyperscaler Google Cloud is also building systems to support HPC demands for industries like manufacturing, health care and life sciences, weather forecasting and electronic design automation.

At the forefront of Google’s HPC initiative is the H4D VM, the company’s high-performance computing virtual machine. Introduced last year, the H4D VM is powered by fifth-generation AMD EPYC processors and offers whole-node VM performance of more than 12,000 GFLOPS and memory bandwidth exceeding 950 GB/s.

An example of how HPC is making inroads in daily life can be seen in the use of H4D VMs by the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration. In July, Google Cloud announced that it had been selected as the primary provider of high-performance computing infrastructure for the Weather and Climate Operational Supercomputing System.

The adoption of HPC to enable meteorologists and researchers to develop future forecasting models is an example of how systems technology will play a critical role in both supercomputing and AI infrastructure moving forward.

“Systems are the key in supercomputing advances,” said theCUBE Research’s John Furrier. “Different architectures. Different bets. Same underlying problem: How do you keep the multiplication engines doing useful work instead of waiting for data? That’s why I think the next era of AI infrastructure won’t be defined by the ‘best chip.’ It will be defined by the best system architecture.”

While the field of HPC is being defined by major players such as Dell and Google, other firms are making contributions as well in areas such as cloud infrastructure and analytics.

Vultr Inc. is building high-performance cloud computing infrastructure for AI, risk management, compliance and fraud prevention. The company is developing its platform across 33 global regions by leveraging CPUs, GPUs and open, composable architectures to position itself as a cloud infrastructure specialist in the agentic AI era.

High-performance computing is also generating a need for consistent data sharing and access across platforms. Omni Analytics Inc. is building a data collaboration solution that can connect directly to cloud data warehouses without needing to preload or duplicate data.

SC26 will offer an opportunity to not only assess the progress of HPC in the enterprise but also examine how AI is continuing to transform the compute stack to generate meaningful business results.

“As organizations invest in increasingly sophisticated AI environments, the competitive differentiator will be the ability to optimize the entire technology stack from data movement and storage performance to application development and deployment,” Nashawaty said. “The central SC26 narrative is that the future of AI supercomputing will be defined not simply by how much compute organizations deploy, but by how effectively they translate that investment into measurable business and scientific outcomes.”

#5542. Why real estate agents wanted Barbara Corcoran for ICNY ’27

Barbara Corcoran (l) onstage at Inman Connect San Francisco 2015, Holly Meyer Lucas (r) onstage at Inman Connect San Diego 2026 |

As our team at Inman began planning Inman Connect New York this January, we asked real estate agents a fairly straightforward question: “In this market, who do you want to hear from most right now?”

The overwhelming response was Barbara Corcoran.

I’ve spent a lot of time thinking about that answer, because I think it tells us something interesting about the current state of real estate, the people who work in it and what they’re looking for from our industry’s leaders.

For context, before becoming Inman’s CMO, I spent years building a $100 million-plus producing real estate team in South Florida. I’ve personally sold more than 1,000 homes, ranging from properties under $20,000 to deals north of $20 million.

I’ve represented distressed sellers, helped families through extraordinarily difficult circumstances and negotiated transactions where getting to the closing table meant everything to the people involved. I’ve also mentored, trained and managed hundreds of agents through slow markets, busy markets and everything the last decade has thrown at us.

My point: I’ve carried the bag, and I understand my real estate agent brethren.

So, all summer when agents told me how much they are struggling (in what should be peak homebuying season), I took that seriously. For the past several months, I’ve heard from some of the most successful agents in the country who were going months without closing a transaction. These are experienced professionals who have built substantial businesses and survived multiple market cycles, suddenly finding themselves in unfamiliar territory.

Meanwhile, the industry around them is in a rather extraordinary state of upheaval. Major brokerages are consolidating, brokerages and MLSs are suing one another, the debate over private listings continues to divide the industry, and NAR is working to rebuild trust following several tumultuous years.

And somewhere in the middle of all this, agents are trying to sell houses while being told to post more on social media, stay hydrated and use more AI.

Our industry has some consequential decisions ahead of it, and the people making those decisions deserve to be questioned. Inman’s newsroom has an important responsibility to cover these issues, and our events should provide a place for the people involved to explain their positions.

But there’s another conversation agents want to have, and I think their overwhelming request for Barbara tells us exactly what it is.

They want to hear from someone who has been in their shoes, knows how to get scrappy in a down market to sell real estate, and can offer an experienced perspective without having to defend a corporate agenda.

One of my favorite anecdotes about Barbara is one that she shares often and seems to take enormous pride in — how gritty she was in her early life. Her LinkedIn bio opens with: “Barbara Corcoran’s credits include straight D’s in high school and college and 20 jobs by the time she turned 23.”

Tell me that doesn’t win the heart of a real estate agent. Our industry has a remarkable way of attracting people who struggled to find their place elsewhere.

Some weren’t great students. Others bounced around between jobs before finding real estate. I’ve met extraordinarily successful agents who can negotiate their way through an impossible transaction, recognize an opportunity before anyone else and build a relationship with practically anyone, and yet were kicked out of school when they were younger. (Looking at you, James Harris!)

Barbara herself has spoken openly about her struggles in school and dyslexia and how the challenges she experienced influenced the way she approached business. (I’ve got a completely unscientific theory about how I think many of America’s top-producing real estate agents who claim they struggled in school but are elite at selling are all actually just dyslexic, but I’ll save that for another time.)

Real estate agents find Barbara’s story particularly inspiring because real estate has always been an industry where people can build extraordinary careers around abilities that aren’t necessarily rewarded in a classroom, and Barbara took those abilities and turned a $1,000 loan into one of the most recognizable real estate brokerages in the country. She is one of us, and she made it out on the other side a literal Shark. And agents love her for it.

To boot, she built The Corcoran Group in New York City, where competition was fierce and standing out required creativity — something agents covet and understand deeply. Long before agents were being told to become content creators, Barbara understood how to make herself and her business interesting to the public. She launched market reports, generated publicity and became a recognizable authority on New York real estate.

She understood personal brand marketing before most of our industry knew what to call it.

She sold her brokerage in 2001 and went on to build another career as an entrepreneur, investor and television personality. And now, after all of that, there she is sitting in a chair on Shark Tank, evaluating other entrepreneurs and deciding which businesses deserve her money.

Barbara understands something that most successful real estate agents figure out, and the new ones need to hear: A willingness to take risks, build relationships and solve problems can take you a very long way in this business.

And she’s spent enough time carrying the bag to know how to find business when everyone else is convinced there isn’t any. Her perspective on this is particularly valuable for agents to hear, if we consider the voices dominating our industry’s conversations right now.

The real estate conversations are dominated by brokerage executives defending their business models, MLS leaders explaining their policies and industry organizations navigating enormous changes; senators are filing FTC complaints against industry leaders, too. It’s overwhelming, and yet, none of it helps Susie Realtor or Mike Agent close a home this quarter.

There are important questions being debated about how homes should be marketed, who controls listing information, and how real estate professionals will operate in the years ahead, and while I do believe all of those discussions deserve a place on highly influential stages such as Inman Connect New York, agents also desperately need to hear from voices right now who don’t have a dog in the fight, who can hunker down on a mic and say, “OK, listen up, this is exactly what I would do right now if I were in your shoes.”

Barbara Corcoran is the real estate fairy godmother who is uniquely positioned to say that, without an obvious bias, something to sell the audience or any other ulterior motive. That dynamic really appeals to agents right now, who are growing tired of the industry’s constant infighting.

A real estate agent trying to figure out how to get their listing sold after sitting for 90-plus days, so they can get their client the win and feed their own family, is less concerned with which brokerage executive launches their AI tool most effectively and who is winning the latest argument about private listings.

Agents need a change of scenery right now, and Barbara knows how to generate business, find the buyer and create buzz around listings that have been sitting for weeks.

She’s also famously candid, and I suspect she will have plenty to say about what is happening in our industry.

My takeaway from the overwhelming request for Barbara is that agents are craving an independent voice of reason. Someone who understands the realities of selling real estate and can speak from experience.

And when our community made that request, we listened.

I want to give credit to Inman CEO Tom Bohn for taking the feedback seriously and making Barbara a priority for New York. One of the things I’ve appreciated about working with Tom is his willingness to listen to the real estate professionals who make up our community with fresh perspectives, while also prioritizing the industry leadership who are critical to our ecosystem as an industry.

We have an opportunity to put some of the smartest people in the business on our stages. I think we should pay particular attention when the people in our audience tell us whose perspective they value.

So, we got Barbara, and she’s going to tell our audience exactly what she would do right now. And we can’t wait to hear it.

Join us at Inman Connect New York, Jan. 26–28, 2027, at the New York Hilton Midtown.

MOUNTAIN VIEW, Calif., Nov. 12, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Tellus App, Inc. ("Tellus"), the proptech company behind the Tellus savings app, today raised the annual percentage yield (APY) on its Reserve Account from 7.75% to 8.00%. That equals its highest Reserve rate, paid from November 2023 to December 2025.

Consumer prices rose 3.7% in the 12 months to September, up from 3.4% in August, according to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics. Energy prices rose 20.4%. October added another 0.4%.
