#5540. 7 ways to breathe new life into a listing that isn’t selling

Don’t jump straight to a price cut when you have a listing not selling. These seven strategies refresh your marketing and put it in front of new buyers.

Listing not selling? If I had a listing that had been sitting on the market for 30, 60 or even 90 days, and I needed to get it sold in the next 60 days, I wouldn’t simply keep doing the same things and hope a buyer eventually showed up. I also wouldn’t immediately call the seller and ask for a price reduction.

I’d start by developing a specific plan to create new interest in the home. These are the seven strategies I’d use.

The first thing I’d do is give the listing a completely fresh look. I want someone who has already seen the property online to notice something different when it shows up again.

I’d start with the MLS description. I’d use AI to help me rewrite it to highlight the most compelling features of the property, tell a better story and give potential buyers a reason to schedule a showing.

Act as an expert real estate MLS copywriter. Rewrite the following MLS description in a fresh, creative and compelling way that helps potential buyers imagine living in this home and encourages them to schedule a showing. Avoid generic real estate language, highlight what makes this property unique and naturally include relevant location and property keywords for SEO and AEO optimization. Ask me any questions needed before writing the new description.

Next, I’d also take a close look at the photos and videos. If the property has been on the market for several months, it may be time for new photography, updated staging or a different approach to showcasing the home.

I’d consider whether an accurately represented twilight photo or a newly staged room could make the property more appealing. If AI-assisted photo editing is involved, I’d make sure any alterations are properly disclosed in accordance with MLS rules and accurately represent the property and its surroundings.

One of the simplest changes you can make is updating the primary listing photo. I’d take five or six of the strongest photos and ask other agents which one would most likely make them stop scrolling. Sometimes it’s the front elevation, but sometimes it’s a beautiful outdoor living area, an incredible kitchen or a view that immediately captures someone’s attention.

I’d also refresh the social media posts promoting the home. Instead of recycling the same graphics and captions, I’d create fresh content tailored to each platform where I’m marketing the property.

The goal is simple. Before doing anything else, make the listing look fresh to give people who may have previously overlooked it a reason to take another look.

The next thing I’d do is identify exactly who the most likely buyers are for this property. Instead of marketing the home to everybody, I’d identify two or three distinct buyer groups who might align with its features and benefits.

For example, a home with a first-floor primary suite, a dedicated office and a low-maintenance yard might appeal to several types of buyers for different reasons. One buyer may be focused on working from home. Another may be interested in reducing the amount of exterior maintenance required. A third may value the floor plan and flexibility of the living spaces.

Once I identified the potential buyer groups, I’d use AI to help me understand which property features, lifestyle benefits and potential concerns might matter most to each group. Then I’d ask AI to help me create separate marketing campaigns that speak to those different priorities.

The key is to focus on the property’s features and the benefits they provide, rather than making assumptions about who should live there. That helps keep the marketing inclusive and aligned with fair housing requirements.

This is a different approach from simply posting the same listing description repeatedly and hoping someone responds. We’re identifying what makes the property attractive to different buyers and creating marketing that helps them recognize those benefits.

When you understand what someone is looking for, you can do a much better job of showing them why a particular property deserves their attention.

The third strategy I’d use is a focused, 10-day campaign to make sure the agents most likely to have a buyer for the property know about it.

I’d start by reviewing MLS data to identify agents who have recently sold comparable homes in the area. I’d also look for agents who have active listings or, where available, buyer activity that suggests they’re working with people interested in similar properties.

Then I’d create a list of the agents most likely to have relationships with buyers who might be interested in my listing. Over the next 10 business days, I’d personally call two of those agents every day.

I’d say something like, “Hey, I know you do a lot of business in this neighborhood and price range. I’ve got a listing I wanted to make sure was on your radar. I’d love to get your feedback on it and see if you might have someone who’s looking for something similar.”

That’s 20 personal conversations with agents who have demonstrated experience selling the type of property I’m trying to get sold. I’d also create an email campaign to share the property’s most compelling features with a broader group of agents, using appropriate contact information and respecting communication preferences.

Another opportunity is reaching out to agents who have competing listings. I’d ask what kind of activity they’re seeing and what feedback they’re receiving. I’d also offer to share information about my listing so that if one of their buyers doesn’t find the right fit in their property, they know about mine. And I’d do the same for them.

The goal isn’t simply to promote my listing. It’s to build relationships with agents who are actively working with the buyers I’m trying to reach. Sometimes the best opportunity to sell a home isn’t through another social media post. It’s through a conversation with the agent who already has the right buyer.

One of my favorite ways to generate new interest in a listing is to stop focusing exclusively on the house and start showing what it might feel like to live there. I’d create videos that help potential buyers imagine the experiences the property and its location make possible.

For instance, I might create a video titled, “Here’s what a Saturday could look like living in this home.” The video could start with coffee on the back porch, move to a nearby farmers’ market, showcase a local restaurant for lunch and end with an evening enjoying the outdoor living space.

Another idea might be, “Here’s what date night could look like if you lived here.” The video could highlight nearby restaurants, entertainment or a relaxing evening at home. If the property is close to a park, I’d show the actual route and how convenient it is to get there. If it’s within walking distance of restaurants or shopping, I’d create a short video showcasing that experience.

I’d also think about the lifestyle opportunities inside the home. Maybe there’s a great outdoor kitchen for entertaining, a flexible bonus room or a covered porch that creates a natural gathering place. The key is to help people see something they may have missed when they first looked at the listing photos.

A buyer may not remember that a home has a 12-by-20-foot covered porch. But they may remember the video showing what a Saturday evening with friends could look like in that space.

Features tell people what a home has. Lifestyle marketing helps them imagine what living there could feel like.

The fifth strategy I’d use is finding ways to make the property more financially attractive than competing homes. We hear a lot about affordability, and for many buyers, the challenge isn’t simply the purchase price. It’s the monthly payment, closing costs or the amount of cash required to purchase the home.

That’s why I’d evaluate potential incentives before assuming that a price reduction is the only option. Maybe the seller could offer a closing-cost credit. Maybe a mortgage rate buydown would make the monthly payment more attractive. Maybe covering a portion of the HOA dues or offering an allowable allowance for improvements could help the property stand out.

I’d approach this the way a new-home builder might. Builders don’t always compete exclusively on price. They often use incentives to create a more attractive financial opportunity for buyers. I’d work with the seller and a qualified lender to determine which incentives are appropriate, what they would actually cost and how they compare with a price reduction.

For example, if a seller is considering a $10,000 price reduction, I’d want to know whether a properly structured $10,000 concession could provide greater value to the right buyer. The answer will depend on the buyer’s financing, the property, lender requirements and the local market. But it’s a conversation worth having.

Then I’d make sure those incentives were clearly communicated in the listing and marketing materials, including any important terms or limitations. Sometimes the opportunity isn’t simply making the house less expensive. It’s finding a way to make purchasing the house more attractive.

Once I’ve refreshed the listing, identified ideal buyer groups, connected with active agents and evaluated potential incentives, I’d launch a 21-day marketing blitz. This is where I’d get creative.

The mistake I see agents make is posting the same property photo and listing information over and over again. They may think they’re marketing the property 10 different times, but in reality, they’re often repeating the same message 10 times. I’d rather create 21 different pieces of content that give people different reasons to take notice.

For example, if the home is listed at $450,000, I’d create a video titled, “What does $450,000 buy you in this neighborhood?” Another video might be, “What the listing photos don’t tell you about this home.” I’d create content about the history of the neighborhood, the builder, nearby amenities and what makes the location unique. I’d showcase individual features that deserve more attention and answer questions buyers might have about the property.

I’d also create content comparing the home with other available options in the same price range. The goal would be to help buyers understand the value and opportunities the property offers. Some content would be short-form video. Some might be photo carousels. Some would be longer walkthroughs, neighborhood videos or educational posts.

I’d also use AI to brainstorm additional angles. I’d ask it to develop a 21-day content campaign that highlights the property from different perspectives without simply repeating the same sales message. The goal is to create enough variety that someone who wasn’t interested in the original listing post might see something new that changes their perspective.

One piece of content might attract someone because of the price point. Another might attract someone because of the neighborhood. Another might reveal a feature a buyer didn’t realize the home offered.

That’s a marketing campaign. Not simply posting the same listing over and over again.

If I’ve done everything I can to refresh the marketing, identify potential buyers, communicate with agents, highlight the lifestyle, create financial incentives and execute a 21-day content campaign, but the property still isn’t generating the activity we need, it’s time to have the conversation most agents dread: the price reduction conversation.

But here’s the difference. I don’t want this to be the first time the seller has heard that a price adjustment might become necessary. I’d communicate with them throughout the entire process. Before launching the marketing blitz, I’d explain exactly what we’re going to do and why. I’d also let them know what happens if those efforts don’t generate the results we’re looking for.

“I want you to know we’re going to make a significant push over the next 21 days to create new interest in your home. We’re going to refresh the marketing, reach out to agents who are active in this price range and launch a series of new campaigns. But if we get through that process and still aren’t seeing the activity we need, my responsibility is to bring you the most current market information so you can make the best decision for you and your family.”

That conversation sets the expectation before the difficult decision arrives. I’d actually recommend having a version of this conversation when you first take the listing. I’d explain that we have a comprehensive listing launch program designed to generate exposure and buyer interest. But if the market doesn’t respond the way we expect, we need to be willing to evaluate what it’s telling us.

Then, when the time comes, I’d bring the seller updated comparable sales, competing listings, properties that have gone under contract, showing activity and buyer feedback. I’d explain what the information suggests and present a specific recommendation.

But I wouldn’t simply ask for a price reduction. I’d show the seller what a strategic price improvement could allow us to do. Maybe it means reaching buyers searching in a different price range. Maybe it creates an opportunity to reconnect with agents who previously showed the property. Maybe it gives us a reason to host another open house, relaunch the marketing and communicate the new value proposition. I’d create a list of the specific activities we would execute following the adjustment.

I’d also be strategic about the timing. Depending on the market, I’d consider making the adjustment before the period when buyers are most actively scheduling weekend showings. I’d review the local data and how the major real estate portals display price changes rather than assuming every market or platform behaves the same way.

The important thing is that we’re not simply changing a number in the MLS. We’re using the new price as an opportunity to create renewed interest through a coordinated marketing plan. And ultimately, I’d remind the seller that the decision is theirs. It’s their home, and my responsibility is to give them the best market knowledge, professional guidance and clear recommendations they need to make an informed decision.

When a listing isn’t selling, continuing to do the same things and hoping for a different result isn’t a strategy. Neither is immediately asking the seller for a price reduction without first evaluating what else can be done.

The most important part of this entire process is communication. Your sellers should never wonder what you’re doing to get their home sold or be surprised when you recommend an adjustment. They should know you’re working on their behalf, evaluating the market and doing everything possible to help them achieve their goal.

This is a market that rewards professionals who are willing to think differently, market more creatively and communicate more effectively. Remember, your sellers didn’t hire you simply to market their home. They hired you to help them get it sold. Our job is to bring the creativity, strategy and professional advice necessary to give them the best opportunity to make that happen.

Jimmy Burgess is the Chief Coaching Officer for HomeServices of America and President of Berkshire Hathaway HomeServices. Get connected on Instagram and LinkedIn.

#5539. HawkEye 360 Announces Third Quarter 2026 Financial Results

Revenue of $59.3 million, up 84% compared to the prior-year period of $32.2 million

Achieved record international revenue of 23.3 million, up 76% compared to the prior-year period

Backlog of $300.3 million as of September 30, 2026

Raising full year revenue guidance to $225-$227 million and non-GAAP Adjusted EBITDA guidance to $38-$40 million

HERNDON, Va., Nov. 12, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- HawkEye 360, Inc. (NYSE: HAWK) ("HawkEye 360" or "the Company"), a global leader in signals intelligence data and analytics, today announced its financial results for the third quarter ended September 30, 2026.

"I am pleased with our third quarter results as we continue to see strong momentum for signals intelligence data and analytics. Importantly, growth on the international side of our business continues to gain significant traction, highlighted by revenue increasing 76% year-over-year to $23.3 million," said Chief Executive Officer John Serafini. "We expect international expansion will continue. We are pleased with the opportunities in front of us, and that our success is translating into tangible financial results."

"More recently, we reached another milestone in our next phase of constellation expansion with the launches of Clusters 15 and 16 in October," he continued. "Following deployment, our space operations team successfully established communications with all six satellites across both clusters. Once commissioned, these clusters are expected to increase our revisit rate and allow us to serve a greater number of customers and mission requirements."

Third Quarter 2026  and Recent Business Highlights:

For full-year 2026, the Company is increasing its total revenue expectations to $225 million and $227 million, and non-GAAP Adjusted EBITDA of between $38 million and $40 million.

The Company has not reconciled its non-GAAP Adjusted EBITDA outlook to the most directly comparable GAAP measure because certain reconciling items, such as stock-based compensation, change in fair value of warrant liabilities, and depreciation and amortization, are uncertain or out of the Company's control and cannot be reasonably predicted. The actual amount of these expenses will have a significant impact on the Company's future GAAP financial results. Accordingly, a reconciliation of the Company's non-GAAP Adjusted EBITDA outlook to the most comparable GAAP measures is not available without unreasonable efforts.

Third Quarter 2026 Earnings Conference Call:

The Company will hold a conference call today, November 12, 2026, at 4:30 PM ET. The call can be accessed by dialing 1-877-407-0792 (U.S. participants) or 1-201-689-8263 (International participants). Participants can also listen to a live webcast of the call by going to the Investors section on HawkEye's website at https://investors.he360.com/. A replay of the call will be available starting on Friday, November 13, 2026, at 11:30 AM ET by dialing 1-844-512-2921 (U.S.) or 1-412-317-6671 (International) and entering the conference ID number:13763186. The replay will be available through Thursday, November 26, 2026, at 11:59 PM ET.

HawkEye 360 is equipping defense, intelligence and national security leaders with mission-critical signals intelligence to enable faster, better decision-making. By detecting, geolocating and characterizing radio-frequency emissions worldwide, HawkEye 360 delivers trusted domain awareness and early-warning indicators to the US Government and allied partners. Our space-based collection, proprietary signal processing and AI-powered analytics transform knowledge of RF spectrum into a strategic advantage. Proven by operational mission success, HawkEye 360 is redefining how signals intelligence strengthens national and global security.

In addition to the financial information prepared in accordance with U.S. generally accepted accounting principles ("GAAP"), the Company reports Adjusted EBITDA and Free Cash Flow, which are non-GAAP financial measures. The Company defines Adjusted EBITDA as net income (loss) before interest income, interest expense, income tax expense or benefit, depreciation and amortization, as well as significant non-cash and/or non-recurring expenses that are not considered part of the Company's operations and revenue-generating activities, or are nonrecurring or infrequent in nature. Management believes these items are not useful in evaluating the Company's core operating performance. These items include, but are not limited to, stock-based compensation expense; acquisition-related costs, one-time costs related to the IPO, settlements, net of related legal expenses, changes in fair value of contingent and deferred consideration, changes in fair value of warrant liabilities, and gains or losses on extinguishment of debt.  The Company defines Free Cash Flow as net cash provided by (used in) operating activities less purchases of satellites, property, and equipment.

The Company uses Adjusted EBITDA and Free Cash Flow in conjunction with other GAAP measures to evaluate the effectiveness of its business strategies, make strategic decisions, and communicate with its board of directors and investors concerning its financial performance. The Company uses these non-GAAP financial measures to assess its financial performance because they allow the Company to compare its operating performance on a consistent basis across periods by removing the effects of its capital structure (such as varying levels of interest expense and income), asset base (such as depreciation and capital expenditures) and other items (such as non-recurring or non-cash costs) that impact the comparability of financial results from period to period.

The Company believes that the presentation of these non-GAAP financial measures will provide useful information to investors and analysts in assessing its financial performance and results of operations across reporting periods by excluding items it does not believe are indicative of its core operating performance. Net Income (Loss) is the U.S. GAAP measure most directly comparable to Adjusted EBITDA. Net cash provided by (used in) operating activities is the U.S. GAAP measure most directly comparable to Free Cash Flow. Reconciliations of these non-GAAP measures to the most comparable GAAP measures are presented below under the headings "Reconciliation of Net Income (Loss) to Adjusted EBITDA" and "Reconciliation of Net Cash Provided By (Used In) Operating Activities to Free Cash Flow." The Company's non-GAAP financial measures should not be considered as an alternative to the most directly comparable U.S. GAAP financial measure. You are encouraged to evaluate each of these adjustments and the reasons management considers them appropriate for supplemental analysis.

In evaluating Adjusted EBITDA and Free Cash Flow, you should be aware that in the future the Company may incur expenses that are the same as or similar to some of the adjustments in such presentation. The Company's presentation of these non-GAAP financial measures should not be construed as an inference that its future results will be unaffected by unusual or non-recurring items. The Company may modify the presentation of Adjusted EBITDA and Free Cash Flow in the future, and any such modification may be material. Adjusted EBITDA and Free Cash Flow have important limitations as analytical tools, and you should not consider these non-GAAP financial measures in isolation or as a substitute for analysis of the Company's operating results as reported under U.S. GAAP. Adjusted EBITDA and Free Cash Flow may be defined differently by other companies in the Company's industry and may not be comparable to similarly titled measures of other companies, thereby diminishing their utility.

Backlog is a key measure of the Company's business. The Company's backlog supports predictable revenue expansion through a recurring model, enabling forward revenue visibility. Management uses backlog to more effectively forecast the Company's future business and results, which supports decisions around capital allocation. It also helps the Company identify future growth or operating trends that may not otherwise be apparent. The Company also believes backlog is useful for investors in forecasting the Company's future results and understanding the growth of its business.

The Company's backlog represents the portion of legally binding contracts that are expected to result in future revenue. Backlog may also include change orders for any contracts that have been formally contracted. This includes firm contracts that contain remaining performance obligations, including the cancellable portion of the contract value for contracts that provide the customer with a right to terminate for convenience without incurring a substantive termination penalty. Backlog also can include up to the remaining ceiling on single award IDIQ contracts where no task orders have been issued. Backlog excludes the value of unexercised options to extend contracts, the value of multi-award IDIQ contracts, and the value of any contracts, or a portion thereof, where management deems execution to be unlikely to result in revenue due to customer-specific or other factors.

#5538. Jeff Glover goes indie after 17 years with Keller Williams (EXCLUSIVE)

Jeff Glover, founder of Live Unreal Companies |

Jeff Glover takes Glover Agency independent after 17 years with Keller Williams, telling Inman the move is about keeping Glover U broker-agnostic.

Glover Agency, the Michigan team Jeff Glover founded in 2008, became fully independent on Nov. 1, ending a 17-year run with Keller Williams. The move comes roughly three months after Glover sold his three Keller Williams market centers.

The team says it has been Michigan’s top homeselling team across all brands in 11 of the past 13 years and has sold more than 10,000 homes. It operates out of four offices in Birmingham, Plymouth, Fenton and Grand Rapids.

Glover Agency will now operate only in Michigan and isn’t affiliated with any franchise or national brand.

With Glover Agency out of the franchise system, none of Glover’s Live Unreal Companies are tied to a single brand, which Glover says frees Glover U to work with agents and leaders at every brokerage in the U.S. and Canada.

In an exclusive interview with Inman, Glover said the decision had a lot to do with Glover U, the coaching and training company where he now spends most of his time. Glover U has long pitched itself as broker-agnostic, but Glover said his KW ties kept closing doors, even after the market center sale.

In August, Glover sold his ownership stakes in three Keller Williams market centers across Michigan, where he served as majority owner and operating principal. He said the sale supported Glover U’s broker-agnostic approach to serving agents across the U.S. and Canada. The three market centers combined closed nearly $1 billion in sales volume in 2025.

“Most of [the potential Glover U clients], if they don’t know me and their agents don’t know me, they’re not going to return my call,” Glover said of leaders at rival brands. “I had leaders of large companies — I mean, the largest that exist today — say, ‘Hey, Jeff, that’s great you sold your franchises, and we’re definitely open to you helping our agents, but I’m sorry, I can’t put a Keller Williams guy on our stage.'”

Joining another brand would have recreated the same problem. Going independent, Glover says, removes it.

“This move furthers the brand-agnostic approach we’ve been working toward, and now there should be little to no objection to somebody trusting me with their agents, because I don’t have a dog in the fight,” Glover said. “They don’t have to worry about me pushing their agents to go to any one company when I’m independent.”

The second driver is marketing. Glover Agency has advertised under its own name for years on TV, radio and billboards, and Glover said most Michigan consumers already assumed the team was independent.

Franchise rules on how the team could advertise, down to how large its name could appear, made it harder for individual agents to build their own brands.

“It’s very hard for them to create a brand within a brand within a brand,” Glover said. “It’s confusing to consumers. It’s confusing to other agents and other companies.”

Glover said top teams that understand marketing already know where consumer loyalty sits.

“The everyday seller and everyday buyer generally doesn’t say, ‘ We’re listing our home with Keller Williams or with Coldwell Banker,'” Glover said. “They say, ‘We’re listing our home with ‘Joe Smith’ or ‘Amy Duncan.'”

For the consumer, Glover said that the brand is “just the gravy on top.” “The brand helps, but today’s consumer resonates more with an agent’s or a team’s brand than with the company’s brand,” he said.

Day-to-day operations at Glover Agency are run by CEO Taylor Kerrigan. Glover remains involved and still lists and sells. He said he was prospecting in front of the team’s agents just before speaking with Inman on Friday.

“For our clients, nothing changes about how we serve them, other than a more personalized approach,” Kerrigan said in a statement. “What does change is that the name on the door is entirely ours.”

Glover joined Keller Williams in 2009, and the company says the team climbed as high as No. 3 nationally among all groups and No. 1 among expansion teams for homes sold. Asked what would be hardest about leaving, Glover didn’t hesitate.

“Without question, my relationship with Gary Keller,” he said, pointing to Keller’s early top 100 mastermind and a smaller circle of about a dozen agents, the Pirate Group, who got regular access to the KW co-founder. “I wouldn’t be where I am today if it weren’t for him.”

Glover said he still considers Keller a mentor and expects to keep speaking at KW events “so long as I’m welcome.”

The timing puts Glover on the opposite side of an industry trend. Consolidation has dominated brokerage headlines this year, including Compass–Anywhere and Real–REMAX, and independents face growing pressure to align with a larger platform.

Glover doesn’t think independence is right for everyone. He said it works for owners who know what agents need today, such as database growth, leverage and help building personal brands, and who have the energy to deliver it.

“For the person who somewhat wants the easy button, and maybe they’re at a point in their life where they don’t have the energy or time to pour into their company,” he said, joining a franchise or a company like Real, eXp or LPT “makes a lot of sense for that individual.”

For Glover, the bigger bet is on Glover U.

“The biggest thing is neutralizing Glover U so that it will be the No. 1 training and coaching company on the planet for real estate agents at the rate we’re growing,” he told Inman. “And I can’t do that if I’m affiliated with any one brand. So that’s a big part of it. The other part is the freedom and flexibility this gives us to help our agents grow their brands even bigger.”

#5537. XTI Aerospace Successfully Completes Restructuring of Approximately $4.7 Million of Promissory Notes and Secures Waiver and Amendment of Revolving Credit Facility with JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A.

FORT LAUDERDALE, Fla., Nov. 12, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- XTI Aerospace, Inc. (Nasdaq: XTIA) ("XTI Aerospace," "XTI," or the "Company"), parent company of Drone Nerds, LLC, ("Drone Nerds"), a leading drone solutions platform serving commercial, enterprise and government customers, today announced the successful completion of an agreement to restructure and amend the terms of certain promissory notes issued on November 10, 2025 in connection with the acquisitions of Drone Nerds, LLC and Anzu Robotics, LLC (the "Seller Notes").

In conjunction with the successful restructuring of the Seller Notes, the Company has also secured a cross-default waiver on its $20 million revolving credit facility with JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A.

Under the terms of the restructuring of the Seller Notes, the parties mutually agreed to modify the repayment schedule and certain financial terms associated with the original promissory note. The revised structure extends the maturity date and establishes a repayment framework that provides additional financial flexibility as the Company continues to execute its business strategy.

Additional details on the restructuring of the Seller Notes and the credit facility waiver and amendment will be available upon the filing of the Company's Form 10Q for the period ended September 30, 2026, which will be filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission and available on the Company's website once filed.

XTI Aerospace, Inc. ("XTI") (Nasdaq: XTIA) is focused on building a leading platform for commercial and government drone adoption in the growing unmanned aircraft systems ("UAS") industry. Through its subsidiary, Drone Nerds, LLC, XTI supports enterprise and government customers in sectors including public safety, agriculture, construction, and energy across the drone program lifecycle, from hardware sourcing and deployment to training, service, repair, and the proprietary Always Flyingâ¢ program. Its established U.S. customer base and reputation as a trusted solutions provider position the company as a go-to-market partner for drone manufacturers and software developers seeking to scale in the domestic market.

For more information about XTI, please visit xtiaerospace.com and follow XTI on LinkedIn, Instagram, X, and YouTube.

#5536. As AI agents take control, Nvidia rethinks the security playbook

Nvidia Corp. recently added a new pillar to its AI networking infrastructure with the unveiling of Scale-In.

Scale-In brings purpose-built acceleration to secure, manage and operate agentic AI factories. It is designed to deliver secure access, high-performance data movement, tenant isolation, simpler operations and more predictable performance as agents assume increasingly larger roles within AI factories.

“In agentic AI, it’s a completely different use case because now we’re dealing with many agents that need to run on the infrastructure,” said Gilad Shainer (pictured), senior vice president of networking at Nvidia. “You need to increase security because you need to make sure that those agents are contained in their sandbox and are not doing the wrong things. You need to build an infrastructure that needs to ensure security all around…what happens in the memory, what happens on storage. This is why we needed to bring an infrastructure which actually enabled the security across everything. And that’s what Scale-In is.”

Shainer spoke with theCUBE’s Dave Vellante for theCUBE + NYSE Wired: AI Factories – Data Centers of the Future interview series on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how Nvidia’s Scale-In architecture is designed to help transform scaled compute into a secure and operational AI factory platform.

Since the August introduction, Nvidia has expanded its agent security strategy. In September, the company introduced its Open Agent Safety Platform, combining OpenShell with Nvidia Sentry for out-of-band monitoring and hardware-based security enforcement. An October announcement added the OpenShell Reference Architecture, integrating Vera Rubin infrastructure, Vera CPUs and BlueField-4 to support secure agent execution across enterprise systems. Nvidia’s announcement outlines the expanded architecture.

Scale-In is powered by Nvidia BlueField-4 and Nvidia DOCA and connected over Nvidia Spectrum-X Ethernet. BlueField-4 is Nvidia’s fourth-generation data processing unit, a networking platform built for agentic AI factories and large-scale infrastructure needs. BlueField is essential to the management of agentic AI security, according to Shainer.

“You can think about BlueField or Blue-Field-4 as a device that has in-silicon security engines that are working out of band and collecting telemetry from everything, from memory, from storage, from GPUs, from CPUs,” Shainer told theCUBE. “That’s why that infrastructure connects to all other infrastructures and ensures security all around. That out-of-band monitoring enables BlueField to actually understand exactly what agents are doing.”

Along with BlueField-4, Nvidia DOCA also powers Scale-In deployment. This software platform enables the rapid creation of apps and services that offload, accelerate and isolate data center workloads.

Using DOCA, developers can create software-defined, cloud-native, DPU- and SuperNIC-accelerated solutions. Like Nvidia CUDA, which provides a programming platform for GPU workloads, DOCA gives developers access to DPU acceleration capabilities.

“DPU brings the in-silicon engines security engines, storage accelerations,” Shainer explained. “DOCA is the framework, the software, the APIs that enable you to access all of those engines that BlueField-4 provides.”

Nvidia has further reinforced agentic AI security with its open-source runtime offering called OpenShell. The tool is designed to govern agent execution, access and inference routing. Nvidia combined OpenShell with BlueField-4 because it wanted a device that could collect information outside the GPU and monitor an environment that no agent could influence.

“I want to also have another device which is completely separated, completely isolated from the agents, that can monitor everything out-of-band,” Shainer said. “That’s what we’re doing with BlueField-4, bringing all the security elements together with OpenShell, and now you have a secure infrastructure for agents. This is how the combination of OpenShell and BlueField-4 brings all the security elements that we need for gen AI.”

The more recent OpenShell Reference Architecture builds on that approach with Nvidia Sentry, which runs on BlueField-4 using DOCA software. According to Nvidia, Sentry continuously monitors agent behavior and can quarantine agents that attempt to move outside their defined software boundaries. The combination extends OpenShell’s runtime controls with an independent enforcement layer.

#5534. Silverfort Named a Leader in the IDC MarketScape for Worldwide Augmented Identity Security Solutions 2026 Vendor Assessment

Silverfort's Runtime Access Protection acts as an identity control plane to stop AI attacks, securing identities from AD to AI

PLANO, Texas, Nov. 12, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Silverfort, the Identity Security company, today announced it has been named a Leader in the IDC MarketScape: Worldwide Augmented Identity Security Solutions 2026 Vendor Assessment (doc# US54116526, November 2026).

The need for Augmented Identity SecurityIdentity Security is evolving. For years it focused on the front door: verify who is logging in, grant access, and trust policy to govern what happens next. That approach partially worked when identities were human, but quickly fell apart when machine identities, then AI agents, arrived on the scene. AI attacks target identity directly, and since the attack surface is outgrowing most organizations' ability to govern it, control has to extend beyond login to what happens next. Identity Security is now where and how organizations can control access, contain risk, and stop attacks. Silverfort protects identities at runtime, before access is granted, so teams can act on identity risk as it happens, without waiting for patches, policies or tech debt to be cleared.

IDC MarketScape's recommendation for when to consider Silverfort

In its guidance to buyers, IDC suggests considering Silverfort when, "Your organization wants visibility across on-premises and cloud identities, or runs Active Directory and legacy protocols that cannot take an agent or an application change, and wants real-time MFA, risk-based access, just-in-time access, and service-account protection on its existing stack, alongside vault, governance, and compliance tooling."

"For years, identity was a checkpoint, built wherever the technology allowed. Everywhere else, protection was taken on faith. Risk never agreed to that arrangement," said Emanuel Figueroa, Senior Research Analyst, Identity and Access Management Security, IDC. "Organizations need identity protections that reach modern and legacy infrastructure alike. Silverfort enforces controls at the authentication layer, including for systems and protocols that cannot support endpoint agents, which gives organizations a way to extend those protections to the environments they already operate."

"Not before the attack and not after it, but at the moment of impact. That's when Identity Security has to step up and stop attacks. AI-powered attacks don't break in, they log in, and they move faster than any human can respond," said Ron Rasin, Chief Strategy Officer of Silverfort. "It's great to see the IDC MarketScape recognize Identity Security as a category. It's a sign of how far it has come and of the market catching up to where it needs to go. Organizations now need to budget for protecting the identity layer, because that's where AI-driven attacks succeed or fail. We're proud to be named to the Leaders Category in the IDC MarketScape."

Silverfort enforces access controls inline at the moment of access to support organizations with four core use cases:

Source: "IDC MarketScape: Worldwide Augmented Identity Security Solutions 2026 - US54116526. Silverfort is positioned in the Leaders Category.

Silverfort is the Runtime Identity Security Platform that pioneered inline enforcement to stop AI attacks, protecting every identity, from AI agents to Active Directory, across on-prem and cloud environments. Its patented Runtime Access Protection sits directly in the authentication path across identity providers and directories, enforcing the right decision at the moment access is requested, without changing the systems or workflows teams already use. Silverfort stops AI attacks, secures privileged access without a vault, protects non-human identities and AI agents, and brings modern runtime controls to legacy infrastructure, securing it from AI. Trusted by more than 1,200 organizations worldwide, including several Fortune 50 companies.

IDC MarketScape vendor assessment model is designed to provide an overview of the competitive fitness of technology and service suppliers in a given market. The research utilizes a rigorous scoring methodology based on both qualitative and quantitative criteria that results in a single graphical illustration of each supplier's position within a given market. IDC MarketScape provides a clear framework in which the product and service offerings, capabilities and strategies, and current and future market success factors of technology suppliers can be meaningfully compared. The framework also provides technology buyers with a 360-degree assessment of the strengths and weaknesses of current and prospective suppliers.

#5532. Figure loan volume rises 135% on platform growth after Kiavi acquisition

Figure said Q3 Loan Marketplace volume rose 135% year over year to $5.8B, including $677M from Kiavi. Net revenue increased 84% to $287M, while net income was $89.3M and adjusted EBITDA rose 91% to $163.6M.  AI Summary

Figure Technology Solutions on Thursday reported a sharp increase in loan marketplace volume in the third quarter, as the blockchain-based lending platform continued expanding its marketplace business and completed its acquisition of real estate investment lender Kiavi.

The company’s Loan Marketplace volume reached $5.8 billion in the three months ending Sept. 30, up 135% from $2.5 billion a year earlier. The total included $677 million in volume contributed by Kiavi, which Figure officially acquired on Sept. 1.

Figure Connect, the company’s capital-light marketplace platform, accounted for $4.3 billion of quarterly volume, up 276% year over year. The platform represented 72% of standalone Loan Marketplace volume during the quarter.

Net revenue increased 84% year over year to $287 million, compared with $156.4 million in the third quarter of 2025.

Net income was essentially flat at $89.3 million, compared with $89.8 million a year earlier. On a quarterly basis, net income rose from its second-quarter figure of $87.4 million.

Net income margin fell to 31%, down from 57%, partly because the year-ago quarter included a one-time $31 million tax benefit related to the recognition of deferred tax assets. Adjusted EBITDA, a non-GAAP measure, rose 91% to $163.6 million. Adjusted EBITDA margin increased to 58% from 55%.

“This was a record quarter for Figure, highlighted by another consecutive quarter of over 100% volume growth and the rapid expansion of our capital-light marketplace, with Figure Connect now making up 72% of our standalone volume,” CEO Michael Tannenbaum said in a statement.

During the company’s earnings call, Tannenbaum said that Figure grew volume 107% year over year, posting a 58% EBITDA margin and maintaining a 3.7% net standalone take rate. Chief financial officer Macrina Kgil said that during the company’s Q2 2026 earnings, it guided Q3 standalone volume to a range of $4.8 billion to $5.2 billion, and that guidance proved reliable as Figure came in at $5.1 billion.

“The Kiavi acquisition … contributed approximately $670 million of volume for the one month in our results this quarter,” Kgil said. Figure Connect volume, including Kiavi, grew to 74% of overall volume, up from 65% last quarter and from 46% a year ago.”

The acquisition expands Figure’s presence in investor-focused mortgage lending, including residential transition loans (RTLs) and debt-service-coverage ratio (DSCR) loans. Figure said the deal added $8 billion in annualized volume and that it had realized $30 million in initial cost synergies since the transaction closed.

“With Kiavi, we have added residential transition loans, RTL, and debt service coverage ratio loans, DSCR, diversifying our platform beyond HELOC into a $200 billion-plus addressable market,” Tannenbaum told investors. He added that the acquisition had closed ahead of schedule and that Kiavi “also brought on a number of new full loan and securitized investors.”

The company also reported continued growth in its small- and medium-sized business lending (SMB) operation, which surpassed a $500 million annualized run rate with more than 150 active partners.

Figure said it expanded its partner network to 612 standalone partners and 894 when including Kiavi. The network includes more than 20 active depository partners.

The company also introduced an artificial intelligence-powered loan officer assistant through a partnership with Sierra. The tool has processed approximately $260 million in funded loans and increased funded dollars per loan approval by 29%, Figure said.

Separately, Figure’s $YLDS stablecoin had $504 million in circulation as of Sept. 30, compared with $328 million at the end of 2025. The company said 28 participants were using the stablecoin for marketplace transactions.

The company’s board also authorized a $200 million increase to its share repurchase program, bringing the total authorization to $400 million.

“Today, we’re announcing an expanded $400 million share buyback plan that will start tomorrow,” Tannenbaum said. “Given our profitability, cash levels, balance-sheet liquidity, and access to the capital markets, we will be opportunistic about share repurchases on an ongoing basis, including beyond this initial $400 million program. That said, we see huge organic growth and look at inorganic opportunities as well, especially those that can accelerate our marketplace reach.”

For the fourth quarter, Figure forecasts Loan Marketplace volume of $6.2 billion to $6.7 billion, along with a gross take rate of 3.1% to 3.4%.

#5531. Exchange Ledgers in the Middle as CFTC and SEC Diverge on What “Delivery” Means

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

A customer buys a token on a U.S. exchange and the app shows the balance. Under the CFTC's December 14 framework, nothing has been delivered yet.

Under the SEC's crypto proposal, delivery doesn't decide the question at all. An October 27 comment letter asks the two agencies to settle on one answer.

Open almost any crypto exchange app after a purchase and you'll see a clean number: 1.0000 ETH, available. To the customer, the asset is theirs. To the exchange's database, it's a row in an internal ledger. To federal regulators, that row is now being judged by two different tests that don't agree on what it means.

The Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) has opened an advance notice of proposed rulemaking on what it calls Regulation Crypto Asset Transactions (CTX) and Regulation Crypto Asset Markets (CAM). It sets out the agency's first formal view of "actual delivery" for crypto since it withdrew its 2020 guidance last December. Comments close on December 14.

The Securities and Exchange Commission's Regulation Crypto Assets proposal takes a different view of the same moment. Then, on October 27, a comment letter on the SEC's file raised the gap directly. It described the situation as "two conflicting definitions of the same physical facts" and asked the agencies to "please coordinate the definitions."

Delivery matters because it decides which rulebook applies.

For the CFTC, the answer comes from Section 2(c)(2)(D) of the Commodity Exchange Act. A leveraged, margined or financed retail commodity trade is treated like a futures contract unless "actual delivery" happens within 28 days. If delivery happens in time, the trade falls outside futures rules. If it doesn't, the exchange is effectively running a futures venue.

For the SEC, the question is whether a token is still part of an investment contract. Under the August proposal, a covered investment contract ends when the issuer has finished or permanently stopped its essential managerial efforts and files a Form TR transition report. Whether the buyer has received the token is not part of that test.

So one agency treats delivery as the deciding question, and the other barely considers it.

The CFTC's position is still preliminary, but it is detailed. Published in the Federal Register on October 13, the notice relies on the Monex case standard: actual delivery requires "the transfer of some meaningful degree of possession or control."

For crypto, the agency suggests that possession and control "may require possession of the credentials (e.g., private key(s))." It takes three positions that matter most to exchanges:

The agency is also asking whether control has to be exclusive, whether delivery can happen while a lien or security interest is outstanding, and how financing offered in an exchange's standard account documents affects whether a trade is covered at all.

The SEC's proposal, released on August 18, deals with a different question. It creates offering exemptions, including a $5 million startup exemption over four years, and a safe harbor for when a crypto asset's investment contract ends. Neither depends on where the token sits.

Under the proposal, a token held in a customer's self-custody wallet and a token recorded on an exchange's books are treated the same way. In both cases, the investment contract question depends on the issuer's managerial efforts and its filings.

That is the gap the October 27 letter tries to close. Its author, who describes themselves as a fintech founder designing a consumer platform, argues that "where the customer holds the private keys or execution is on-chain, with custody evidence, the asset should be treated as delivered and the covered-investment-contract analysis should end there."

Running four common exchange transactions through both frameworks shows where the tests split.

Trade one: a fully paid purchase left on the exchange.

Trade two: the same purchase withdrawn to a self-custody wallet on day three.

Trade three: a margined purchase kept on the exchange's ledger for 30 days.

Trade four: an on-chain swap that settles directly into the user's wallet.

The pattern is consistent. Self-custody is the only position that clearly counts as delivery under the CFTC's view and also ends the analysis under the letter's proposed SEC fix. Everything left on an exchange's internal ledger stays in an unclear position. The CFTC treats it as undelivered and the SEC's text doesn't address it.

The letter was filed on October 27, a week after the SEC's October 20 comment deadline. It is anonymous and brief, but its main concern is practical. If the definitions stay separate, it warns, founders will have to design products around whichever rule is stricter.

It is the only filing on either docket so far that sets the two definitions side by side.

The CFTC process is still at the advance-notice stage, so a formal proposal will follow. For U.S. platforms, though, the direction is clear. Under the CFTC's preliminary reading, an exchange that keeps customer assets in internal ledger accounts has not delivered them. If that exchange also offers margin or financing, it is on track to be treated as a futures venue.

The SEC's final rule could adopt the letter's custody-based approach or keep delivery out of its analysis entirely. Until one of those happens, the same ledger entry can be undelivered for one regulator and irrelevant for the other.

Exchanges and their customers have until December 14 to say which definition should prevail. The real decision is whether "delivered" ends up meaning the same thing at both agencies.

#5529. Compass pushes back on antitrust claims, says it owes StreetEasy nothing

Compass filed a motion to dismiss an amended antitrust complaint in SDNY tied to pulling rental listings from StreetEasy. Compass argues the suit conflates sales and rentals, lacks causation, and cites the FARE Act as a driver of inventory visibility.  AI Summary

Compass International Holdings is seeking to dismiss an antitrust lawsuit alleging that it created a monopoly through its acquisitions, which it used to harm consumers as well as competitors like Zillow when it decided to pull its rental listings from StreetEasy in early August.

Filed in late August, the lawsuit claims that Compass’s removal of listings from StreetEasy reduced consumer choice, while also driving up rents and brokerage fees.

In a filing on Tuesday, Compass told the court it was seeking to dismiss the amended complaint with prejudice, which would prevent the plaintiff from refilling the lawsuit.

In the filing, Compass claims that the plaintiffs have confused the residential sales market with the rental market, noting that the information cited in the complaint pertains to for-sale homes and not rental listings. The filing also notes that Compass does not own rental properties or set rental prices, claiming instead that Zillow and StreetEasy dominate the online listing-search market. The defendant also claims that the plaintiff cannot demonstrate that Compass’s alleged conduct caused his higher rent.

The filing also notes that rental inventory in New York City began to decline seven months prior to its acquisition of Anywhere and more than a year before Compass began instructing agents to pull rental listings from Street Easy. Instead, Compass points to the June 2025 implementation of New York City’s Fairness in Apartment Rental Expenses (FARE) Act, which prohibits brokers hired by landlords from charging broker fees to tenants and requires landlords to disclose applicable fees before a lease is signed, as the reason behind the drop in visible inventory.

Compass also claims that it does not have monopoly power in the rental listings market and that it has no legal obligation to share its listings with platforms like Street Easy.

According to a notice on the court docket, the plaintiff has until December 8, 2026, to respond to Compass’s motion to dismiss the suit. While the parties wait for the court to rule on the motion, Compass is also asking the court to stay discovery. The court has not yet ruled on that motion.

#5528. Vuzix Reports Third Quarter 2026 Results

ROCHESTER, N.Y., Nov. 12, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- VuzixÂ® Corporation (NASDAQ: VUZI) ("Vuzix" or the "Company"), a supplier of AI-powered smart glasses, waveguides for smart glasses and co-packaged optical data center interconnects, and related augmented reality technologies, today reported its financial results for the third quarter ended September 30, 2026.

"During the third quarter, Vuzix continued to advance its transition towards a more OEM-focused business built around advanced waveguide technologies, optical engineering and its U.S.-based manufacturing capabilities," said Paul Travers, President and CEO of Vuzix. "While sales of our established enterprise smart glasses products declined year-over-year, reflecting models we discontinued at the end of 2025, we are seeing new tangible progress in defense and other customer-directed opportunities. Our defense business is becoming an increasingly important part of this strategy, supported by just under $1.0 million in recently secured new orders, additional expected defense opportunities are now progressing through the award contracting process, and ongoing production and next-generation development work with Collins Aerospace. The recent launch of our SHRIKE Defense Display Platform and our expanded domestic manufacturing capabilities further position us to address specialized defense and security requirements."

The following table compares condensed elements of the Company's unaudited summarized Consolidated Statements of Operations data for the three months ended September 30, 2026 and 2025, respectively:

For the three months ended September 30, 2026, total revenues decreased by 38% to $0.7 million versus $1.2 million for the comparable period in 2025. Product sales were $0.5 million versus $0.9 million, a decrease of 45%. Engineering services and OEM product sales were $0.2 million versus $0.3 million, a decrease of 17%.

There was an overall gross loss of $0.9 million for the three months ended September 30, 2026 as compared to a gross loss of $0.4 million for the comparable 2025 period.

Research and Development expense was $3.3 million for the three months ended September 30, 2026 versus $2.9 million for the comparable 2025 period, an increase of 13%. This increase was largely due to increased external consulting expenses related to the Company's new waveguide-based optical interconnect components being developed for CPO solutions.

Selling and Marketing expense was $1.6 million for the three months ended September 30, 2026 versus $1.1 million for the comparable 2025 period, an increase of 43%. This increase was largely due to increased external consulting expenses related to the Company's new waveguide-based optical interconnect components being developed for CPO solutions.

General and Administrative expense for the three months ended September 30, 2026 was $2.5 million versus $2.6 million for the comparable 2025 period, a decrease of 3%.

For the third quarter ended September 30, 2026, the net loss attributable to common shareholders was $8.4 million or $0.10 per share as compared to a loss of $7.4 million or $0.09 per share for the third quarter of 2025.

Net cash used in operating activities was $6.7 million for the third quarter of 2026 versus $5.0 million for the comparable 2025 period. As of September 30, 2026, the Company had $9.2 million in cash and no current or long-term debt obligations.

Total operating expenses for the third quarter of 2026 were $7.6 million and included approximately $1.0 million of external consulting costs related to the Vuzix Causeway platform, which the Company does not expect to recur. Excluding these costs, operating expenses were approximately $6.6 million, approximately 7% below the third quarter of 2025, and the Company expects fourth-quarter operating expenses to be in the mid-$6 million range.

"We are encouraged by the increasing breadth and pace of progress across our growth initiatives," continued Mr. Travers. "In defense and security markets, we are executing upon awarded work and advancing additional opportunities involving advanced research, specialized optical systems and initial production programs. We have also begun shipping our first SHRIKE display platform units for customer evaluation and integration into their offerings."

"On the OEM front, customers are approaching Vuzix with more defined applications, specific technical requirements and clearer commercial milestones. Our global automotive OEM customer has progressed to production-validation systems and procurement contract negotiations, while other customers continue to evaluate our various Ultralite OEM platform offerings. These developments reflect a meaningful shift toward customer-driven programs with more clearly defined paths to commercialization."

"The Vuzix Causeway Optical Interconnect platform has evolved rapidly in the last 90 days, progressing from its introduction to physical evaluation samples to active engagements with more than 10 companies across the AI optical interconnect ecosystem. This momentum underscores the potential of our waveguide technology to now address emerging optical connectivity requirements in AI data centers. Our next priorities are characterizing integrated-link performance and converting these technical engagements into customer-funded development programs, establishing a potential pathway toward future production opportunities."

"We believe the opportunity emerging around optical interconnects and co-packaged optics warrants continued strategic investment as we advance Causeway from initial evaluations toward integrated system demonstrations. The third quarter included approximately $1.0 million of external market assessment and consulting costs that we do not expect to recur, and we expect to continue advancing Causeway without a significant increase in development spending. By leveraging our existing waveguide expertise, intellectual property and manufacturing infrastructure, we believe we can make meaningful technical and commercial progress while maintaining a disciplined approach to capital allocation."

"We have completed the installation and upgrades to our Rochester waveguide manufacturing facility, including improvements to processing, handling and production flow, while advancing high-index material processing and functional single-plate color waveguides toward customer qualification," concluded Mr. Travers. "These capabilities, together with our established optical technologies and intellectual property, provide a common foundation for pursuing significant opportunities across defense, OEM smart glasses and AI optical interconnects. We believe the progress we are making today is laying the foundation for stronger financial performance and long-term shareholder value."

#5527. UWM rolls out 40 bps year-end pricing bonus, expands Bilt partnership

United Wholesale Mortgage introduced “40 to the Finish,” a year-end pricing incentive that adds 40 basis points to all products for loans with 700+ FICO scores when brokers use UWM’s Underwriting+, TRAC+ or virtual closing tools through Dec. 31. At the same time, UWM expanded its partnership with Bilt to integrate Bilt Neighborhood OS into its servicing platform.   AI Summary

United Wholesale Mortgage (UWM) this week announced the launch of a year-end pricing incentive for broker loans and an expansion of its partnership with Bilt.

Effective immediately through Dec. 31, brokers who use UWM’s Underwriting+, TRAC+ or virtual closing tools will receive 40 basis points on all agency and nonagency products when the borrower has a credit score of at least 700, UWM said.

The incentive is intended to give brokers more pricing flexibility in the final weeks of 2026 while encouraging use of the lender’s underwriting and closing technology. Year-end pricing specials are common in the wholesale channel as lenders seek to pull volume into the current year, clean up pipelines and help partners hit production goals.

UWM – which was more aggressive on pricing in the past but is seeking to deleverage its balance sheet amid a deal with Oaktree Capital Management and the Ishbia family – saw its gain-on-sale margins decline to 124 basis points in the third quarter, down from 133 basis points in the second quarter.

UWM chairman, CEO and president Mat Ishbia told analysts he expects margins to be steady, adding that “people don’t use UWM because we’re the lowest rates” and arguing that competitors offering lower rates are not good partners.

Separately, UWM said it’s expanding its partnership with Bilt, a neighborhood commerce and rewards platform, to bring Bilt Neighborhood OS into its servicing ecosystem.

Bilt Neighborhood OS is designed to help businesses reach customers and build loyalty through neighborhood-level experiences. Through UWM, it links mortgage servicing with homeownership tasks and local commerce, while keeping independent brokers visible to borrowers after closing.

“The broker who helps you buy your home should be your first call when you’re ready to take the next step, whether that’s refinancing, accessing equity or buying again,” Ishbia said in a statement. “With Bilt Neighborhood OS, we’re making the servicing experience more valuable to homeowners and creating more reasons for them to stay connected to their broker between those major decisions.”

UWM already services hundreds of thousands of loans through Bilt, giving these homeowners a single place to manage their mortgage and access rewards. With Neighborhood OS added, UWM said the experience will extend into more day-to-day homeownership activities, from finding a local contractor to exploring neighborhood offers, or reconnecting with a broker about a home equity or refinance opportunity.

Bilt said it has delivered more than $1 billion in value to its 8 million members, who redeem rewards toward travel, housing payments, student loans, dining and other categories. The company also says it powers one in four U.S. rental homes, primarily through the Bilt Alliance of large owners and operators.

#5526. CISCO REPORTS FIRST QUARTER EARNINGS

SAN JOSE, Calif., Nov. 12, 2026 /PRNewswire/ --

Cisco (NASDAQ: CSCO) today reported first quarter results for the period ended October 24, 2026. Cisco reported first quarter revenue of $18.5 billion, net income on a generally accepted accounting principles (GAAP) basis of $4.6 billion or $1.14 per share, and non-GAAP net income of $5.6 billion or $1.40 per share.

"In Q1, we delivered the strongest revenue and non-GAAP earnings per share growth rates for Cisco in over 15 years," said Chuck Robbins, chair and CEO of Cisco. "Organizations are turning to Cisco for our trusted, market-defining technology and our expertise to help them scale, secure and optimize their environments for the agentic AI era. We are in the very early stages of a multi-year networking supercycle, and we're confident in our ability to continue capturing the multi-billion-dollar opportunity it represents for Cisco."

"Q1 FY27 was another record quarter for Cisco, with revenue, non-GAAP operating margin, and non-GAAP EPS all exceeding the high end of our guidance ranges. The strength of our Q1 performance gives us confidence to raise our revenue and non-GAAP EPS guidance for FY27," said Mark Patterson, CFO of Cisco. "As our business continues to scale, we are unlocking significant operating leverage which is enabling us to grow earnings much faster than revenue. Looking ahead, we remain focused on delivering durable growth and driving continued capital returns."

Reconciliations between net income, EPS, and other measures on a GAAP and non-GAAP basis are provided in the tables located in the section entitled "Reconciliations of GAAP to non-GAAP Measures."

Cisco has declared a quarterly dividend of $0.42 per common share to be paid on January 20, 2027, to all stockholders of record as of the close of business on January 4, 2027. Future dividends will be subject to Board approval.

All comparative percentages are on a year-over-year basis unless otherwise noted.

Revenue -- Total revenue was $18.5 billion, up 24%, with product revenue up 32% and services revenue up 1%.

Revenue by geographic segment was: Americas up 28%, EMEA up 18%, and APJC up 21%. Product revenue performance reflected growth in Networking up 43%, Security up 7%, Collaboration up 8%, and Observability up 2%.

Gross Margin -- On a GAAP basis, total gross margin, product gross margin, and services gross margin were 63.7%, 61.8%, and 70.9%, respectively, as compared with 65.5%, 64.5%, and 68.4%, respectively, in the first quarter of fiscal 2026.

Total gross margins by geographic segment were: 64.1% for the Americas, 68.9% for EMEA and 66.5% for APJC.

On a non-GAAP basis, total gross margin, product gross margin, and services gross margin were 65.6%, 63.7%, and 72.9%, respectively, as compared with 68.1%, 67.2%, and 70.7%, respectively, in the first quarter of fiscal 2026.

Operating Expenses -- On a GAAP basis, operating expenses were $6.2 billion, down 3% year over year, and were 33.4% of revenue. Non-GAAP operating expenses were $5.1 billion, up 2%, and were 27.8% of revenue.

Operating Income -- GAAP operating income was $5.6 billion, up 66%, with GAAP operating margin of 30.2%. Non-GAAP operating income was $7.0 billion, up 37%, with non-GAAP operating margin at 37.8%.

Provision for Income Taxes -- The GAAP tax provision rate was 17.2%. The non-GAAP tax provision rate was 18.5%.

Net Income and EPS -- On a GAAP basis, net income was $4.6 billion, an increase of 59%, and EPS was $1.14, an increase of 58%. On a non-GAAP basis, net income was $5.6 billion, an increase of 39%, and EPS was $1.40, an increase of 40%.

Cash Flow from Operating Activities -- $4.4 billion for the first quarter of fiscal 2027, an increase of 36% compared with $3.2 billion for the first quarter of fiscal 2026.

Balance Sheet and Other Financial Highlights

Cash and Cash Equivalents and Investments -- $15.8 billion at the end of the first quarter of fiscal 2027, compared with $15.9 billion at the end of fiscal 2026.

Remaining Performance Obligations (RPO) -- $46.2 billion, up 8% in total. Product RPO was up 7% and services RPO was up 9%.

Deferred Revenue -- $30.1 billion, up 7% in total, with deferred product revenue up 6% and deferred services revenue up 9%.

Capital Allocation -- In the first quarter of fiscal 2027, we returned $3.7 billion to stockholders through share buybacks and dividends. We declared and paid a cash dividend of $0.42 per common share, or $1.7 billion, and repurchased approximately 18 million shares of common stock under our stock repurchase program at an average price of $112.38 per share for an aggregate purchase price of $2.0 billion. The remaining authorized amount for stock repurchases under the program is $6.1 billion with no termination date.

In the first quarter of fiscal 2027, we closed the acquisition of WideField Security Inc., a privately held security company.

#5525. Google releases Gemini 4 Hydrogen, a lower-cost model said to outscore Argon

Google LLC today released Gemini 4 Hydrogen, a lower-cost model in its Gemini 4 artificial intelligence family that it says outscores its frontier Gemini 4 Argon model on an independent intelligence ranking.

Measured on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index at its default high thinking level, Hydrogen scored 51 to Argon’s 50, according to Google. A fourth thinking level called xhigh, new with Hydrogen, takes the score to 54.

The rollout is different, too. Argon spent nearly two weeks with members of Google’s Fairwind Program, a group of vetted cybersecurity defenders, before paying developers could get at it on Oct. 13. Hydrogen skipped that stage. Anyone can use it from today, including people on the free version of the Gemini app.

Koray Kavukcuoglu, who became head of Google DeepMind in August when Demis Hassabis moved into a chairman role, wrote in the announcement that Hydrogen is “built for rapid execution.”

Orchestrator, which Google added to its Antigravity coding tool today, picks between Hydrogen and Gemini 4 Carbon as a session goes along. Google’s runs of the Terminal-Bench 4.0 coding test found Orchestrator getting close to Carbon’s success rate on an average of 24% less quota.

Gemini 3.8 Flash, which came out in September, is the yardstick for most of the other numbers in the announcement. Against it, Hydrogen finished tasks 2.5 times faster at the default setting. On Terminal-Bench 4.1, which tests work done at a command line, Hydrogen more than tripled the older model’s 18.2% with a score of 57%.

Among the early testers Google quoted, Andrew Carr, a former OpenAI scientist who is now chief scientist at 3D animation startup Cartwheel Inc., said the model caught two problems with an approach his team had been stuck on for 10 days. Discovery Loop Inc., the startup former Google Chief Scientist Jeff Dean co-founded after leaving in August, was another.

#5524. Newrez partners with Upgrade to add personal loans for servicing customers

Newrez is adding unsecured personal loans for eligible servicing customers through a partnership with fintech firm Upgrade, which will originate and service the loans via issuer Cross River Bank. The product gives existing Newrez borrowers a way to access cash without using their home as collateral or changing their mortgage, with no prepayment fees and soft-credit prequalification.  AI Summary

Multichannel lender Newrez partnered with financial technology firm Upgrade to offer unsecured personal loans to eligible mortgage servicing customers, giving homeowners another option to access cash without tapping home equity or refinancing.

The loans, originated and serviced by Upgrade and issued by its partner Cross River Bank, do not change the existing Newrez mortgage. Newrez funded $12.9 billion in mortgages in the third quarter and reached $878.9 billion in unpaid principal balance across its mortgage servicing rights (MSR) portfolio at the end of September.

According to the company, the loans can be funded in as little as one business day for qualified borrowers, have no prepayment fees and allow customers to see prequalified offers through a soft credit inquiry.

Newrez framed the launch as an extension of its relationships with homeowners beyond the mortgage, with loans designed for uses such as debt consolidation, home improvements and unexpected expenses.

“Our relationship with homeowners doesn’t begin and end with a mortgage,” Leslie Gillin, Newrez’s chief commercial officer, said in a statement. “Homeowners’ financial needs often extend beyond their monthly mortgage payment, and we’re proud to broaden the ways we can support them, including helping identify opportunities for savings as they navigate important financial decisions.”

The launch comes as many homeowners are struggling with revolving debt. In a June 2026 survey conducted by Morning Consult on behalf of Newrez, 51% of homeowners reported carrying credit card balances, with 59% saying the debt is negatively affecting their finances. The online survey of 2,203 U.S. adults was conducted in June 2026.

“The findings show that many homeowners are looking for ways to improve their financial position but may not know where to start,” Gillin said. “By combining education with access to responsible financing options, we can help customers make informed decisions that support their long-term financial goals.”This article was generated using HousingWire Automation and reviewed by a HousingWire editor before publication. The system helps convert company announcements and industry data into HousingWire-style news coverage.
