#5502. 5 financial products and where FDIC deposit insurance stops

Free daily briefing on global business news.

FDIC insurance follows the product and the issuer, not the label. See how it treats 5 familiar products, from checking accounts to Treasurys.

Few financial promises have held up as well as federal deposit insurance. Since the guarantee began in 1934, no depositor had lost a cent of insured money as of 2022, according to the FDIC. For money inside the guarantee, the protection is about as certain as anything in finance. With a record like that, the question that matters is not whether the guarantee works but what it actually covers. Coverage depends on the type of product and on who issued it, not on the bank name over the door or the label on a monthly statement. As a result, the money people assume is protected and the money that really is protected do not always match.

Insured and uninsured products can look alike to a customer, so lawmakers and regulators have put the job of telling them apart on the label. In 2012, banks were already required by law to tell customers whether the FDIC insured a product and to print that on account statements and advertising, according to Carol Kaplan, a spokeswoman for the American Bankers Association, in remarks reported by CNBC. Regulators have since revised those rules. Provisions of Part 328, the FDIC regulation on how banks present deposit insurance, took effect on April 1, 2024, according to the Federal Reserve, FDIC and OCC. Regulators' continued attention to these rules suggests the confusion is real. A disclosure can tell a customer that a product lacks insurance, but it cannot tell them what that means for their money. That second question is the one a customer actually needs answered.

Investopedia set out to sort which financial products FDIC deposit insurance protects and which it leaves out. Its picks include checking accounts and cashier's checks, which the guarantee covers, as well as mutual funds and Treasury bills, which it does not. That sorting is a starting point rather than an answer. A product on the covered side can still fall outside the guarantee when a company other than an insured bank holds or issues the money. The uncovered side includes products as different as a stock fund and a government bond, and a product's place on that side says nothing by itself about how safe the money is. For each product, the useful question is what actually stands behind the money and where that protection stops.

A checking account is the plainest case of protected money. Investopedia counts it as a deposit at an insured bank, which means it is covered automatically up to $250,000 in each ownership category. The limit applies to each ownership category rather than to each person, so one customer's total insured amount can rise above $250,000 when the money is held in different categories. For most households, the dollar cap is not where a checking account's protection ends. The weak point is something a monthly statement never shows.

Automatic coverage depends on a condition that the words "checking account" don't reveal: the customer's money has to be on deposit at an insured bank. A customer who signs up through another company is covered only after that company has placed the money with an insured institution, according to the Federal Reserve, FDIC and OCC. The guarantee protects the customer against the failure of that bank. It does nothing for the customer if the nonbank company in between collapses. Checking accounts are counted among covered products, yet the people who run the insurance say customers may not see this gap. "End users may not be aware that access to their funds may depend on the third party and that deposit insurance does not protect against losses resulting from the failure of the third party," the Federal Reserve Board, FDIC and OCC said in a joint statement. The useful test is whether the company holding the money is an insured bank, and if it isn't, which bank is.

Even with an insured bank behind the account, the records decide whether the guarantee reaches each customer. When a company pools many customers' money at one bank, regulators require that each owner's identity and interest can be determined from the records, according to the Federal Reserve, FDIC and OCC. If the company keeps poor records, a customer's claim can be left in doubt. An insured balance is also not always one the customer can reach right away, because the guarantee covers the amount but not a quick way to get it back.

The name describes the product, but the safety of the money depends on who holds it and whether the records prove it belongs to the customer.

A savings account receives the full protection the guarantee was built to give, because it is a deposit, and that protection covers the interest a saver earns as well as the money the saver puts in. Savings are protected dollar for dollar, interest included, up to $250,000, according to Investopedia. Coverage begins automatically when a saver opens the account at an insured bank, so being protected takes no form and no choice from the saver. Because interest is protected under the same limit, it also counts toward that limit. A saver whose balance sits near $250,000 can move past the insured amount through earned interest alone, without depositing another dollar. The guarantee does not fail in that case. The insured amount stays fixed while the balance grows, and the saver has to keep track of the total.

A saver can insure more than $250,000 at a single bank by owning money in more than one way. The limit covers each depositor, at each insured bank, in each ownership category, and every category carries its own limit. The categories are ordinary ones that many savers already use, such as individual, joint, pay-on-death and certain retirement accounts. A saver who opens a second savings account in the same name at the same bank gains no extra protection, while a saver who titles money under a different category can. Someone who spreads assets across several qualifying accounts could in theory reach insured totals of $500,000, $750,000 or $1 million. Those totals depend on arranging the accounts correctly and are not a guaranteed amount.

The savings guarantee is generous but literal: it protects money according to how each account is owned, not according to how safe the saver believes it is.

A cashier's check or a bank money order is a single payment that the issuing bank has promised to honor. When a bank issues these official items, they count as covered deposits, though they are not ordinary accounts, according to Investopedia. The slip in a buyer's hand is protected as a deposit at that bank. That protection comes from the bank's promise to pay and not from the paper itself, so the issuer is the detail that decides everything.

The words "money order" on a slip do not tell the buyer who issued it, and only a bank-issued money order is insured. The FDIC says it never insures companies that are not banks and offers nothing when such a company goes bankrupt. Deposit insurance exists to protect customers when the issuer collapses. Only a buyer whose money order came from a bank has that protection if the issuer fails. For any sum the buyer can't afford to lose, buying the money order from a bank rather than from a non-bank seller is the safer choice.

A bank-issued item carries the same ceiling as other covered deposits. The guarantee reaches at least $250,000, counted separately for each depositor at each bank in each ownership category. That ceiling matters most when people buy these items for large payments, because any amount above it falls outside the guarantee. Buyers can work out their coverage with the FDIC Electronic Deposit Insurance Estimator.

An official item is protected only when a bank issued it, and only up to the limit the guarantee sets.

A mutual fund is outside deposit insurance because of what it is. FDIC coverage depends on whether a product is a deposit product, Investopedia reports, and investments such as mutual funds fall outside that coverage. The FDIC lists mutual funds among the products it does not cover. No bank name on the door, branch location or design of the account statement changes that, because the exclusion rests on the type of product. Knowing that the FDIC will not protect the money settles one question. An investor still needs to know whether anything else protects it.

A fund held in a brokerage account does have some protection, but it comes from a separate program with a narrower purpose. The likely protector of a brokerage account is the Securities Investor Protection Corporation, whose coverage reached up to $500,000 in 2023, with a lower limit for cash, according to CNBC. That is a high limit for an ordinary investor's account if the brokerage firm fails. That coverage depends on how and where the fund is held, so an investor does not receive it automatically the way a bank depositor receives deposit insurance. SIPC also pays nothing when the securities in an account lose value. It guards an investor against the collapse of the firm, not against a drop in market prices.

Deposit insurance guarantees the dollars a saver puts in. SIPC protects an investor only if the firm holding the account fails, and it promises nothing about what the fund is worth. A mutual fund can be worth less tomorrow than it is today, and that possibility is what makes it an investment. No program insures against that risk, and investors accept it in exchange for the chance of a higher return.

Before buying a mutual fund, an investor should decide whether they can afford to see it lose value, because no program will make up the loss.

A U.S. Treasury bill, bond or note is not covered by FDIC deposit insurance because it is not a bank deposit at all. Investopedia lists Treasury bills, bonds and notes among the products the FDIC does not cover, and these securities carried no insurance in 2012, according to CNBC. The exclusion comes from the form of the product, not from any weakness in it. Treasurys therefore show most clearly that "uninsured" and "risky" are separate questions. No insurer backs a Treasury because the buyer is lending to the government itself, not to a bank that could fail.

Financial planners treat Treasurys as the standard for safety even though the FDIC does not cover them. "They're as good as it gets from a safety standpoint," Jude Boudreaux, a CFP and senior financial planner at The Planning Center in New Orleans, told CNBC in 2023. Top-tier safety and a lack of FDIC coverage both apply to Treasurys because of who makes the promise to repay. Deposit insurance backs a bank's promise to its customers. With a Treasury, the government makes that promise directly, with no bank in between. A saver who compares a Treasury with an insured account is weighing two routes to government-backed protection, not a safe product against an unsafe one.

The "not covered" label cannot tell a buyer which uninsured investment is sound. Bond investments are also excluded from the FDIC guarantee, so the same label applies to the government's own debt and to debt from other borrowers. For any product the FDIC does not insure, the safety of the money depends on who issued it.

For a Treasury, the useful question is not whether the FDIC covers it but whose promise the buyer holds, and here that promise comes from the government itself.

#5501. Seattle startup OneCourt brings tactile tablets for blind and low-vision fans to NHL games

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 5, 2026 at 2:01 pmNovember 6, 2026 at 7:00 am

Seattle startup OneCourt is bringing its haptic devices for blind and low-vision sports fans to hockey, with the NHL and Ticketmaster making the tablets available free at the league’s marquee events this season and at all home games for four teams.

The device turns real-time game data into vibrations that users follow with their fingertips. For hockey, OneCourt draws on the NHL’s EDGE puck and player tracking data.

The tablets debuted at the Heritage Classic on Oct. 25, and the Washington Capitals, Colorado Avalanche, Chicago Blackhawks and Detroit Red Wings are the first clubs to offer them at every home game.

“Our community has been asking us for hockey since day one, and launching it with Ticketmaster and the NHL is a milestone for OneCourt,” CEO Jerred Mace said in a news release.

The hockey launch builds on OneCourt’s work in other leagues, starting with the NBA’s Portland Trail Blazers. Since 2025, Ticketmaster has offered the tablets at every home game for nine NBA teams, and it backed an NFL pilot during the 2025 season with four clubs, including the Seattle Seahawks, along with Super Bowl LX.

Mace started OneCourt as a University of Washington student studying industrial and product design. His co-founders are three fellow UW grads: COO Antyush Bollini, CTO Andrew Buckingham and CIO Nick Durand.

Time named OneCourt’s tablet to its Best Inventions of 2026 list last month, in the accessibility category. It was one of several Seattle-area innovations on the list.

#5500. The IRS is raising 401(k) limits for 2027. But IRA savers get no higher limit

Free daily briefing on global business news.

The 401(k) catch-up limit for workers 50 and older rises too, while income ranges for IRA deductions and Roth eligibility increase

The Internal Revenue Service raised the 401(k) employee contribution limit by $1,000 for 2027, setting the cap at $25,500 versus the $24,500 that applies this year, the agency said on Thursday.

The same limit covers 403(b) plans, governmental 457 plans and the federal Thrift Savings Plan. The IRS issued technical guidance on cost-of-living adjustments for 2027 in Notice 2026-66.

The limit on annual contributions to an Individual Retirement Account remains $7,500, the IRS said. The IRA catch-up limit for people 50 and older remains $1,100.

The catch-up limit for most 401(k), 403(b), governmental 457 and Thrift Savings Plan participants 50 and older rises to $8,500 from $8,000. Those participants can contribute up to $34,000 a year starting in 2027, the IRS said. Under SECURE 2.0, employees aged 60 to 63 in these plans have a higher catch-up limit of $11,750 for 2027.

"Along with the Working Families Tax Cuts, this increase in the pension limitations will help American families keep more of their hard-earned income," IRS Chief Executive Officer Frank J. Bisignano said in a statement.

Income ranges that determine eligibility for deductible traditional IRA contributions, Roth IRA contributions and the Saver's Credit all increased for 2027. For single taxpayers covered by a workplace retirement plan, the traditional IRA deduction phases out between $83,000 and $93,000, up from $81,000 to $91,000 for 2026. For married couples filing jointly, where the spouse making the IRA contribution has a workplace plan, the range is $133,000 to $153,000, up from $129,000 to $149,000.

The Roth IRA contribution phase-out range for singles and heads of household rises to $158,000 to $173,000, from $153,000 to $168,000. For married couples filing jointly, it rises to $250,000 to $260,000, from $242,000 to $252,000.

The general contribution limit for SIMPLE retirement accounts increases to $17,500 from $17,000. The general SIMPLE catch-up limit for employees 50 and older remains $4,000.

The announcement arrives a week after the agency published a separate batch of cost-of-living updates for 2027, among them the tax brackets for federal income, according to CNBC.

#5499. Agility Robotics co-founder on its Nasdaq debut, lessons from Amazon, and the future of work

by Todd Bishop on Nov 5, 2026 at 6:51 pmNovember 5, 2026 at 6:51 pm

Agility Robotics of Salem, Ore., made its Nasdaq debut Thursday as the first publicly traded U.S. company devoted solely to humanoid robots — offering an ambitious vision for how the technology will change work, and a cautious view of how long it will take.

“Maybe we’ll never have faster-than-light travel. Maybe we’ll never have transporters from Star Trek,” said Jonathan Hurst, the company’s co-founder and chief robot officer. “But we absolutely will have machines that can do all of the physical work that a person can do.”

However, he cautioned, “It’s not going to be next year or five years from now. It’s really a grand challenge.”

Agility went public through a merger with Churchill Capital Corp XI, a special purpose acquisition company, or SPAC, led by financier Michael Klein. The deal valued Agility at $2.5 billion before the new investment and brought in about $465 million in gross proceeds. Its shares trade on the Nasdaq under the ticker AGLT.

After initially dipping below its opening price, the stock closed Thursday at $11.51, up 2.2%, bucking the trend on a day when the Nasdaq fell 5.5%, its worst day in 18 months.

Agility’s robot: The company’s main character is Digit, a two-legged robot with two arms mounted near the top of its torso that let it lift bins high and recover from falls. It moves totes and containers in warehouses and factories.

Digit 5, the latest version, was unveiled in September. Standing 5-foot-11 and weighing 284 pounds, it’s covered in sensors, with cameras and antennas in its head and safety-rated sensors in protective housings around its body. Agility says it can lift 50 pounds, reach 7.2 feet high and work more than 20 hours in a 24-hour day.

But the big advance is that Digit 5 was designed to work alongside people without a barrier. Earlier versions had to be fenced off from workers, which limited where customers could use them.

Agility learned how much that mattered at Amazon, an early investor in the company, which tested prior versions of Digit for moving and stacking bins in its warehouses.

Digit did useful work in tests there, Hurst said, but when Agility asked about scaling up, Amazon said it couldn’t deploy the robots. It showed Agility what it had taken to get its own wheeled robot through three to four years of safety certification, and said it didn’t know how a balancing robot would ever get there.

“The safety case to do this is unbelievably hard,” Hurst said. “Nobody has ever deployed a dynamically stable balancing machine, and it brings new risks.”

Getting a robot out from behind the barrier took years of engineering and standards work. Agility has been co-authoring ISO safety standards for the category and making its case to insurance companies and warehouse operators who want proof in numbers before putting a balancing machine next to a person.

Digit 5 uses AI and multiple sensors to watch for nearby people. Depending on the situation, it steers around them, stops or sits down. Visual and audio cues signal what it’s about to do, and a safety controller triggers its responses when someone gets too close.

Hurst credits the lessons from Amazon, along with ones from GXO, Toyota and Schaeffler, with shaping the design of Digit 5.

“Amazon was a huge, huge part of getting us to that point,” he said.

Amazon made an initial deposit in 2024 toward a $1.05 million purchase of five robots, according to Agility’s filings. Agility recorded about $1.04 million in net sales from Amazon in 2025, 58% of its total for the year. Hurst said he couldn’t speak to whether Amazon is a customer now.

With the safety improvements and other advancements, Hurst called Digit 5 “the scaling moment” for Agility. “That is the unlock,” he said.

One customer, which Agility has not named, has committed to a $300 million, three-year contract for 1,000 Digit 5 robots, according to its filings. The robots would be rented rather than sold, the commitment is subject to milestones and specifications, and the customer gets warrants that vest as the robots are deployed.

Agility has built about 10 Digit 5 robots, Hurst said, with the first prototypes just coming off the line. Its factory in Salem was built to eventually produce as many as 10,000 robots a year.

Financial picture: Agility’s business is still small, with revenue of $1.78 million last year and about $174,000 in the first six months of this year. It lost $362 million in the first half, up from $71.8 million a year earlier. Stock-based compensation, an accounting charge for employee equity awards, rose by about $252 million over the same period.

Agility had $14.7 million in cash at the end of June, before the deal closed, and management said in its interim financial statements that there was substantial doubt about the company’s ability to keep operating.

Hurst called the public markets his biggest unknown.

“I’m completely confident in our market path, our technological path,” he said. If public shareholders agree, he said, Agility will be able to “continue on this mission successfully and raise money when we need to.” If they doubt the company, “that’s going to make our life a lot harder.”

What Agility has that most rivals don’t is robots doing commercial work. As of May, its Digit 4 model had logged more than 65,000 hours across nine committed customer deployments, according to its filings. Digit 4 robots have moved more than 100,000 totes since June 2024 at a Georgia facility run by the logistics company GXO.

Investors have put far higher values on rivals still working largely in pilots, including Figure AI at a reported $39 billion, more than 15 times Agility’s valuation in the merger.

“Digit is doing real work in customer operations today, taking on repetitive, physically demanding tasks,” said Peggy Johnson, Agility’s CEO, in a statement. Going public, she said, gives the company more resources to put Digit into more workplaces.

Johnson became CEO in March 2024, when Hurst moved from CTO to chief robot officer. She previously ran Magic Leap, and before that spent six years as a Microsoft executive, leading business development and dealmaking under CEO Satya Nadella.

In an interview with GeekWire earlier in the week, Hurst took the long view on the stock listing, calling it a milestone on a much longer path. Treating a listing day as the achievement, he said, is a finance person’s frame: “I just don’t live in that world.”

From CMU to OSU: Hurst has been on that path for almost three decades.

He built his first walking robot in 1997, as a freshman at Carnegie Mellon University in Pittsburgh. He stayed at Carnegie Mellon for a Ph.D. in robotics, finishing in 2008, when fewer than 100 people in the world had earned one, he said.

That year he joined Oregon State University in Corvallis, planning from the start to eventually spin a company out of his research. In his Oregon State lab, Hurst’s team built ATRIAS, a two-legged robot that didn’t look like any animal because it was based on a mathematical model of walking and running. It was the first machine to reproduce the dynamics of human walking.

He started Agility in 2015 with Damion Shelton, a Carnegie Mellon classmate who was CEO until 2024, and Mikhail Jones, one of his Oregon State students, out of his lab there.

Being in Oregon helped from the start, Hurst said. Agility was almost alone in trying to build humanoid robots, and the engineers who moved to Oregon to join it were committed to that mission. The company had almost no turnover, unlike the Silicon Valley pattern of people jumping to a new job every six months.

But as it passed 400 employees, it needed experienced engineering managers, and Oregon had no robotics industry large enough to have produced them. Agility had been hiring those people in California and flying them north, so it opened an office there. Today Agility has offices in Pittsburgh and Fremont, Calif., in addition to Oregon.

Impact on jobs: For the time being, Agility pitches Digit as a way to fill jobs that are difficult to staff. Johnson told TechCrunch this week that the company has focused on “manual, very repetitive jobs, that it’s hard to find humans to do.”

Hurst calls the first commercial uses of the technology “step one” toward what he describes as the dream: “robots as part of everyday human life, doing the things people would rather not do.”

Asked what happens to the people whose work the robots replace, Hurst pointed to farming as an example of automation improving people’s lives.

“Early in American history, 90% of Americans worked in agriculture, and today 2% do,” he said. “And the only reason that’s true is because of automation.”

#5498. Kalshi is dropping Donald Trump Jr. as an advisor over Polymarket conflict

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Trump Jr.'s firm 1789 Capital holds a stake in Polymarket, where he remains an advisor, as Democrats take power in Congress

Kalshi is cutting ties with Donald Trump Jr. as an advisor because 1789 Capital, his venture firm, owns a piece of competing prediction market Polymarket, according to CNBC.

A Kalshi spokesperson said the company and Trump Jr. both concluded that it was a conflict of interest for the president's son to advise Kalshi while also being a major backer of Polymarket, according to CNBC. Discussions about his departure got underway in August, following 1789 Capital's announcement of its Polymarket stake, the spokesperson said.

"We have mutually agreed to end Don's advisory role after his firm's significant investment in a competitor this past summer. We are grateful for his contributions in helping us market Kalshi to more customers," the spokesperson said, according to Bloomberg.

Trump Jr. remains an advisor to Polymarket, according to CNBC. He was paid in Kalshi equity for the advice he provided, according to Bloomberg. A spokesperson for Trump Jr. had not responded to a request for comment.

The departure follows Democratic gains in the House and the Senate, according to CNBC. The party is anticipated to take a harder line on prediction markets. Bloomberg reports that Democrats are entering their new congressional majority pledging to examine the Trump family's dealings with prediction markets and crypto firms.

Kalshi named Trump Jr. a strategic advisor in January 2025, according to CNBC. Bloomberg reports that Kalshi CEO Tarek Mansour said at the time that Trump Jr. would advise on strategy, including expansion. Kalshi has said Trump Jr. gives advice on marketing strategy, not regulatory matters, according to Bloomberg.

Early in October, Mansour told MS NOW that the company's tie to Trump Jr. amounts to an "optics issue." He added that Kalshi has never used the connection to win over government officials, according to CNBC.

Trump's appointees at the Commodity Futures Trading Commission have adopted a friendlier stance toward prediction markets since the president returned to office, according to Bloomberg. Democrats have led most of the pushback, though some Republicans have voiced concern. Several states have filed lawsuits against Kalshi and Polymarket, contending that the platforms break state gambling laws.

#5497. LIVE – Bitcoin Price Rebounds Despite Quantum Threat as Nvidia’s Jensen Huang Faces Ouster After Two Affairs

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

Bitcoin price has rebounded from recent lows as Nvidia board considers ousting CEO Jensen Huang following revelations about two extramarital affairs. Meanwhile, Glassnode data shows that 7.12 million BTC, worth more than $500 billion, already has publicly visible keys that future quantum computers could potentially exploit.

The developments put two of the technology industry’s biggest names under pressure. Bitcoin faces growing questions about its long-term cryptographic security, while Nvidia confronts a leadership crisis that could draw its AI dominance and ambitions in quantum computing.

Nvidia shares plunged more than 8% in extended trading after reports emerged that directors were preparing to remove Huang. The board is also considering an interim CEO before launching a wider search for a permanent replacement.

Bitcoin price recovered from its November 10 low of $72,600, reaching around $74,000 before easing to $73,700 this morning. The rebound offers bulls some relief after a sharp correction earlier this month. However, Glassnode has identified a potentially huge vulnerability affecting more than a third of Bitcoin’s issued supply.

According to a Glassnode update, approximately 35.4% of Bitcoin’s supply, equivalent to 7.12 million BTC, has publicly visible keys. At current market prices, those holdings are valued at more than $500 billion.

The exposure largely comes from address reuse. When Bitcoin holders spend from an address, their public keys become visible on the blockchain. Any remaining coins associated with those keys could become targets for sufficiently powerful quantum computers. Glassnode also says moving those coins to fresh addresses ends this exposure.

The concern centers on Shor’s algorithm, which could theoretically allow quantum computers to derive private keys from publicly available information. That would undermine the cryptographic security protecting vulnerable Bitcoin holdings.

Bitcoin developers are already exploring ways to address the challenge. BIP 360 proposes new transaction structures designed to reduce public-key exposure, while BIP 361 outlines a potential migration away from vulnerable signature schemes.

Nvidia’s leadership crisis has escalated dramatically after Reuters reported that its board was meeting late Wednesday to decide whether to remove Huang. The 63-year-old founder has led Nvidia for more than three decades, transforming it into the dominant supplier of AI processors. But revelations about two extramarital relationships have triggered an internal investigation and intensified scrutiny of his leadership.

The first controversy involves Alice Huang, a businesswoman whose relationship with Jensen Huang has attracted attention from US intelligence officials. BREAKING: Nvidia, $NVDA, is now working with an "outside firm" to find a new CEO to replace Jensen Huang, per Bloomberg.The company is also reportedly weighing naming a temporary CEO while searching for a replacement.

Huang acknowledged being unfaithful to his wife in a message to employees, taking responsibility for his actions. The board’s response has shifted rapidly. It should be noted that Nvidia has 11 directors, with all but Huang considered independent. Its bylaws allow a majority vote to remove the CEO.

Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress has emerged as a potential interim successor, while data-center executive Ian Buck has attracted attention as a possible longer-term candidate. The timing is particularly sensitive, with Nvidia scheduled to release quarterly results on November 17.

Bitcoin’s market recovery remains an important counterpoint for all these developments. Bitcoin price has managed to recover from its November 10 sell-off, with buyers stepping in around $72,700. Reclaiming $74,000 would give bulls another opportunity to challenge higher resistance levels.

The quantum threat is pushing developers to consider changes that could strengthen Bitcoin’s security over the coming years. Nvidia faces a different challenge. The $500 billion quantum exposure has added another major scare to the market. But Bitcoin’s ability to adapt could become just as important as its price performance.

#5496. Let there be LEDs: Tech upgrade helps James Turrell’s Skyspace shine again at UW art museum

Geek Life: Fun stories, memes, humor and other random items at the intersection of tech, science, business and culture.  SEE MORE

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 6, 2026 at 8:01 amNovember 6, 2026 at 9:42 am

For most of the past dozen years, a James Turrell artwork on the University of Washington campus in Seattle — built to glow at sunrise and sunset — has been running on daylight alone.

That changes Nov. 14, when UW’s Henry Art Gallery relights “Light Reign,” its Turrell Skyspace, after a restoration that replaced aging lights with hundreds of new fixtures and a control system synced to the sun.

Originally installed in 2003 near the Henry’s entrance along 15th Avenue N.E., “Light Reign” is one of dozens of skyspaces by Turrell, the 83-year-old artist known for turning light itself into his medium.

Inside the artwork’s oval chamber, LEDs bathe the walls in slowly shifting color, and when the weather cooperates, a retractable lid opens to an oculus that frames the sky. From outside, the glass-paneled shell lights up with its own program — a 21st-century mood ring just steps from a bronze George Washington who has been gazing west toward the Olympics since 1909.

The relighting comes as the Henry, Washington’s first public art museum, heads into its 100th year. The museum opened on campus in February 1927, and officials are hinting that bigger changes are on the way for the centennial.

Trouble with “Light Reign” started around 2015, said Sage Sommer, the Henry’s director of exhibitions and collections. The original lights, by then more than a decade old, were reaching the end of their lifespan, and over time the museum lost the ability to run them.

Through those years, the Skyspace stayed open. Visitors could still sit inside, meditate and watch clouds and birds pass over the oculus, just without the color.

After years of planning, the Henry settled on a full lighting overhaul that also folds in ideas Turrell has used in his newer skyspaces. The exterior already ran on LEDs, but a very early generation of them, while the interior and oculus were lit by neon tubes made by Western Neon.

The museum didn’t work with Turrell directly. Instead it worked with lighting designer Ryan Pike, whose company, RHMP, works only on Turrell installations, from upgrades of existing pieces to new projects. Pike has worked on Turrell artworks since 2013.

For Pike, the toughest part was the exterior. “It’s just over 700 lights, in nine DMX universes, so each fixture can output independently of the rest,” he said in an email. DMX is the standard protocol for controlling stage and architectural lighting. Splitting the facade across multiple universes lets every fixture be programmed on its own.

Sommer said the Skyspace isn’t strictly time-based media, a museum term for art that relies on equipment and unfolds over time. But it raises the same questions. Sometimes the fix is simple, like converting a VHS tape to a digital file. Other times the hardware is integral to the work. Some artists insist a piece be shown only on a CRT TV, and some come back with a remastered version and want only that one shown.

“We work really closely with the artists to make sure that it is as they envision,” she said.

The Henry isn’t the only museum to face the problem. In 2023, Minneapolis’ Walker Art Center restored its own Turrell skyspace, “Sky Pesher,” after it became impossible to find the cold cathode tubes — a 1920s-era technology — that powered its sunrise and sunset lighting program.

Working with Turrell and his studio, the Walker switched to LEDs, which allowed more control and a much wider range of color. What had been “shades of tinted white” is now multicolored, Joe King, the Walker’s director of collections and exhibition management, said in an interview published by the museum.

The Henry’s new system uses roughly 840 LED fixtures, about 710 outside and 130 inside, Sommer said. The exterior program kicks in a half-hour before dawn and dusk. The morning show is brief, about 36 minutes, while the evening one currently runs about four hours after sunset.

“The very cool thing about this space, because we are so far north, is just how connected to sunrise and sunset it is, and how drastically different it is throughout the year,” Sommer said.

The roof has its own engineering pedigree. The Skyspace’s hydraulic lid, which lifts and slides out of the way, was designed by submarine manufacturers in Everett. It stays shut in the rain.

The museum closed the Skyspace in late July and used the downtime for physical restoration, too: repainting the interior, refinishing the teak benches, waxing floors, replacing worn locks, refitting doors that had swollen and cleaning out the gutters. Everything had to be rewired, and the project took longer than expected.

“Light Reign” is the most visible piece in the Henry’s collection of about 30,000 objects, including more than 18,000 textiles and 7,000 works on paper. Only a sliver is ever on view, so the Henry is putting its collection database online. The project was funded by UW’s Student Technology Fee. Anyone can book an appointment at its study center to see a piece up close.

Technology is also the focus of the Henry’s centennial exhibition, opening in late February. Swagato Chakravorty, associate curator, said he was surprised that no major museum had mounted a large, ambitious show on contemporary art and technology in decades, even as Seattle was transformed around it. His show looks at technology “from below,” focusing on the people and communities most directly affected rather than a “great man” story.

The exhibition is loosely organized around three threads. One is bioethics, including a work the Henry commissioned in 2002 with UW geneticist Mary-Claire King, which is being revived 25 years later. Another pairs Indigenous knowledge with tools like 3D printing and algorithms. The third is technology’s material toll, from data centers to water use.

Chakravorty said he deliberately avoids taking a side on whether technology is good or bad for art.

“Writing is a technology. Cave painting was a technology,” he said. As for AI: “It’s not going to kill art.”

The public unveiling of the refurbished “Light Reign” runs 3:30 to 6 p.m. Nov. 14, with remarks from Henry Executive Director Kris Lewis and the exterior illumination starting at 4 p.m. Admission is free, though the Henry encourages RSVPs, and interior viewing is limited to 25 people at a time for about 10 minutes each.

#5495. Fed officially set October 2027 as its first no-vote strategy session

Free daily briefing on global business news.

The revised tentative 2027 calendar sets Oct. 26-27 for broad strategy talks, with no policy decision to be announced

The Federal Reserve designated its Oct. 26-27, 2027, meeting as a session on broad monetary policy strategy, and the Federal Open Market Committee will not announce a policy decision at the end of it.

The Fed announced the revised tentative 2027 schedule on Thursday. It lists meetings on Jan. 26-27, March 16-17, April 27-28, June 8-9, July 27-28, Sept. 14-15, Oct. 26-27 and Nov. 16-17. The committee will announce its policy decision on the second day of each meeting except the October session, the Fed said.

The calendar has seven meetings with rate decisions in 2027 and none in December, according to CNBC. The October session will give policymakers additional room to debate policy, with no rate vote and no statement issued afterward.

Fed Chair Kevin Warsh announced the move at his Oct. 28 news conference, though he left unspecified which meetings would lose their rate votes. The Fed will keep its eight annual meetings.

"In 2027, one meeting will focus exclusively on broad monetary policy strategy, with neither a vote on the federal funds rate nor a policy statement anticipated," Warsh said. He said he expects two strategy meetings in 2028 and six for setting policy.

Warsh said what the Fed might release after a strategy meeting is "not obvious yet" and that details will not come until fall 2027. He said it is "equally important we reserve time and space, as an intellectually diverse group, for strategic deliberations."

#5494. Quantum software startup Q-CTRL raised $290 million at more than $1 billion valuation

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Salesforce Ventures led the Series C round for the quantum software company, which makes GPS-free navigation tools

Q-CTRL, a quantum software company, raised $290 million in a Series C round led by Salesforce $CRM Ventures, the venture arm of Salesforce, the company said on Thursday. The round values Q-CTRL at more than $1 billion, according to Bloomberg.

Q-CTRL said it will expand its software work and scale globally to meet customer demand across sectors from finance to energy. It also plans to continue autonomy and aerospace programs.

The company's main product, Ironstone Opal, is a quantum navigation system that works when GPS is unavailable or denied. Q-CTRL said the system is being deployed on commercial aircraft with Airbus and in autonomous platforms with Lockheed Martin.

Q-CTRL counts DARPA, a U.S. military agency, the navies of Australia and Britain, and Airbus among its contract customers, Chief Executive Michael J. Biercuk told Bloomberg. The technology can fix its location with an error of no more than 10 meters (about 33 feet), according to Bloomberg. Jamming and spoofing have degraded satellite navigation signals amid the conflicts in Ukraine and the Middle East.

Q-CTRL's software can also make quantum computers more stable by cutting their error rates, according to Bloomberg. "Think of our software as the equivalent of noise-canceling headphones," Biercuk told Bloomberg.

"The hard problem in quantum is not building the machine, it is getting useful output from it," Robert Keith, a partner at Salesforce Ventures, said in a statement. Keith said Q-CTRL's control software is the reason Salesforce Ventures led the round.

"Q-CTRL is one of the few quantum companies with real customers and real revenue," Per Roman, founding partner of Bullhound Capital and a Q-CTRL board member, said in a statement.

#5493. Amazon’s AI shopping agent moves into text messages, taking orders and tracking prices

by Todd Bishop on Nov 6, 2026 at 8:07 amNovember 6, 2026 at 9:35 am

Amazon is rolling out a new feature to let customers shop by text message — sending requests to its Alexa for Shopping AI agent, which will search for products, compare options and place orders on their behalf.

The idea is to make shopping work more like messaging a personal assistant. Amazon says the agent works in the background after it gets a request or a photo, and texts back when the task is done.

It’s part throwback and part hot new thing, reflecting a broader shift in how tech companies are offering AI agents for everyday use. OpenAI added texting to Dot, its personal AI agent, last month, and DoorDash rolled out text ordering in September.

The expansion of Amazon’s AI shopping assistant comes amid a larger fight over who controls online shopping when agents do the buying. Amazon has moved to block outside agents from Meta, Perplexity, Google and OpenAI from shopping its site while building its own.

The text thread is also a new place for Amazon to sell. The company says order updates, delivery notifications and deals will eventually land in the same conversation.

Digiday reports that sponsored products can appear among the options the agent texts back, free to advertisers for now, while purchases the agent completes on its own stay ad-free. Amazon reported $68.6 billion in advertising sales in 2025.

The text feature started rolling out Friday to a small group of U.S. customers by invitation, and millions more will get access in the coming weeks, the company says.

Customers who opt in get a contact called “Alexa Shopping” and can send it requests that range from a note that they’re out of dog food to a photo of a recipe they want turned into a grocery order, according to Amazon’s examples.

The agent searches, texts back with options and completes the purchase with the customer’s approval. Customers can also turn on auto-buy to have it purchase an item automatically when the price hits their target. It can also watch for price drops, reorder past purchases and check on packages, and Amazon says a conversation started by text will carry over to the Amazon app, the website and Alexa devices.

Amazon launched Alexa for Shopping in May, merging its Rufus shopping chatbot with Alexa+, the generative AI version of its voice assistant.

#5492. Is the Crypto Market Walking Into a Bull Trap? Bitcoin ETF Records Five Straight Days of Outflow

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

Bitcoin’s latest recovery attempt is running into a serious problem: institutional investors are pulling money out of the market. U.S. spot Bitcoin ETF recorded five consecutive days of net outflows, shedding $1.44 billion between November 5 and November 11.

Bitcoin is now trading near $73,500, struggling to reclaim the $75,000 level. Bitcoin ETF outflow streak raises a bigger question: Is the crypto market walking into another bull trap?

The timing is particularly concerning. Bitcoin briefly reclaimed $80,000 on November 4 before reversing sharply the following day. Crypto has since struggled to regain momentum, leaving us questioning buyers’ decisions and whether we are stepping in too early.

The latest Bitcoin ETF withdrawals included $430.2 million on November 5, followed by another $411.9 million on November 6. Outflows continued on November 9, 10, and 11.

BlackRock’s iShares Bitcoin Trust (IBIT) accounted for most of the selling pressure. The fund alone recorded $269.7 million in net outflows yesterday.

The latest Bitcoin ETF outflow streak shows that institutional demand is struggling to support the market’s recovery. Five consecutive sessions of withdrawals have removed $1.44 billion from U.S. spot Bitcoin funds. BlackRock’s IBIT accounted for three-quarters of that amount.

However, institutional demand has not disappeared entirely. Morgan Stanley’s Bitcoin ETF attracted $9 million yesterday, offering a small counterpoint to the ETF-wide selling.

Glassnode’s latest Week 46 report adds another warning. Bitcoin has fallen below the short-term holder cost basis of $75,600. This leaves recent buyers sitting on unrealized losses.

The research firm also points to shrinking stablecoin supply and continued ETF selling. Both developments display that fresh capital is struggling to enter the market.

This creates an uncomfortable setup for anyone buying the latest dip. A short-lived recovery could attract retail investors before another wave of selling pushes prices lower.

Bitcoin’s derivatives market offers another piece of the puzzle. BTC futures open interest remains above $50 billion, while funding rates remain positive. This number somehow paints a clear picture: leveraged traders are still paying to maintain bullish positions.

However, leverage has already started coming out of the market. Open interest has declined, and much of the long-side leverage near current prices has been flushed.

That creates two possible outcomes. If spot demand returns, reduced leverage could help Bitcoin recover without triggering another major liquidation cascade. Alternatively, another failed breakout could leave remaining leveraged buyers exposed to further downside.

For now, $75,600 is the important recovery threshold. Reclaiming that level would put Bitcoin back above the short-term holder cost basis and improve market sentiment.

A grinding climb toward $80,000 would offer stronger evidence that buyers are regaining control, but losing the $72,000 area could expose BTC to another test of $70,000.

The bull trap argument also has a counterpoint. There is accumulation among two large wallet cohorts, while selling momentum has started weakening. This shows that some investors are already positioning for a recovery.

The market does not need another dramatic crash to trap investors. Sometimes, all it takes is a convincing bounce that runs out of buyers.

#5491. AI giants face a new lawsuit to freeze frontier model development

Free daily briefing on global business news.

The plaintiffs invoked a California law to challenge practices they allege threaten public health, safety and property. They say a freeze is needed to protect public safety

Irreplaceable Education Fund, Public Citizen, Heat Initiative and The Alliance for Secure AI filed a lawsuit on Thursday seeking to freeze development of advanced AI models at Anthropic, Google $GOOGL, Meta $META, OpenAI and SpaceXSI. The suit, filed in San Francisco Superior Court, alleges that executives at the companies have warned that advanced AI systems pose imminent and catastrophic risks to humanity.

The plaintiffs invoke California's Unfair Competition Law to challenge practices they allege threaten public health, safety and property. They say a freeze is needed to protect public safety before a catastrophe occurs.

Former New Jersey Attorney General Matthew Platkin, who filed the complaint on behalf of the plaintiffs, said the companies are creating a public nuisance. "AI companies are causing a public nuisance by knowingly developing and deploying AI systems that pose catastrophic risk," Platkin said in a statement.

The complaint cites incidents involving existing, less powerful AI systems, the plaintiffs said. These include AI agents hacking private companies, gaining unauthorized access to government databases and submitting a false police report without human control. OpenAI's ChatGPT independently breached the systems of a different AI firm in July, according to The Associated Press.

"Our lawsuit asks the court to apply existing law and find the AI corporations' reckless practices unlawful and freeze further AI development," Robert Weissman, co-president of Public Citizen, said in a statement.

Phil Aroneanu, founder and executive director of Irreplaceable Education Fund, said in a statement: "We must freeze frontier AI development until the technology is under control and the American people have a say and a stake in its future, instead of leaving it to a handful of billionaire Big Tech CEOs."

The groups also say they have been forced to shift money and staff off their other scheduled projects to confront the dangers they say the companies' models pose, according to The Associated Press. The companies did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

The suit follows the midterm elections, in which Democrats won control of Congress. President Donald Trump has pushed the companies to oversee their own safety practices, while Congress has yet to put any rules on the technology, according to The Associated Press.

Around 400 scientists, including Geoffrey Hinton and Yoshua Bengio, called in October for an international body with authority over containment standards and security incident reporting for advanced cyber-capable AI systems. The signatories argued that voluntary industry commitments are insufficient and urged governments to work toward a formal oversight regime.

He holds bachelor’s, master’s and doctoral degrees in electrical engineering from the UW.

#5489. Binance’s $6.3B Hack Fix Is Coming Tomorrow: Why the ZK Math Doesn't Tell the Whole Story

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

On-chain data shows the attacker behind the $6.3 billion Binance theft depositing about $4 million into three Binance deposit addresses.

At the same time, Binance's first post-hack reserve snapshot shows its biggest assets covered with buffers as small as 2.7 ETH and $6 of USDT. Binance's full zero-knowledge proof of those figures is due by Tuesday.

Some of the money stolen from Binance has started going back to Binance.

Blockchain intelligence firm Arkham has flagged the entity it tracks as "Binance Hacker" depositing about $4 million into three Binance deposit addresses. Arkham says those addresses "likely represent nested service(s)." These are third-party exchanges that use Binance for liquidity and custody, giving their own customers deposit addresses that sit on Binance's infrastructure.

If Arkham is right, the hacker isn't depositing into an ordinary Binance account. The money would be going to smaller platforms that operate through Binance. Exchanges have long known this is a weak point for stolen funds moving into normal trading. Either way, Binance is now receiving stolen funds at its own deposit addresses while it works to show customers it has replaced what was taken.

The FBI has attributed the October 29 theft to North Korea. The deposits come at a sensitive moment. Binance has just published its first reserve snapshot since the hack and has promised a full cryptographic proof of it by Tuesday.

$4 million is a small slice of a theft worth about $6.3 billion, but it matters for two reasons.

It shows how the laundering works. Nested services are a common way into the regulated financial system. A third-party platform that relies on Binance for custody may run weaker identity checks on its own users. Funds deposited there can be swapped and withdrawn without the hacker ever opening a Binance account.

Binance can act on it. Binance can't freeze bitcoin and ether sitting in wallets nobody controls, and it doesn't control the stablecoins that issuers like Tether and Circle have frozen. Deposits that land at its own addresses are different: they are on Binance's platform, so Binance can freeze them itself. One of the first tests of how Binance handles the money still in the hacker's hands is whether it freezes these funds and identifies the services that own the addresses.

While the hacker's funds move, Binance has been rebuilding its reserves. Its proof-of-reserves page now shows:

The first page covers Binance's six largest assets. Customer balances are what users hold. Reserves are on-chain wallet balances, including assets held with outside custodians.

The second page has four more assets, and two of them stand out:

Why USD1 and RLUSD matter: these are two of the stablecoins whose issuers froze stolen funds after the attack. World Liberty Financial froze $27 million of USD1, and Ripple began freezing RLUSD the same night. Both now show reserves above what Binance owes customers.

Assets with outside custodians: part of several reserves sits with outside custodians rather than in Binance's own exchange wallets:

The striking part isn't that the ratios reach 100%. It's how closely they stop there.

Compared with October's report: Binance's previous monthly report, published in early October before the hack, showed BTC at 100.35% and USDT at 103.88%. ETH was already at exactly 100.00%. After the theft:

Not every asset is that tight. USDC, ZEC and BNB carry buffers of 1.3% to 6%. The thinnest buffers are in BTC, ETH, USDT and SOL, which are among the assets the attacker took in the largest amounts.

How Binance says it got here: the pattern fits Binance's account of replacing the stolen assets in stages. It reported 80% replaced on Friday, 90% on Saturday and 95% on Sunday. The remaining 5% is in less-liquid tokens it is still buying. The money came from:

Binance confirmed taking 7,499 BTC from SAFU and has pledged to refill the fund to about $1 billion.

What the snapshot can't show: it was taken a little over a day after the theft, once the rebuild was under way. It shows the balance sheet after the replacement, not how large the gap was on October 29.

Binance says the full proof takes 40 to 50 hours to compute. Its latest update says it will be ready "by Tuesday, 2026-11-03 (UTC)." The system is open source, in Binance's zkmerkle-proof-of-solvency repository.

What the proof guarantees, according to the project's circuit design document:

The design also guards against a "dummy user attack" identified by Ethereum Foundation researcher Enrico Bottazzi. In that attack, fake accounts holding cheap tokens are used to offset debts in major assets.

What it doesn't prove: the reserve side. The project's verifier config describes the totals as information "published by CEX, it represents CEX's liability." The reserve figures are checked a different way, against the wallet addresses Binance publishes through the page's "Download All Address" option.

What customers can do: each user can get a Merkle proof for their account and check it against the published root. They can use the verifier code in Binance's repository rather than Binance's own interface. That doesn't prove Binance is solvent, but it confirms the user's balance was counted.

Binance has rebuilt its reserves to 100% across its ten largest assets, but on several of them the buffer is only a few coins. Meanwhile, stolen funds are reaching its deposit addresses through platforms that run on its infrastructure. Tuesday's proof can confirm customer balances. It can't show how Binance handles the stolen money arriving at its own door.

#5488. Torus raised $500 million to manufacture container-sized AI computing units with batteries

Free daily briefing on global business news.

The Series C round, led by Magnetar, will fund production of Foundry units that range from 1 to 20 megawatts in size

Torus raised $500 million in a Series C round to build a product about the size of a shipping container that pairs battery storage with AI computing power, according to Bloomberg. The Salt Lake City-based energy-storage startup said it will use the funding to build its Foundry product.

Magnetar led the round, with participation from ICONIQ, Origin Ventures and Trinity Capital, according to Bloomberg. Hydra Host, a firm focused on AI infrastructure, counts itself as one of Torus’s customers, according to the startup.

Torus founder and CEO Nate Walkingshaw told Bloomberg the containers can be placed on-site at businesses or plants whose local grid has unused electrical headroom. That can head off infrastructure upgrades that would strain customers' utility bills, he said. Walkingshaw said the units are designed for AI inference work, come in sizes from one to 20 megawatts, and can be installed within four months.

"The Foundry product is our version of a distributed data-center approach to move the chips to the power that's already there," he said, according to Bloomberg.

U.S. data-center developers are scrambling to secure sufficient electricity for power-hungry AI workloads, according to Bloomberg. Developers planning huge campuses whose power demand rivals that of an entire city could face closer scrutiny and extended schedules in states such as Texas and Ohio. Democrats who ran on tougher curbs for data centers took the governorships in those states in last week’s midterm elections, Bloomberg said.

Torus has so far sold modular battery systems that let businesses and factories control their energy consumption and cut electricity costs. Walkingshaw said the changing political climate gives an advantage to firms able to deliver computing capacity while keeping power rates flat and avoiding extra neighborhood noise or pollution.

#5487. How to be unemployed: Glenn Kelman on life after Redfin

by Glenn Kelman on Nov 6, 2026 at 12:47 pmNovember 6, 2026 at 12:52 pm

After 20 years at Redfin, and 10 months of unemployment, I’ve co-founded a new company. My business partner and I will announce our plans after we’ve built our product, but in the meantime GeekWire asked me to explain what I learned in the transition between Redfin and this new venture.

Many of us are in transition because society is in transition, with AI hollowing out big companies and making it easier to start new companies.

In the past, my own transitions had been harrowing, because I ran out of money or lost my sense of purpose. Leaving Redfin, I thought “here we go again.” I felt self-conscious being in the grocery store at 11 a.m. on a weekday. I was ashamed when I couldn’t come up with an idea for a company. But I made it to the other side.

To do that, I had to convince myself that I was an intrepid explorer, even if what I was exploring wasn’t Mount Everest, but instead what I could be. I wanted to feel brave about encounters I otherwise would’ve found embarrassing. Over the last year, I met people about becoming a high school teacher, a Whistler bagel shopkeeper, a candidate for the state legislature, the founder of a tree-planting nonprofit, the CEO of a pre-IPO company and a project leader for Sound Transit.

The way to prepare yourself to do one thing for a long time is first to consider everything else.

At the beginning of my exploration, a CEO recruiter told me the startup scene in Seattle was “dead” and that, for all of Seattle’s talent, more companies were forming in New York and even LA. I Googled “high-growth Seattle startups” and the list included one company that went bankrupt in 2023, and Redfin, which was acquired in 2025.

Another friend told me that she was on a Discord channel with a bunch of CTOs who were miserable trying to do “AI transformations” at businesses with legacy codebases. At least for me, the logical response to all this has been to start an AI-native company in Seattle.

“The way to prepare yourself to do one thing for a long time is first to consider everything else.”

It took me months to feel ready to do that. In January, a friend told me I wasn’t allowed to make any big decisions until September. Another said I had to wait until the frenzy of my last job had subsided. “You’ll know it has happened,” he said, “because food will start tasting better” (it never happened).

At a conference, a fashion entrepreneur who’d built and abandoned vast residences in Jackson Hole and Costa Rica, and got divorced twice in the past three years, gave me a bracelet that said “we are enough.”

Since I’d often been thinking I hadn’t done enough in the morning to deserve lunch, it was a relief to feel that I didn’t have to be creative or productive in order to justify my existence. But relieving that pressure also made it easier to be creative and productive.

On a call walking through Volunteer Park, I told a friend that the bracelet reminded me I could be happy and never start a company again. She said, “YOU JUST NEED A CO-FOUNDER.”

She told me to share flawed ideas with people who could make them better. I set up meetings with potential co-founders, and we shared our ideas before they were ready, because our meetings had become deadlines. Then we used AI to turn our ideas into products, so we could see what was good and bad about each idea. Starting a company started to feel like a natural progression, instead of Athena sprouting out of Zeus’s head.

When I confessed to a friend that everything we were working on still seemed so small, she said, “What about breakfast burritos?” She outlined her vision for a shop serving breakfast burritos all day, with a line out the door. Then she started talking about inventing a nursing home “that makes everyone happy.” Rather than running a McKinsey market-sizing analysis, she just thought about what she wanted to exist in the world.

That’s something almost anyone can do. In her living room, I suddenly felt that humanity would always have an instinct — this is a bizarre word, but it’s what popped into my head — to fructify. I remember walking home from her house with my wife and hearing the thick sound of insects humming in the night as proof of life’s rich pageant. This is what I mean by surrounding yourself with good vibes.

The last step in my process maybe should’ve come first, choosing where I wanted to make a difference. I thought about all the companies that I honestly would’ve been proud to start, and they were all in the same industry. I had no experience in that industry, but a friend said I could offset that if I were willing to give it everything I have, which is what I’m now doing. I met amazing, generous investors who gave me a good idea, and a business partner who helped me think it through.

Through all of this, I depended on my wife more than any husband ever should. She works herself to the bone treating people with cancer, but she took my calls in the middle of her workday, when I would talk in detail about what to cook for dinner and then — one more thing! — what’s the meaning of my life?

Once, she was getting into our Chevy Bolt for her morning commute while I was rounding the corner with the dog, and I saw her brighten in the way many people did back when I was Redfin’s CEO.

I found myself full of anticipation. She reached into the car, as if to grab a small gift, and heaved something at me from across the street, saying it “needs reprogramming.” Before I realized it was a garage clicker, I thought she had said I was the one who needed reprogramming. “Maybe that’s true,” I said to myself, trudging past the browned lawn, and the dirty dishes, and into a world of possibilities.

#5486. Jensen Huang's exit has investors asking if Nvidia will keep bankrolling the AI boom

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Nvidia stock was down 14% Thursday as Colette Kress became interim CEO and the board began a search to replace Huang

David Paul Morris / Bloomberg via Getty Images

Nvidia $NVDA named Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress interim CEO on Thursday after founder Jensen Huang resigned, and the board has begun a search for a permanent successor.

Nvidia stock fell as much as 14% in Thursday trading before paring losses and closing down around 4%. The stock is still en route to a sixth consecutive week of losses, the longest run of that kind since 2012, according to CNBC. The company will post its next earnings figures on Tuesday.

Kress will keep her CFO role while she serves as interim CEO. The board is looking at both insiders and outsiders for the permanent job. Kress said in a statement that she plans to expand on the base Huang spent 33 years laying.

Kress joined Nvidia as CFO in 2013, after finance roles at Cisco $CSCO, Microsoft $MSFT and Texas Instruments $TXN, according to CNBC. Kress has held the post for more than double the typical length of service among CFOs at S&P 500 and Fortune 500 companies, according to Bloomberg.

Dan Ives, an analyst at Yorkville Ives & Co., told CNBC before the announcement that Huang "didn't do anything without her." Ives called Kress "a Swiss Army knife for Nvidia."

Boards frequently look to their finance chief to lead temporarily when trouble hits, according to Bloomberg. "In a time of crisis, you want to convey the message of stability and confidence, even though there's tremendous instability right now," said Cathy Logue, a managing director at executive search firm Stanton Chase, according to Bloomberg.

Huang resigned after reports of two extramarital affairs, one of which involved a businesswoman that American spy officials suspect works for China's intelligence services. Huang admitted infidelity in a note to employees on Sunday, and the board opened an independent investigation the same day. He also left the board, effective immediately.

The board named Harvey C. Jones, a former CEO and executive chairman of Synopsys $SNPS, as its first chair. "We expect the company's operations, customer commitments and product roadmap to continue without interruption," Jones said in a statement.

Investors are concerned that Nvidia could scale back its financing of data centers under new leadership, which would slow the AI boom, according to Reuters. In its latest earnings report, Nvidia disclosed $164.5 billion in financial commitments.

Shares of CoreWeave and Naver, both Nvidia customers, fell 6% or more, while shares of Broadcom $AVGO and AMD $AMD rose.

#5484. Is Microsoft 365 down or is it your device? 5 checks to run

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Is Microsoft 365 down, or is the problem on your end? These 5 checks show real-time outage status, from Microsoft's own pages to crowd-sourced trackers

When Outlook refuses to load or a Teams call drops mid-sentence, the useful question is not what broke. It is where it broke. A fault on Microsoft $MSFT's side calls for patience and a reliable source of updates. A fault on your own laptop, network or account calls for action, and waiting will not fix it.

Telling those two situations apart takes more than a glance. Microsoft 365 is not a single product. It bundles separate services, including Outlook, Teams, SharePoint and OneDrive. One service can stumble while the others keep working. A colleague may have no trouble at all while your inbox sits frozen.

That is why the search "is Microsoft 365 down" rarely has a one-line answer. Different sources answer different parts of the question. Microsoft's own channels tell you what the company has confirmed. Crowd-sourced trackers tell you what other users are experiencing, whether or not Microsoft has acknowledged anything yet. Neither replaces the other. The clearest picture comes from reading them together.

This guide walks through five checks in a practical order. It starts with Microsoft's public service status page, which anyone can open without signing in. It then moves to the Service health dashboard in the Microsoft 365 admin center. That is where administrators see incidents and advisories tied to their own organization. From there it covers Microsoft's official status account on X $TWTR, formerly Twitter, as another public channel for incident updates. It also covers independent outage trackers such as Downdetector, which chart spikes in user-submitted problem reports.

The final step turns the question around. If none of those sources shows a Microsoft 365 outage, the cause may sit closer to home. A few quick tests on another device, another network or the browser version of the apps can narrow it down. So can a question to your IT team.

Each source also has limits. A public status page can be less detailed than what an admin sees. A spike in user reports confirms that people are having trouble, not why. Knowing what each source can and cannot tell you turns a stalled workday into a short diagnosis.

Microsoft $MSFT's public status page at status.cloud.microsoft shows whether Microsoft 365 services are running normally or have a reported incident. It is Microsoft's own public view of the suite's health.

The page's older address is status.office.com, which some readers may still have bookmarked.

The page lists services one by one. Outlook, Teams, SharePoint and OneDrive are among them. Each entry shows either a normal status or a reported incident.

That layout lets a reader match the check to the symptom. Someone whose inbox will not load can go straight to the Outlook entry. Someone whose shared files will not open can look at OneDrive or SharePoint. A dropped Teams call points to the Teams entry.

The entries for other services carry less weight. An incident listed for SharePoint does not explain an Outlook inbox that will not load. A normal Teams entry says little about a OneDrive folder that will not sync.

The page needs no account, so it suits anyone, not only IT staff. A remote worker, a small-business owner or a student can check it as easily as an administrator. It can also be checked when a person cannot sign in to Microsoft 365 at all. In that case, the status check does not depend on the very account that is failing.

The result sends the next step in one of two directions. A reported incident on the affected service suggests the fault sits on Microsoft's side. A normal status suggests looking more closely at the device, the network or the account.

The public page also has limits. It gives a general picture of the suite rather than a view of one organization. It is typically less detailed than what administrators see in their own organization's Microsoft 365 admin center. A normal reading here does not rule out a problem confined to a single workplace.

Administrators can check whether a Microsoft $MSFT 365 outage is hitting their own organization by signing in to the Microsoft 365 admin center at admin.microsoft.com. Selecting Health, then Service health, opens a dashboard of active incidents and advisories for that tenant.

The tenant focus is what separates this view from Microsoft's public status page. A problem can affect one organization or one region without appearing on that public page at all.

Service health is where those issues show up. It lists what affects the organization's own tenant, not a general summary for every customer. For an IT team fielding calls about Outlook or Teams, it is the place to confirm whether a reported problem is already known.

Every incident on the dashboard carries an ID, and the letters at the start point to the service involved. An ID beginning with MO relates to the Microsoft 365 suite. One beginning with EX relates to Exchange Online.

The ID gives everyone a shared reference. An admin can quote it to colleagues or a help desk. Every report then points to the same issue rather than a loose description of symptoms.

Each incident also includes status updates posted by Microsoft. Reading them in one place shows how the issue has been described since it first appeared, without piecing the story together from several sites.

Admins do not need to keep the dashboard open to stay informed. Service health supports email notifications for incidents. Admins can set these up to send alerts to an inbox.

Access depends on the account. Only administrators with the right role can open Service health. Regular users who sign in for email, chat or files will not find it in their view.

For those users, the direct route is to contact the organization's IT team or Microsoft 365 administrator. Asking whether an incident appears in Service health, and for its ID, helps show whether the fault sits with Microsoft.

Microsoft $MSFT runs an account on X $TWTR called @MSFT365Status that posts about Microsoft 365 service incidents. It can serve as a quick public signal of trouble when the official status page is slow to update.

X used to be called Twitter. Older help articles and forum threads may still refer to the account as a Twitter feed.

The account belongs to Microsoft. That makes it an official channel, not a fan page or a community-run tracker. A post there reflects an incident that Microsoft itself has acknowledged.

The feed covers the Microsoft 365 service rather than a single app. A post can concern a problem with the whole suite. It can also concern one service, such as Outlook, Teams, SharePoint or OneDrive.

Other Microsoft accounts on X focus on product news. For incident information, @MSFT365Status is the status-focused account.

Type the handle exactly when searching for it. A misspelled search can surface unofficial accounts with similar names. Those accounts have no link to Microsoft. Their outage claims carry no official weight.

Replies under each post come from other X users. They can show that people elsewhere see the same fault. They are not statements from Microsoft. They do not confirm the cause or scope of a problem.

Following the account and turning on post notifications in X brings new updates to a phone or browser. That removes the need to keep refreshing a page during a suspected Microsoft 365 outage.

A post on the account is a public notice, not an organization-specific report. It does not show whether a particular company's tenant is affected. Administrators can check that in the Service health dashboard in the Microsoft 365 admin center.

A single post is short by design and may not spell out every detail of an incident. The public status page at status.cloud.microsoft shows which services are running normally and which have a reported incident. Reading the account alongside those channels gives a fuller picture of a Microsoft 365 outage.

Downdetector and similar sites collect problem reports from users and show a spike when many people report trouble with a service such as Outlook or Teams. A spike signals widespread complaints. It does not prove what caused them.

These trackers run independently of Microsoft $MSFT. Their data comes from the public, not from Microsoft's own systems. A tracker reflects what users say they are experiencing. That can differ from what Microsoft has formally listed as an incident.

Reports are grouped by service. A reader who cannot open Outlook can look at Outlook's page on a tracker. A reader whose Teams calls keep dropping can check Teams instead. Microsoft 365 bundles several services. One of them may show a cluster of reports while another stays quiet.

A spike cannot explain itself. A rise in reports shows that many people are having trouble at the same time. It does not show whether the fault lies with Microsoft, with an internet provider in one area or with something else. A user-submitted report records a symptom, not a diagnosis.

Pairing a tracker with the official status page at status.cloud.microsoft helps separate a Microsoft-side outage from a local fault. Read together, the two sources point in a few distinct directions. A spike on the tracker plus a listed incident on the status page points to a Microsoft-side outage. A spike with no listed incident means many users see trouble, but the cause remains unconfirmed. Checking the official page again later is the next step.

No spike and no listed incident point the other way. If other users are not reporting the same symptom and Microsoft lists nothing, the problem is more likely local. The reader's own device, network or account then becomes the main suspect.

An incident on the status page without a matching spike is also possible. Not every affected user files a report. A quiet tracker does not rule out an official incident. In that case, the official listing is the firmer evidence.

If no Microsoft $MSFT 365 outage is reported, the fault may lie with your own device, network or account. Testing the service on a second network or device, and in a web browser, can narrow down the cause.

Start with the connection. Switch from office Wi-Fi to a phone hotspot, or from a home network to mobile data, and try again. If Outlook or Teams works on the second connection, the first network is the likely source of the trouble. That points to the network rather than to Microsoft.

Next, try a different device. A laptop that cannot load mail while a phone on the same account can points to something specific to that laptop. If every device fails on every network, the problem is more likely tied to the account or to the service itself.

The browser offers a clean comparison. Outlook on the web at outlook.office.com runs without the desktop client. The other Microsoft 365 apps can also be opened in a browser. If mail loads in the browser but not in the installed Outlook app, that points to a client-side fault. The same test applies to Word, Excel or Teams when only the desktop version fails.

Account problems can produce symptoms that look like an outage. Signing out of Microsoft 365 and signing back in is a simple first account check. Confirm that the password is still valid and has not expired or been changed. Check that the account still holds a valid Microsoft 365 license. A lapsed license or an expired password can block access while the service runs normally for everyone else.

People using Microsoft 365 through an employer or school have one more step. The public status page does not show every problem. An issue can affect a single organization or region without appearing there. An administrator can check the Service health dashboard for an incident tied to the organization's own tenant. A quick question to the IT team can confirm a tenant-level incident before anyone spends time on device fixes.
