#5483. JPMorgan and Mastercard back Seattle startup Firmly’s bet on AI shopping agents

by Todd Bishop on Nov 7, 2026 at 10:23 amNovember 9, 2026 at 6:47 am

Firmly, a Seattle-area startup that helps online retailers sell through AI shopping assistants, raised a $15 million Series A round led by Squarepoint Capital, with participation from J.P. Morgan Payments, Mastercard, Samsung Next and others.

The company, founded in 2019, connects retailers’ existing online stores to AI assistants, marketplaces and other shopping channels, so people can buy products inside those third-party apps and services without going to retailers’ websites. Retailers keep their own payment providers and customer relationships.

“Every new AI assistant, marketplace or shopping platform is another place to sell. But connecting to each one can take serious engineering, because catalogs, inventory, payments, and checkout all have to work together,” wrote Kumar Senthil, Firmly’s co-founder and CEO, in a blog post announcing the round.

Mastercard is a commercial partner as well as an investor. Firmly handles the merchant side of Mastercard Agent Connect, a service launched in September to link merchants, AI agents and payment providers through a single integration.

Senthil told Axios Pro that Mastercard is recruiting merchants for the service, giving Firmly a route to new customers.

Firmly charges merchants $2,000 to $15,000 a month, depending on the total value of merchandise they sell, Senthil told Axios. He said connecting a merchant took four to six weeks in 2024 and now takes a day or less, including testing.

The company lists Best Buy, Furniture.com and Backcountry among its retail customers. RetailMeNot and an AI shopping app called Wizard also use its technology.

The funding comes as AI shopping agents move into the mainstream. Meta’s Muse assistant can browse retail sites and buy items with a user’s approval. Amazon has blocked Muse from its site and is suing Perplexity over a shopping agent in the startup’s Comet browser.

Firmly takes a different approach from those agents. Instead of having software click through a retailer’s web pages, it connects directly to the retailer’s systems with its permission.

The company this week also launched Ask Agent, an AI shopping assistant for retailers’ own websites. Shoppers describe what they want, get product recommendations and can check out without leaving the chat.

Other investors in the round include Alumni Ventures, ARK Invest, Benhamou Global Ventures, Granada Funds, Hike Ventures, The Mercantile Companies and Versus Ventures.

The round brings Firmly’s total funding to about $20 million. The company had raised $5.2 million when it partnered with Perplexity in March 2025 on shopping features inside the AI search app.

Senthil spent eight years at Microsoft and later led e-commerce products at Samsung. He co-founded Firmly with Damien Balsan, a co-founder of LoopPay, the mobile payments startup acquired by Samsung, and Murali Krishnamurthy, Firmly’s CTO and a former chief technical architect for Samsung’s U.S. and global e-commerce business. Firmly is based in Issaquah, Wash., and its engineering leaders work in Seattle. The company also has engineering teams in Sao Paulo, Brazil, and Chennai, India.

#5482. Microsoft 365 outage credits: 7 things businesses should know about SLA claims

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Microsoft 365 outage service credits exist, but businesses buying through a Cloud Solution Provider claim them via that provider, for the affected service only, prorated by outage length

A Microsoft $MSFT 365 outage can earn a business a service credit. Microsoft's partner guidance describes that remedy as a credit and does not call it a cash refund. The way to claim it depends on who sold the subscription.

For companies that buy through Microsoft's Cloud Solution Provider program, known as CSP, the process is set out in Microsoft Learn documentation for Partner Center. The page is titled "How and when to request a credit from Microsoft" and was last updated on June 16, 2026. It is written for partners, not end customers. That means the business that lost access to a service does not file the claim itself. Its provider does.

The guidance covers products bought in the legacy commerce experience as well as the new commerce experience, which Microsoft abbreviates as NCE. It applies the service level agreement policy to services sold through CSP. The scenarios that qualify for a credit are listed in a separate document, the Online Services Consolidated SLA. The Partner Center page points to that document rather than restating its terms.

Credits are also limited in scope. A credit attaches to the service that went down, not to every app in a bundled plan. Its size is prorated according to which service was affected and how long the disruption lasted. Requests for Azure credits follow a different filing deadline from requests for all other services.

Microsoft's Partner Center page also handles credits that have nothing to do with downtime, such as credits for accidental purchases and duplicate orders on legacy products. Those follow their own rules and are not remedies for an outage.

The direct-purchase path is a separate question. The Partner Center guidance does not describe how organizations that buy straight from Microsoft claim SLA credits. The steps below should not be read as covering them.

The seven slides below are a selection of points about Microsoft 365 outage service credits for CSP-sold services, not a full rulebook. They cover who can file, how credits are scoped and prorated, and the deadline split. They also cover the evidence a request needs, where to find an incident ID and how advisory incidents differ from outages.

Only Cloud Solution Provider direct providers and indirect providers can submit a service level agreement credit request for a Microsoft $MSFT 365 outage on services sold through CSP. Indirect resellers are not permitted to file these requests.

That rule comes from Microsoft's Partner Center guidance on Microsoft Learn, which sets out how partners request credits from Microsoft. The page is written for partners in the CSP program, not for end customers. Its outage rules apply to services sold through that channel.

The CSP program has two partner tiers that matter here. A direct provider buys Microsoft cloud services from Microsoft and sells them straight to customers. An indirect provider supplies those services to indirect resellers, who then sell them to business customers. Under the credit rules, the right to ask Microsoft for an outage credit sits with the provider in both models. An indirect reseller cannot file one on a customer's behalf.

For a business customer, the practical effect is that an outage claim starts with whichever company sits on the provider tier of the relationship. A customer that buys from an indirect reseller depends on the indirect provider behind that reseller to file the request.

Inside the provider, the task falls to a specific role. Partner Center is the portal Microsoft partners use to manage customers, orders, billing and support requests. The Admin agent role gives partner staff administrative access to the customer tenants that partner manages. A person in the Admin agent role handles credit requests. The request goes to Microsoft as a support ticket filed in Partner Center.

The rules are not limited to newer subscriptions. Microsoft's guidance applies the SLA outage policy to products bought under the legacy commerce experience. It applies equally to products bought under the new commerce experience, known as NCE. A customer with a mix of older and newer CSP subscriptions follows the same provider-led route for both.

A Microsoft $MSFT outage credit covers only the service that went down, not the full subscription. Microsoft's Partner Center guidance gives an example: an Office 365 suite customer whose only outage was in SharePoint can receive service level agreement (SLA) credit for SharePoint alone.

The credit does not reach the rest of that customer's plan. Microsoft decides credits according to which services an outage affected.

An Office 365 suite bundles several online services under one subscription, and SharePoint is one of them. In the SharePoint example, the services that kept running stay outside the claim. Only the service that failed is part of it.

The guidance refers to affected services in the plural. That wording ties a credit to each service an incident touched, not to the subscription as a whole. A disruption confined to SharePoint produces a claim for SharePoint and nothing else in the bundle.

The way a business pays and the way a claim is assessed do not line up. The suite arrives as one subscription on one bill. An outage claim is still weighed service by service, and the bill does not set its boundaries.

The example comes from Microsoft's page on how and when to request a credit. That page is written for partners in the Cloud Solution Provider (CSP) program, and it applies its SLA policy to services sold through CSP. It does not describe how customers who buy directly from Microsoft claim credits. The SharePoint example belongs to that CSP context.

For a business reviewing an outage, the starting point for any claim is the specific service that failed. The plan the business holds does not set the scope of the credit.

Microsoft $MSFT prorates SLA credits for services sold through its Cloud Solution Provider (CSP) program. The size of a credit depends on two things: which service went down and how long the outage lasted.

Proration means the credit is a proportional amount rather than a flat payment. A qualifying outage does not produce a fixed sum that is the same for every customer and every incident. The amount moves with the details of the disruption.

The first factor is the affected service. Microsoft's Partner Center guidance on credits ties the calculation to the product that suffered downtime. It looks at the service that failed, not at the full subscription that service belongs to.

The second factor is duration. Under the same guidance, the length of the outage feeds into the size of the credit. A short interruption and a long one on the same service are not treated as the same event.

The two factors apply together. Two outages of equal length on different services need not produce matching credits. Two outages on the same service need not match either if one ran longer than the other. Neither factor alone settles the amount.

Whether an outage qualifies at all is a separate test. Microsoft lists the qualifying scenarios in the Online Services Consolidated SLA, its service level agreement for online services. The Partner Center guidance states that this document also applies to services sold through CSP.

The Online Services Consolidated SLA is also where the detailed terms sit, including credit percentages, downtime thresholds and uptime commitments. A business weighing a claim can read the section of that document covering the service that went down. That check shows whether the disruption meets a qualifying scenario before a request is filed.

Microsoft $MSFT applies one deadline to outage credit requests for Azure and a different deadline to requests for all other services sold through its Cloud Solution Provider (CSP) program. Microsoft's Partner Center guidance on requesting credits places Azure in its own category for timing.

A business that buys both Azure and Microsoft 365 through a provider therefore works with two request deadlines, not one. An Azure outage is claimed under the Azure deadline. A Microsoft 365 outage falls under the deadline that covers every other service.

The split also applies when one disruption affects both Azure and a Microsoft 365 service. Each affected service is claimed under its own category's timing. An organization that runs workloads on Azure alongside Microsoft 365 apps cannot treat one request window as covering both.

The business does not submit the request itself. A CSP direct provider or an indirect provider files it as a support ticket in Partner Center. Indirect resellers are not permitted to file. A customer that wants a credit for downtime has to bring the outage to its provider. The provider's filing then has to land within the deadline for the affected service.

That handoff adds a step between the outage and the claim. A customer that reports an incident late leaves its provider less time to prepare and submit the ticket. Raising the outage with the provider soon after it happens helps keep the request inside the window.

Meeting a deadline does not by itself make an outage eligible. Whether a period of downtime qualifies for a credit is set out in Microsoft's Online Services Consolidated SLA, not in the deadline rules.

A Microsoft $MSFT 365 SLA credit request must include identifying details. Among them are the customer's tenant GUID, the outage ID and the customer's email address.

Microsoft's Partner Center guidance lists these as items a Cloud Solution Provider partner supplies with an outage claim. They connect the request to one customer and one recorded incident.

The tenant GUID is the globally unique identifier assigned to a customer's Microsoft 365 tenant. It points the claim at a single organization's environment.

The outage ID identifies the service incident behind the claim. It links the request to a specific event Microsoft recorded, not to a general report of downtime.

The customer email gives a contact address tied to the affected business.

These details go into the credit request, which a CSP direct provider or indirect provider submits as a Partner Center support ticket. The end customer does not file it.

The guidance asks for further items beyond these three. A business that buys Microsoft 365 through a provider can keep its tenant GUID and the relevant outage ID on hand. The provider then has them ready when it opens the ticket.

The outage ID that a Microsoft $MSFT 365 SLA credit request needs is listed in the Microsoft 365 admin center. Each incident ID shown there includes an abbreviation for the affected service.

Microsoft's Partner Center guidance names the outage ID as a required part of a credit request. The ID ties a claim to one specific recorded incident rather than to a general report of downtime.

The abbreviation inside the ID shows which service the incident involved. That label connects the incident to the specific product a credit would cover.

For services sold through the Cloud Solution Provider program, the provider that files the claim puts the outage ID in its Partner Center support ticket. A business that buys Microsoft 365 through a provider can find the incident in the admin center and pass its ID along to that provider.

Microsoft $MSFT's Partner Center credit guidance treats an advisory incident as a separate category from an outage. It also sets out what follows once a credit request is approved.

Both points apply to Microsoft 365 services sold through the Cloud Solution Provider program, known as CSP. The guidance applies its service level agreement policy to those services.

The credit process in the guidance is built around outages. Advisory incidents sit outside that outage category. Anyone preparing a claim should therefore confirm which type of incident they are dealing with before they file.

An approved request produces an SLA credit for the affected service. Microsoft's guidance presents that outcome as a credit.

#5480. Why Microsoft keeps going down: 7 common causes of cloud outages, explained

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Common causes of cloud outages, from bad configuration changes to DNS and sign-in failures, explain why Microsoft services like Azure and Microsoft 365 sometimes go down

When Outlook stops loading or Teams calls drop for many users at once, the cause is rarely a server room going dark. Many large cloud failures start smaller than that. One setting, one piece of code or one shared component breaks. Then the cloud's own automation can copy the problem across a global system faster than any person can step in.

That speed is the trade-off at the heart of modern cloud computing. Microsoft $MSFT runs Azure, its cloud platform, alongside Microsoft 365 and Teams, the online services that handle email, documents and meetings for many organizations. These products are separate brands, but they sit on shared infrastructure. They share data centers, networks, deployment systems and a common sign-in service. A fault in one of those layers can surface in many products at the same moment. To a user, it looks as if all of Microsoft has gone down.

The same design that makes the cloud efficient also makes its failures visible. A company that once ran its own email server might have suffered an outage that only its staff noticed. When that company moves to a large cloud provider, it shares the provider's strengths and its weak points with many other customers on the same platform. A single problem can reach businesses, schools, hospitals and government agencies across several continents at once.

The causes of cloud outages tend to fall into a handful of recurring categories. Some are human, such as a mistyped configuration value or a software update with a hidden bug. Others involve technical plumbing, such as the Domain Name System that directs traffic or the identity service that checks who is allowed in. Some are physical, such as power, cooling and network hardware. A few come from outside, including floods of hostile traffic designed to knock services offline.

The seven slides that follow walk through a selection of these common failure types. They are not a ranking, and they do not explain any specific incident. Each one describes how a particular kind of failure works, why it can spread and what cloud providers do to contain it.

For businesses that depend on Microsoft's cloud, these patterns matter in practical terms. Knowing where failures start helps IT teams read status updates, plan backup options and ask sharper questions about resilience before the next disruption arrives.

A single incorrect setting, pushed automatically to thousands of servers, can break a cloud service before engineers notice anything is wrong. Faulty configuration changes are among the most commonly cited causes of large cloud outages. They can happen without anyone writing a line of new code.

Configuration is the set of instructions that tells software how to behave. It covers details such as which servers accept traffic, how much capacity a service may use, which network paths data should follow and which security rules apply. Changing a configuration value does not alter the program itself. It alters the conditions the program runs under.

At the scale of Azure or Microsoft $MSFT 365, nobody edits those settings by hand on each machine. Providers use automated configuration management systems that write a change once and distribute it across fleets of servers in many regions. That automation keeps settings consistent from one machine to the next. It also means a mistake travels as fast as a correct update.

The errors themselves are often small. A single wrong number can be enough. So can a missing entry in a list of allowed addresses, a limit set too low or a rule applied to the wrong group of machines. A setting that looks harmless on its own can also conflict with another setting elsewhere in the system.

Providers try to catch these problems before they spread. Common safeguards include automated validation that checks a change against expected formats and rules. Peer review by a second engineer adds another check. Many systems also keep a record of the last known good configuration.

Rollback is the standard recovery tool. If a change causes failures, engineers revert to the previous settings and push that version out instead. In principle, reverting a setting is quicker than writing and shipping a code fix.

Rollback has limits, though. A bad change can disrupt the management tools, network access or permissions that engineers need to undo it. Servers that crashed may have to restart and reload before service returns. As a result, a configuration error that takes seconds to deploy can take much longer to reverse.

New code can break a cloud service when it carries a defect that testing did not catch. Cloud providers ship software updates constantly. A single flawed release can slow down or take offline the email, meeting and file storage tools that businesses depend on every day.

Software in a large cloud platform is never finished. Engineers release fixes, security patches and new features on a rolling basis, often across many parts of the system in the same week. Each release carries risk. Code that passed every check in a test environment can still behave differently once it meets real customers.

The gap between testing and reality is the core problem. Test environments are smaller and quieter than production. They rarely reproduce the full volume of traffic or the variety of customer setups in a global service. They also miss many of the odd combinations of old and new software that build up over time. A memory leak that takes days to grow can slip through. So can a race condition that appears only when thousands of requests arrive at once.

Providers limit the damage with staged rollouts. A change goes first to a small share of customers or servers. Engineers watch error rates, response times and crash reports before sending it further. If something looks wrong, the release stops before it reaches everyone.

A canary release is one version of this approach. The name comes from the caged canaries that miners once carried to detect dangerous gas. The first small group of servers plays the same role and signals trouble early. Feature flags add another safeguard. They let engineers ship code with a new function switched off. The function can then be turned on gradually, or shut off again without a fresh deployment.

These methods reduce risk, but they do not remove it. Some defects stay hidden until a release reaches full scale. Others are triggered by a rare event, such as a date change or an unusual request, long after the rollout looks complete. Monitoring can also miss a problem when the early symptoms are subtle.

A bad release that gets through is usually undone by redeploying the last version that worked. Finding the culprit comes first. A large platform may have several releases moving through it at once. Each one is a suspect until engineers rule it out. Code that changes how stored data is structured adds another obstacle. The older version may not be able to read data the new one has already rewritten. In that case, shipping a corrected update can be faster than going back.

A Domain Name System failure can make a Microsoft $MSFT service vanish for users even when every server behind it is running normally. The servers have not crashed. The system that tells computers where to find those servers has stopped giving answers.

DNS works like a phone book for the internet. People type names such as outlook.com, but computers connect using numeric IP addresses. Before a laptop or phone can open a mailbox, it has to ask DNS which address belongs to that name. The connection can begin only after a reply comes back.

That lookup passes through several layers. A device usually sends its question to a recursive resolver. An internet provider, an employer or a public DNS service typically runs that resolver. The resolver then works through the DNS hierarchy until it reaches the authoritative name servers for the domain. Those authoritative servers hold the official records for the name.

Problems can start at any point in that chain. Authoritative servers can become overloaded or unreachable. A record can be edited incorrectly, pointing a name at the wrong address or removing it altogether. A resolver can fail and leave everyone who relies on it unable to look anything up.

From the user's side, the result looks like a complete outage. A browser reports that the site cannot be found. Desktop apps such as Outlook or Teams retry and eventually show a connection error. Nothing in the message tells the user that the mail and chat servers are still working.

Caching makes DNS failures uneven and slow to clear. Resolvers store answers for a set period called the time to live, or TTL. The domain owner chooses that period. A user whose resolver still holds a valid cached answer may keep working while someone relying on a different resolver is cut off.

The same mechanism works against recovery. If a bad record has been cached, the corrected version reaches users only as the old entries expire. Engineers may restore the right records quickly, yet the service comes back in waves rather than all at once. That lag explains why complaints can continue after a fix is in place.

DNS also matters to Microsoft's business customers directly. Microsoft offers Azure DNS, a service that hosts DNS records for customers' own domains. Businesses that use it rely on that service to point visitors to their websites and apps. Short TTL values let an organization redirect traffic faster during trouble. The tradeoff is a higher volume of lookups, which adds load on the name servers answering them.

When Microsoft $MSFT Entra ID cannot confirm who a user is, Outlook, Teams, SharePoint and the Azure portal can all look broken at the same moment. The apps themselves may be running normally. People cannot get past the sign-in step to reach them.

Entra ID is Microsoft's cloud identity service. It was previously called Azure Active Directory, and many IT administrators still use the older name or its abbreviation, Azure AD. The service checks credentials, applies security rules and decides which accounts can open which resources across Microsoft 365 and Azure.

The system works by issuing tokens. After a user signs in, Entra ID gives the app a digitally signed token that vouches for the person's identity and permissions. The app accepts that token instead of asking for a password again. The exchange follows industry standards, including OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect.

Single sign-on extends the same arrangement across products. One successful login can unlock email, chat, file storage and the third-party business apps a company has connected to Entra ID.

That convenience creates a single front door. If the identity service slows down or rejects valid requests, every product behind it inherits the problem. For a person at a desk, mail, chat and files all seem to fail together.

Security checks add more steps that can fail. Multifactor authentication may ask for a code or an approval in the Microsoft Authenticator app. Conditional Access policies can weigh a device's compliance status, location or sign-in risk before granting entry. Each check depends on another system answering on time.

Timing shapes how an identity problem appears. Tokens expire after a set period and must be renewed. Someone already signed in may keep working for a while. A colleague opening a laptop fresh may be turned away. That uneven pattern can make an identity fault hard to diagnose at first.

Mistakes inside a customer's own tenant can produce a similar lockout. A badly scoped Conditional Access rule can block an organization's whole workforce, including the administrators who need to fix it. Microsoft recommends that organizations keep emergency access accounts for this situation. These are often called break-glass accounts, and they sit outside normal sign-in policies.

Physical faults inside a data center can take servers offline even when every line of software works. A power interruption, a cooling breakdown or a failed piece of network equipment can each cause it. Cloud providers build layers of backup to absorb these faults, but each layer has limits.

Power is the first point of exposure. A large data center draws electricity from the utility grid. A sudden drop or surge on that feed can cut power to whole rows of server racks.

Facilities bridge that gap with uninterruptible power supplies. These run on batteries for the short window it takes backup generators to start. The generators usually run on diesel and can carry the site until grid power returns.

The handoff between those systems is a weak spot. A transfer switch can fail. A generator can fail to start, or batteries can run down before backup power takes over. In each case, servers lose power abruptly. Machines that shut down without warning can take time to restart. Some come back with failed components or data that needs checking.

Cooling is a second vulnerability. Servers produce heat constantly. Data centers remove it with chillers, air handlers and, in some facilities, liquid cooling. When cooling capacity drops, temperatures in the server halls climb quickly.

Server hardware is designed to slow itself down or switch off before heat damages it. That protects the equipment. It also removes computing capacity from the service running on it. Hot weather adds strain. Cooling systems must work harder when the outside air is warmer.

Ordinary hardware also wears out. Hard drives, memory modules, power supplies and network switches fail routinely across any large fleet of machines. Most of these failures stay invisible to users. Software moves the work to healthy machines.

A failed core network switch or storage cluster is a different matter. It can cut off many servers at once.

Microsoft $MSFT limits the reach of these problems through geography. Azure divides its infrastructure into regions, and many regions contain availability zones. Each zone is a physically separate location with its own power, cooling and networking. A service spread across several zones can keep running if one zone goes dark.

That protection depends on how a workload is set up. Applications deployed in a single zone or a single region have no fallback when that location fails. Failing over to another region also takes time. Data written moments before a fault may not have copied across yet.

Network problems can cut users off from Microsoft $MSFT services that are still working normally. A faulty routing change, an overloaded link or a distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attack can each stop traffic from reaching its destination. The application stays healthy in its data center, while customers see timeouts and error pages.

The internet is a patchwork of separate networks, each run by a different company or institution. They share directions using the Border Gateway Protocol, or BGP. Through BGP, each network announces which blocks of IP addresses it can deliver traffic to. Its neighbors then pass that information along to their own neighbors.

That arrangement depends on trust. A network might announce routes it should not, or withdraw routes it still needs. Traffic can then be sent down the wrong path or dropped entirely. A large provider's address ranges can effectively disappear from parts of the internet when this happens. The servers behind those addresses keep running, but packets no longer find a way to them.

Large cloud providers also run their own private wide area networks, which link data centers across countries and continents. Routing inside that backbone follows the same logic. A mistake in how traffic is steered between regions can cut off services in one location from the users and systems that depend on them.

Congestion is a quieter version of the same problem. Every network link has a fixed capacity. When demand exceeds it, routers start dropping packets and response times climb. A fiber cut or a sudden shift of traffic onto fewer paths can push the remaining links past their limits. Users then see slow page loads, choppy Teams calls and failed file uploads rather than a clean shutdown.

DDoS attacks create congestion on purpose. An attacker directs traffic from many machines at once — often a botnet of compromised computers, home routers and internet-connected cameras — at a single target. Some attacks try to fill network pipes with raw volume. Others exhaust server resources with a flood of connection requests or with requests for pages that are costly to generate. The goal in each case is to leave no capacity for legitimate users.

Cloud providers defend against these floods by spreading and filtering traffic. Anycast routing lets the same address be announced from many locations. An attack's load is then split across sites instead of landing in one place. Filtering systems inspect incoming traffic and discard requests that match attack patterns before they reach the application. Microsoft offers this kind of protection to Azure customers through a service called Azure DDoS Protection.

Those defenses can still be strained. A very large or unfamiliar attack may take time to recognize and filter. Mitigation systems can also misfire and block real users along with attack traffic. Telling a hostile flood apart from an ordinary surge in demand, such as a spike after a major product launch, is not always straightforward.

A single failed component can look like Microsoft $MSFT going down everywhere because cloud services are built on top of one another. When many businesses run on the same small group of providers, one fault inside a shared layer reaches far beyond the product where it started.

Modern cloud platforms are assembled from internal building blocks. A storage service, a messaging queue, a monitoring system and a database may each support many customer-facing products. Engineers call these links dependencies. A product that looks independent on the surface often relies on several of them underneath.

Shared building blocks let a provider build a capability once and reuse it across email, collaboration tools and developer platforms. They also create a dependency chain. If a component near the bottom of the chain slows down or fails, every service stacked above it can stall in turn.

This pattern is known as a cascading failure. It rarely shows itself at the source. Users see Teams messages that will not send or an Azure dashboard that will not load. The actual fault may sit several layers deeper, in a system those users never touch directly.

Recovery can make things worse before it makes them better. Software is usually written to retry a request that fails. When thousands of clients retry at once, the combined traffic can overwhelm a service that is trying to come back online. Engineers call this a retry storm, or a thundering herd. Providers counter it with exponential backoff, which spaces out each retry over longer intervals. They also use circuit breakers, which stop calls to a failing component for a set period.

Customer concentration widens the impact. Much of the world's corporate computing runs on a few hyperscale providers, including Microsoft Azure, Amazon $AMZN Web Services and Google $GOOGL Cloud. When one of them has a problem, unrelated companies in different industries can lose the same tools at the same time. The disruption becomes a public event rather than a problem inside one company.

Concentration also reaches businesses that never signed a contract with the affected provider. A company may host its own website elsewhere but depend on a payment processor, a customer-support tool or a software vendor that runs on Azure. Those indirect links often stay invisible until something breaks.

Organizations plan around this risk in several ways. Some run critical workloads in more than one cloud region, so a fault in one geography does not take everything offline. Others adopt a multicloud strategy, spreading systems across two or more providers. That approach adds cost and engineering complexity. It also does not remove the shared dependencies inside each individual platform. A third approach is mapping which vendors a business relies on and writing down how it will operate if a key service goes dark for several hours.

#5479. Trevor Noah on AI

by Oren Etzioni on Nov 8, 2026 at 9:52 amNovember 8, 2026 at 9:52 am

On Oct. 19, Trevor Noah launched Luminaries, a science conversation series at Boston’s Museum of Science. I joined him onstage, and Rana el Kaliouby moderated. Rana is a pioneer of emotion AI, software that reads human emotion, and the host of the Pioneers of AI podcast. She wrote afterward that she expected Trevor to be witty and funny, but “didn’t expect to be so blown away by his humanity and depth of ideas.”

Here are a few of his insights with his own words highlighted.

When an AI matchmaker Rana built in ChatGPT picked Trevor as her match, he pointed out that it knew very little about either of them. It assembled a plausible answer from what’s on the internet.

Trevor added that when you tell AI it made a mistake, it thanks you but often fails to correct the error: “It’s like a friend who’s been to a lot of therapy but doesn’t actually change.”

When asked how we protect ourselves from AI’s downsides, Trevor said the answer “goes back to something that is very un-technological and very un-AI.” He cited Robert Putnam’s book Bowling Alone, noting that places where communities form accrue many surprising benefits including more accountable governments.

I pushed back that communitarianism, the 1990s movement my father helped found to foster communities, had failed. Trevor responded that we hand too many ideas to intellectuals, who then “apply too much academia” to them. Communitarianism failed, he deadpanned, “because it’s called communitarianism.” An overly academic name.

He noted that nobody calls a phone a failure when the first version doesn’t sell; companies keep re-releasing it. He vowed never to stop investing in community.

Despite his concerns, Trevor has “yet to see a technology that blew up and then left everyone behind.” Cars, computers and the internet all spread to ordinary people.

AI has reached what he calls “work intelligence”: it can do the jobs we invented, but we keep inventing new ones. Salt and ice used to be precious. Now restaurants hand them out for free. What we value changes, and in Trevor’s view, we’re expendable only if we define being human by the tasks we value today.

Our conversation turned to AI’s impact on jobs.

Touring as a comic, Trevor saw towns hollowed out after Kodak and the automaker Studebaker left. Factory workers were told automation was progress. “White-collar workers are now experiencing what many blue-collar workers experienced for decades,” he said. The difference, he argued, is that white-collar workers are closer to power, so newspapers are covering it.

Trevor is confident new jobs will come, as they did after telephone exchange operators disappeared. What worries him is the gap. His analogy is the highway, where the following distance is the space that lets you stop before you hit the car ahead:

Trevor tells tech leaders that “it’s easier to be patient when you are in a position of privilege,” and added, “But ironically, they don’t have patience when it comes to quarterly earnings.”

After ChatGPT took off, show hosts kept telling him weak jokes that ChatGPT had written in a pale imitation of Trevor’s style. He rattled off four reasons AI struggles with humor: there isn’t enough comedy data, the model is a frozen snapshot while what society finds acceptable keeps shifting, comedy depends on knowing your audience (there are jokes you know are funny but you wouldn’t tell your mom), and companies have made models risk averse.

In addition to being the former host of The Daily Show, an award-winning author and a sought-after comedian, Trevor Noah is Microsoft’s Chief Questions Officer.

I reminded him of Picasso’s famous verdict on computers, “They are useless. They can only give you answers,” and joked that as Chief Questions Officer he has something rare these days: job security. He chuckled. Of course, his real job security comes from his depth and humanity, which feed his exceptional humor and wit.

Rana noted that everybody’s getting replaced by AI, but Trevor had played an AI, voicing Griot in Black Panther: Wakanda Forever.

He quipped: “Yeah, I’m coming for AI’s job.”

In just a few weeks, AWS re:Invent brings advanced and expert-level sessions on the services you build on every day, from serverless and containers to databases and developer tools. Go hands-on with new launches the same week they’re announced, and hear directly from the engineers who built them. Experience the depth you won’t find anywhere else.

#5478. What is Exchange Online? The Microsoft service behind Outlook outages

Free daily briefing on global business news.

What is Exchange Online? A guide to the Microsoft 365 email service behind Outlook, from mail flow and security to why its outages reach so many users

When Outlook stops sending mail, the program on the screen is often not the part that failed. The problem can sit one layer down, in a service most people never open or log into directly. That service is Exchange Online, and it holds the mailboxes Outlook displays.

What is Exchange Online? It is Microsoft $MSFT's cloud-hosted messaging platform, part of the Microsoft 365 suite. It stores and delivers email, and it also keeps calendars, contacts and tasks. Microsoft hosts and operates it. It is the hosted counterpart of Exchange Server, the product organizations run on their own servers.

That split between app and service explains why a single fault can look so widespread. Outlook for Windows, Outlook for Mac, Outlook on the web and the Outlook mobile apps can all connect to the same back end. When that back end has a fault, every one of those clients can misbehave at the same moment. A user may restart a laptop, reinstall an app or switch phones and find the same problem waiting.

The reach goes beyond the inbox. Companies, schools and public bodies of every size keep their mailboxes in this one service. Other Microsoft 365 tools draw on it as well. Teams, for example, pulls its calendar data from the user's Exchange mailbox. A problem in Exchange Online can therefore surface in places that do not look like email at all.

Knowing how the service works helps people read symptoms more accurately. Someone who can still read old messages but cannot send new ones may be looking at a local copy of the mailbox. That copy is not a live connection. An administrator who knows where Microsoft posts incidents can confirm a wider issue before spending hours on a single machine.

The 10 slides that follow cover the service piece by piece. They explain what the service is and how it differs from Outlook. They show why its outages spread and how to check Microsoft 365 service health. They also cover how mail reaches the service, how it filters spam and malware and which mailbox types it supports. The final slides look at compliance tools, hybrid setups with Exchange Server and the protocols and programming interfaces clients use to connect.

The service handles four kinds of data. Email is the most visible, but the same mailbox also holds a person's calendar appointments and meeting invitations. It keeps personal contacts, along with the tasks and to-do items a user creates. All four live in one mailbox, so they follow the user to any device that signs in.

Exchange Online is the hosted counterpart of Exchange Server. Exchange Server is software that organizations install and run on their own hardware. With the online version, Microsoft runs the servers in its own data centers instead. The customer manages users and settings, while Microsoft handles the hardware, the operating systems and the software updates underneath.

Each subscribing organization gets its own tenant. A tenant is the customer's private space inside Microsoft's cloud, holding its users, mailboxes, domains and policies. Exchange Online shares that tenant with other Microsoft 365 services, including Teams, SharePoint Online and OneDrive. Those services draw on the same user accounts. That shared foundation makes Exchange Online more than a stand-alone mail server.

Microsoft sells access per user through subscriptions. Many Microsoft 365 business and enterprise plans include Exchange Online as part of a wider bundle. Organizations that only need hosted mail can also license it on its own through Exchange Online Plan 1 or Plan 2.

Everyday users reach Exchange Online through an email app, most often a version of Outlook. That app reads and writes the data held in the mailbox. Administrators see more of the service. They manage mailboxes and settings through the browser-based Exchange admin center and the Microsoft 365 admin center.

Customers do not patch or upgrade Exchange Online themselves. New features and fixes reach each tenant as Microsoft deploys them across its service.

Outlook is the email program people open on their screens. Exchange Online is the Microsoft $MSFT 365 service that stores their mailboxes and delivers their messages. One is the client, and the other is the server it talks to.

The split is easy to miss because the two are sold and used together. A worker at a company on Microsoft 365 rarely sees the name Exchange Online anywhere. They see an Outlook icon, an inbox and a calendar. The stored mail, the folders, the meeting invitations and the contact list all sit on Microsoft's servers, not inside the app.

Outlook comes in several forms that can connect to Exchange Online. There are desktop apps for Windows and Mac, a browser version and mobile apps for iOS and Android. Each is a separate piece of software with its own interface and its own update schedule. All of them draw on the same mailbox.

That shared mailbox is why a message read on a phone shows as read on a laptop. A meeting accepted in the browser appears on the desktop calendar too. A folder created in one app shows up in the others. The apps do not keep a master copy of their own. They display what the server holds.

Neither side is tied exclusively to the other. Outlook can add accounts from other providers, including Gmail and other IMAP services. Exchange Online, in turn, accepts connections from mail apps that are not Outlook.

Outlook.com adds another source of confusion. It is Microsoft's free consumer email service. A business mailbox in Exchange Online is a separate, paid offering. Organizations buy it through Microsoft 365 plans or as a standalone Exchange Online subscription.

The server side is where a fault can reach every device together. Each Outlook app depends on the same mailbox, so trouble there shows up in all of them. A user who switches from a laptop to a phone meets the same error. To that user, it looks like Outlook has broken.

The reverse case looks different. A problem confined to one copy of Outlook, such as a damaged desktop profile or an outdated mobile app, usually affects only that device. If Outlook on the web still works while the desktop app does not, the mailbox itself is likely reachable.

An Exchange Online outage spreads widely because one shared service holds mailboxes for a large number of organizations. Several other Microsoft $MSFT 365 tools also draw on those mailboxes. A single back-end fault can stall email, calendars and scheduling for many workplaces at the same moment.

Each of those organizations keeps its mail in Microsoft's hosted platform rather than on servers of its own. That concentration is the first reason a problem travels so far.

When a shared piece of the service misbehaves, the effect is not confined to one employer's server room. It can reach customers in many sectors at once. An office worker, a teacher and a council employee may all find their inboxes unreachable together.

The second reason is that Exchange Online sits underneath more than email. The mailbox is also where a user's calendar, contacts and tasks live.

Microsoft Teams reads calendar data from that same mailbox. The meetings list inside Teams depends on the back end that serves Outlook. A person who switches from Outlook to Teams to check an afternoon meeting can run into the same gap in both apps.

The service is built to survive the loss of individual machines. Exchange mailbox databases are copied across several servers using database availability groups. Exchange Online inherits that design from Exchange Server.

If one server fails, another copy of the database can take over. That replication reduces the chance that a single broken server takes mailboxes offline.

Replication has limits. It guards against the failure of a single server, not against faults in the shared systems that every mailbox server depends on.

Authentication is one of those shared systems. Users sign in to Microsoft 365 through Microsoft Entra ID, Microsoft's identity service. Outlook cannot open a mailbox until that sign-in succeeds, no matter how many healthy database copies exist.

Networking is another shared layer. It sits between the user and every copy of the database. Extra replicas behind it do not help if the path to them is broken.

A bad configuration change is a third category. A setting pushed across shared infrastructure reaches every server it touches, including the ones holding duplicate copies. Redundant databases offer no protection against a mistake applied to all of them.

That is why the breadth of an incident says more about which layer failed than about any one machine. A problem limited to one mailbox usually stays local. A problem that hits mail, calendars and sign-in across many organizations at once traces back to a component they all share.

The most direct way to confirm an Exchange Online problem is the service health dashboard in the Microsoft $MSFT 365 admin center. Microsoft posts incidents there. That helps show whether a fault sits in the cloud service or closer to the user.

The dashboard sits inside an administration console. That makes it a tool for IT staff rather than for most employees. A worker who suspects an outage usually needs an administrator to check it.

Symptoms can narrow the question before anyone opens the dashboard. Every Outlook version, from the Windows desktop app to the mobile apps, reads from the same mailbox in Exchange Online. Comparing two of them is a simple test a user can run without admin access.

If mail fails in the desktop app but works in Outlook on the web, the problem more likely sits on that one computer. A failure that shows up in both at once shifts suspicion toward the service.

The same test reaches beyond Microsoft's own apps. Exchange Online also accepts connections over IMAP and POP, where an organization has enabled them. A third-party mail app linked to the same mailbox can serve as one more point of comparison.

Outlook desktop in cached mode complicates that test. It keeps a local copy of the mailbox. Messages that had already arrived can still open during a back-end failure. That makes reading old mail a weak sign that the service is healthy. A better check is whether a new message leaves the outbox and whether fresh mail arrives.

When no incident is posted, administrators can look closer to home. The Exchange admin center and Exchange Online PowerShell let them review their own organization's mail settings.

Several of those settings can stop mail without any fault at Microsoft. Connectors and mail flow rules, also called transport rules, control how messages move between Exchange Online and outside systems. A connector or rule set up incorrectly can disrupt mail for a whole organization while the service runs normally.

Protocol settings are worth a look as well. Admins can enable or disable each connection protocol on a per-mailbox basis. A protocol switched off for one person can explain why a single app fails for that user and nobody else.

Email sent to a Microsoft $MSFT 365 organization finds its way there through the domain's MX records, which point to Microsoft's servers. Once a message arrives, connectors and mail flow rules decide how it moves between Exchange Online and outside systems.

An MX, or mail exchanger, record is an entry in the domain name system. It tells every sending mail server on the internet where to deliver mail for a given domain. For a domain set up in Microsoft 365, that record typically names a host ending in mail.protection.outlook.com.

The domain has to be added to the Microsoft 365 tenant and verified first. The domain owner proves control by publishing a DNS record that Microsoft checks before the domain goes live.

The MX record lives with the domain's DNS host, not inside Microsoft 365. Each record carries a time-to-live setting. That setting controls how long other servers keep using a cached answer. A switch of mail providers therefore does not take effect everywhere at the same moment.

Connectors handle the less direct routes. An inbound connector accepts mail from a specific partner or service. An outbound connector sends mail through a chosen path instead of straight to the internet. Organizations use them to pass mail through a third-party filtering service, to exchange mail with a business partner or to link Exchange Online to an on-premises server. A connector can also require Transport Layer Security, the standard that encrypts mail in transit, on its route.

Mail flow rules, also called transport rules, act on messages as they pass through the service. Each rule pairs conditions with actions and can include exceptions. One rule might add a legal disclaimer to outgoing mail. Another might block certain attachment types, redirect messages to a reviewer or apply encryption. Admins build these rules in the Exchange admin center or with Exchange Online PowerShell.

These layers matter when mail stops arriving. A misconfigured connector or an overly broad rule can block or reroute mail for a whole organization while Exchange Online itself runs normally. The message trace tool in the Exchange admin center shows the path a specific message took and where it stalled.

SMTP, the protocol mail servers use to hand messages to one another, also tolerates short delays. A sending server that cannot reach its destination generally queues the message and retries for a limited time. Mail held up by a temporary fault often arrives late rather than vanishing.

Exchange Online Protection is the filtering service built into Exchange Online. It scans incoming and outgoing mail for spam and malware. Microsoft $MSFT Defender for Office 365 is a separate security layer that sits on top of it for organizations that license it.

Every organization with Exchange Online mailboxes gets Exchange Online Protection, usually shortened to EOP. It works at the edge of the service, before a message reaches an inbox. Microsoft also sells EOP as a standalone service for companies that still host mailboxes on their own Exchange servers.

EOP checks mail in stages. Connection filtering looks at the reputation of the sending server. Anti-malware scanning inspects attachments for known malicious code. Anti-spam filtering then gives each message a verdict, such as spam, high-confidence spam or phishing.

Those verdicts decide where a message ends up. By default, ordinary spam goes to the recipient's Junk Email folder. Messages judged more dangerous, such as malware or high-confidence phishing, are held in quarantine. Admins control who can review and release quarantined items.

Filtering also covers outbound mail. EOP watches for accounts that suddenly send spam, a common sign of a compromised mailbox. An outbound spam policy can block such a user from sending. That protects the reputation of Microsoft's mail servers and of the organization's own domain.

Sender authentication belongs to the same layer. EOP evaluates SPF, DKIM and DMARC results to judge whether a message really came from the domain it claims. Spoof intelligence adds a check for senders pretending to be someone at the recipient's own organization.

Microsoft Defender for Office 365 targets threats that basic filtering can miss. It comes in Plan 1 and Plan 2. Plan 1 adds Safe Attachments, which opens files in a sandbox before delivery. It also adds Safe Links, which checks a URL at the moment a user clicks it. Plan 1 brings stronger protection against impersonation as well.

Plan 2 includes everything in Plan 1 and adds tools for security teams. These include Threat Explorer, automated investigation and response, and attack simulation training. Microsoft 365 E5 includes Plan 2.

Admins manage these policies in the Microsoft Defender portal. Microsoft offers preset Standard and Strict protection policies as starting points. Organizations can also build custom policies of their own.

The filtering layer is worth checking when someone reports missing mail. A message that never appears may have been quarantined or routed to junk rather than lost to a service fault. Reviewing quarantine and running a message trace can separate a filtering decision from a wider problem.

Exchange Online offers several kinds of mailboxes and groups, each built for a different job. User mailboxes belong to individual people. Shared mailboxes, room and equipment mailboxes, distribution lists and Microsoft $MSFT 365 Groups serve teams, spaces and shared resources.

A user mailbox is the standard account tied to one licensed person. It holds that person's email, calendar, contacts and tasks. It is the mailbox Outlook opens by default when that person signs in.

A shared mailbox gives a team a common address, such as a support or sales inbox. Several people can read and reply from it without sharing a password. Nobody signs in to a shared mailbox directly. Admins grant permissions to individual users rather than handing out credentials.

Three permissions do most of the work. Full Access lets a person open the shared mailbox and read its contents. Send As makes a reply appear to come from the shared address itself. Send on Behalf shows both names, so recipients can see who answered for the team.

Shared mailboxes do not require a license of their own in most cases. Microsoft requires one when a shared mailbox needs litigation hold or more storage than the unlicensed allowance.

Room mailboxes represent physical spaces such as conference rooms. Equipment mailboxes cover items that are not tied to a location, such as projectors or company cars. Together they are known as resource mailboxes. People book them by adding the room or item to a meeting invitation. The resource can accept or decline automatically, based on whether its calendar is free.

Admins can set booking rules for each resource. These include how far ahead someone can reserve it, how long a meeting may run and whether a delegate must approve requests.

Distribution lists, also called distribution groups, work differently. They store no mail of their own. A message sent to the list's address is copied into each member's mailbox. Dynamic distribution groups build their membership automatically from attributes such as department or office location.

Microsoft 365 Groups go further than a distribution list. Each group gets a shared inbox and calendar in Exchange Online, plus a SharePoint site for files. Every team in Microsoft Teams is backed by a Microsoft 365 Group.

Admins create and manage all of these in the Exchange admin center, a browser-based console. Exchange Online PowerShell handles the same tasks from the command line and suits bulk changes. The New-Mailbox cmdlet can create shared, room or equipment mailboxes. Set-CalendarProcessing controls how resource mailboxes respond to booking requests.

Exchange Online includes built-in compliance tools that decide how long email is kept and how it can be searched later. Retention policies, litigation hold, archive mailboxes and eDiscovery all work on the same mailboxes people open every day in Outlook.

Retention policies set the rules for how long content stays in a mailbox and what happens when that period ends. An organization can keep messages for a set period, delete them once they reach a certain age, or keep them and then delete them. A single policy can cover every mailbox in a tenant. It can also target specific users or groups.

Microsoft $MSFT 365 retention policies are configured in Microsoft Purview, the company's compliance portal. Older Exchange retention tags belong to a feature called messaging records management. They apply rules to individual folders or messages and can still be managed through Exchange Online PowerShell.

Litigation hold preserves everything in a mailbox, including items a user deletes or edits. Organizations apply it when they expect a lawsuit, an audit or an internal investigation. Deleted items and the original versions of edited items are kept in the Recoverable Items folder. Most of that folder is hidden from the normal mailbox view. Its contents stay available to searches. The user can keep working in Outlook while the hold is in place.

Archive mailboxes give each user a second storage area for older mail. The archive appears as a separate folder tree in Outlook and Outlook on the web. Archive policies can move messages there automatically once they pass a set age. This keeps the primary mailbox smaller without deleting anything.

eDiscovery tools let authorized staff search across many mailboxes at once. Searches can filter by keyword, sender, recipient and date range. They can reach archive mailboxes and items preserved under hold. Results can be exported for review by legal or compliance teams.

The features available depend on the license. Mailbox storage allowances differ between Exchange Online Plan 1 and Exchange Online Plan 2. Plan 2 includes litigation hold. Plan 1 customers can add it, along with expanded archive storage, through the Exchange Online Archiving add-on.

These tools control what is kept and what can be found. They do not restore access during a service disruption. Archive mailboxes and held items are stored inside Exchange Online itself, not in a separate system. They depend on the same service as the primary mailbox.

Exchange Online and Exchange Server are the same messaging platform delivered in two ways. Microsoft $MSFT hosts and operates Exchange Online as part of Microsoft 365. Exchange Server is licensed software an organization installs on its own hardware. A hybrid deployment connects the two.

The practical difference is who carries the operational load. With Exchange Server, the organization supplies the hardware and installs the software on Windows Server. It also applies Microsoft's cumulative and security updates itself. Its own staff handle backups, capacity planning and recovery when a server fails.

Exchange Online moves that work to Microsoft. The company runs the servers, applies updates and manages the underlying infrastructure. Customers still configure mailboxes, policies and mail flow, but they no longer maintain the machines underneath.

That split also changes what an outage touches. Users whose mailboxes sit on the organization's own Exchange Server can usually keep opening them when the hosted service has a problem. Users with Exchange Online mailboxes cannot count on that. Mail passing between the two environments can still be delayed.

A hybrid deployment runs both environments side by side. Organizations choose it for two reasons. Some use it as a bridge during a gradual migration, moving mailboxes to the cloud in stages rather than all at once. Others keep certain mailboxes on their own servers indefinitely and place the rest in Exchange Online.

Microsoft provides the Hybrid Configuration Wizard to set up the connection between the environments. Once it is configured, users in both locations can share one email domain and one address book. They can also see each other's calendar free/busy information. Meeting scheduling therefore works across the divide.

Mailbox moves in a hybrid setup are handled in migration batches. A user's mailbox moves to the cloud, and Outlook reconnects to the new location. The person's email address stays the same.

Hybrid also adds moving parts. Mail between the two environments travels over connectors, and the on-premises servers still need patching. An organization in hybrid mode depends on both its own infrastructure and Microsoft's.

Mail apps reach Exchange Online through a handful of protocols, chiefly MAPI over HTTP, Exchange ActiveSync, IMAP, POP and SMTP. Software that reads or changes mailbox data in code uses Microsoft $MSFT Graph, the current programming interface for the service.

MAPI over HTTP is the connection the classic Outlook desktop client for Windows uses to talk to Exchange Online. It carries mail, calendar items, contacts and other mailbox data inside standard web traffic. That design lets the desktop client work over an ordinary internet connection, with no dedicated network link to Microsoft.

Exchange ActiveSync is a synchronization protocol built for phones and tablets. Mobile mail apps use it to keep email, calendars and contacts in step with the mailbox on the server. The built-in mail apps on many phones rely on it when a user adds an Exchange account.

IMAP and POP are open internet standards that Microsoft does not own. IMAP keeps messages on the server and mirrors folders across devices. POP is designed to download messages to a single device. Neither protocol carries calendars or contacts. Apps that read mail over IMAP or POP use SMTP to send it.

Admins can switch each of these protocols on or off for individual mailboxes. In Exchange Online PowerShell, the Set-CASMailbox cmdlet controls those settings. The Exchange admin center offers the same choices for a single mailbox. Turning off POP and IMAP for accounts that do not need them reduces the number of ways a mailbox can be reached.

Microsoft Graph is one API that spans data across Microsoft 365, reached through the graph.microsoft.com endpoint. For Exchange Online, it exposes mail, calendar events and contacts to developers. The same interface also reaches data in other services, such as Teams and OneDrive. An app can work with a user's mailbox and files through one set of calls.

Exchange Web Services, or EWS, is the older interface that applications have used to work with Exchange data. Microsoft has announced plans to retire EWS in Exchange Online. The announcement concerns the cloud service specifically. Microsoft points developers to Microsoft Graph as the replacement. Tools that still depend on EWS will need to move before the retirement takes effect.

#5477. From paper routes to fighter jets: Shield AI’s bet on Seattle is a homecoming for its co-founders

by Todd Bishop & John Cook on Nov 9, 2026 at 6:36 amNovember 9, 2026 at 6:36 am

As a kid on Mercer Island, Brandon Tseng delivered The Seattle Times and the Mercer Island Reporter for extra cash. Now he and his older brother, Ryan Tseng, are making news of their own in the Seattle region.

Shield AI, the San Diego defense tech company the brothers co-founded in 2015, announced a deal last week to buy Kirkland, Wash.-based radar maker Echodyne for up to $5.3 billion. Shield, now valued at $28.8 billion, had already unveiled plans in September to build its AI-piloted X-BAT fighter jet at a factory south of Seattle.

“I believe we will become one of the largest, or at least the fastest-growing employer in this region over the next several years,” Brandon Tseng said in an interview with GeekWire in the hours after the Echodyne acquisition was announced.

The company projects that it will employ about 4,000 people in the Seattle area by the early 2030s. It estimates the X-BAT could support about 8,000 jobs across the region in all, including jobs at Shield and its suppliers, according to an economic analysis drawing on company figures.

Tseng said Shield expects to have “well north of a million square feet” in the area before long, up from its initial 420,000-square-foot facility in Des Moines, Wash.

“That will really just be the beginning,” he said.

Brandon Tseng said the biggest reason Shield chose the Pacific Northwest for X-BAT production was the region’s “density of engineering and manufacturing talent,” pointing to Boeing, Microsoft and Amazon.

Inside the Echodyne deal: Shield believes the defense tech companies that succeed will need products that “sense, think, and act,” Tseng said. Its Hivemind autonomy software handles the thinking, and its V-BAT drone and X-BAT jet will handle the acting.

Echodyne becomes “the cornerstone of the sensing piece,” he said.

Tseng said Shield got a closer look at the market for sensors when it bought Australian optics company Sentient Vision Systems in 2024. That led the company to start looking seriously at other sensor makers, and eventually to Echodyne.

Shield and Echodyne had first crossed paths in 2016, when both were fledgling companies in the Department of Homeland Security’s Silicon Valley Innovation Program.

Nearly a decade later, the two companies’ teams were talking about working together when Echodyne began exploring a sale, Tseng said. The deal came together over several months. Tseng was at Echodyne the day it was announced last week, as the companies held all-hands meetings with their teams.

It’s an unusual deal: one venture-backed startup buying another, funded in part by a new venture round. Shield is raising $2.5 billion to help pay for the deal, including $1 billion in new funding at the $28.8 billion valuation — more than double what it was worth in March.

Echodyne has about 400 employees, after opening a $40 million radar factory in Woodinville in July. No layoffs are planned, the companies said. Eben Frankenberg, Echodyne’s co-founder and CEO, will stay in that role, reporting to Shield CEO Gary Steele. The combined company will have about 2,700 employees.

The deal is expected to close in early 2027, pending regulatory approval. Tseng said Shield plans a light touch for roughly the first year after that. Echodyne will keep selling radar to other manufacturers, many of them in counter-drone systems, while pursuing performance targets that could add $500 million to the price.

Deeper product integrations will be announced later, he said.

“They’ve been on a tear growth-wise, and we don’t want to get in their way,” Tseng said. “We don’t want to slow them down. We just want to supercharge them.”

He called the two companies’ cultures a strong match, describing both as mission-oriented and engineering-first. Echodyne’s best-selling radar, EchoShield, is designed to protect U.S. and allied service members from incoming drones.

Echodyne spun out of Intellectual Ventures, the Bellevue invention lab, in 2014 with a $15 million round led by Bill Gates and Madrona. Madrona and other Echodyne investors will become significant Shield shareholders.

Tim Porter, the Madrona Venture Group managing director who has served on Echodyne’s board since 2014, called the deal another sign of the defense tech industry’s rapid growth in the Pacific Northwest.

Echodyne “rarely, if ever, showed up on lists of the hottest defense tech companies,” he wrote. Now it’s “under the radar no longer.”

X-BAT bet: Much of Shield’s growth in the region depends on an aircraft that hasn’t flown yet. Shield unveiled its first full-scale X-BAT prototype this month and shipped it to Kansas for flight testing, with first flight targeted by the end of the year. Shield has said low-rate production will start in Des Moines in mid-2027, with the first locally built jet due in early 2028.

The Pentagon and Shield have committed a combined $400 million to X-BAT’s development, but Shield hasn’t announced any production orders.

Ryan Tseng, speaking to Breaking Defense on the sidelines of the International Fighter Conference in Munich last week, said Shield expects to announce European X-BAT orders and partnerships but declined to discuss quantities, saying only, “Watch this space.” Andrew Hawkes, Shield’s X-BAT director for Europe, told Breaking Defense the company has “several active” sales campaigns there but declined to name customers.

Asked about the X-BAT schedule in the interview last week, Brandon Tseng acknowledged the challenge but pointed to the engineering and manufacturing teams that brought the prototype together in about a year. “There was no quit in them,” he said.

“It’s hard as hell, right? Just to move out on production that fast, but you have to be confident,” he said. “I’m confident.”

Tseng, a Naval Academy graduate who deployed twice to Afghanistan as a Navy SEAL, compared Shield’s pace to that experience, when small, mission-driven groups with the right tools and resources would “do things that people didn’t think were possible.”

Ryan Tseng, an electrical engineer, previously founded wireless charging company WiPower, which was acquired by Qualcomm. The brothers started Shield with Andrew Reiter, Shield’s first CTO, who returned to the company this year.

Seattle roots: The Tseng brothers and their sister grew up on Mercer Island. Brandon Tseng spent summers swimming in Lake Washington and played water polo for Mercer Island. Ryan Tseng, who was Shield’s CEO for about a decade, graduated from Mercer Island High School, and their sister graduated from the University of Washington.

Their father, Carlos Tseng, was CEO of Seattle-based Foss Maritime from 1996 to 2001, according to Tseng and Shield. He would stop at Pike Place Market on the way home from work, and the family “probably ate salmon every other day,” Brandon Tseng said.

The family moved to Florida in 2001. None of the Tsengs live in the area anymore, but Brandon Tseng still has friends here from middle school and high school and stops by Mercer Island when he has time on his visits to the region.

Shield’s Washington state connections go further. Steele, the company’s CEO since May 2025, grew up in Yakima and graduated from Washington State University.

Brandon Tseng called Shield’s expansion in the region “a fun homecoming” for him, his brother and Steele. He is based in Washington, D.C., but expects to spend more and more time in the Seattle area.

Tseng delivered the Times, then the afternoon paper, seven days a week from age 10 to 14, making his rounds every day after school and on weekends. He credits those routes with teaching him about hard work.

“It’s always felt like home,” he said. “It’s great to be back here.”

Go hands-on with new launches the same week they’re announced, and hear directly from the engineers who built them. Experience the depth you won’t find anywhere else.
