#5476. 15 key moments in Jensen Huang's path from Computex to resignation

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Fifteen dates track former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's rising favor in Washington beside reported warnings about Alice Huang, up to the Nov. 9 fallout

When the White House and a handful of chief executives decide between themselves which American artificial intelligence chips may be sold in China, an executive's private life no longer stays private. In that arrangement, an executive who is close to the president can win sales for his company. The people close to that executive also gain a possible route to the officials who set policy. Few executives hold more of that access than Jensen Huang, who co-founded Nvidia $NVDA and still runs it. His judgment about the people around him matters to investors in a company that analysts expect to bring in nearly $694 billion in sales in fiscal 2028, according to FactSet estimates reported by CNBC. Any question about who stood close to Huang, and why, is also a question about how advanced chips reach China.

The story follows two tracks that may have run at the same time. In public, Washington showed Huang more and more favor. Inside the government, officials reportedly worried about a businesswoman tied to an Nvidia customer. The gravest claim against her is that she worked for Chinese intelligence. VnExpress reports that the claim appears in a classified U.S. intelligence memo and that the Chinese Embassy denies it. No criminal charge against her has been publicly reported, according to Yahoo News. Every mention of spying in this story is therefore an allegation rather than a finding, even though officials took the concern seriously enough to put it in writing. That uncertainty does not make the story smaller. It moves the focus away from what Huang did and toward what officials knew, and when they knew it. Neither question has a settled public answer, so the dates of each honor and each reported warning matter.

ABC News traced how Huang's relationship with Alice Huang, who is no relation, led to his downfall. His path took him to a White House state dinner, onto Air Force One on the way to Beijing, to a crowded Taipei restaurant during a tech expo, and to a presidential science medal. Huang's rising standing in Washington grew alongside reported warnings about the woman at his side, and how those two records fit together remains unresolved. How officials explain that overlap will shape how far Washington trusts the chip industry's leaders on China from here on.

At Computex, the technology trade show in Taipei, Nvidia $NVDA's chief executive spends his days among partners and buyers, and one more meeting there draws little notice. ABC News reports that Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was with Alice Huang in Taipei during Computex on June 7, 2024. It was the second time the two had met, according to Korea JoongAng Daily, so they already knew each other when they met at the trade show. Reuters obtained a photo of the two together. That image made an ordinary trade-show meeting into a fixed point that anyone could go back to, and everything that follows on this timeline is read against it.

Alice Huang had a business reason to be near Nvidia's chief. She first met him as a representative of Megaspeed, a company based in Singapore, according to Korea JoongAng Daily. For the head of the world's leading AI chipmaker, time with buyers at an industry event is part of the work. "Meetings with customers are part of a CEO's job," Nvidia spokesperson John Rizzo said. Taken on its own, the Taipei encounter shows nothing more than a chief executive spending time with a customer's representative at a trade show.

Her ties to Megaspeed began before Taipei. Singapore's company registry listed her as a Megaspeed director from March to November 2023, according to Korea JoongAng Daily, though her broader career has not been independently confirmed. The company itself soon drew federal attention when the Commerce Department opened an investigation into Megaspeed in late 2024. Within months of the trade show, the business that had brought her into Huang's circle was under scrutiny in Washington.

The photo from Taipei never changed. What changed was what officials came to suspect about the woman beside him.

Jensen Huang went to the White House as an executive whose sales were bound up with rules the new president had the power to undo. He met President Donald Trump there on Jan. 31, 2025, according to ABC News. CNBC reports that Trump could reverse the diffusion rules on AI chip exports, so the visit put Huang in front of a man able to change the terms of Nvidia $NVDA's sales. From that point on, Huang's personal standing with Trump had commercial value for Nvidia, and the company had reason to protect it.

China was likely to come up from the very first meeting. People familiar with the plans expected the two men to discuss China's DeepSeek, according to CNBC, and the diffusion rules were expected to take effect in 2025. The meeting therefore took place while those export limits were still pending, with a Chinese AI rival expected to be a topic. The question of where American AI chips can be sold, which would later turn Huang's private life into a public matter, was already part of his dealings with the president on this date.

Nothing in public at this stage pointed to trouble in Huang's personal life. He appeared as a chief executive with growing ties to a new administration and a direct line to the president on the policy his company cared about most. That clean start is why what followed reads as a sharp reversal rather than a slow decline. The more Nvidia's interests depended on Huang having Trump's attention, the further any later question about the people around him would reach beyond one company.

Jensen Huang was filmed with Alice Huang during the busiest week of Taiwan's tech calendar, at a dinner he hosted rather than at a hidden meeting. The dinner took place in Taipei during the Computex tech expo, ABC News reports, and Huang himself was the host, according to VnExpress. That put the evening on Nvidia $NVDA's business calendar, with the company's chief at the head of the table. Cameras caught the two leaving the restaurant, and they reportedly got into the same car, a public exit at one of the most watched moments of the industry's year. A chief executive with this much riding on his judgment kept no distance between this relationship and his company's most visible week.

The dinner matters beyond gossip because of where Alice Huang had worked. Megaspeed International, a data center company based in Singapore, had employed her as a senior executive, according to VnExpress. The man beside her that night was Nvidia's co-founder and CEO. Data center companies buy the kind of hardware Nvidia sells, so Megaspeed did business in Nvidia's own market rather than in some unrelated industry. Any board would have to weigh a close personal tie between people on either side of the chip market, even with no espionage question attached.

Taiwanese broadcaster TVBS captured video of the evening, but accounts of the dinner reached the public only in November 2026, more than a year later. AFPTV obtained CTI footage of the dinner on Nov. 9, 2026, according to VnExpress. What the two said at the table has not been reported, so the night shows that they were close and nothing more. It shows no exchange of business or secrets.

Every meeting and honor that followed came after cameras had already recorded this evening.

In the fall of 2025, the suspicion that Alice Huang was a spy reportedly reached the president himself, and he took no action at the time, according to ABC News. From that point, the government was on notice. Before, people could treat the worry about the woman close to Jensen Huang as talk circulating around Washington. Now the president had heard it, and the White House took no step against Huang in response. Leaving things as they were was itself a decision. Trump left his ties to an executive who had his ear on chip policy toward China unchanged while a serious question about Alice Huang remained unanswered.

The warning that reached Trump was a belief held by sources, not an established finding that any spying took place. Officials faced a suspicion, with no evidence of a crime before them. That leaves two ways to understand the inaction. A president could reasonably decide that an unproven belief did not justify cutting off one of the country's most important executives. He could also have set aside a security concern to protect a relationship that was valuable to his administration. Nothing on the public record shows which reading is correct. Either way, the central question changes here. People no longer need to ask whether anyone raised the concern. They need to ask what was done with it once it reached the top.

From this season on, every new sign of favor toward Huang has to be read against a warning that, by the sources' account, the president had already heard. That is why this quiet season, in which no decision was announced, is among the most important in the story.

Nvidia $NVDA collected its clearest reward from its ties to the White House on this date. President Donald Trump personally cleared Nvidia's H200 chip for sale in China, according to CNBC, so the company won access to that market from the president rather than through an agency ruling. ABC News reports that the U.S. government would take 25% of those sales. Even with that cut, Nvidia's stock gained about 2% in trading after the market closed. From then on, Washington held a direct financial stake in Nvidia's China business, and the company's interests and the government's were tied together.

Trump made the promise before the rules were written, while the Commerce Department was still finalizing the details, according to CNBC. The concession had a ceiling. The H200 outranks the H20, but Nvidia makes better chips than either. The deal's main safeguard was a requirement that only approved customers, vetted by the Commerce Department, could buy the chip. That safeguard depended on judging who the buyers were and who stood behind them, and the president announced it after a briefing about Huang in the fall of 2025. It remains an open question whether that briefing had any bearing on how the customer rules were drawn up.

Nvidia answered the president as a company, through a spokesman rather than its founder, and presented the bargain as a national interest. "Offering H200 to approved commercial customers, vetted by the Department of Commerce, strikes a thoughtful balance that is great for America," an Nvidia spokesman said in a statement to CNBC. Rival chipmakers, AMD $AMD and Intel $INTC among them, were due to get identical terms. That made the deal a rule for the industry's China trade rather than a personal favor to Huang.

A deal this valuable to Nvidia raised the cost of any doubt about the people near its chief.

Huang's access to Washington became an official role on this date, when he took a formal seat advising the president on science and technology. Trump appointed him to the President's Council of Advisors on Science and Technology, according to ABC News. The White House lists him among the council's first appointments, announced March 25, 2026, which puts Huang among the people chosen to define the council from its start. The new role gives his private associations a new weight. An outside executive's associations are a problem for his company, but an adviser's associations are also a question for the administration that appointed him.

The seat placed Huang among the best-known founders and chief executives in the technology industry. He joined as Nvidia $NVDA's chief executive, and the White House names Zuckerberg, Ellison, Su, Dell $DELL, Brin and Andreessen among the other appointees and says the council can hold up to 24 members. The council had 13 members after its first appointments, so Huang was among those picked first while the rest of the roster was still being filled in public. That visibility cut both ways. On a council with seats still open, any later change in a founding member's standing would be hard to miss.

Huang's appointment was an honor, not a disclosure. It records the day he joined the council rather than any briefing, so it says nothing about what anyone in government knew at the time about the woman close to him. It shows only that the administration chose to elevate him. Whatever officials were saying about the people around Huang, the White House was moving him closer to the president, and how those two facts fit together remains the open question from here on.

On April 28, 2026, Jensen Huang appeared in public as a settled family man. He attended as a guest with his wife, Lori, and as Nvidia $NVDA's CEO, so anyone watching saw the head of the company and one half of a long marriage at the same moment. That marriage had lasted more than 40 years, according to ABC News, and the partnership on display had been part of his whole adult life. Huang's appearance that day gave outsiders no visible reason for doubt, even though warnings about the people around him were reportedly already circulating inside the government.

A marriage of four decades helped make Huang look like the steadiest kind of executive. In Washington, personal standing with the powerful counts as an asset, and that image of steadiness made him an easy person to bring close to the president and to the officials shaping chip policy toward China. His public image combined a long marriage with his record at Nvidia, and that combination raised the stakes for him. The more his standing drew on his family life, the further it could fall once questions about the people around him reached the public. A founder who looks this settled gives critics little reason to ask about his private associations, and he leaves himself more exposed if those questions arrive anyway.

Every later date on this timeline should be measured against the image of a long and steady marriage that Huang showed on April 28.

By spring 2026, the worry about the woman at Huang's side had become a written allegation that named a specific spy service. A memo that season accused Alice Huang of ties to China's Ministry of State Security, according to CNBC. The public knows of the memo only through earlier New York Times reporting described by ABC News, and no government has released it. The person named in it was a Megaspeed International executive with a business identity of her own, so the suspicion could not be dismissed as gossip about a private companion. The memo still records what officials were told to believe, not a proven case.

The warning reportedly stayed inside the government for months before news reports brought it into public view. Even now, people familiar with the memo who spoke to ABC News are the only basis for its existence, and Washington has acknowledged nothing. By their account, officials had the warning in writing by spring. Through those same months, Huang kept his job and his standing in Washington. A written warning about the woman close to him and the government's continued favor toward him existed at the same time.

A suspected state-security operative close to the head of the company whose chips sit at the center of export decisions on China is a policy problem, not a private one. The memo cannot settle whether Alice Huang worked for Chinese intelligence, and nothing in it amounts to a court finding. It can show that officials had been told she might, and roughly when they were told.

From this spring on, every honor Washington gave Huang has to be read against a warning his government reportedly already held.

Jensen Huang was a late addition to the president's trip to China. Yahoo News reports that his name was missing when the delegation was first drawn up. ABC News reports that he joined the entourage in Alaska on May 12, 2026, and Trump then told his followers on Truth Social that Huang was flying with him on Air Force One. That post put the Nvidia $NVDA chief's presence on the public record. The head of the company whose chips sit at the center of the China export question was flying with the president to China itself.

That same plane is where the warning about the woman close to Huang reportedly reached the president. Yahoo News reports that, by officials' account, Secretary of State Marco Rubio raised the subject of Alice Huang with Trump during the flight. A briefing from the secretary of state made the warning a cabinet-level matter. Trump has denied hearing about it at that time. "No, I didn't hear about it then," he said. The State Department, whose chief reportedly gave the briefing, declined to comment. That leaves the president's denial against the officials' account, with nothing on the record to settle which is true.

The timing matters beyond the affair because of who Alice Huang is. She is a Chinese national associated with Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company, according to Yahoo News. Huang reached Beijing the next day, May 13, 2026, as part of the president's delegation. If the warning was given on board, Trump heard it about a Chinese national close to Nvidia's chief while he was bringing that chief along on his visit to China.

The open question from this date is whether anyone in charge knew enough to ask why Huang was on the plane.

Trump gave Huang his most symbolic sign of favor yet when he included him at an evening built around China's own leader. President Donald Trump hosted a White House state dinner for Chinese President Xi Jinping on Sept. 24, 2026, according to ABC News. CNBC reports that it was Xi's first U.S. state visit since the Obama presidency, which made the evening a rare high point in relations between the two countries. Huang attended as Nvidia $NVDA's CEO. That gave the chipmaker at the center of the fight over which chips can be sold to China a place at the summit. The allegations about his relationship with Alice Huang did not become public until Oct. 29, so he sat at Xi's dinner more than a month before they surfaced.

The guest list showed which businesses the administration wanted in the room for its dealings with Beijing. CNBC reports that a person briefed on the preparations was unaware of any invitations to Chinese companies, even though business leaders had been expected to attend. Not every American AI company had a seat either, since the AI developer Anthropic was not on the guest list. Huang's place at the dinner was a choice the White House made, not a courtesy that every major technology company received.

The government put Huang in the room with China's leader at the height of its diplomacy with Beijing. By then, warnings about the woman close to him had reportedly already reached top officials, and those warnings did not cost him the seat. The administration's favor toward Huang continued in the most public setting it could offer.

Once the allegations surfaced, the question became what the White House knew when it seated him.

Washington's most public show of trust in Huang came as an honor from the government itself, not as a deal or a private meeting. Huang received the National Medal for Science and Technology and Innovation from President Donald Trump on Oct. 8, 2026, according to ABC News. With that medal, the government put national prestige behind the Nvidia $NVDA chief, on top of the president's personal goodwill.

The award came months after Secretary of State Marco Rubio reportedly warned Trump on May 12 about the woman at Huang's side. The disputed point is when the president actually learned of the allegations. Trump's account of that differs from New York Times reporting that he had been briefed, according to CNBC. If the reports are accurate, the president gave a national honor to a man he had already been warned about. Whatever Trump took from those briefings, the ceremony raises the question of whether anyone in the White House checked a public honor against a private security briefing.

Trump presented the medal in person, so critics now treat the ceremony as a test of his judgment as much as Huang's. "Trump has been busy trying to defend Jensen Huang when he ought to be defending our national security. It's that simple, it's obvious," Sen. Charles Schumer, D-N.Y., the Senate minority leader, said, as reported by CNBC. The charge comes from the opposition party, but the question behind it has nothing to do with party. That question is whether an honor this public was ever weighed against what the government's own security officials were reportedly saying about the people close to its recipient.

Every answer about what officials knew, in the weeks that follow, will be measured against this ceremony.

On Oct. 29, 2026, Jensen Huang's relationship with Alice Huang became public, and it turned one executive's private judgment into a question about chip policy. ABC News reports that the first public account that day described the two as personally close. Her job is what made the tie a concern. Alice Huang was an executive at Megaspeed, a chip buyer that had earlier been suspected of helping evade U.S. chip export controls, according to CNBC. A relationship that connects the head of Nvidia $NVDA to a company suspected of helping evade those rules is a policy question, whatever it means in private.

The reported worry centered on the president himself. The fear was Huang's direct line to Trump, according to New York Times reporting described by CNBC. That put an executive of a company suspected of evading export controls one personal step from the president, through the chief of the company whose chips those controls cover. The access Washington had given Huang could now serve someone else as a way to reach Trump. The open question therefore moves from Huang's conduct to what officials understood about the people around him while they kept him close.

Nvidia defended a customer and left the relationship unaddressed. CNBC reports that an Nvidia spokesperson said the claims that the regional cloud provider had diverted chips had been looked into closely and shown to be false the previous year. That answer did not mention the CEO's tie to an executive at the same firm. The company also leaned on trust in Washington. "We're confident that if the U.S. government believes that any person is a threat to American industry, it would let us know," the spokesperson said. In effect, Nvidia was saying it had received no warning.

That confidence puts the next question to the government: whether it had concerns about the people around Huang, and whether it ever passed them on.

By the end of October, officials in three governments reportedly shared a worry about the woman close to Huang. Intelligence officials in the United States, Singapore and Taiwan had grounds to suspect that Alice Huang could be a spy, according to Wall Street Journal reporting described by ABC News. When officials in three governments reach a similar view, critics cannot easily dismiss it as one administration's politics or one agency's guess. Even so, the concern is still a suspicion and not a proven case, and no one has publicly shown that she worked for Chinese intelligence.

A concern held in three countries makes the question of timing harder to avoid. Congress and the public will want to know how long American officials had been watching her while the White House kept honoring Huang. When officials in Singapore and Taiwan first formed their view has not been made public. That gap leaves the question open, and it settles nothing in Huang's favor or against him. For an executive whose business with China depended on his access to the president, a doubt shared by officials in three countries was no longer a matter of his private life.

It had become a test of the judgment Washington had been trusting on chips.

Nvidia $NVDA answered the allegations against its founder in two separate parts on the same day. The company's board opened an independent investigation on Nov. 8, ABC News reports, as Huang sent his own message to staff. CNBC reports that Huang admitted in that email that he had been unfaithful to his wife. With that admission, Huang addressed the personal side of the story in his own words. The investigation would decide whether the relationship had put anything at risk, and the board, not Huang, would deliver that answer.

The directors addressed the security question in terms that neither accused Huang nor cleared him. "While the Board has no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised, the Board's inquiry will examine all available information," Nvidia's board said in a statement, as reported by CNBC. The board offered a reassurance and promised a full review in the same sentence, so the outcome remains open. For anyone weighing what this means for chip sales to China, the central question remains unanswered. Nobody at Nvidia had yet said whether anything leaked.

Handling the private matter and the security matter separately made one result possible: Huang could keep his job while the inquiry ran. He remained CEO and was committed to continuing in the role, according to CNBC. The investigation would therefore run under the executive it was examining.

Nvidia tied Huang's future to an inquiry it had only just opened, and it could keep that position only as long as the two questions stayed apart.

President Trump stood behind Huang within a day of his confession. On Sunday, the day Huang told his staff in a memo that he had been unfaithful to his wife, Trump praised him as an honorable man, according to CNBC. Huang's answer to the gravest charge reached the public through Trump after the two men spoke by phone the next day, according to ABC News. "He said he had absolutely no idea that the person in question was a spy," Trump said at a press briefing. That denial came secondhand, in the president's words rather than Huang's. It covers only what Huang knew about the woman at his side, not what the government knew while it honored him.

Trump's backing carried less weight that Monday because his party had just lost control of Congress. Democrats won majorities in both the House and the Senate, CNBC reports, and the committees that can summon Huang and administration officials now belong to the president's critics. Sen. Chris Coons of Delaware has already promised a congressional inquiry. Sam Bresnick, a research fellow at the Center for Security and Emerging Technology, expects Democrats to put the Trump administration's awareness of the matter near the top of what they examine. Trump's relayed denial does not reach that question.

Investors reacted to the election result as well as to the affair. They drove Nvidia $NVDA shares down 12% over the two days that followed the vote, according to CNBC. For shareholders, the new Congress may matter as much as Huang's private conduct. Huang also has a public appearance he cannot easily avoid, a keynote at a Washington conference on Dec. 1, in the city where the new majority is preparing its questions.

Huang still had the president on his side, but Trump cannot answer the questions that matter most for him.

#5475. New tax incentives give Washington’s sustainable aviation fuel industry a boost

Challenges, breakthroughs and big ideas in the race to protect our planet. SEE MORE

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 9, 2026 at 9:38 amNovember 11, 2026 at 7:41 am

Washington has cleared a milestone in its effort to become a hub for lower-carbon jet fuel, unlocking tax incentives aimed at attracting production to the state.

Gov. Bob Ferguson announced Friday that Washington has reached the capacity to produce at least 20 million gallons of sustainable aviation fuel annually. That triggers incentives taking effect Jan. 1, including a tax credit starting at $1 per gallon for qualifying fuel. The credit rises to as much as $2 for fuels with greater emissions reductions.

The Department of Ecology recently surveyed potential producers and confirmed that Phillips 66’s Ferndale refinery alone has enough capacity to meet the threshold. The benchmark measures production capacity, not actual output.

Sustainable aviation fuel, or SAF, is widely seen as one of the most promising near-term options for cutting aviation’s carbon emissions because it can be blended with conventional jet fuel and used in existing aircraft. But it remains more expensive than petroleum-based fuel, and production is orders of magnitude below the industry’s needs.

“We have so many unique assets in Washington that position us to be global leaders in the SAF transition, and this tax incentive is the final element needed to really unleash the tidal wave of opportunity,” said Jake Gentry, executive director of the Cascadia Sustainable Aviation Accelerator, in a GeekWire interview.

The accelerator launched in January, bringing together airlines, SAF producers, public officials, researchers and others to promote the industry in the Pacific Northwest. Its work includes helping producers secure financing, develop feedstock supplies and connect with customers.

SAF can be produced from used cooking oil, grease and fats, plants and agricultural waste, and captured carbon. Its climate benefits depend on the raw materials and energy used to make it.

The fuel still produces carbon dioxide when burned. But unlike petroleum-based jet fuel, which releases carbon that would otherwise stay trapped underground, SAF recycles carbon already in circulation in plants, animals and the atmosphere. Washington’s per-gallon tax credit requires emissions at least 50% below those of conventional jet fuel.

Washington’s production capacity is below that of some larger facilities elsewhere. A Diamond Green Diesel plant in Texas can produce up to 235 million gallons of SAF annually, according to its partner Valero. That figure also represents capacity, not actual production.

With the minimum threshold being met, all Washington SAF producers will be eligible for the tax credit regardless of their volumes.

A startup called Twelve is already making the fuel in the central Washington city of Moses Lake. The company opened its AirPlant One facility last year and began commercially producing SAF this summer from captured carbon dioxide and water. The technology has the potential to create the most climate-friendly SAF available, potentially unlocking the largest state tax credits.

Nicholas Flanders, Twelve’s CEO and co-founder, welcomed the announcement.

“This is an extraordinary signal of support for our industry,” Flanders said via email. “Washington is building the leading foundation in the country for next-generation domestic fuel production, and Twelve is ready to build upon it.”

Twelve’s first-of-its-kind facility is designed to make up to 50,000 gallons of SAF per year. AirPlant Two, a much bigger plant that would make tens of millions of gallons a year, is in development. The company hasn’t said where it will be located.

Dutch-owned SkyNRG is building a SAF facility in Walla Walla, Wash., and plans to use renewable natural gas that’s captured at landfills and from dairy waste as a feedstock. Earlier this year, leaders said the company had secured key environmental approvals and plans to start commercial operations in 2030.

Washington’s relatively affordable hydroelectric power has historically helped attract climate tech companies. But growing electricity demand, including from data centers, is putting pressure on the region’s power supply.

Washington also faces competition from other states offering SAF tax incentives. Illinois and Minnesota already offer credits, and Nebraska’s program starts next year. Meanwhile, a federal credit was reduced from $1.75 per gallon to $1 after President Donald Trump returned to office.

Washington leaders tout other perks that could attract SAF production. It’s the only state that offers both a SAF tax credit and a clean fuel standard. Together, the policies help make cleaner jet fuel more cost-competitive by providing tax benefits and allowing SAF producers to earn credits they can sell to other fuel suppliers that need to meet the state’s emissions requirements.

The accelerator also supports efforts with Washington State University to develop regional feedstock supplies, including waste from logging and agriculture.

“Between our long history of aviation innovation, our intentional investments into the sector and our climate-forward policies, we’re making sure Washington is the best state in the country to produce sustainable aviation fuels,” Ferguson said in a statement.

The Climate Pledge is a commitment to reach net-zero carbon emissions by 2040, co-founded by Amazon and Global Optimism in 2019.

Seven years later, the community has grown to over 700 signatories across 62 industries and 49 countries and territories, reducing emissions, scaling emerging climate solutions, and addressing challenges across operations and value chains.

#5474. Anthropic’s blockbuster IPO just got harder after Jensen Huang’s dramatic exit as Nvidia CEO

Anthropic is about to embark on one of the most hotly anticipated IPOs in history. After a dramatic turn of events, it will now be doing so a week after the industry lost one of its most powerful figures and best salesmen.

Nvidia’s longtime CEO and co-founder Jensen Huang resigned from the company on Thursday following reports alleging he had engaged in two extramarital affairs: one with a customer suspected by U.S. intelligence to be a Chinese intelligence asset and another with an Nvidia executive who reports to him.

The timing has thrown new pressure on Anthropic’s listing, which was already seen as a stress test for investors’ appetite for AI. The AI lab is expected to list on Wednesday or Thursday next week, days after Nvidia reports quarterly earnings—the company’s first-ever without Huang at the helm.

Nvidia is a close partner of Anthropic and intimately involved in the lab’s upcoming IPO. According to Anthropic’s filings, the chipmaker has agreed to buy about $10 billion of shares in a $26 billion private placement alongside the IPO. The two companies are also closely tied commercially, with Anthropic committing to tens of billions of dollars to secure access to Nvidia’s most advanced chips.

Investors and analysts told Fortune that while they don’t expect the Nvidia shock to affect Anthropic’s core business, it could cause problems for the broader AI story.

Jay Goldberg, an analyst at Seaport Research Partners and one of the few on Wall Street with a sell rating on Nvidia’s stock, doesn’t expect Huang’s exit to derail the deal. “They’re going to go public right in the face of Nvidia’s earnings call, and I don’t think that derails it,” he said. “It’s such a massive IPO and there’s so many people behind it now that they don’t pull the IPO.”

The bigger risk, he said, comes once Anthropic is a public company. Speaking shortly before Huang’s departure but after reports that he was likely to be leaving the company, Goldberg warned that turmoil at Nvidia, including the loss of its CEO, would create a headwind for Anthropic when it reports its first quarterly results. “At the very least it will create this narrative of, ‘Can the AI narrative maintain? Can we keep doing this?’” he said. “They’ll get much tougher questions.”

Karl Alomar, a partner at venture firm M13, agreed that Anthropic’s fundamentals haven’t changed. “From where I stand, Anthropic is still in as good, as strong a position as it was before this news came out,” he said. “Anthropic’s numbers are fantastic, and they’ve clearly shown that they have excess capacity for what they need. They haven’t spent that much money.”

Anthropic is also less dependent on Nvidia than some of its rivals, running some models on Google’s TPUs, Amazon’s Trainium chips, and AMD’s GPUs, as well as Nvidia’s hardware. Anthropic has also reportedly been exploring building its own chips.

“Nvidia has committed to invest $10 billion in the Anthropic IPO. That will likely still happen when the IPO eventually happens,” said Francine McKenna, an accountant and investigative journalist who has taught at the Wharton School. “But anyone who was looking at Nvidia to bail out CoreWeave if needed should probably look elsewhere.”

However, the recent trouble at Nvidia and questions surrounding the CEO’s judgement could spill over into more scrutiny for its partners, according to Jason Schloetzer, an associate professor at Georgetown University’s McDonough School of Business. He said he expected there to be “much closer scrutiny of [Anthropic’s] ties to Nvidia and customers associated with Nvidia.”

For Silicon Valley, Anthropic and competitor OpenAI have needed so much capital that almost every venture capital firm in town owns a piece of them—making them the private market equivalent of an index fund. That makes Anthropic’s expected IPO next week a high-stakes liquidity event—not only for the more than 400 backers of Anthropic, but for the AI boom as a whole. There’s a broad sense that if Anthropic succeeds, the AI boom has far more runway. If it flops or pushes back indefinitely, it would be an unequivocal negative signal that the AI bubble is heading towards a pop.

It may not be a bust. Indeed, at least one venture capitalist sees a clear upside for Anthropic. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has long pushed for tighter controls on chip exports to China, putting him at odds with Huang. The AI lab has similarly clashed with Huang on AI regulation, with Huang particularly keen to avoid any licensing requirements that would make it more difficult for customers to adopt open-source AI models.

“If anything, I think Anthropic is a beneficiary here,” said the investor, who asked not to be named given the situation’s sensitivity and their investments across AI. “They weren’t that close to Jensen…They’re building their own chip, and so the supply chain considerations that get freed up are good for Anthropic.”

Beatrice Nolan is a tech reporter on Fortune’s AI team, covering artificial intelligence and emerging technologies and their impact on work, industry, and culture. She's based in Fortune's London office and holds a bachelor’s degree in English from the University of York. You can reach her securely via Signal at beatricenolan.08

Allie Garfinkle is a senior writer and editor at Fortune, where she runs Term Sheet; leads coverage of private capital, investors, and startups; and co-chairs the Brainstorm conference series.

#5473. Flash flood watch vs. warning vs. emergency: what each alert means

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Flash flood watch vs. warning vs. emergency: what each National Weather Service alert means, how the three levels differ and what to do when one is issued

A flash flood can turn a dry creek bed or a city street into fast-moving water within about six hours of heavy rain. The National Weather Service (NWS) uses three escalating alert levels for this hazard. A watch says flash flooding is possible. A warning says it is happening or about to happen. An emergency says an ongoing or imminent flash flood poses a severe threat to human life and could cause catastrophic damage.

Each level calls for a different response. Confusing them costs time. Someone who treats a warning like a watch may still be gathering information while water is already rising. Someone who reads a flash flood emergency as a routine warning may miss that it is the rarest and most severe flash flood alert the NWS issues.

Getting flash flood watch vs. warning vs. emergency right starts with what each word describes. A watch is about conditions that favor flooding. A warning is about an event in progress or close to it. An emergency is not a separate product at all. It is enhanced wording added to a flash flood warning when the threat reaches its highest level.

The system has more layers than those three terms suggest. Flash flood alerts are distinct from ordinary flood alerts, which also cover slower rises on rivers and streams. Flash flood warnings carry damage threat tags. Those tags help decide whether a warning reaches phones through Wireless Emergency Alerts. That is why a person inside a warned area may not get a phone alert for every warning.

The physical danger is also easy to misjudge. Fast-moving water does not need to be deep to knock an adult down or float a car. Some landscapes also turn rain into rushing water faster than others.

The 10 slides that follow explain what a flash flood is and what each alert level means for people in its path. They compare flash flood alerts with standard flood alerts and break down the NWS damage threat tags. They also explain why phones sound for only some warnings, how little water it takes to move a vehicle and which kinds of terrain flood fastest.

A flash flood is a rapid rise of water that usually arrives within about six hours of heavy rain or another cause. River flooding moves more slowly, and the National Weather Service (NWS) covers it with a separate set of alerts.

Timing is what sets a flash flood apart. The definition turns on how quickly water comes up after the event that caused it. It does not depend on how deep the water gets or how big the waterway is. A small creek that overtops its banks soon after a downpour can qualify, just as a larger stream can.

Heavy rain is the one cause the definition names outright. The words "or another cause" leave room for floods that do not come from a storm directly overhead. A flood counts as a flash flood when the speed of the rise fits, whatever started it.

River flooding follows a different timeline. The water comes up gradually rather than in a sudden surge. The NWS does not fold this kind of flooding into its flash flood products.

The NWS reflects that difference in pace by keeping two families of flood alerts. One family is built around fast water and short notice. The other covers flooding that develops more gradually, including rises on rivers.

The short timeline also changes what a flood means for people in its path. When water can rise within hours of heavy rain, the gap between the first sign of trouble and dangerous conditions is narrow. A slower river rise generally leaves more room to react.

The flash flood side of the system has three alert levels: the watch, the warning and the emergency. All three deal with fast-rising water. Each one marks a different stage, from flooding that is possible to flooding that threatens lives.

Knowing whether a flood is the fast or the slow kind is the first step in reading any NWS flood alert. With a flash flood, the time to act is short.

A flash flood watch means conditions are favorable for flash flooding in or near the watch area. Flooding is possible, but it is not yet happening or confirmed. The watch is a signal to prepare and stay alert.

The National Weather Service issues flash flood watches, and its definition uses precise terms. "Favorable" describes the setup. The ingredients for a rapid rise of water are present, but the water is not yet rising. A watch is a forecast of risk, not a report of an event.

The phrase "in or near the watch area" also shapes how to read the alert. The risk is not confined to the outlined zone. A person just outside the boundary should treat the watch as relevant to them.

The main value of a watch is the time it provides. While flooding is only a possibility, there is room to plan routes, check devices and decide where to go. Those choices are harder to make once water is already rising.

Preparation during a watch comes down to three steps. The first is to know the local evacuation route. That means knowing which road leads to higher ground from home, from work and from any place a person expects to spend time during the watch.

The second step is to enable emergency alerts on a phone. A watch can escalate if flooding begins. A phone set to receive alerts is one way to learn about that change quickly.

The third step is to keep a NOAA Weather Radio as a backup. The radio offers a second path for alerts if a phone is switched off, out of battery or without signal.

A watch on its own does not tell people to move to higher ground. It calls for readiness — a known route, alerts turned on and a backup source of information — for as long as the watch remains in effect.

A flash flood warning means flash flooding is occurring or about to occur. The National Weather Service (NWS) tells anyone in the warned area to move to higher ground right away.

That instruction separates a warning from a flash flood watch. A watch describes conditions that could lead to flooding. A warning describes water that is already rising or is expected to rise very soon.

The NWS does not need to wait for water to reach homes before issuing one. The phrase "about to occur" means a warning can arrive before flooding is visible at a given spot. The guidance to seek higher ground applies either way. Waiting for visible water before acting would give up the time the warning is meant to provide.

Three kinds of evidence usually trigger a warning. Radar estimates show how much rain is falling and where the heaviest rain is concentrated. Rain gauges record the rain that has actually reached the ground. Eyewitness reports describe what is happening on streets, streams and roads.

Each source covers a gap the others leave. Weather radar scans a wide area, but it estimates rainfall indirectly from the signal that precipitation reflects back. A gauge gives a direct measurement, but only at the spot where it sits. A report from someone on the scene describes the flooding itself rather than the rain behind it.

Taken together, the three sources let forecasters check one signal against another. Heavy rain on radar, a high gauge reading and a report of water over a road point to the same conclusion from different angles.

A warning covers a defined area, not an entire state or region. The practical question for a reader is whether their home, workplace or current location falls inside it.

Higher ground means a place the rising water cannot reach. Basements, underpasses and low spots along creeks sit in the path of the water rather than above it.

A flash flood emergency is the most serious flash flood alert the National Weather Service issues. The agency reserves it for an ongoing or imminent flash flood that poses a severe threat to human life and catastrophic damage.

Both parts of that definition matter. The danger to people has to be severe. The expected damage has to reach the catastrophic level. A flash flood that falls short of that threshold still gets a flash flood warning, but without the emergency designation.

The flood does not have to be underway yet. The NWS can declare an emergency for a flash flood that is imminent as well as for one already in progress. That means the alert can come before water reaches a given street or neighborhood.

There is no separate flash flood emergency product. The NWS issues it as enhanced wording inside a flash flood warning. On a phone screen, a radio broadcast or a weather app, the alert still appears as a warning. The emergency language in its text is what marks the escalation, so anyone in a warned area should read past the headline of the alert.

The designation also lines up with the strongest NWS damage threat tag. Flash flood warnings are tagged base, considerable or catastrophic, and the catastrophic tag goes with a flash flood emergency. A warning carrying that tag can trigger a Wireless Emergency Alert on phones in the warned area.

The NWS issues flash flood emergencies rarely. Most flash flood warnings never carry the label. Its use signals that forecasters see a threat beyond routine flooding.

The required response matches the threat. A flash flood warning already tells people in its path to move to higher ground right away. An emergency adds that lives are at severe risk and catastrophic damage is expected. That move to higher ground cannot be delayed to watch how the water behaves.

A flash flood watch and a flood watch are two different National Weather Service (NWS) alerts. The flash flood watch is about sudden, fast-rising water. The flood watch covers a broader chance of flooding, including slower rises on rivers and streams.

The two names differ by one word, and that word carries the meaning. "Flash" points to speed. A flash flood watch tells people that conditions in or near the watch area could produce that kind of fast-moving event.

A flood watch casts a wider net. It is not limited to fast-rising water. It also accounts for water that climbs gradually as rivers and streams fill. Slower flooding of this kind is a separate hazard, and the NWS handles it with its own set of products.

Both alerts share the same basic status. A watch of either kind means flooding is possible but is not yet happening or confirmed. Neither one tells people in the area that water is already rising.

The practical difference is the pace of the threat each one describes. Under a flash flood watch, the concern is water that can rise quickly. Under a flood watch, the concern can also include rises that build over a longer stretch.

The alert's name is the simplest way to tell which one applies. The word "flash" is the signal to look for. Its presence means the NWS is flagging the possibility of sudden, fast-rising water rather than only the broader chance of flooding.

A flash flood warning covers rapid flooding that is happening now or is about to happen. Flooding that builds more slowly, such as a gradual rise on a river or stream, falls under separate National Weather Service flood products.

The split between the two comes down to timing. The NWS treats flash flooding as its own hazard because the water climbs fast. That leaves people little room between the first heavy rain and dangerous conditions. A flash flood warning is built for that compressed timeline.

The threat a flash flood warning describes is already underway or close at hand. Its purpose is to prompt immediate action, not to start a planning process. The guidance for anyone in the warned area is to get to higher ground right away.

River flooding moves on a slower schedule. Water on a river or stream rises gradually, and the NWS keeps that hazard out of its flash flood alerts. It tracks slower flooding through a separate set of flood products instead.

That separation matters when two alerts appear close together on a phone or a broadcast. A flood alert and a flash flood alert are not interchangeable labels for the same event. Each one describes a different kind of water behavior.

The word "flash" in an alert's name is the signal to look for. It tells the reader that the gap between rain and dangerous water may be short. An alert that leaves the word out covers the broader category of flooding the NWS handles through its other products, including slower rises on rivers and streams.

Reading the full alert name, rather than skimming for the word "flood," is the quickest way to tell which situation applies.

National Weather Service flash flood warnings carry an impact-based tag that rates the expected damage threat as base, considerable or catastrophic. The tag tells people in a warned area how severe the flooding is expected to be.

The tag sits on top of the warning's basic message. Every flash flood warning carries the same core meaning: flash flooding is occurring or about to occur in the warned area. The damage threat label adds a second layer. It describes how much harm that flooding could do, not whether it is happening.

The three labels form a scale. Base is the lowest of the three. Considerable sits in the middle. Catastrophic is the highest.

A base tag does not soften the warning itself. Flash flooding is still occurring or imminent under a base-level warning. The label only places the expected damage at the low end of the scale.

The product name alone does not separate one flash flood warning from another. Two warnings can share the same name and carry very different labels. The tag is what tells them apart.

The term "impact-based" describes what the tag rates. It looks at the expected damage threat, meaning the effect the water could have on the area it reaches. That is a different question from where or when the flooding is happening, which the warning itself already answers.

The top of the scale connects to the top of the alert system. The catastrophic tag goes with a flash flood emergency, the most severe flash flood alert level. A warning carrying that label signals the threat the NWS reserves for danger to human life and catastrophic damage.

Flash flood warnings tagged with a considerable or catastrophic damage threat can trigger Wireless Emergency Alerts on phones in the warned area. Warnings tagged at the base level generally do not set off those phone alerts.

That split explains why people see some flash flood warnings on their phones and not others. One warning can make phones across a neighborhood sound at once. A later warning for the same area may never appear on a phone at all. Both are genuine National Weather Service flash flood warnings. The difference lies in the damage threat tag the NWS attached to each one.

Those tags come in three levels: base, considerable and catastrophic. Only the upper two are linked to Wireless Emergency Alerts. A catastrophic tag accompanies a flash flood emergency.

Wireless Emergency Alerts reach devices in the warned area. The alert depends on where a phone is at the moment, not where its owner lives. That makes the alert a signal about present location rather than a home address. A driver passing through a warned area can receive one. Someone whose home lies inside the warned area but who is elsewhere when the warning goes out may not.

A silent phone does not mean no warning is in effect. A base-level flash flood warning still means flash flooding is occurring or about to occur in the warned area. The lower tag describes the expected scale of damage. It does not make the water any less dangerous for someone caught in it.

A person who relies on phone alerts alone can miss a base-level warning entirely. Nothing arrives on the device, even though the warning covers the area they are in.

The NWS guidance under any flash flood warning stays the same whether or not a phone sounds. People in the warned area should move to higher ground right away.

Six inches of fast-moving water can knock an adult off their feet, according to the National Weather Service. A foot of water can float many cars. Two feet can carry away most vehicles, including SUVs and trucks.

Those three depths form the core of the agency's safety campaign, Turn Around Don't Drown. The slogan is a plain instruction. When water covers a road or path ahead, the guidance is to turn back rather than go through it.

The first threshold applies to people on foot. Six inches of water sits well below the knee of most adults. Moving water at that depth can still take a person down. Wading across a flooded street is a hazard in its own right, separate from driving through one.

The second threshold applies to cars. A car that begins to float loses the grip of its tires on the road. The driver can no longer steer or brake. The current, not the driver, decides where the vehicle goes.

The third threshold reaches larger vehicles. The NWS places SUVs and trucks among the vehicles that two feet of moving water can carry away. Extra height and weight do not take them out of danger.

Read together, the three depths show that the danger to people and the danger to vehicles overlap. Water deep enough to float a car is already deeper than the depth that can knock an adult down. A driver whose car is lifted by the current cannot count on stepping out and walking to safety. The vehicle offers no refuge, and the water outside it offers none either.

The figures also show why depth alone is a poor guide. Every number in the campaign describes fast-moving water, not still water. The force of the current, not just the height of the water, is what moves people and vehicles. A driver who reaches a flooded road has one safe option under the campaign's guidance. Turn around, and find another route.

Flash flooding strikes fastest where rainwater cannot soak into the ground or has little room to spread out. Steep canyons, paved urban areas, low-water road crossings and recent wildfire burn scars all fit that description. Each one concentrates runoff in its own way.

Narrow canyons work like funnels. Rain that falls across a wide area of rock and steep slopes drains into a single channel. The water rises quickly because the canyon walls leave it nowhere to go but up and downstream.

The storm producing that water does not have to be overhead. Heavy rain miles upstream can send a surge through a canyon where the sky is clear. A forecast for the entire drainage area, not only the trailhead, gives a fuller picture of the risk inside a slot canyon.

Cities create a similar problem with concrete instead of rock. Roads, parking lots and rooftops shed rain rather than absorbing it. That water collects in streets, storm drains and culverts within minutes. When drains back up or fill beyond capacity, underpasses and low-lying intersections can flood quickly, even in neighborhoods far from any river.

Low-water crossings are places where a road dips through a creek bed instead of passing over it on a bridge. They are common on rural roads and in hilly regions such as central Texas. During a storm, the creek can rise over the roadway faster than a driver expects. Muddy water also hides how deep it is and whether the pavement underneath has washed away.

Wildfire burn scars change how the ground behaves for months or even years after a fire. Burned slopes lose the plants and leaf litter that normally slow and absorb rain. Intense heat can also leave some soils repelling water instead of taking it in.

As a result, a storm over a recent burn area can produce far more runoff than the same rain would on unburned land. That runoff can pick up ash, mud, rocks and fallen trees as it moves downhill. Communities below a burn scar can face fast-moving debris flows, not just rising water.

#5472. Amazon’s Ring tries again with a $250 flying home security drone and a $1,000 patrol robot

by Todd Bishop on Nov 10, 2026 at 5:30 amNovember 10, 2026 at 5:42 am

Amazon’s Ring unveiled a $249.99 flying indoor security drone and a $999.99 mobile patrol robot for businesses, bringing back two ideas that stalled in earlier incarnations.

The Ring Drone Cam and Ring Rover Cam, announced Tuesday, are the first products under the Ring Robotics name, which the company calls “a new category of autonomous, mobile security.” Both devices use a system Ring calls AI Pilot to map a home or business, suggest spots worth checking, and find their own way around obstacles such as furniture and shelving.

The drone stays docked with its camera off until it’s sent out on a schedule, on demand, or automatically when another Ring device is triggered. The Rover patrols stores and offices, using a periscope camera to see over counters and shelving.

The Rover is available for preorder in the U.S. and is scheduled to ship Dec. 16. The Drone Cam is slated for Jan. 27, 2027, but Ring is only taking email sign-ups for now. The fine print notes that the drone hasn’t yet received the required authorization from the Federal Communications Commission.

Scheduled flights and patrols, and reviewing the Rover’s recorded video, require a Ring Protect subscription plan. Ring didn’t say which plans qualify.

Ring says customers wanted to see spots a fixed camera can’t reach, and rooms where they wouldn’t want one mounted.

“The honest answer wasn’t more cameras; it meant reimagining what a security device could be,” said Jamie Siminoff, Ring’s founder and chief inventor, in a statement. “That kind of invention is hard, and it takes time.”

Ring unveiled a flying indoor camera called the Always Home Cam in 2020, also priced at $249.99. The company later opened an invitation list, but the device never went on general sale.

The original drone flew only along paths that owners mapped out with it in advance. Ring says the new one builds a floor plan as the owner carries it through the house, suggests spots to check, and plans its own routes.

The Rover Cam traces back to Astro for Business, a rolling security robot that Amazon launched in November 2023 at a starting price of $2,350. Amazon discontinued it less than a year later, refunding customers and shutting the robots off.

Astro for Business was a spinoff of Amazon’s Astro home robot, an Alexa-powered device on wheels that debuted in 2021 and can patrol the house on its own.

Ring says the new robot was inspired by Astro customers who said roving security was their favorite feature. The Ring team “leveraged the best of Astro” to build it, the company says. Ring is pitching the Rover as “not a home robot that also does security, but a purpose-built security robot.”

The original Astro for the home remains an invite-only product. Amazon has redeployed much of the Astro team to work on a new home robot, CNBC reported Sunday. In March, Amazon acquired Fauna Robotics, a New York humanoid robot startup, saying it would become part of a new Personal Robotics Group. Ring’s announcement doesn’t mention either effort.

The Rover also extends Ring’s push into commercial security, following a $5,000 surveillance trailer for parking lots that it unveiled in January. In security robots, it competes with companies such as Knightscope, which rents its robots through a subscription, and Cobalt AI. At $999.99, the Rover costs less than half what Astro for Business did.

On the security drone front, Indoor Robotics makes a ceiling-docking drone that patrols offices and warehouses, but flying security cameras for the home remain rare.

Siminoff, who launched Ring’s predecessor, Doorbot, in 2012 and sold Ring to Amazon in 2018, left the company in 2023 and returned last year to lead Ring and Amazon’s related home security businesses. Last month, Ring unveiled its first smart lock, a $249 deadbolt with no keyhole and a dial that recharges a dead battery by hand.

In just a few weeks, AWS re:Invent brings advanced and expert-level sessions on the services you build on every day, from serverless and containers to databases and developer tools. Go hands-on with new launches the same week they’re announced, and hear directly from the engineers who built them. Experience the depth you won’t find anywhere else.

#5471. Standard Chartered profit jumps 46% as CEO bets on a fragmenting global economy: ‘An advantage for us’

The CEO of British multinational bank Standard Chartered says “geopolitical fragmentation is an advantage for us,” after the lender reported a 46% jump in third-quarter net profit to $1.5 billion.

Speaking at a media roundtable, Bill Winters said the splintering of global trade is creating new business for the bank, which helps multinational corporations manage cross-border deals, the South China Morning Post reported.

His remarks come as companies rethink where they make things amid rising trade tensions. Many have adopted a “China plus one” strategy, shifting some production to Southeast Asia to offset China’s rising costs. That shift has proven more complicated than expected, as many factories in the region still rely on Chinese inputs, Fortune reported in October.

Geopolitical fragmentation refers to the structural shift in the global economy as supply chains, trade, and policy realign along political lines.

For banks, that shift changes where money flows. A company moving manufacturing from China to Southeast Asia, for instance, needs new banking relationships and financing arrangements in each new market.

Standard Chartered operates in 54 markets, with a significant presence in Asia, Africa, and the Middle East. That network lets it follow clients as their trade and investment move.

“We’ve really focused on getting a few things right and one is to serve multinational corporations and multinational individuals on their cross-border needs,” Winters said.

The bank’s third-quarter results, released Oct. 28, show how much it now leans on fee-generating businesses beyond traditional lending. Operating income rose 13% to $5.8 billion, and pre-tax profit climbed 27% to $2.25 billion.

Wealth Solutions income rose 26% to $1.1 billion, while Global Markets income grew 20% to just over $1 billion. The bank raised its 2026 outlook and now expects a return on tangible equity of about 14%.

The industry as a whole is flush. Banks earned a record $1.3 trillion in net income in 2025, up 7% from a year earlier, according to McKinsey’s Global Banking Annual Review, which argues that AI will reward lenders that move quickly. Winters cautioned that the AI boom may lead to some misallocated capital, and said the bank’s role is to avoid those risks.

Fragmentation cuts both ways. Trade restrictions and political instability add friction to the cross-border transactions at the heart of Standard Chartered’s business, and if tensions choke off trade, demand for those services could fall.

Operating across dozens of jurisdictions also means keeping up with each country’s regulations and compliance requirements, which can shift with politics. Even so, the bank’s economists have argued that fears of a broad retreat from the U.S. dollar are overstated, Fortune reported in July.

Winters named five structural trends he expects to redefine finance over the next decade: the transition to a low-carbon economy, wealth creation across Asia, the Middle East, and Africa, changes to banking infrastructure, geopolitical fragmentation, and the digitization of money.

Hong Kong, where regulators are building frameworks for digital assets, is central to that last bet. This month, Standard Chartered launched tokenized deposits in Hong Kong and piloted a liquidity facility to support Ant International’s investment in tokenized money market funds. The bank ranks No. 7 on the 2026 Fortune Crypto 100.

“We’re positioned for the themes that we think are most important for the next 10 to 20 years, and we intend to keep our focus on those things,” Winters said.
