#5470. Car caught in a flash flood: what drivers should do before, during and after

Free daily briefing on global business news.

What to do if your car is caught in a flash flood, from judging water depth to escaping a sinking vehicle and dealing with the damage afterward

A car feels like shelter. It has a roof, locked doors and a heater, and it sits between the driver and the storm outside. In a flash flood, that sense of protection can be misleading. A vehicle is a hollow metal box that can float once enough water gets underneath it. Moving water can then push it off the road with the people still inside.

Flash floods differ from slow river flooding. They form fast, often after intense rain over a small area. They can turn a dry street, creek bed or underpass into a channel of fast water with little warning. Roads often follow low ground, where water collects first. That puts drivers directly in the path. A route that was clear on the way out can be underwater on the way home.

Knowing what to do if your car is caught in a flash flood comes down to a short chain of decisions. Each one depends on where you are in that chain. Before reaching the water, the choice is whether to drive in at all. If the engine stalls in still water, the question becomes how fast to get out and where to go. If the car is sinking or caught in current, the order of actions narrows to seconds. Once the water drops, a different set of choices determines whether the car can be saved and how an insurance claim proceeds.

The National Weather Service, FEMA and Ready.gov publish guidance for each of these moments. Their advice is consistent on the basics. Avoid flooded roads and take official alerts seriously. Leave a stalled vehicle when water starts rising around it. Treat floodwater as dangerous whether you are inside a car or standing in it.

The 10 steps below follow that sequence. They start with reading the road and the weather alerts. They move through escaping a stalled or sinking vehicle and finish with what to do once the flood has passed. Each step covers one situation. A driver facing a specific problem can find the relevant guidance without reading the rest first. None of it requires special training. Most of it requires deciding early, before rising water removes the easier options.

If water covers the road ahead, turn around before your tires reach it. The National Weather Service sums up that rule in its slogan, "Turn around, don't drown." Do not try to test how deep the water is.

The reason is what sits under the surface. Water flowing over a road can hide a washout, where the current has carried away the ground beneath the pavement. It can also hide a stretch where the pavement itself is gone. Once both are covered, a collapsed roadbed and an intact one look the same from the driver's seat.

Floodwater is rarely clear. It usually carries mud and silt, which block any view of the road below. Lane markings, curbs and the edge of the road disappear. A driver has no reliable way to tell whether the water is a thin layer over solid asphalt or the top of a much deeper gap.

The surface of the water gives no better clue. Smooth, calm-looking water can still be flowing across the road. A flooded stretch can look shallow when the road beneath it has dropped away.

Another vehicle crossing without trouble does not prove the road is sound. Moving water keeps eroding the roadbed. A section that held one car can give way under the next. During a flash flood, conditions can change within minutes as more rain drains into the same low ground.

That is why the NWS answer to the common question "can you drive through flood water" is no. Its guidance makes no exception for drivers who believe they can judge the depth by eye.

Turning around takes only a few steps. Stop well short of the water. Check that the road behind you is clear, then reverse or make a U-turn. Take a different route, or wait on higher ground until the water recedes and the road surface is visible again. A detour adds time. Driving into water of unknown depth puts the car and everyone inside it at risk.

About 12 inches of moving water can float many cars, and about two feet can carry away most vehicles, including SUVs and pickup trucks. Those are the depth thresholds the National Weather Service and FEMA give drivers.

Water at either depth can sit well below a typical car's windows. From the driver's seat, it can look manageable. The risk does not start when water reaches the doors. It starts lower, at the tires.

A car stays on the road because its weight presses the tires against the pavement. That contact lets a driver steer, brake and accelerate. Floodwater undermines it in two ways.

The first is buoyancy. A vehicle's tires, body and cabin hold air. Water pushes upward on anything that holds air. As the water rises, that upward force offsets more of the car's weight. The tires press down with less force, and their grip on the road weakens.

The second is current. Moving water pushes against the whole side of the vehicle. Friction between the tires and the road resists that push. Once buoyancy has lightened the car, the same push can slide it sideways. Steering and braking no longer work in any useful way. The car then moves with the water.

Depth lifts the car. Current carries it. Together they can move a vehicle that looks firmly planted.

A larger vehicle is not immune. A taller SUV or pickup truck keeps its cabin above shallow water for longer. It also presents a larger body for water to lift and push against. The NWS and FEMA place both vehicle types within the two-foot threshold.

The figures are approximate rather than exact cutoffs. How quickly a specific vehicle floats depends on its weight, its shape and the speed of the water around it. A heavier vehicle may hold the road slightly longer than a light compact car. Neither is safe once the water reaches these levels.

The takeaway from these thresholds is simple. Water does not have to look deep to move a car.

A flash flood watch means conditions could produce flash flooding. A flash flood warning means flooding is happening now or is about to, and anyone in the warned area should move to higher ground immediately.

The National Weather Service issues both alerts. The two names sound alike, but they call for very different responses from anyone behind the wheel.

A watch is an early signal. It means the ingredients for flash flooding are in place, such as heavy rain falling on saturated ground or slow-moving storms over the same area. A watch usually covers a broad region. It is often issued well before any water rises, and nothing may be flooding yet.

For drivers, a watch is the time to plan. Check the forecast before leaving. Consider delaying a trip that isn't essential, or pick a route that stays on higher ground. Keep a phone charged and weather alerts switched on. That way, an upgrade to a warning won't go unnoticed.

A warning carries more urgency. It means flooding is underway or imminent in a specific area. The NWS guidance at this stage is to move to higher ground at once. A driver already on the road should head for elevated ground rather than press on toward a destination.

Flash floods can strike where little or no rain is falling. Runoff from storms upstream can rush down creeks, dry washes and canyons far from where the rain fell. A clear sky overhead does not cancel a warning.

The NWS also issues a rarer and more serious alert, the flash flood emergency. It is reserved for cases where a flash flood poses a severe threat to human life and catastrophic damage is occurring or expected.

Alerts reach drivers through several channels. NOAA Weather Radio, local TV and radio broadcasts and smartphone weather apps all carry them. Wireless Emergency Alerts can also push urgent warnings straight to a phone with a distinctive tone.

Reading the alert correctly buys time. Under a watch, that time goes into planning a safer trip or skipping it. Under a warning, it goes into getting to higher ground.

If a car stalls and floodwater starts rising around it, the driver should get out and move to higher ground. Ready.gov advises abandoning the vehicle when the water around it is climbing but not moving, rather than waiting inside for help.

A stalled engine changes the situation. The car can no longer drive out of the water, and it cannot back up to a safer spot. At that point, the vehicle offers no way out of the rising water.

Still water is the scenario where leaving on foot is most manageable. Without a current pushing against the body, a person stepping out of the car has a better chance of staying upright and reaching dry ground. That chance shrinks as the depth increases.

The National Weather Service and FEMA put the depth at which many cars begin to float at about 12 inches. A car that floats can drift into deeper water or into a current. Water that is calm at the moment of a stall may not stay calm.

Staying inside carries its own problems. Electrical systems can fail once they are submerged. That can leave power windows unusable. Doors also become hard to push open once water presses against them from outside. Each minute spent waiting makes the exit harder.

The order of action is to leave the car first. The vehicle can be inspected and reported to an insurer once the water recedes.

Higher ground means a spot above the water line and away from the path the water is taking — a raised road shoulder, a hill or an elevated structure. Low ground near the stalled car can flood next.

This advice applies to standing water. If the water around the car is moving fast, the situation is different. Wading into swift current is dangerous, and the guidance shifts to climbing onto the roof and calling 911. Reading which kind of water surrounds the car is the first decision a stranded driver makes.

If a car goes into water and begins to sink, unbuckle, open a window and climb out right away. The window, not the door, is the exit, and the best moment to use it is the first moment the car is in the water.

Every second in the water makes escape harder. As water rises along the outside of the car, it presses against the doors. That pressure can make a door difficult or impossible to push open, even for a strong adult.

An open window avoids that problem. It gives a direct route out that does not depend on fighting the weight of the water outside. Electrical systems can fail once they are submerged. Lowering a power window while the car still has power gives it the best chance of moving.

The seat belt comes first. A buckled belt holds a driver in place, and panic can make the release harder to find by feel. Unclipping it immediately frees the body to turn toward the window.

Waiting inside does not help. Some drivers assume they should stay put until the cabin fills and the pressure on the doors evens out. That approach leaves them in a flooding space with less air, less time and less control. The safer choice is to leave early, while the car is still near the surface.

Passengers change the order of operations only slightly. Children who cannot unbuckle themselves need help with their harnesses or belts. They should go out through the window ahead of the adult. That way, no one is left behind in a cabin taking on water.

A phone call can wait. Dialing 911 from inside a sinking car uses up seconds that are better spent leaving it. The call can be made once everyone is out of the vehicle.

Once out, the priority is getting clear of the vehicle and toward safety. If the side windows will not open at all, breaking the glass becomes the fallback route.

A spring-loaded window punch or a hammer-style escape tool can break a car's side window when floodwater has knocked out the power windows. Aim it at a side window, not the windshield, which is built to resist breaking.

Power windows depend on the car's electrical system. Once that system is submerged, it can fail and leave the window switches dead. A driver who planned to lower the glass and climb out may find it stuck in place. An escape tool gives that driver another way through.

The two common designs work in different ways. A spring-loaded punch is pressed firmly against the glass. Pressure builds inside the tool until a spring drives a hardened pin against the window. It needs almost no swinging room. That helps in a cramped cabin or with water around the driver's arms.

A hammer-style tool has a pointed steel head on a short handle and is swung against the glass. Many hammer-style models also carry a recessed blade for cutting through a jammed seatbelt.

Glass type decides which window to target. Side windows are usually tempered glass. Tempered glass is heat-treated so that a sharp, concentrated impact breaks the whole pane into small, granular pieces. That is why a small pointed tip can clear a side window opening.

Windshields are laminated, with a layer of plastic bonded between two sheets of glass. When struck, laminated glass cracks but tends to stay in one piece, held together by that interlayer. Breaking through it is much harder, so it is a poor escape route.

Some vehicles also use laminated glass in their side windows, often to cut road noise. The small printed marking in the corner of each window often identifies the glass type. The owner's manual can confirm it. If the front side windows are laminated, a rear side window may be the better exit.

A tool helps only if the driver can reach it quickly. One kept in the trunk or under clutter in the glove box may be out of reach once water enters the cabin. A keychain, a door pocket or the center console keeps it within the driver's grasp. Every adult who rides in the car regularly should know where it is and how it works.

If moving floodwater traps your car, get onto the roof if you can and call 911. Do not try to wade through fast-moving water to reach dry ground.

This advice covers a different situation from a car stalled in still water. When a strong current flows around the vehicle, stepping off it puts a person directly into the flow. The roof keeps the body above the water and out of its push.

The roof is usually the highest point a stranded driver can reach. Sitting or lying flat there keeps the body lower and steadier than standing. Holding onto a roof rack, the edge of the roof or the top of the door frame helps if the car rocks or shifts.

A 911 call from the roof should start with location. Dispatchers need the road name, the direction of travel and the nearest cross street or highway exit. A nearby landmark, such as a bridge, a business sign or a mile marker, can narrow the search. Saying plainly that people are on top of a car in moving water tells the dispatcher what kind of rescue is needed. The number of people, along with the color and type of vehicle, helps responders find the right car.

Text-to-911 works in many U.S. areas, though not everywhere. Where the service is not offered, the sender should receive an automatic reply saying so.

Wading out is the step to avoid. Fast water pushes against the legs with steady force, and the ground beneath it cannot be seen. A stretch that looks shallow can drop away without warning. The current also carries branches and other debris that can strike or pin a person.

Once on the roof, the safer course is to stay put and wait for trained rescuers instead of swimming or walking out. At night, a flashlight or a lit phone screen can help crews spot the car. Keeping the phone dry and saving its battery keeps the line to dispatchers open.

Walking through floodwater exposes a person to hazards they cannot see, including submerged debris, open storm drains, contamination and downed power lines. Anyone who has left a car should head straight for higher ground and stay out of the water wherever possible.

Murky water hides what lies underneath. A path that was solid before a storm can be covered with branches, broken fencing, rocks or pieces of damaged vehicles. Any of these can trip a person or cut a foot or leg. A fall in moving water is much harder to recover from than a fall on dry pavement.

Open drains are a separate risk. Rushing water can push manhole covers and storm drain grates out of place. A pedestrian has no way to tell where the opening is. A single step can drop a leg, or a whole body, into a drain that is pulling water downward.

Current adds force to every one of these hazards. The National Weather Service and FEMA put the threshold low: about six inches of moving water can knock an adult off their feet. Water that shallow can look harmless from the edge of a road. Once a person is down, the current can carry them into debris or toward a drain.

Floodwater is also dirty. It can carry sewage, fuel, chemicals and other contamination picked up as it moves across streets, yards and industrial sites. Cuts and scrapes from hidden debris give that contamination a way into the body. Anyone who touches floodwater should wash with soap and clean water as soon as possible.

Electrical hazards are easy to miss. Storms bring down power lines, and a line lying in water can sit hidden below the surface. Water conducts electricity. A downed line can energize the water around it. Stay well away from any downed line and report it to the local utility.

The safest route is the one that avoids water entirely. After leaving a vehicle, look for the nearest high point, such as a hill, a raised embankment or an upper floor of a sturdy building. Move there without wading through current. If every way out crosses moving water, waiting on the highest available ground is safer than attempting the crossing.

Never drive around a road barricade during a flood. Low-water crossings, underpasses and dips are among the first places to fill with water in heavy rain. Darkness or a downpour makes that water much harder to see from behind the wheel.

A barricade marks a road that crews have already closed because of a hazard. Whatever made them close it may sit under the water or farther down the road, out of view. Moving a barrier or steering around it throws away the clearest warning a driver will get. It can also leave the road looking open to the drivers who arrive next.

Dips collect water because they are the lowest point on a stretch of road. Rain running off the surrounding pavement and ground drains toward them. In a heavy storm, a dip can fill with standing or moving water long before the rain stops.

Underpasses carry the same risk for a similar reason. A road that passes beneath a railway or highway sits below the ground around it. During intense rain, water can flow in from several directions faster than drains can clear it. A driver entering an underpass may not see how deep the water is until the car is already in it.

Low-water crossings are built where a road meets a creek or wash at stream level instead of on a bridge. They are designed for water to flow over them when the stream rises. In a flash flood, the creek can run across the road with force. The water feeding it may come from rain that fell well upstream, out of the driver's sight.

Night driving adds another layer of risk. Headlights show only a limited stretch of road ahead. Floodwater can look like ordinary wet pavement in the dark. Heavy rain cuts visibility further, even with wipers on their fastest setting.

Planning helps before the storm arrives. When heavy rain is in the forecast, drivers can choose routes that avoid known dips, underpasses and creek crossings. A flooded crossing or underpass can also be reported to local authorities, who decide when a road needs to be closed.

Do not restart a car that has sat in floodwater. Turning over an engine with water inside it can cause serious damage. Photograph the vehicle and contact your insurer before making any other decision about it.

A flooded car can look normal once the water drains away. The floor mats dry out and the body panels shed their mud. The engine may even seem ready to run. None of that shows what happened inside the engine or under the dashboard.

An engine is designed to compress a mix of air and fuel. Water does not compress. If water has reached the cylinders, starting the engine can force the moving parts against it. Mechanics call this hydrolock, and it can bend internal components. The ignition key, the push-button start and any jump-start attempt should all stay off-limits.

The engine is not the only system at risk. Electrical systems can fail once they have been submerged. A car that powers up normally may still have water in its wiring. Have the car towed rather than driven, even if it appears to work.

Return to the car only after the water has gone down and the area is safe to reach. Floodwater can carry contamination. Soaked seats, carpets and trim may hold more than water. Wearing gloves while handling wet items inside the cabin limits contact with whatever the flood left behind.

Photographs are the core of any damage record. Take wide shots of every side of the car, then close-ups of the seats, floor, dashboard and engine bay. Capture any line the water left on the doors or upholstery, because it shows how high the flood rose. Take these pictures before cleaning anything or having the car towed.

Then call the insurer and start a claim. Whether flood damage is covered depends on the specific policy. Do not assume the damage is either covered or excluded. Ask the insurer which part of the policy applies and what documentation it needs. Ask, too, whether an adjuster will inspect the car before any repair begins.

#5469. PitchBook to give early-stage startups free access, using their data to feed a new tool for VCs

by Todd Bishop on Nov 10, 2026 at 7:23 amNovember 10, 2026 at 7:25 am

PitchBook announced a new program to give early-stage startups free use of its private-market data, if they share their financials and other company details.

The Seattle-based company says the new program, dubbed PitchBook for Startups, will feed PitchBook Origin, a new deal-sourcing product that helps venture capitalists and other investors find startups before they raise their first institutional round.

PitchBook announced both offerings Tuesday morning at Web Summit in Lisbon. Owned by Morningstar since 2016, the company has more than 3,000 employees and sells subscriptions to venture firms, private equity investors and dealmakers.

The launches come as first-time startup financings hit a record. There were an estimated 8,625 such deals in the U.S. through the third quarter, already more than the 8,507 in all of 2021, according to the PitchBook-NVCA Venture Monitor. PitchBook attributes part of the surge to AI, which it says is making it easier to start companies.

The startup program is open to pre-seed and bootstrapped companies that haven’t taken money from a venture firm or other institutional investor, or raised a priced round, the type of funding round that sets a valuation.

Founders can use PitchBook to find investors who are active in their sector and stage, and to compare their valuation and growth against similar companies.

To keep their free access, startups must update their company information every quarter. PitchBook says that information can include financials, team growth and product milestones. Only “select portions” of that data will go into Origin, the company said, without saying which.

Origin covers about 25 million companies, including stealth, pre-funding and bootstrapped companies. About 15 million of them are new to PitchBook. It scores companies on how well they match an investor’s criteria and sends alerts when they show new activity.

“What’s been missing is visibility into the stage before a company raises, when the most important signals are the hardest to see,” said Paul Santarelli, PitchBook’s chief solutions officer, in a statement announcing the products.

PitchBook didn’t disclose pricing for Origin, and the product’s web page currently asks investors to join a waitlist.

In just a few weeks, AWS re:Invent brings advanced and expert-level sessions on the services you build on every day, from serverless and containers to databases and developer tools. Go hands-on with new launches the same week they’re announced, and hear directly from the engineers who built them. Experience the depth you won’t find anywhere else.

#5468. Silicon Valley’s richest outspent supporters more than 10 to one to kill California’s billionaire tax—and won

California voters rejected a proposed tax on the state’s billionaires after some of Silicon Valley’s wealthiest executives and investors spent $378.4 million to defeat it—delivering a victory to a coalition led by Google cofounder Sergey Brin.

The Associated Press called the race on Monday, with 52.8% of voters opposing Proposition 40 and 47.2% supporting it. The votes needed to pass the measure had trailed for days.

The defeat means—at least for now—an effort to make California the first state to impose a one-time tax on its billionaires has ended. It also represents a significant win for the Silicon Valley executives who have come together to block the measure.

Approximately 52.8% of voters opposed Proposition 40, whereas 47.2% supported it. According to CalMatters, ultrawealthy opponents collectively contributed $378.4 million to efforts opposing the tax and related countermeasures like Props 41 and 42. That amount is more than 10 times the $33.5 million raised by supporters of Proposition 40.

Proposition 40 would have imposed a one-time 5% tax on the net worth of individuals worth more than $1 billion who were California residents on Jan. 1, 2026. The proposed tax covered financial assets and other forms of wealth, rather than just income.

Under the proposal, approximately 90% of the revenue would have gone toward healthcare services, with the remaining 10% allocated to education and food assistance. The Legislative Analyst’s Office estimated that the measure could generate “tens of billions” of dollars.

The initiative was introduced by Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West, which argued that California needed additional revenue to address healthcare funding shortfalls following federal spending reductions under President Donald Trump’s tax and spending legislation. The measure also received support from Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders, U.S. Rep. Ro Khanna, the California Democratic party and several labor organizations.

But not every Democrat and Californian was on the same page. The proposal faced opposition from prominent Democrats including Gov. Gavin Newsom, who argued that a state-level wealth tax would push wealthy residents and their businesses out of the state. Instead, Newsom said he would support a national wealth tax. San Francisco Democrats also opposed the measure, voting 17-4 against Prop 40 in August, while U.S. Rep. Nancy Pelosi, a member of the local party, voted “no endorsement.”

“Here is what I support: A national billionaires’ tax,” Newsom wrote in a post on Substack in June. “A true minimum tax on billionaires—a modern Buffett Rule—that ensures the people at the very top pay at least the tax rate their own workers pay.”

The campaign against the proposition was financed by some of the most prominent figures in the tech, finance and investment industries—with Brin emerging as its largest individual financial backer.

Brin contributed approximately $102 million to Building a Better California, a political committee he established in January that became the main vehicle opposing the wealth tax. The contributions made Brin one of the most consequential financial players in California’s 2026 ballot-measure fight. He relocated to Nevada in December 2025—making his fortune, estimated at $231 billion by Bloomberg, potentially exempt from the tax.

Eric Schmidt, Google’s former CEO, was also a major contributor to the opposition effort. According to campaign finance filings, he contributed $40.2 million to the campaign.

Other prominent tech executives and investors also contributed millions, including DoorDash CEO Tony Xu, Stripe cofounder Patrick Collison, venture capitalist John Doerr, cryptocurrency entrepreneur Chris Larsen and former Sequoia Capital partner Michael Moritz.

The contributions were also not limited to Building a Better California’s fight against Prop 40. Through Oct. 20, Building a Better California spent more than $304 million supporting efforts to defeat Proposition 40 and advance Propositions 41 and 42—direct counters to the wealth tax. Of that amount, approximately $118.5 million went toward opposing Proposition 40, while the other $186 million supported Propositions 41 and 42, according to Capital & Main.

Proposition 41 would “require preelection audits for initiatives proposing special taxes and additional audits every four years. It also would prohibit new tax revenue from being exempted from state spending limits,” making it harder for the state to use funds raised by the billionaire tax. Proposition 42 would “prohibit taxes on personal savings, assets and retirement holdings”—outlawing retroactive taxation, directly countering Proposition 40. According to the Legislative Analyst’s Office, if either one gets more “yes” votes than Proposition 40, the wealth tax could be stopped even if it is approved.

And while the wealth tax didn’t get approved, a ballot measure meant to block it did. According to the AP, Proposition 41 did not pass by voters while Proposition 42 did—meaning Proposition 40 would have been shot down if it had passed regardless.

According to Politico, more than 70 current and former California billionaires had spent a record $612 million into the state elections this cycle. Of that money, at least 30 billionaires had contributed more than $293 million specifically to the wealth tax fight.

Joshua Hong is a News Fellow at Fortune covering data, AI, cybersecurity, energy, and retail.

#5467. 10 flash flood checklist steps for your home, car and household

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Knowing how to prepare for a flash flood starts long before the rain, with 10 practical steps covering alerts, emergency kits, insurance, evacuation routes and safer driving

A flash flood leaves almost no room for improvisation. The National Weather Service defines it as rapid flooding of low-lying areas, usually within six hours of heavy rain or a similar cause. That short window means the useful decisions happen well before the storm. Once water is rising in a street or a basement, the time for gathering supplies, reading insurance terms or choosing a route has passed.

That is the core of how to prepare for a flash flood: move as much of the work as possible to a calm, dry day. A household that already knows its risk, its alerts and its exit routes can act on a warning quickly instead of scrambling under pressure.

Risk also extends beyond the obvious places. Official flood maps are a useful starting point, but flash flooding does not stay inside mapped high-risk zones. Dry creek beds and land scarred by wildfire can turn dangerous during heavy rain.

The 10 steps that follow are a practical selection of preparations, grouped into three broad stages. The first steps cover knowing your exposure and making sure an alert actually reaches you. The next ones turn to supplies and paperwork: an emergency kit and protected documents. The rest address plans that are hard to make in the moment. Those include evacuation routes, flood insurance, readying the home, driving near water and caring for relatives and pets with extra needs.

Each step stands on its own. A reader can start anywhere and work through one item at a time.

Most of the resources named here are U.S. agencies and programs. They include the Federal Emergency Management Agency, the National Weather Service, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, the National Flood Insurance Program and Ready.gov, the federal government's preparedness site. Readers outside the U.S. can apply the same principles through their own national weather service and local emergency authorities. Alert systems and insurance options differ by country.

The aim is not to predict the next storm. It is to make sure that when a warning arrives, the household's next moves are already settled.

U.S. residents can look up the flood risk for a specific address through FEMA's Flood Map Service Center at msc.fema.gov. That result is a first reading, not a guarantee. Flash floods also strike places outside mapped high-risk zones.

The Flood Map Service Center is run by the Federal Emergency Management Agency. A user enters a street address, and the site shows the flood map information on file for that location. The same lookup works for a current home, a rental or a property a household is considering buying.

A map is one layer of information. A home can sit outside a zone labeled high risk and still lie in the path of a flash flood. Three kinds of terrain show how that can happen.

Dry creek beds are the first. A channel that holds no water for most of the year can fill quickly during heavy rain. A house beside a dry wash or arroyo carries flash flood exposure, even when no stream is visible from the yard.

Low-water crossings are the second. These are spots where a road dips through a creek or drainage channel instead of crossing it on a raised bridge. A home reached only by such a crossing can be cut off even if the building itself stays dry.

Burn scars are the third. Land stripped of vegetation by wildfire is one of the places where flash floods can occur outside mapped zones. Residents near recently burned hillsides should count that as part of their risk.

Knowing the risk at an address shapes the rest of a household's flood planning. It helps decide where an emergency kit and important papers are stored. It also helps determine which routes out of the neighborhood make sense when water starts to rise.

FEMA's maps cover U.S. addresses only. Readers in other countries can check with their national weather service or local authorities for comparable flood risk information.

A flash flood watch means conditions are favorable for flash flooding. A flash flood warning means flash flooding is occurring or imminent, and anyone in the warned area should move to higher ground immediately.

The National Weather Service issues both alerts. The two names differ by a single word. The similarity makes them easy to mix up when a notice arrives late at night or in the middle of a heavy storm. In practice, one signals a time to get ready and the other signals a time to leave low ground.

A watch describes the setup, not the event. It tells people that the conditions for a flash flood are in place across the covered area. It does not mean water is rising yet, and it does not mean a flood will definitely happen.

That makes a watch the point to finish any preparation that would be hard to do later. Charging phones, confirming the emergency kit is where it should be and reviewing the household's route to higher ground each take minutes under a watch. The same tasks become much harder once water is moving.

A warning describes the event itself. It means flash flooding is already happening or is about to start in the warned area. The guidance at that stage is direct: move to higher ground right away. Waiting to see whether the water reaches the house uses up time that may not be available.

The two alerts also call for different questions. Under a watch, the useful question is whether the household is ready to leave quickly. Under a warning, the question is how to reach higher ground by the safest route available.

Readers outside the U.S. should check how their own national weather service labels flood alerts. Other agencies may use different terms, and those terms may not line up with the NWS watch and warning system.

A flash flood alert only helps if it reaches you. Keep Wireless Emergency Alerts turned on, keep a NOAA Weather Radio with battery backup at home and join your local government's alert system if it runs one.

Wireless Emergency Alerts are messages that authorities such as the National Weather Service send to compatible phones in an affected area. Delivery is based on where a phone is, not on a home address. A household member at work, at school or on the road can receive a warning for wherever they are at that moment. The same applies to a visitor passing through an unfamiliar town, who may have no idea which local roads tend to flood. Every phone user in the household should confirm that emergency alerts are switched on in the device settings.

Phone alerts have a weak point. They depend on cell service, and the phone depends on a charged battery. A severe storm can knock out power, cell service or both.

A NOAA Weather Radio covers that gap. A model with battery backup keeps working when the power goes out or the cell network fails. Place it where people in the household will hear it, including overnight, when phones may be silenced or out of reach. It also reaches anyone at home who does not carry a phone, such as young children or some older relatives. Check its batteries on a regular schedule so the backup is ready when it is needed.

Many local governments also run their own alert systems. These are opt-in, which means residents have to sign up to receive them. A city or county website or emergency management office is the place to find out whether one exists and how to enroll. Enrolling before storm season avoids hunting for the sign-up page while a storm is already underway.

Each channel protects against a different failure. Using all three makes it less likely that one outage leaves a household without warning.

A flood emergency kit built to Ready.gov guidance starts with water: one gallon per person per day, enough for several days. Store the finished kit above the level floodwater is likely to reach. That keeps the supplies dry and within reach.

Water takes up more space than anything else in the kit. The amount adds up quickly. A household of four needs four gallons for each day the kit is meant to cover. Plan the storage space around the water first, then fit everything else in.

Nonperishable food is the next layer. These items keep for long stretches without refrigeration. That matters if a flood knocks out power. Pick foods the household already eats and that need little or no cooking. Unfamiliar or hard-to-prepare items are harder to use when a household is under pressure.

Light and information come next. Ready.gov lists a flashlight, extra batteries and a battery-powered or hand-crank radio. A hand-crank model makes its own power when the handle is turned. It keeps working after the spare batteries run out. A radio lets a household follow updates when phones are dead or networks are down.

Health supplies belong in the same container. A first aid kit covers minor cuts and scrapes. Medications are on the Ready.gov list as well. Anyone in the household who takes a daily prescription should have a supply packed with the kit, not left in a bathroom cabinet.

Ready.gov also lists a whistle. It is small and light, and it gives someone a way to signal for help if they are stranded or trapped.

Copies of important documents round out the list. Packing a set in the kit means proof of identity and insurance leave the house with everyone else.

Where the kit sits matters as much as what is in it. A shelf on an upper floor or a high closet shelf works better than a basement or garage floor, where water tends to collect first. Keeping everything in one container that a single person can carry makes it easy to grab when it is time to leave.

A kit also needs regular upkeep. Swap in fresh batteries, rotate food and water before they go stale, and replace medications before they expire.

Seal passports, insurance policies, birth certificates and property deeds in waterproof containers, and keep digital copies somewhere you can reach from anywhere. Doing both gives a household a backup if the originals are soaked, lost or left behind.

A flash flood can leave very little time to gather paperwork. Documents sorted into one sealed container ahead of time can be picked up in seconds on the way out the door.

The papers worth protecting first are the ones that prove identity, citizenship and ownership. Passports and birth certificates establish who each household member is. Deeds document who owns a property. Insurance policies record the coverage a household has in place.

Where the container sits also matters. Floodwater rises from the ground up. An upper floor is a safer spot for a document box than a basement or a ground-level closet.

A copy of the insurance policy is useful after the water recedes. It keeps the policy number and the insurer's contact details on hand, which a household needs to start a claim.

Digital copies add a second layer of protection. Scanning or photographing each document and saving the files to a secure cloud account makes them retrievable from a phone or another computer. That access holds even if the house cannot be reached. Losing the physical box does not mean losing the record.

A portable drive is the other option for digital backups. A drive left behind in the house offers no backup if the house floods. Packed in its own waterproof container alongside the paper originals, it can leave with the household during an evacuation.

The stored set needs to stay current. When an insurance policy renews or a passport is replaced, the copy in the container and the file in the cloud should be swapped for the new version.

Keeping the document container near the household's flood emergency kit, above likely water levels, lets both be carried out in a single trip.

Choose at least two routes from your home to higher ground, and plan both so they avoid low-lying roads, underpasses and bridges over creeks. Then agree on a household meeting place and name a contact person who lives outside your area.

The second route exists for the moment the first one is cut off. Floodwater collects in the lowest ground first. The roads most likely to become impassable are the ones that dip below their surroundings, run beneath rail lines or highways, or cross a stream. A route that avoids all three gives a household a better chance of getting out before water closes the way.

Start by tracing each route on a map. Follow it from the front door to the destination and mark every point where the road drops, passes under something or crosses water. Each marked point is a spot to plan around. Two routes that share the same weak point are really one route.

A meeting place matters because a flash flood can arrive while a household is spread out, with people at work, at school or on the road. Pick a single spot on higher ground that every member can reach by at least one of the planned routes. Everyone then has the same destination, even if they cannot reach home or contact one another.

The out-of-area contact serves a different purpose. A person living outside the flooded area is less likely to be dealing with the same emergency. Each household member can check in with that one person, who can pass updates along to the others. Write the contact's number on paper as well as saving it in a phone. A paper copy still works if a phone is lost or its battery dies.

Share the routes, the meeting place and the contact with everyone in the household, including children old enough to follow the plan. Revisit the plan after a move or a change in the roads nearby.

Standard homeowners insurance policies generally do not cover flood damage. Flood coverage is a separate purchase, and a National Flood Insurance Program policy typically takes 30 days to take effect.

That waiting period is the reason to buy early. Coverage needs to be in place well before rain shows up in a forecast. Unlike an emergency kit or an evacuation route, a flood policy cannot be pulled together at the last minute. The calendar, not the weather, decides when it starts.

The first move is to read the current homeowners policy. Its terms, or a direct question to the insurer, will show whether flood damage is excluded.

The National Flood Insurance Program, known as the NFIP, is run by FEMA, the U.S. Federal Emergency Management Agency. It is not the only source of flood coverage. Private insurers also sell flood policies. A homeowner can compare both routes before choosing. A useful comparison looks at when each policy begins and what each one covers, not only at the price.

A flash flood can develop within hours of heavy rain. The typical NFIP wait is 30 days. A household that starts shopping for coverage after a flash flood watch is issued has already missed the window. Under the typical rule, an NFIP policy bought at that point would not cover the flood that follows.

A limited number of exceptions to the wait exist. An insurance agent or the NFIP can confirm whether any of them applies to a particular purchase.

A home's flood map designation does not change what a standard policy covers. A homeowners policy generally excludes flood damage wherever the home sits. An owner outside a high-risk zone faces the same exclusion as one inside it.

Private flood policies set their own terms, which can differ from the NFIP's. The start date printed on any flood policy shows when protection actually begins. Comparing that date with the purchase date shows whether a waiting period applies.

Find your home's main electrical panel, main water valve and gas shutoff before storm season, and move valuables and electronics to an upper floor ahead of heavy rain. Both tasks are simple on a dry day and much harder once water is coming in.

Start with the utilities. Walk through the house and note where each shutoff sits, whether that is a basement wall, a garage, a utility closet or an outside meter. Every adult in the household should know these locations. Each of them should also know how to operate every valve and switch, not just where it is. A flash flood can arrive when the person who usually handles home repairs is away.

The most important rule involves electricity. Never touch electrical equipment, including the breaker panel, appliances and extension cords, while standing in water. If the floor around the panel is already wet, leave it alone. Shutting off power is a step to take while conditions are still dry. It is not a reason to wade back inside.

Then move the things you can least afford to lose. Computers, televisions, game consoles and external drives belong on an upper floor rather than in a basement or on the ground floor. Family photographs, heirlooms, jewelry and other valuables belong there too. In a single-story home, high shelves and upper cabinets are the closest substitute. Unplug electronics before carrying them upstairs.

Outside, clear gutters, downspouts and nearby drains of leaves and debris. Blocked drainage leaves heavy rain fewer places to go, and water that cannot run off collects around the foundation. Check them again when heavy rain is in the forecast.

Sandbags are a limited measure. A row of them may help in some situations, but they do not make a house floodproof. Filling and stacking them should never take priority over leaving when officials tell residents to move to higher ground.

Never drive into a flooded road, and never steer around a barricade that blocks one. The National Weather Service sums up that rule in four words: "Turn Around, Don't Drown."

The slogan rests on how little water it takes to cause harm. The National Weather Service has said that six inches of moving water can knock an adult off their feet. The agency has also said that 12 inches of moving water can carry away a small car.

Those two figures describe two separate dangers. The first applies to anyone who leaves a stalled vehicle or tries to wade across a flooded street. The second applies to anyone who stays behind the wheel and expects the car to push through.

A foot of water is also enough to float many vehicles. A car that floats has lost its grip on the road. Its driver can no longer steer it. From that point, the current decides where the vehicle goes.

The key word in the agency's figures is "moving." A flash flood sends water across roads with force, and that force acts on anything in its path. A stretch of road that looks shallow can still push hard against a person or a car.

Barricades follow the same logic. Authorities close a flooded road because crossing it is unsafe. Driving around the barrier puts a driver into the exact conditions the closure was meant to prevent.

Walking through floodwater carries its own risk beyond the current. Floodwater can carry contaminants. That makes contact with it a health hazard as well as a drowning hazard. Anyone moving on foot should choose a path that stays out of the water entirely.

The practical step is to settle the decision before the rain starts. Agree as a household that no one drives into water covering a road, whatever its apparent depth. If a road ahead is underwater, the response is fixed in advance: stop, turn back and find another way out.

A flash flood evacuation plan must cover household members who cannot simply grab a bag and go. People who rely on medical devices, mobility aids or regular medications need their own arrangements, as do pets. Those arrangements belong in place well before a warning arrives.

Start with the people. List anyone in the home who uses equipment that runs on electricity, such as an oxygen concentrator or a powered wheelchair. Power can fail during a flood. A device that stops working turns an evacuation into a medical emergency. Ask the equipment supplier or prescribing doctor about battery backup options and how long a full charge lasts.

Mobility aids raise a different problem. A walker, cane or manual wheelchair has to travel with its owner. Someone who moves slowly also needs more lead time than the rest of the household. Decide in advance who will help that person and which vehicle has room for the equipment. Pick an exit from the home that avoids stairs or steep ground.

Regular medications call for a written record. Keep a current list of drug names, doses and prescribing doctors, along with pharmacy contact details. That list helps a shelter clinic or an unfamiliar pharmacy refill a prescription if the original bottles are lost or soaked.

Local emergency management offices are the next call. Some keep assistance registries for residents who would need help evacuating. Enrolling can alert responders in advance that a household may need help. Contact the county or city office directly to ask whether a registry exists and how to enroll.

Pets need a parallel plan. Keep a carrier for each animal that rides in one, plus leashes, several days of food and copies of vaccination records. Those records make it easier to place an animal in a shelter, kennel or boarding facility on short notice. Not every emergency shelter takes pets. Identify the ones that do ahead of time. Line up pet-friendly hotels or friends outside the flood area as backups.

The plan should also cover the trip home. Wait for local officials to give an official all-clear before bringing anyone back. Confirm that powered medical equipment will have a working outlet or a charged battery when the household returns.

#5466. Allen Family Philanthropies gives $10M to hundreds of small arts groups across Washington state

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 10, 2026 at 7:30 amNovember 9, 2026 at 2:56 pm

Allen Family Philanthropies and Seattle nonprofit ArtsFund awarded $10 million to 745 small arts and culture organizations across Washington state, and renewed the grant program for another $10 million next year.

The latest Community Accelerator Grant awards range from $2,500 to $25,000 and reach organizations in 37 of the state’s 39 counties. The 2027 renewal brings the program’s total to $50 million over five years.

For 2026, the program focused on groups with annual budgets under $1 million, which raised the average award by about 25%, from $10,753 last year to $13,423.

The change followed a sector analysis by Allen Family Philanthropies and SMU DataArts. It found that smaller arts groups lost an average of one staff position between 2023 and 2024, while organizations with budgets over $1 million added an average of five.

“The incredible reach of this program across our state, along with the significant findings from our report, show just how much this type of flexible support is needed to bolster Washington’s rich and diverse arts and culture sector,” said Lara Littlefield, executive director of Allen Family Philanthropies.

Of this year’s grantees, 496 are in Northwest Washington, 132 in Southwest, 67 in Eastern and 50 in Central Washington. Recipients include 12 of the state’s 29 federally recognized tribes, and more than 22% are in rural counties.

A handful of the organizations blend art and technology, including Tacoma’s Fablab Nonprofit ($25,000), Seattle-based Simulated Immersive Experimental Realities ($15,000) and Bellingham Makerspace ($2,500).

The Old Hotel Art Gallery in Othello, in Adams County, has received a $25,000 grant each year since 2024. The gallery used the money to pay staff a living wage, to keep operating until its annual fundraiser, and to renovate its historic building, which now brings in rental income.

Gallery director Samantha Copas said the 2025 award “truly kept our doors open.”

Allen Family Philanthropies, formerly known as the Paul G. Allen Family Foundation, was founded in 1988 by the late Microsoft co-founder and his sister, Jody Allen. Arts and culture is one of its core program areas, along with youth and the environment. Last year the foundation committed nearly $7 million to eight Seattle Center nonprofits, including KEXP and the Museum of Pop Culture, to expand youth access to the arts.

ArtsFund will hold a virtual webinar in the spring for organizations interested in applying for 2027 grants. Details will be posted here.

See the full list of 2026 grant recipients here.

#5465. Yield-Bearing eZAR Blurs the Line Between Stablecoin and Investment Product

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

eZAR opened its rand-pegged token to the public on November 2 with R303 million in circulation. Its reserve yield is the feature that puts the stablecoin label to the test.

Most stablecoin launches promise a token that never moves. eZAR's disclosures say its holders can make money or lose it. The rand-pegged token went live to the public on November 2, and its fine print reads more like an investment product than a payments coin.

According to launch reports, eZAR is now open to the public and to new institutional partners after almost a year of pilot operations. The company says R303 million worth of tokens had been issued and were in circulation as of October 30.

The project is a partnership between eZAR Ltd, asset manager Ninety One and AVBOB Financial Services, with AVBOB acting as lead institution and liquidity partner. CEO Sean Emery said the team put "getting it right" ahead of "getting it big" during the pilot. The message now is that eZAR is ready to scale.

The model also departs from the typical single-issuer coin. Neobanks, retailers, insurers and payment firms can plug the token into their own branded wallets and share in the economics. Transfers between participating wallets settle within seconds at any hour and, according to the company, cost nothing.

The reserves backing eZAR are invested through a money market strategy run by Ninety One, mainly in the Ninety One Money Market Fund. Returns are distributed daily to partners after partnership fees, and each partner then decides on what terms its own customers receive a share.

Ninety One's head of digital assets, Adam Duxbury, described it as new rails under an old discipline. His firm has run money market strategies for 25 years, he said, and South Africa should build its own digital rand rather than import a dollar coin.

The framing is clever, since it presents the yield as a feature of "digital cash that can grow." Yet that same feature makes the classification question hard to avoid.

The risk language is the most revealing part of the launch. eZAR describes itself as a crypto asset issued by the eZAR En Commandite Partnership. It states that the token is not legal tender, not a bank deposit and not a banking product, and that it carries no guarantee.

The details that follow set it further apart. The R1 redemption value depends on available liquidity. Money market returns can be positive or negative, so capital is at risk. Holders also own no units in the underlying fund and have no direct claim on it.

"Capital at risk" rarely appears in stablecoin terms. A payments token is meant to hold its value and let users redeem at par, yet eZAR's own documents hedge on both counts. Back in March, a market survey from Blockhouse had already noted that eZAR doesn't qualify as a stablecoin under most regulations. The live launch now tests that observation against a real product.

In the major rulebooks, the yield is the sticking point. The US GENIUS Act bars permitted payment stablecoin issuers from paying holders any form of interest or yield solely for holding, using or retaining the token. The EU's MiCA framework takes a similar line on interest. The logic is that a payment token paying a return starts to function like an unregulated deposit.

The OCC issued its final GENIUS Act rules on October 21, and they confirmed that ban for covered issuers. The contested ground lies elsewhere, in who sits between the issuer and the holder. Earlier OCC proposals set a rebuttable presumption against yield arrangements run through affiliates and related third parties, whereas the statute itself names only issuers.

eZAR's design lands squarely in that gray zone. Returns flow to partners, and the partners decide how customers share in them. Whether that amounts to an issuer paying yield or a partner passing on profit is precisely the kind of question US regulators are now wrestling with, and it would be a difficult one to argue before the OCC.

eZAR doesn't operate under the US or EU regimes, so none of those rules apply to it directly. eZAR Ltd is described as an authorised financial services provider responsible for the main technology and services behind the partnership. That technology also draws on the South African Reserve Bank's Project Khokha 2, where eZAR's parent company, Block Markets Africa, was a technical contributor.

This background signals a serious, institution-backed build rather than a speculative launch. Even so, the rand stablecoin field is getting crowded. ZARU launched earlier this year as an institutional-grade rand coin, and a pattern is emerging of different models competing for the same local payments niche.

The bigger question is whether South Africa will define stablecoins narrowly, as the US and EU do, or leave room for hybrid products like this one. Because the network is permissioned, the reported circulation figure also rests on company disclosure rather than a public ledger, which makes the regulatory and disclosure framework matter even more.

For everyday users, the appeal is easy to see. A rand token that moves in seconds, costs nothing to send and might earn a daily return makes an attractive pitch. For partners, shared infrastructure with a revenue share offers a way into digital payments without building a coin from scratch.

The trade-off sits in the disclaimers. A holder who treats eZAR like a bank balance could be caught off guard by liquidity-dependent redemption, or by a money market return that dips below zero. That gap between how the product feels and how it is legally defined is where regulators tend to step in.

eZAR is best understood as a hybrid: a payments token with an investment return attached. It may well succeed on those terms. Still, as more jurisdictions tighten the stablecoin definition around no-yield, par-redemption tokens, products like this will increasingly be judged on what they are rather than what they are called. How South African regulators treat eZAR in the coming months will show which way that debate is heading.
