#5464. Flood insurance explained: 10 things to know about the NFIP, private policies and claims

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Standard homeowners insurance does not cover flood damage, and this guide explains how the NFIP, private flood policies, waiting periods, coverage limits and claims work

A burst pipe and a swollen river can leave the same water stain on a living room floor. A standard homeowners policy treats them very differently. Water that escapes suddenly from plumbing inside the house is generally covered. Water that rises from outside and pours through the front door generally is not.

That line answers a basic question: does homeowners insurance cover flood damage? For most U.S. homeowners with a standard policy, the answer is no. Flood is written into the policy as an exclusion, alongside surface water and the overflow of a body of water. Protection against rising water has to be bought separately.

Two main sources fill the gap. The National Flood Insurance Program, or NFIP, is administered by FEMA. It sells policies through participating private insurers and directly to consumers. Private insurers also write their own flood policies, with terms that differ from the federal program and from one another.

The line between a flood and other kinds of water damage has more than one edge. Water that backs up through a sewer or drain is treated as a separate risk from flood. Standard policies usually exclude it too. Covering it takes an optional endorsement.

Buying a policy is only part of the picture. Several rules shape what a flooded homeowner actually recovers. Flood insurance does not take effect the moment it is purchased. Some mortgage borrowers are required by federal law to carry it, depending on where the home sits on FEMA's flood maps. Federal flood policies cap what they pay and leave out certain parts of a home, belongings and expenses. Claims carry their own paperwork and deadlines. Federal disaster aid comes with conditions of its own and does not replace insurance.

The 10 slides that follow walk through each of these points. They start with the standard exclusion and how the federal program defines a flood. They explain which kinds of water damage a homeowners policy does pay for. They outline how the NFIP and private flood insurance work, and when sewer backup coverage applies. They close with flood zone requirements, waiting periods, coverage limits and the steps for filing a claim.

A standard homeowners insurance policy does not pay for flood damage. The HO-3 form, a widely used policy for owner-occupied single-family homes, names flood as a specific exclusion. A homeowner who wants protection from rising water has to buy a separate flood policy.

The HO-3 is often called a special form policy. It covers the house itself against any cause of loss the contract does not expressly rule out. That structure puts the weight of any water claim on the exclusions section. Flood is listed there by name.

The exclusion reaches further than the word flood alone suggests. Standard policies also rule out surface water, such as heavy rain that collects on the ground and flows into a home. They exclude the overflow of a body of water, such as a river, lake or stream that tops its banks. The standard wording used by many insurers also names waves, tides and tidal water.

That exclusion applies whether or not wind drives the water. The distinction shapes claims after hurricanes and other coastal storms. One storm can cause two kinds of damage to the same property. Wind that tears off shingles or breaks a window is generally a covered loss under the homeowners policy. Storm surge that pushes seawater into the ground floor is treated as flood and falls under the exclusion.

The standard form also contains what is known as an anti-concurrent causation clause. It says the exclusion applies regardless of any other cause that contributes to the loss at the same time or in sequence. A covered event that happens alongside flooding does not bring the flood damage itself into coverage.

The gap is not limited to the HO-3. Renters policies, known as HO-4, and condominium unit-owner policies, known as HO-6, exclude flood as well. Tenants and condo owners who want flood protection for their belongings or units need a separate policy too.

The exclusions section of an existing homeowners policy lists which kinds of water the contract leaves out. Wording can differ from one insurer to the next. The language in the policy itself decides how a water claim is handled.

The National Flood Insurance Program defines a flood as a general and temporary condition of inundation. It applies when two or more acres of normally dry land, or two or more properties, are partly or completely covered by water.

That definition is central to every flood policy the NFIP backs. It decides whether an event counts as a flood before any question of dollar amounts comes up. Water damage that falls outside it is not a flood under the program's terms.

The word "general" points to scale. A flood under this definition affects an area rather than a single room. The program sets two ways to meet that threshold. Water can cover at least two acres of land that is normally dry. Or it can reach at least two properties.

The word "temporary" matters as well. The definition describes a condition that arrives and then recedes. Land that sits underwater all the time, such as a pond, is not normally dry land. It cannot supply the acreage needed to meet the test.

Inundation can be partial or complete. A property does not need to be submerged to the roofline. Water covering part of the lot or part of the building can still count, as long as the scale test is met.

The NFIP names three causes. The first is the overflow of inland or tidal waters. Inland waters include rivers, streams and lakes that spill past their banks. Tidal waters include the ocean and connected bays. Seawater pushed ashore by a coastal storm falls into this category.

The second cause is an unusual and rapid accumulation or runoff of surface water. This part of the definition reaches homes far from any river or coastline. A heavy downpour can qualify when it pools across a neighborhood faster than the ground and drains can absorb it.

The third cause is mudflow. The definition counts mudflow as a flood when it inundates property in the same general and temporary way.

For a homeowner with a flood policy, the definition frames the first questions in a claim. Did the water come from one of the three named causes? Did it cover at least two acres of normally dry land or reach at least two properties? A yes to both places the loss within the program's meaning of a flood.

A standard homeowners policy generally pays for water damage that is sudden and accidental and starts inside the home. A burst pipe, a leaking dishwasher and a split washing machine hose are typical examples of covered losses.

The key test is how the water arrived and how quickly. Water that escapes from a plumbing, heating or air-conditioning system usually falls within the policy. The same is generally true of water from a household appliance or a fire sprinkler system.

Coverage often extends beyond the soaked floors and drywall. Standard forms such as the HO-3 typically pay to tear out and replace part of a wall or floor to reach the source of a leak. The broken pipe or failed appliance itself is usually not covered. The policy pays for the damage the water caused, not for the part that wore out.

Frozen pipes are a winter risk with their own condition attached. Damage from a pipe that freezes and bursts is generally covered. The standard HO-3 form sets a condition for vacant, unoccupied or under-construction homes, though. In those cases, the owner must have used reasonable care to maintain heat. The alternative is to have shut off the water supply and drained the system.

Rain is treated differently depending on how it gets inside. Rain that enters through a roof or window already damaged by a covered peril, such as wind or hail, is generally covered. Rain that seeps through an aging roof or a failed window seal, with no storm damage, typically is not.

Time is the other dividing line on water claims. Policies typically exclude damage from gradual leaks and from poor maintenance. A slow drip under a sink that rots a cabinet over months usually falls outside coverage. So does damage traced to wear and tear, deterioration or a neglected repair. Mold that grows from a long-running leak is often excluded or subject to a separate limit.

The exact terms vary by insurer and by state. The policy wording decides any individual claim. Homeowners can check the declarations page and the perils section of their own policy. Those pages show which water events are listed and which are excluded.

The National Flood Insurance Program, or NFIP, is the federal program that sells flood coverage to U.S. property owners. Congress created it through the National Flood Insurance Act of 1968, and FEMA, the Federal Emergency Management Agency, administers it.

Congress set up the program at a time when private flood coverage was hard to find. The NFIP gives owners in eligible areas a way to buy a separate flood policy backed by the federal government.

Most buyers never deal with FEMA directly. NFIP policies reach the public through two channels. The first is the Write Your Own program. Under it, private insurance companies sell and service flood policies under their own brand names. The federal government carries the flood risk behind those policies.

The second channel is buying a policy directly through the NFIP. FEMA sets the rates and coverage terms for program policies. The same federal rules apply whichever channel a buyer uses. Many agents who sell homeowners insurance can also write NFIP policies.

Eligibility depends on the community as well as the house. A home qualifies for an NFIP policy only if its community participates in the program. A community joins by agreeing to adopt and enforce floodplain management rules. These rules govern how and where new construction happens in high-risk areas. FEMA publishes a Community Status Book that lists participating communities.

Residents of a community that does not participate cannot buy NFIP coverage. A private flood policy is the remaining option for them.

FEMA also changed how it prices policies. Its current pricing method, called Risk Rating 2.0, took effect Oct. 1, 2021 for new policies. Existing policyholders moved to the new method at renewals starting April 1, 2022.

The older approach leaned heavily on a property's flood zone and elevation. Risk Rating 2.0 weighs more property-specific factors. These include the home's distance to a water source, the types of flooding it faces and the cost to rebuild it. Two homes in the same flood zone can receive different prices as a result.

Private insurers sell flood policies outside the National Flood Insurance Program, and some offer higher coverage limits than the federal program. Certain private policies also pay additional living expenses, a benefit the NFIP does not provide.

Additional living expenses cover applies when a flood forces a household out of its home. It is meant to pay the extra cost of living elsewhere during repairs. That can include a rental or hotel stay and meals beyond a household's normal spending. An NFIP policy pays nothing toward those costs. Not every private policy includes this benefit. Whether a given policy does is spelled out in its written terms.

Higher limits are the other main difference from the federal program. Owners of larger or more expensive homes may find that the cost to rebuild exceeds what an NFIP policy will pay. A private policy can be written for a larger amount. Some insurers also sell excess flood insurance, which sits on top of an NFIP policy and pays after the federal coverage is used up.

The tradeoff is variety. NFIP policies use standard federal wording, known as the Standard Flood Insurance Policy, whether a private company sells them or the program sells them directly. Private flood policies have no single template. Each insurer writes its own terms, exclusions and waiting periods.

As a result, two private policies with similar limits can respond differently to the same flood. One may exclude property that another covers. One may begin coverage sooner after purchase than another. A reliable comparison comes from reading the policy documents side by side, not from a marketing summary or the quoted limit alone.

Mortgage lenders add another check. A homeowner who is required to carry flood insurance can sometimes use a private policy instead of an NFIP policy. The private coverage has to meet federal standards to satisfy the lender. Confirming acceptance with the lender before buying, or before dropping an existing NFIP policy, avoids a lapse in required coverage.

Water that backs up through a sewer line or floor drain, or that collects because a sump pump fails, is usually excluded from a standard homeowners policy. Many insurers sell that protection as an optional endorsement, commonly called water backup coverage.

The exclusion applies even though the water enters from inside the house. It can surface through a basement floor drain, a toilet or a shower on the lowest level. The source is the drainage system, not a sudden break in the pipes that supply water to the home.

Backups have several common causes. A municipal sewer main can be overwhelmed during heavy rain, pushing wastewater back toward connected homes. Tree roots, grease or debris can block the private line that runs from a house to the street. A sump pump can stop working during a power outage, after a mechanical failure or in a storm that delivers more water than it can move.

An endorsement is a written change added to an existing policy. Water backup coverage attaches to the homeowners policy rather than standing alone as a separate contract. It carries an added premium.

The insurer sets the coverage limit for the endorsement. That limit is often lower than the dwelling limit on the main policy. A homeowner with a finished basement full of flooring, drywall and furniture can face a loss larger than the endorsement pays. The endorsement wording spells out which events and items it includes. Those terms differ from one insurer to the next.

Water backup coverage is not flood insurance. Flood cover addresses water that rises from outside and inundates the property, such as an overflowing river or storm surge. A backup endorsement addresses water that enters through the home's own drains and sewer connection. A house in a low-lying area can face both risks, and each requires its own coverage.

The two risks can meet in a single storm. Under a standard NFIP flood policy, sewer or drain backup is covered only when a flood in the area directly causes it. A backup without a general flood falls outside that policy. In that case, the endorsement's terms decide what gets paid.

Federal law requires flood insurance on a building in a Special Flood Hazard Area when the mortgage comes from a federally regulated or insured lender. These zones carry a 1% annual chance of flooding. FEMA maps label them with codes that begin with A or V.

The requirement is tied to the loan, not only the location. A high-risk home with no mortgage falls outside the federal mandate. So does a home financed by a lender outside federal oversight. Any lender can still make flood coverage a condition of the loan.

The mandate dates to the Flood Disaster Protection Act of 1973. That law added a mandatory purchase requirement to federal flood insurance. It applies to banks and credit unions under federal supervision. It also covers loans insured or guaranteed by government agencies such as the Federal Housing Administration and the Department of Veterans Affairs.

The zone designation comes from FEMA's Flood Insurance Rate Maps. A zones mark areas at risk from river, lake or shallow flooding. V zones mark coastal areas that also face wave action from storms, and they carry stricter building standards. The 1% annual chance flood is often called the 100-year flood. That label describes a yearly probability. It does not mean a flood arrives once a century, and a property can flood in back-to-back years.

Lenders check a property's designation when a loan is made, using a standard flood hazard determination form. If the borrower does not buy coverage or lets it lapse, the lender must send a notice. If the borrower still does not act, federal rules require the lender to buy a policy and charge the cost to the borrower. This is known as force-placed insurance.

Flood maps change. When FEMA issues a revised map that moves a property into a Special Flood Hazard Area, the lender can require coverage on an existing loan. Anyone can look up an address on FEMA's Flood Map Service Center.

Homes outside these zones can still flood. Areas marked B, C or X $TWTR carry moderate or low mapped risk. Heavy rain, overwhelmed drainage and storm surge can still reach properties beyond mapped boundaries. Owners there are not required to carry flood insurance. They can buy it through the National Flood Insurance Program or a private insurer.

A flood insurance policy from the National Flood Insurance Program generally takes effect 30 days after purchase. A homeowner who buys cover today is not protected against a flood that arrives next week.

The rule closes off one specific approach. A homeowner cannot watch a storm forecast, buy a policy as the weather system approaches and expect the NFIP to pay for the damage. If floodwater arrives inside the 30-day window, the new policy is not yet in force.

Two dates matter on any new flood policy. One is the day the policy is bought. The other is the day cover begins. Under the standard NFIP rule, those dates sit 30 days apart. The second date decides whether a flood falls inside the policy.

The NFIP waiting period has exceptions. One applies when flood insurance is bought in connection with a loan closing. In that case, the standard 30-day wait does not hold back cover. A buyer whose lender requires flood insurance can have it in place as part of closing on the loan.

That exception is tied to the loan transaction, not to a change in the weather. A homeowner who already owns a property and decides to add flood cover ahead of a storm season generally faces the standard wait.

Private flood insurance follows different rules. Private insurers set their own waiting periods rather than using the NFIP's 30-day standard. The length can vary from one company to another. The start date appears in the policy terms, which a buyer can review before signing.

For a homeowner comparing a private policy with an NFIP policy, the waiting period belongs on the list of terms to check, next to exclusions. Both can differ by insurer. A premium quote alone does not show when protection begins.

The practical result is that flood cover has to be arranged before a threat appears, not in response to one. A policy bought during calm weather can already be in force when floodwater arrives.

A National Flood Insurance Program policy on a single-family home pays at most $250,000 for the building and $100,000 for its contents. Contents cover is a separate, optional purchase. A policy that insures only the structure pays nothing for furniture, clothing or electronics.

Building coverage applies to the house itself and the systems built into it. If rebuilding a home would cost more than $250,000, the owner carries the difference unless another policy picks it up.

Each of the two coverages carries its own limit. Owners who skip contents cover are insured for the walls and floors but not for the belongings inside them. The declarations page of a flood policy shows which coverages it carries and at what amounts.

Basements get narrower treatment than the rest of the home. The NFIP covers essential equipment there, including the furnace, the water heater and the electrical panel. Some appliances in a basement are covered as well. Most improvements that turn a basement into living space are not. Finished walls, flooring and similar upgrades below ground level generally fall outside the policy.

Several common flood losses sit outside an NFIP policy entirely. It does not pay additional living expenses. The cost of a hotel or rental while a flooded home is repaired falls to the owner. It also does not cover outdoor landscaping, such as lawns, trees and shrubs.

Vehicles are excluded too. A car damaged by floodwater falls under an auto policy instead. The comprehensive portion of that auto policy is the usual route for flood damage to a car.

One NFIP benefit reaches past repairing the damage itself. Increased Cost of Compliance coverage can pay up to $30,000 to bring a flood-damaged home in line with local building rules. Elevating the house is one use of that money. The benefit addresses a cost that can follow a major flood. Some communities require changes before a badly damaged home can be rebuilt or repaired.

A flood insurance claim starts with prompt notice to the insurer and photos of the damage taken before any cleanup begins. Under a National Flood Insurance Program policy, the policyholder generally must also submit a signed proof of loss within 60 days of the flood.

Prompt notice puts the claim on the insurer's record early. That notice goes to the insurer that issued the policy. A private flood policy follows the claim procedure written into that insurer's contract. Its deadlines and steps can differ from the federal program's.

Photographs taken before cleanup show the damage as the flood left it. Cleanup changes the scene. Waterlogged flooring gets pulled up, ruined furniture goes to the curb and walls get opened so they can dry. Once that work starts, the original condition of the home can no longer be seen directly. Pictures of each affected room and the damaged contents in it give the insurer a record to compare against the claim.

The proof of loss is a separate step from the first notice. It is a signed statement in which the policyholder sets out the amount being claimed. The NFIP clock for it runs from the date of the loss, not from the date the homeowner first contacts the insurer. FEMA has extended that deadline after some declared disasters. An extension is not automatic. A homeowner relying on one needs to confirm that it covers the specific event.

Federal disaster assistance works differently from insurance and does not replace it. FEMA aid for individuals becomes available only after a presidential disaster declaration. A flood that damages homes without prompting a declaration opens no path to that help.

Small Business Administration disaster loans are a second federal source of money after a disaster. They are loans rather than grants, and borrowers must repay them.

A flood policy is a contract the homeowner holds before the water arrives. Its payout does not depend on a declaration. FEMA individual aid does. An SBA disaster loan, by contrast, leaves the homeowner with debt.

#5463. Jensen Huang built Nvidia into a $4 trillion AI giant but owned less than 4% of it, leaving him without the super-voting power to protect his CEO role

Jensen Huang, the billionaire ex-Nvidia CEO who took the company from a small player in the video game graphics industry to the chipmaker at the center of the AI revolution, once made a surprising revelation: He could be fired at any time.

“In a well-governed company, the CEO was always designed to report to the board of directors and the board of directors report to shareholders,” Huang said in a January podcast interview with Jodi Shelton. “If the CEO doesn’t do his job according to 12, 13, 15 board members, however sized the board is, that CEO is let go.”

This reality sets Nvidia apart from other Silicon Valley companies, especially those still run by a cofounder. That includes Meta, where CEO and cofounder Mark Zuckerberg wields considerable power over the board due to its dual class share structure.

On Thursday, Huang resigned from the company that he cofounded and led over the past 33 years after publicly admitting to being unfaithful to his wife. Nvidia’s board opened an independent investigation into Huang and the possibility he may have been a target of a foreign intelligence operation after reporting by the New York Times explored his close relationship with a businesswoman that U.S. intelligence identified as a Chinese spy. Huang reportedly had another affair with an Nvidia executive who reported to him, according to the New York Times. On Thursday, the board appointed CFO Colette Kress as interim CEO.

Still, Huang said in that January interview any future Nvidia CEO would not measure up to him.

“There will never be one like me, and the reason for that is because I was raised by the company,” he said at the time.

Nvidia did not immediately respond to Fortune’s request for comment.

Despite being the company’s largest individual shareholder, Huang did not have unparalleled voting control over his company or outsized control over the company’s board, like other founders.

Huang owned about 870.6 million Nvidia shares, or about 3.58% of the company as of March, according to the company’s 2026 proxy statement. His holdings were far greater than that of  other executives and directors, including Kress, who held 4.4 million shares. Vanguard and BlackRock both owned more than 7% of the company each.

Because of Nvidia’s one-share-one vote system, Huang’s stake doesn’t come with special privileges, despite his status as a cofounder. That means the number of votes he has directly corresponds with his number of shares.

As Huang alluded to in his January podcast interview, Nvidia’s bylaws are written in such a way that the company’s CEO can be removed by the board for any reason and at any time—still, Huang lacked enough voting power to independently elect or remove Nvidia’s directors.

While founders with majority voting control, such as Zuckerberg, can effectively determine who sits on their boards, Huang would have needed support from other Nvidia shareholders to do the same.

That differs from other companies run by tech founders including Meta, Snap, and even Google.

At Meta, a dual class voting structure (it said last month it would add a third non-voting tier next year) gives Zuckerberg outsized power over voting.  Despite owning 13.4% of the company, Zuckerberg controls about 60% of the company’s voting power because his class B shares give him 10 votes each compared to one vote for every class A share. With this voting power, Zuckerberg can effectively elect Meta’s entire board and is the deciding voice on most matters sent to shareholders.

Snap, the social media company, has a similar arrangement with CEO and cofounder Evan Spiegel controlling 53% of the company’s voting power while only owning about 9.3% of the company.

Even at Google parent company Alphabet, where cofounder Sergey Brin and cofounder and former CEO Larry Page no longer run day-to-day operations, the pair still collectively retain majority voting control of the tech giant. Both still serve on the company’s board.

Nvidia’s stock plummeted by as much as 14% Thursday following the announcement of Huang’s departure, before rebounding. It was down about 4.7% as of 1:30 p.m. EST on Thursday. With a nearly $4 trillion market cap, the company makes up about 6% of the S&P 500 and about 10% of the Nasdaq 100, meaning any reckoning it experiences will trickle through the broader market and everyday Americans’ 401(K) accounts.

Huang was key to Nvidia’s operations with a flat management structure and direct involvement in the company’s product strategy and its supplier and customer relationships. In recent months, he has also cultivated a close relationship with President Donald Trump, who has been a vocal proponent of boosting the AI industry and the infrastructure backing it in the U.S.—although Trump was quick to back ex-Apple CEO Tim Cook as Huang’s successor on Thursday.

The board has now made changes to its own structure as well. It previously operated without a board chairman, opting instead to rely on lead independent director Stephen Neal to oversee management. On Thursday, it appointed Harvey C. Jones, a former semiconductor company CEO and Nvidia board member since 1993, as its chairman of the board, it said in a statement.

Kress, the company’s CFO since 2013, said for her part she is planning to build on Huang’s legacy at Nvidia as interim CEO she said in a Thursday statement.

In the January interview, Huang said while he didn’t love his job every day, he always tried his “mightiest” because of two reasons.

“One, I’m the best person for the job. I believe that,” he said. “And, two, I have to earn being the best person for that job every day.”

Role: Reporter Marco Quiroz-Gutierrez is a reporter for Fortune covering general business news.

#5462. Data center developers brace for new reality as election backlash sinks in

Challenges, breakthroughs and big ideas in the race to protect our planet. SEE MORE

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 10, 2026 at 10:25 amNovember 11, 2026 at 7:41 am

Data center developers already knew they had a public relations problem. This month’s midterm elections showed how much of a political problem it has become.

Voters approved data center restrictions in 44 of 45 local measures across a dozen states. Candidates who support stronger regulation of the facilities won 32 of the 34 gubernatorial races called so far. And political campaigns reportedly spent more than $380 million on TV ads referencing data centers, according to the Associated Press.

The results capped a year of accelerating resistance as tech giants plan to spend hundreds of billions of dollars on new facilities.

So what comes next? More outreach, more transparency and the expectation that states and local governments will pass data center rules, said leaders in the Pacific Northwest.

“We’ve been working and adapting our approach to meet the moment,” said John Wilson, chief financial officer of Sabey Data Centers, in an interview. “There used to be a time where we would say that our track record could speak for itself, and that’s clearly no longer the case.”

Communities nationwide have raised concerns about the facilities’ effect on rising electric bills, their water use for cooling electronics and the noise they generate.

Broader fears about artificial intelligence are also stoking the pushback, including worries that it will replace workers and appropriate human-created content, and that it can provide erroneous information, foster unhealthy relationships with users, or facilitate scams or terrorist attacks.

A renewed effort to regulate data centers is expected in January in Washington state — home to the headquarters of Sabey, Microsoft and Amazon.

Earlier this year, state Rep. Beth Doglio, D-Olympia, pushed legislation that included ratepayer protections, transparency on environmental impacts and clean energy requirements. Microsoft and the national Data Center Coalition opposed the bill, which failed.

“It’s going to be a very tech-heavy session,” Doglio said.

Before voters weighed in this month, tech companies launched efforts to assuage public fears.

In January, Microsoft released its “Community First AI Infrastructure” initiative, which includes promises to pay the company’s full power costs, reject local property tax breaks, replenish more water than it uses, train local workers and fund AI education and community programs.

Last month, Amazon announced its “Built Together” program, pledging to invest $1 billion over five years in the U.S. communities where it operates data centers, including support for education and civic projects. The initiative offers similar commitments to Microsoft’s on transparency and covering its energy costs.

Wilson said Sabey also works with communities to understand and meet their needs. When a proposed campus in Indianapolis triggered significant pushback, the company brought community members to Quincy, a central Washington data center hub, to tour a Sabey facility and hear from locals about their experience.

“It requires a lot of patience. It requires a lot of transparency in our communication,” Wilson said. Sabey’s Decatur Technology Park in Indianapolis is moving ahead, and the company aims to bring it online in 2030.

But the even bigger challenge now is statewide moratoriums and data center bans — a scale of resistance that is difficult to address even when there is local support.

Oregon Gov. Tina Kotek in October directed a state agency to pause processing and issuing permits for new and expanding data centers until July 2027. Umatilla, where Sabey is developing its first Oregon campus, declared a local state of emergency over the potential loss of investment and revenue, the Oregon Capital Chronicle reported.

Even with the surge in resistance, “we’ve been able to find our way through on every project that we’ve had,” Wilson said. “I’m knocking on wood as I say that.”

Corporate commitments alone may no longer be enough to win public confidence, said Brad Smith, Microsoft vice chair and president, in a GeekWire interview. Communities increasingly want laws requiring all data center developers to build responsibly — a shift he called a “watershed” moment, “but one we anticipated.”

“[P]eople want to see everyone who builds a data center do it in a responsible way,” Smith added, “and they feel that the only way that one can obtain that result is to have some new laws that are put in place.”

Come next year, that could include Washington and impact local tech giants, Sabey and others. Baxtel, a data center industry research firm, lists 29 Microsoft facilities operating in Washington and four under construction, with Sabey operating eight facilities.

Amazon plans to build its first large-scale data centers in Washington, with proposed campuses in Walla Walla County and the Tri-Cities. Amazon did not respond to repeated requests for comment on this story.

Doglio said the next version of her bill will be more stringent. “We have to have a strong bill,” she said, adding that the public and members of her party are calling for it. Microsoft did not publicly specify which provisions triggered its opposition to the previous bill.

Wilson hopes any legislation, in Washington or elsewhere, allows flexibility and recognizes that data centers vary widely in size, impact and application. Sabey provides data center space and infrastructure for customers ranging from major cloud companies to corporations and community organizations.

“Describing all data centers as one thing is just not accurate,” Wilson said, “and it doesn’t understand the realities of the industry itself.”

Smith expressed optimism that U.S. lawmakers can find a middle ground that meets the needs of communities and tech companies.

“There’s plenty of room to draft laws that enable people to go forward and build responsible data centers without chilling the economic contributions these data centers make, especially to local communities,” he said.

The Climate Pledge is a commitment to reach net-zero carbon emissions by 2040, co-founded by Amazon and Global Optimism in 2019.

Seven years later, the community has grown to over 700 signatories across 62 industries and 49 countries and territories, reducing emissions, scaling emerging climate solutions, and addressing challenges across operations and value chains.

#5459. Why flash floods are so deadly: 10 things to know about how fast water rises

Free daily briefing on global business news.

How fast flash floods rise and why they turn deadly so quickly, explained through 10 points on water depth, vehicles, canyons, burn scars and warnings

A flash flood can turn a dry streambed, a parking lot or a two-lane road into a fast, churning current with very little notice. That compressed timeline sits at the heart of the danger. Most river floods build over days. That gives forecasters time to issue outlooks and gives residents time to move cars, pets and belongings to higher ground. A flash flood offers no such cushion.

Understanding how fast flash floods rise and why they are so deadly comes down to several forces working at once. Intense rain can fall faster than the ground can absorb it. Steep terrain and narrow channels funnel runoff into a single path. Pavement sheds water almost immediately. Wildfire-scarred slopes can behave much the same way. Each condition shortens the gap between the first heavy rain and a fast-moving surge.

The depth of the water is only part of the threat. Moving water is heavy, and it pushes far harder than its depth suggests. A current that looks shallow from behind a windshield can knock a person down or lift a vehicle off the road. Many flood drownings involve drivers who tried to cross a flooded road that looked passable, not swimmers caught in deep water.

Geography shapes the risk as well. In arid country, a storm miles away can send a flood down a dry wash while the sky overhead stays clear. In cities, storm drains and paved surfaces can send runoff to low-lying streets faster than the drainage system can carry it away.

This slideshow walks through 10 explanations and examples of how these floods form and why they kill. It starts with the official definition and how a flash flood differs from a river flood. It then covers the depth thresholds the National Weather Service uses in its safety guidance, the physics of flowing water and the role of vehicles in flood deaths. Later slides look at canyons, cities and wildfire burn scars, along with the difference between a flash flood watch and a warning. The final slide explains how a warming atmosphere can make heavy downpours more intense.

Knowing which conditions produce a flash flood, and how little moving water it takes to become dangerous, makes it easier to recognize the moment to turn back.

A flash flood is flooding that begins quickly, generally within about six hours of heavy rain, according to the National Weather Service. The agency also counts sudden failures, such as a dam or levee giving way, as causes. That short window separates it from the slower river floods most people picture.

The defining feature is timing, not size. A flash flood can be confined to a single creek, a city street or a narrow canyon. It can also spread across a wide area. What makes it a flash flood is how little time passes between the cause and the arrival of dangerous water.

Rain is the most common trigger. A thunderstorm can stall over one spot. A line of storms can also pass repeatedly over the same ground. Either pattern can drop more water than soil and channels can absorb. The excess runs downhill and collects in streams, gullies and low-lying roads.

Structural failures work differently. When a dam or levee breaks, water that had been held back is released all at once. That can send a surge downstream even where no rain is falling. A river ice jam can do something similar when it breaks apart and releases the water pooled behind it.

A river flood follows a slower pattern. Water rises as rain from a large area, or melting snow, drains into the main channel and moves downstream. A river may crest days after the rain that caused it has stopped.

That slower pace changes how communities respond. The National Weather Service runs River Forecast Centers that model how high a river will rise. They also estimate when it will crest at specific gauges. Forecasts like these give officials time to stack sandbags, close roads and order evacuations before the water peaks.

Flash floods rarely allow that kind of preparation. The storm that creates the flood may still be overhead when the water arrives. The National Weather Service treats the two as separate hazards. It issues one set of alerts for ordinary flooding and a separate set for flash flooding.

A flash flood often gives people minutes rather than hours to get out of the way. It can turn an ordinary street or creek bed dangerous before many people recognize the threat.

The difference starts with what forecasters can see. On a large river, water from upstream rain has to travel down the channel before it reaches a town. River gauges track that rise along the way. The National Weather Service uses those readings to forecast when and how high a river will crest, often days ahead. Residents downstream get a timeline they can plan around.

A flash flood rarely offers that buffer. The rain that causes it often falls on the same small area or just upstream of it. The runoff arrives soon after. Forecasters can flag the conditions in advance. The exact creek, road or neighborhood that floods may not be clear until the water is already moving.

Timing compounds the problem. Thunderstorms that produce flash flooding can linger or repeat over one spot into the evening and overnight. A flood that arrives after dark can find people asleep, and an alert can go unheard. Darkness also makes rising water harder to notice from a house, a tent or a parked car.

Travel adds another layer of risk. A driver, camper or hiker passing through an unfamiliar area may not know which roads dip into low crossings. They may not know which creeks drain a large area upstream. They may not have heard the local forecast at all.

Rain does not have to be falling where the flood hits. Heavy rain several miles upstream can send a surge into a channel where no drops are falling. That removes the most obvious cue people rely on to judge danger.

With so short a window, the National Weather Service advises moving to higher ground as soon as flooding is threatened. Its guidance is not to wait and watch the water rise. Choosing a destination in advance, along with a route that avoids low spots, leaves less to decide once a warning arrives.

No single speed describes how fast flash flood water rises. The rate depends on rainfall intensity, the steepness and shape of the land, how wet the ground already is and the size of the area draining into a stream or channel.

For flash flooding, the pace of the rain can matter more than the storm's total. Soil can take in water only so quickly. Once rain arrives faster than that, the excess runs across the surface almost at once. A moderate rain spread across a full day may mostly soak in. The same amount falling within an hour can send much of it downhill.

The condition of the soil changes the outcome. Ground already saturated by earlier storms has little room left. Even modest rain on that ground becomes runoff. Very dry, hard-baked soil can also shed water at first. Its crusted surface resists infiltration. Bare rock, such as the sandstone common across the American Southwest, sheds most of the rain that lands on it.

Terrain controls how quickly that runoff gathers. Steep slopes move water downhill faster than gentle ones. Narrow valleys and channels squeeze the flow into a smaller space. The same volume of water then stacks up deeper than it would across an open floodplain.

The size of the drainage area — the watershed feeding a stream — sets the timing. Hydrologists use a measure called time of concentration. It describes how long runoff from the most distant point in a watershed takes to reach a given spot downstream. Small, steep watersheds have short times of concentration. Their creeks can climb sharply soon after heavy rain begins. Large river basins respond far more slowly.

Not every flash flood starts with a downpour. A dam or levee failure can push a surge downstream with almost no buildup. So can the sudden release of water held back by an ice jam or a pile of debris. In those cases the water can arrive as a moving front rather than a steady climb.

The U.S. Geological Survey runs a nationwide network of stream gauges that record water levels as they change. Those records show how a particular creek tends to behave in heavy rain. They also show that two streams hit by the same storm can respond in very different ways. One may rise gradually while the other jumps within a short window.

About six inches of moving water is enough to knock an adult off their feet, according to the National Weather Service. On most adults, that depth reaches only around the ankle or the bottom of the shin.

The danger comes from depth and motion together. Standing water at the same level mostly gets shoes wet. Flowing water pushes steadily against the feet and lower legs. A person wading through it has to lean into the current just to stay upright.

Footing is the weak point. A person stays standing because body weight presses the soles of the feet against the ground. Friction between shoe and surface keeps the feet from sliding. Moving water adds a sideways push on the legs. The submerged part of the body is also slightly buoyed. That buoyancy takes some weight off the feet. Less weight on the ground means less grip to resist the push.

The ground underneath rarely helps. Floodwater is usually brown with mud and silt. A person wading through it cannot see where they are stepping. A curb, a pothole, an open drain or a stretch of broken pavement can sit just below the surface. A single step onto an uneven or slick spot can be enough to break balance.

Once someone falls, the situation changes fast. A person lying in moving water presents far more of their body to the current than someone standing. The flow can then carry them downstream toward deeper water, storm drains, culverts or piled-up debris. Getting back up in a current is much harder than staying up in the first place.

Smaller people reach the threshold sooner. The same six inches covers a larger share of a child's leg. Children also weigh less, which leaves them less body weight holding them to the ground.

The National Weather Service builds its public safety message around this risk. Its slogan, "Turn Around, Don't Drown," applies to people on foot as much as to drivers. The guidance is to treat flowing water across a path, trail, street or low-water crossing as impassable instead of testing it.

The same logic covers everyday situations. Walking along the edge of a flooded street, fording a creek on a hiking trail and stepping off a curb into fast runoff all carry the same basic risk. Moving to higher ground and waiting removes the need to judge the water at all.

About 12 inches of moving water can float many vehicles, according to the National Weather Service. The agency's guidance adds that about two feet of rushing water can carry away most vehicles, including SUVs and pickups.

Buoyancy explains why. Archimedes' principle holds that an object in water is pushed upward by a force equal to the weight of the water it displaces. A car is a large, mostly hollow shape. Its cabin, trunk and engine bay hold air, and its tires are filled with air as well. As water climbs the sides of the body, the vehicle displaces more of it, and the upward push grows.

A car does not need to float completely free to be in trouble. As buoyancy takes on part of the vehicle's weight, the tires press less firmly on the pavement. Less pressure means less grip. Steering and braking depend on that grip. A driver can lose control well before the tires leave the pavement.

Once traction is gone, the current can shove the vehicle sideways. It can slide off the roadway, drift into a ditch or a deeper channel, or tip onto its side. At that point the people inside have no way to steer out of the water.

Bigger vehicles are not exempt. A tall SUV or a full-size pickup weighs more than a compact sedan. It is also larger, so it displaces more water as the level rises. The Weather Service's two-foot guidance names SUVs and pickups explicitly. Higher ground clearance can keep the cabin dry a little longer. It does not anchor the vehicle to the road.

Water can also cause mechanical trouble. If it reaches an engine's air intake, the engine can stall. That leaves a car stranded in a rising current with no power to back out. Electrical systems that run power windows and door locks can also be affected once water gets inside.

These depths are guidance, not fixed limits. The point at which a particular vehicle floats depends on its weight, its shape and how fast the water is moving. A lighter car or a faster current can reach that point at a shallower depth.

Fast-moving floodwater hits hard because water is heavy and its push grows much faster than its speed. Fresh water weighs about 62.4 pounds per cubic foot. The force a current exerts on an object rises with the square of how fast that current is moving.

The weight is the starting point. A cubic yard holds 27 cubic feet, which puts a cubic yard of fresh water at roughly 1,685 pounds. In metric terms, one cubic meter of fresh water has a mass of about 1,000 kilograms, or one metric ton.

That mass does not sit still in a flash flood. It moves downhill through channels, streets and low-lying roads. Anything in its path has to absorb the momentum the water carries.

Speed is the larger factor. In fluid dynamics, the drag a current places on an object depends mainly on three things. They are the water's density, the area of the object facing the flow and the square of the current's velocity. The squared term is what makes speed the dominant variable.

Doubling a current's speed roughly quadruples the force it applies. Tripling the speed raises the force about ninefold. A modest rise in speed therefore produces a much larger rise in push.

Area matters as well. A narrow post in the water presents little surface to the flow. A car door or the side of a house presents a great deal. The same current delivers far more total force against a wide, flat surface than against a slim one.

Floodwater is also rarely clean water. Flash floods pick up silt, sand and gravel. That sediment makes the water denser than the 62.4-pound figure for fresh water, and denser water pushes harder at the same speed.

Debris turns the current into a battering ram. Fast flows can carry tree limbs, logs, fencing, trash bins and even vehicles. Each object strikes whatever lies downstream with the speed of the water behind it. Floodwater is usually brown and opaque. People in or near it often cannot see what is coming.

The force acts on the ground, too. Fast water scours soil and gravel from beneath pavement, bridge supports and embankments. That erosion can undermine a structure that still looks intact from above.

These relationships describe how force scales, not a fixed number for any single flood. The actual force in a given flood depends on its depth, its speed, the shape of the object in its path and the material the water is carrying. All of those vary from one channel to the next.

Vehicles sit at the center of flood fatalities. About half of flood-related drownings happen when someone drives a vehicle into hazardous floodwater, according to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

The choice to drive in can feel routine. A flooded road often looks like a broad, shallow puddle stretched across the pavement. A driver who has crossed the same dip or low-water crossing many times may assume it is safe to cross again. In a flash flood, conditions at that crossing can change from one storm to the next, and from one minute to the next.

Depth is hard to judge from the driver's seat. Floodwater is usually brown with mud and sediment. The road surface disappears beneath it. Nothing on the surface reliably shows how deep the water is in the middle of the crossing, where the road often dips lowest. At night, headlights glare off the water and reveal even less.

The road itself may no longer be there. Fast-moving water can scour away pavement and the soil beneath it. That can leave a collapsed section or a deep hole hidden under the surface. A car that rolls onto a washed-out stretch can drop suddenly into water far deeper than the edge of the flood suggested.

Control can disappear quickly. Once the tires lose firm contact with the road, the driver can no longer steer or brake. The vehicle then goes wherever the current carries it.

The engine is another weak point. Water drawn into the air intake can stall it. The occupants are then stuck in the flow, unable to reverse out.

Escape becomes difficult once a car is in the water. Pressure from the water against the doors can make them hard to push open, and occupants may have very little time to act. Rescue crews trying to reach a stranded car must contend with the same current.

The safest decision comes before the tires touch the water. Choosing another route, or waiting for the water to recede, removes the risk behind the CDC figure.

A dry canyon or desert wash can flood under a clear sky. Rain that falls miles upstream collects in the channel and moves downstream as a surge. It can reach people who never saw a storm cloud overhead.

That disconnect makes desert drainages especially hazardous. Across the southwestern U.S., an arroyo is a creek bed that carries water only after storms. It can sit empty for months. Hard, thin desert ground absorbs little of a sudden downpour. The runoff gathers in the lowest channel available.

Slot canyons narrow the problem further. These are deep, tight passages carved into rock, sometimes only a few feet wide, with walls that rise far above a visitor's head. Water entering a slot has no floodplain to spread across. It climbs the walls instead. Smooth sandstone sides offer few ledges to scramble onto. Exits can be far apart.

Antelope Canyon in Arizona shows how that plays out. On August 12, 1997, a flash flood swept through Lower Antelope Canyon, a slot canyon on Navajo Nation land near Page, and killed 11 tourists. The rain that fed it fell upstream, away from where the group was walking.

Colorado's Big Thompson Canyon is a different landscape. It is a steep mountain river canyon rather than a desert slot, but the same mechanics applied. On July 31, 1976, a thunderstorm stalled over the upper part of the canyon and dropped roughly 12 inches of rain in about four hours. The Big Thompson River turned into a flood that killed 144 people.

U.S. Highway 34 follows the river through that canyon. Residents, campers and travelers were spread along the road and the riverbanks when the water came down. The flood struck on the eve of Colorado's centennial, during a holiday weekend.

These settings share two traits: a limited view of the sky and limited ways out. Someone standing in a narrow channel can see only a strip of sky. The storm cell feeding the drainage may sit beyond the rim, out of sight. Warning signs on the ground tend to arrive late. They include water turning muddy, floating debris or a roar from up-canyon.

The practical response follows from the terrain. Check the forecast for the whole watershed rather than only the trailhead. Inside a canyon or wash, the safer move is to climb to higher ground rather than try to outrun the water along the channel floor.

Cities and freshly burned hillsides both turn rainfall into runoff faster than natural ground does. Pavement and storm drains rush water to low points, while wildfire-scarred slopes shed rain and can unleash debris flows of mud, rock and trees.

On undeveloped land, soil and vegetation soak up part of a storm before water reaches a stream. Roofs, roads and parking lots absorb almost none of it. Nearly all the rain that lands on them flows off the surface.

Storm drains are built to move that water away quickly. That speed is the purpose of the system, but it also concentrates runoff in channels, culverts and the lowest streets. When a downpour exceeds what the pipes can carry, the excess runs across the surface instead. Underpasses, basements, sunken roads and older districts built along creeks tend to fill first.

Ellicott City, Maryland, shows how the pattern can repeat in the same place. The historic town's Main Street flooded on July 30, 2016. It flooded again on May 27, 2018, less than two years later. The downtown sits in a narrow valley where small streams run down to the Patapsco River. Water from the surrounding hills drains toward that low ground.

Burned ground behaves differently but produces a similar result. A wildfire strips away the plants, roots and leaf litter that slow water and hold soil in place. Intense heat can also leave a water-repellent layer in the soil. Rain then runs off the surface instead of sinking in.

On steep slopes, that runoff can pick up ash, loose soil, boulders and fallen trees. The resulting mixture is called a debris flow. It is far denser than floodwater alone, and it can destroy buildings in its path.

Montecito, California, experienced this in January 2018. The Thomas Fire had burned the mountains above the community the previous month. When heavy rain fell on the bare slopes, debris flows surged down creek channels and into neighborhoods. The flows killed 23 people.

The danger does not end with the first storm after a fire. Burned slopes can remain prone to fast runoff and debris flows for several years, until vegetation returns and the soil recovers. In cities, the hazard is more lasting. As more ground is paved, less of each storm can soak in, and more of it reaches the low points at the same time.

A flash flood watch means conditions are favorable for flash flooding, according to the National Weather Service. A flash flood warning means flooding is happening or about to happen. The agency also issues a third, higher alert, the flash flood emergency. It is the Weather Service's most severe flash flood alert.

The watch and the warning call for different responses. A watch is a signal to prepare. It is the time to check the forecast, learn the route to higher ground and decide where to go if conditions worsen. No flooding has to be under way for a watch to be issued.

A warning removes that margin. It tells people in the affected area that water is rising now or will be shortly. Under a warning, the Weather Service's guidance is to move to higher ground right away. Waiting to see the water before leaving can use up the time needed to get out.

The flash flood emergency is reserved for rare situations. The Weather Service uses it when a flash flood poses a severe threat to human life and catastrophic damage is happening or expected. It is not a different kind of flood. It marks an existing warning that has reached its gravest level.

These alerts reach the public through several channels. Flash flood warnings can trigger Wireless Emergency Alerts on mobile phones inside the warned area. NOAA Weather Radio also broadcasts them around the clock.

The flash flood alerts are separate from the Weather Service's flood watches and flood warnings. Those cover flooding that develops more gradually.

Temperature affects how much rain a storm can deliver. Warmer air can hold about seven percent more water vapor for each one degree Celsius of warming. This is known as the Clausius-Clapeyron relationship.

More moisture in the atmosphere gives storms more water to release. That can raise the intensity of heavy downpours, the short, hard bursts of rain that drive flash flooding. The relationship describes the atmosphere's capacity to hold water, not the outcome of any single storm. Whether a given downpour becomes a flood still depends on where the rain falls, how long it lasts and how much the ground below can absorb.

#5458. ‘The plot twist’: A study of 73,000 adults found America’s richest still die sooner than most Europeans

Americans have never earned more or lived longer. Median household income hit $87,460 in 2025, the highest since the Census Bureau began tracking it in 1967, according to Census data released in September. Life expectancy reached 79 years in 2024, also a record.

Yet money still can’t buy Americans a European lifespan. A Brown University study published last year in the New England Journal of Medicine found that Americans die sooner than Europeans at every level of wealth, and that the richest Americans fare no better than the poorest people in much of Western Europe.

“The plot twist is that even the wealthiest quartile of Americans does not have better outcomes than most of northern and Western Europeans,” says Sara Machado, a research scientist at Brown’s Center for Health System Sustainability. “That was unexpected and counters a lot of the narrative that we’re used to.”

The researchers tracked more than 73,000 adults ages 50 to 85 in the U.S. and 16 European countries, starting in 2010 and following them for about a decade, using data from the U.S. Health and Retirement Study and Europe’s SHARE survey.

The wealthiest people in northern and western Europe had a mortality rate about 35% lower than the wealthiest Americans. Survival among America’s richest quartile was statistically equivalent to that of the poorest quartile in countries like France, Germany, and the Netherlands.

Across the board, people in continental Europe died at rates about 40% lower than Americans over the study period, according to Brown. In southern Europe, death rates were about 30% lower.

Wealth still matters within each country. “We found that where you stand in your country’s wealth distribution matters for your longevity, and where you stand in your country compared to where others stand in theirs matters, too,” Machado says.

The U.S. spent an estimated $14,775 per person on health care in 2024, nearly $7,000 more than the average comparable wealthy country, according to the Peterson-KFF Health System Tracker. Those countries averaged a life expectancy of 82.7 years, 3.7 years longer than the U.S. Fortune has reported on why U.S. health care costs run about twice those of peer nations.

The spending doesn’t buy universal access. About 26.7 million Americans went uninsured for all of 2025, Census data shows, and about 2.6 million fewer Americans had ACA marketplace plans in early 2026 than in early 2025.

“Fixing health outcomes is not just a challenge for the most vulnerable – even those in the top quartile of wealth are affected,” says Machado.

Lifestyle plays a role. Americans tend to have less healthy diets and a more sedentary lifestyle, and heart disease and cancer remain the two leading causes of death nationally. The researchers noted that smoking and rural living, both tied to poorer health, were more common in the U.S.

Europe is also home to two of the so-called blue zones, Sardinia in Italy and Ikaria in Greece, where longevity is credited to activity, diet, rest, and strong social ties, though some researchers dispute the claims.

When Fortune first reported on the study, senior author Irene Papanicolas pointed to higher U.S. rates of avoidable deaths from firearms, alcohol, and suicide; higher cardiovascular mortality; and a thinner social safety net, with health coverage tied more closely to employment.

Inequality compounds it. The U.S. has a far wider gap between rich and poor than Europe, a divide that Creative Planning CEO Peter Mallouk recently warned is unsustainable.

“Our previous work has shown that while wealth inequality narrows after 65 across the U.S. and Europe, in the U.S. it narrows because the poorest Americans die sooner and in greater proportion,” explains Papanicolas, a professor of health services, policy, and practice who directs Brown’s Center for Health System Sustainability.

The recent gains in U.S. longevity came largely from the end of the pandemic, and a drop in overdose deaths and suicides also occurred in 2024, according to the CDC. Those gains have not closed the gap with Europe.

“If we want to improve health in the US,” explains Papanicolas, “we need to better understand the underlying factors that contribute to these differences – particularly amongst similar socioeconomic groups – and why they translate to different health outcomes across nations.”

“There is a lot of it that is a collective issue,” Machado agrees. “But I would say to individuals that you really need to think about your retirement—about when you’re going to retire, how you’re going to retire, and how you can be happy as a person that has retired.”

Machado adds, “If you look at other countries, there are better outcomes, and that means we can learn from them and improve. It’s not necessarily about spending more — it’s about addressing the factors we’re overlooking, which could deliver far greater benefits than we realize.”

#5457. Microsoft awards $20K grants to 25 Seattle-area nonprofits amid state budget crunch and tax debate

by Todd Bishop on Nov 10, 2026 at 10:48 amNovember 11, 2026 at 10:27 am

The Lighthouse for the Blind is adding braille displays to its computer lab. Friends of the Issaquah Salmon Hatchery is taking its lessons to low-income schools. And Lake Washington High School’s band boosters are replacing marching capes that date to the MS-DOS era.

Those are among 25 King County nonprofits that received $20,000 apiece from Microsoft in grants announced this week. It’s the first round of the company’s Community-First Grants, a $1 million program launched in September.

Microsoft said it received 813 applications.

“Boy, I think we hit a nerve,” said Jane Broom, Microsoft’s senior director of Community Affairs, during an event Monday recognizing the nonprofits on the company’s Redmond campus, featuring Mariners catcher Cal Raleigh and the team’s mascots.

The grants are meant for immediate needs, such as replacing a broken-down van or a failed freezer, Broom explained. Nonprofits that already received or were invited to receive Microsoft corporate grants in 2026 weren’t eligible.

Funding and the tax debate: Nonprofits are dealing with rising costs and tighter budgets. As a group, their largest funding source is the state government, which is in the middle of an ongoing debate with members of the business community over taxes and economic competitiveness amid a budget crunch.

Microsoft is among the companies asserting that current and proposed taxes are hurting the business climate. It’s also the second-largest funder of the state’s nonprofits, behind only the state itself, said Brad Smith, the company’s president and vice chair.

“In my view, a healthy nonprofit community actually has aspects of support from more than one source,” Smith said in an interview after the event, noting that state grants are often at risk when a recession forces budget cuts.

Where the money goes: Demand is climbing for many of the grant recipients. At Community Lunch on Capitol Hill, which serves free hot meals, it’s up 40% this year, and the diaper bank at Byrd Barr Place has grown from 720 families in 2021 to 1,600, Microsoft said at the event.

Friends of the Issaquah Salmon Hatchery gives more than 700 tours during the salmon season. It will use its grant to bring lessons to classrooms, mainly at Title I schools, which serve large numbers of low-income students and often can’t afford a field trip to the hatchery, said Mark Clemens, the group’s executive director.

“If they can’t bring the school to the hatchery, we will go out to the school,” said Clemens, a former Scientific American art director, who was creative director of the Modernist Cuisine cookbook project before taking over the nonprofit in 2023.

One bonus for the group, which goes by the clever acronym of FISH, was the appearance of the Mariners’ salmon mascots, which joined the group onstage for a photo op when Clemens and his colleagues accepted its grant.

The Lighthouse for the Blind, a Seattle-based nonprofit that employs blind people in manufacturing, retail and other jobs, will use its grant to upgrade its computer training lab with Windows 11 PCs, braille displays and wireless keyboards, said Antonio Rozier, the nonprofit’s IT director.

The goal is to keep employees current on screen readers and other tools so they can work alongside sighted colleagues, Rozier said. The Lighthouse also has computer labs at its three manufacturing plants, and employees can use them for personal tasks, since some don’t have that equipment at home.

Rozier called the upgraded lab “a game changer for the future.”

The Lake Washington High School Band and Jazz Boosters will buy 150 uniforms for the school’s marching band, which returned in 2025 after a 40-year absence and has been performing in capes from 1981.

Microsoft’s company culture: Most of the company’s local giving is directed by its employees. Microsoft matches their donations and adds $25 for every hour they volunteer, up to a combined $15,000 a year per person, Smith said.

That program accounts for most of the $1.9 billion that Microsoft and its employees have given to about 13,000 Washington nonprofits over the past 30 years, he said.

“We let our people decide where the money goes,” Smith said.

Microsoft’s employee base is going through a period of major change. After layoffs in July and September, the company offered voluntary buyouts last month to about 60,000 people, roughly a quarter of its global workforce. Employees have described mounting pressure to use AI, stagnant pay and a growing sense of job insecurity, The New York Times reported.

Asked about the buyouts, Smith said it’s a good time for Microsoft to keep investing in the employee experience, and he described the giving program as part of that.

Silicon Valley companies may offer more free food as a perk, he said, but Microsoft matches employee donations, giving workers who often move to the region from elsewhere a way to get involved in the community.

This year’s Microsoft Give campaign in October, the company’s biggest month for employee donations, was again a success, Smith said, showing that “employee participation and employee giving is alive and well.”

Microsoft plans to open a second round of applications for the Community-First Grants in the spring of 2027.

#5456. Seattle mayor lifts pause and will expand police surveillance cameras with new safeguards

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 10, 2026 at 1:10 pmNovember 10, 2026 at 1:28 pm

The move comes a day after NYU’s Policing Project released an independent audit of the Seattle Police Department’s Real Time Crime Center (RTCC), which Wilson commissioned during the pause. The audit found the city had built “an important foundation” for overseeing the system but that “significant policy gaps remain.” It made 19 recommendations.

Cameras in the Stadium District, installed before this summer’s FIFA World Cup, will be turned on immediately, according to the mayor’s office. Cameras around Garfield High School and in the Capitol Hill nightlife district still need to be bought and installed, which will take months. The City Council approved all three areas in 2025.

Wilson briefly turned on the 22 stadium-area cameras during the World Cup, citing “credible threats” reported by law enforcement, and said they would go off after the tournament. The audit noted that police streamed live feeds throughout the event, despite a department policy against monitoring cameras without an active call or case.

“After reviewing the evidence, the recommendations, and the safeguards available to us, I believe there is an important and responsible role for the RTCC within Seattle’s public-safety system,” Wilson said in a statement.

Wilson said the city will adopt most of the audit’s recommendations. The police department will publish a public dashboard on how the crime center is used and tighten its rules on data retention, permissible uses and requests from outside agencies. A new advisory group will help write policies for privately owned cameras, protests and where future cameras go.

No Flock cameras in Seattle, ever. New protections against potential abuses drawn from an outside audit. A handful of cameras in new neighborhoods. Here's what the RTCC looks like from the inside. pic.twitter.com/QeYUg8ZkW3

The Real Time Crime Center, which launched in 2025, pulls live video from hundreds of cameras into a single command room at police headquarters. They include 303 police-owned cameras at 61 sites, 116 security cameras at police buildings, 96 city traffic cameras, and 23 cameras owned by three local businesses that share their feeds with police.

Analysts watch 911 calls as they come in and pull up nearby cameras to give officers details callers may have missed, such as what a suspect is wearing or which way they ran. They also comb through recorded footage to help detectives investigate past crimes. The system runs on Fusus, software from Axon, the Arizona-based maker of police body cameras and Tasers.

Police are barred from using facial recognition with the system. The software does include an AI tool that searches video for people, vehicles and other objects, but analysts told auditors they use it only as a last resort because it is unreliable. In one case, a search for a man in a gray top and gray pants returned an image of a pigeon.

Whether the system reduces crime remains an open question. The Seattle Police Department has said officers and detectives are three times more likely to make an arrest with help from crime center analysts, and that the center assisted in 17 homicide cases in 2025, helping close 10. But the audit notes that the department counts any analyst action as “support,” such as checking a camera, even if it produced nothing useful.

Broader research on crime centers is thin, the audit found, and studies of surveillance cameras on their own show mixed results. A University of Pennsylvania evaluation of Seattle’s program, commissioned by the city’s inspector general, isn’t expected until late 2027.

Critics have warned that footage could end up with federal immigration agents or out-of-state prosecutors pursuing people who come to Washington for abortions or gender-affirming care. The audit found that state and city laws limit such sharing, but they can’t fully prevent it. Outside agencies could still get footage through public records requests or court orders served on the city or on Axon, which stores some of the police department’s video in its cloud.

“Used together, CCTV and RTCC supercharge law enforcement’s capabilities to monitor, track, and reconstruct people’s movements across the city,” Sannon said. Protecting residents, she said, requires strict, enforceable limits on how the technology is used, how long data is kept and who it’s shared with, along with independent oversight.

Wilson said the expansion and the new safeguards go together. “We can gather evidence to hold those who commit violent acts accountable and protect our neighbors targeted by federal overreach,” she said.

“Residents and businesses have sent a clear message: they want our officers to have the tools to keep them safe,” said former Gov. Chris Gregoire, CEO of Challenge Seattle.

City Councilmember Bob Kettle, who chairs the council’s public safety committee, said the committee will take up the audit’s recommendations, along with those from the city’s inspector general and auditor.

The city also plans to lay groundwork for connecting cameras run by Seattle Center tenants and nearby businesses to the crime center, according to the mayor’s office, citing interest from those businesses after the Bite of Seattle shooting in July. The audit flagged private camera integration as a key area to watch: the police department has bought about 100 devices that let businesses stream video to the center but hasn’t decided who will get them.

The advisory group, which will include members of the Community Police Commission, the Community Surveillance Working Group, police and other city staff, will meet over the next few months. Its recommendations will then go through the police department’s policy review process.
