#5455. After Jensen Huang is Howard Lutnick the prime target of national security inquiry?

When questioning the motives of certain public leaders, the Roman orator Cicero was said to have used as a shorthand, “cui bono?” meaning, whose interests come first? That line rings true as Secretary of Commerce Howard Lutnick falls under rapidly escalating bipartisan scrutiny over his role in the flow of Nvidia chips into China.

Nvidia founder and CEO Jensen Huang resigned Thursday after reports of affairs with a direct report and with Alice Huang, a suspected Chinese spy, yet the national security questions he leaves behind keep growing amidst escalating congressional investigations. Megaspeed, the Nvidia customer where Alice Huang was an executive, was suspected of funneling advanced chips to China for years, yet the U.S. government took little action. Many are now asking: Who knew what, and when? And why is this surfacing only now?

We have already described Nvidia directors’ exposure to shareholder lawsuits over their own failures of oversight. Now the scrutiny is shifting to Washington. How did the U.S. government look past so grave a threat to national security for so long, and let these sales go on? As the reporting accumulates, all roads lead to one person, who by multiple accounts blocked action over the objections of fellow cabinet members and leading voices in both parties in Congress: Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick. He is now squarely on the hot seat, and it grows hotter by the day as more information comes to light.

Megaspeed has long been a major target of U.S. government focus amidst pervasive allegations that the Singapore-based data center company helped Chinese firms evade U.S. export controls on sensitive Nvidia chips.

The Department of Commerce’s own agents began investigating Megaspeed, the Singapore firm that bought billions of dollars of Nvidia chips and is suspected of diverting them to China, in 2024, under the Biden Administration. After the change of administration but amidst the ongoing probe, The New York Times reported that in 2025, Nvidia’s general counsel emailed those agents directly, citing permission from Lutnick’s export-control chief, Jeffrey Kessler, with Commerce soon pausing its work on the investigation.

That sparked many concerns even within the GOP, with respected Senate Intelligence Committee Chair Tom Cotton writing to Lutnick directly, urging Commerce to investigate Megaspeed more carefully. Still, Megaspeed never landed on the entity list, the blacklist kept by the Department of Commerce that cuts suspect firms off from American technology; even though other agencies repeatedly agreed on proposing to add Megaspeed to the list, with the Financial Times reporting that the State Department, Treasury Department, Energy Department and the Pentagon were pushing particularly aggressively to add Megaspeed to the entity list. Despite these entreaties, Lutnick’s Commerce Department was unmoved, steadfastly refusing to add a single company to the entity list for more than a year.

Then came the memo. This spring, the New York Times reports, Secretary of State Marco Rubio oversaw the drafting of a highly classified assessment built on electronic surveillance of Alice Huang. Its conclusion was as stark as can be: China’s Ministry of State Security had recruited her to gather intelligence on Jensen Huang and on America’s AI chips, and she had grown close to the Nvidia CEO. U.S. officials assessed that Beijing’s aims may have gone further, to steering Nvidia into pressing Washington for greater Chinese access to its most advanced chips.

The memo went to a handful of senior officials before President Trump’s May trip to China, with Axios reporting that Lutnick was among those who received the memo directly. Perhaps not coincidentally, Jensen Huang was originally left off the delegation of business leaders traveling to China with Trump, before being added at the very last possible minute during an Alaska refueling stop.

That same month, Reuters reported that Commerce had cleared about 10 Chinese companies to buy H200s.

Perhaps even more alarmingly, but less widely known than the existence of the memo; Axios also reports that President Trump approved a crackdown on chip diversion to China no less than three times, in May, in August, and on Nov. 5, with even Elon Musk supportive, and that Lutnick and his deputies had resisted carrying out each order. As Maria Curi and Marc Caputo of Axios reported pithily, “One administration official has repeatedly stood in the way: Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick,” noting that virtually every other Administration official was supportive of these crackdowns.

Just last week, after news of the Jensen Huang spy scandal broke, Axios reported that Bessent confronted Lutnick about why his department has resisted implementing the export controls, particularly on Megaspeed, the company at the center of the spy scandal, with virtually all other Admin officials siding with Bessent; yet Lutnick apparently continued to stall. Already, there has been speculation that the leaks over the last week that felled Huang came from sources within the Trump Administration, perhaps from within the National Security Council, who were frustrated at Lutnick pushing what they perceived to be pro-China policies, with many remarking about the suspicious timing of these leaks right after midterm elections, even though the original memo was circulated in May this year, six months ago.

What makes this scrutiny so hot is who is turning up the temperature. Lutnick’s chief antagonists on the issue of China chip controls are almost entirely his own colleagues within the administration, ranging from Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer and National Security Adviser and Secretary of State Marco Rubio, to U.S. Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton, all of whom reportedly favor a far tougher approach than Lutnick has been willing to impose.

Lutnick’s Republican detractors are plenty outside the administration as well, particularly within the GOP congressional ranks. Republican Sen. John Kennedy says Lutnick must explain himself “in front of God and country.” Rep. Bill Huizenga has attacked Lutnick’s lack of responsiveness to Congress as “frustrating,” and the Republican chairs of the House China and Foreign Affairs committees, Rep. John Moolenaar and Rep. Brian Mast, have made their unhappiness with Lutnick just as vivid.

All these intraparty critics join legions of Democratic senators who are demanding records from Lutnick, and after last week’s midterms, their party takes the committee gavels in January with detractors making clear that Lutnick is one of their top targets – for reasons extending far beyond merely his role in sensitive U.S. technology making their way to China.

Many congressional Democrats are practically salivating at the prospect of being able to issue subpoenas to examine Lutnick’s perceived business conflicts of interests, and their files are already thick with hard questions Lutnick will have to answer.

Start with rare earths as one prominent example. In January, Commerce announced a tentative $1.6 billion deal that gives the government a roughly 10% stake in USA Rare Earth. To close it, the company raised $1.5 billion in a private stock offering and chose as its lead placement agent Cantor Fitzgerald, the firm Lutnick led for decades and which his son Brandon Lutnick, 27 when he took over, now oversees as chairman. By the lawmakers’ account, the company’s CEO credited Lutnick’s personal involvement for the deal. Sens. Elizabeth Warren, Ron Wyden and Chris Van Hollen have pressed for documents since February.

Crypto brings another witches’ brew of problems for Lutnick. Cantor has been custodian of the reserves of Tether, the largest stablecoin issuer, since 2021, and holds a stake that Sen. Richard Blumenthal says has swelled from about $600 million to an estimated $10 billion since Trump returned to office. A trust for Lutnick’s children reportedly borrowed from Tether around the time he transferred his Cantor stake to them. Cantor also launched Twenty One Capital, the bitcoin treasury company known by its ticker, XXI, with Tether, with Blumenthal already raising questions about the arrangement.

That doesn’t even factor in any potential lingering issues related to Lutnick’s longtime ties to Jeffrey Epstein, his onetime next-door Manhattan neighbor. Lutnick long maintained that he cut ties with Epstein in 2005, but Justice Department files showed a 2012 family visit to Epstein’s island, a shared investment and emails as late as 2018, which many called “grossly deceptive.” Republican Rep. Thomas Massie called on him to resign in February, and his closed-door testimony to House Oversight in May left Democrats on the panel calling him evasive.

For Lutnick, each of these issues raises the exact question Megaspeed poses: Whose interests came first, and whose side was he really on?

Defenders of Lutnick point out that he is merely carrying out Trump’s wishes as part of a broader implicit trade deal with China where the U.S. continues to provide cutting-edge chips and in exchange, the Chinese continue to provide the U.S. with rare earth minerals. But this is a misleading and misguided argument on several counts.

First, the U.S. is not nearly as dependent on China for rare earth minerals as many imagine, with the U.S. possessing tremendous reserves of rare earth minerals but merely needing some sustained investment to extract and process them. Second, this implicit deal did not apparently restrain other cabinet members, such as Secretary of State Rubio and Treasury Secretary Bessent, from registering their concerns with Lutnick’s stances. Third, Trump himself has endorsed the widely admired former CEO of Apple, Tim Cook, as the next CEO of Nvidia, echoing our own earlier endorsement of Cook. Cook has scrupulously abided by national security policies while capably and successfully balancing commerce in China with protection of US national security, and there is nothing to suggest that Cook would knowingly undermine US national security by continuing the illicit flow of chips into China.

As the questions pile up, there is no easy way out for Lutnick.  As Thomas More is said to have warned King Henry VIII, “Trust is as fragile as liquid in your hands, once you separate your fingers, its forever gone.”

Steven Tian is the director of research at the Yale Chief Executive Leadership Institute.

#5454. Can You Be Too Honest at Work? Here Are 3 Questions to Ask Before Giving Feedback.

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

It is possible to be too honest in the workplace.

Saying exactly what you think isn’t always the best career move.

Social psychologist Vanessa Bohns recently said in an interview with NPR that knowing when to speak up and when to stay quiet can be more challenging than figuring out how to phrase your thoughts.

“There are times when honesty is the best policy,” Bohns said. “On the other hand, honesty is not the best policy if whatever we say is going to be honest without any instrumental value.”

In her book Should I Say Something? The Science of What to Share—and What to Keep to Yourself, published in October, Bohns draws on research to explore which thoughts and feelings are worth voicing, and which are better left unsaid. Her guidance spans everything from offering an honest opinion to celebrating a win, apologizing or opening up.

People can find it hard to deliver criticism, even comments meant to help. “It pains us to embarrass or hurt other people,” Bohns said. Researchers call it the MUM effect, or minimizing unpleasant messages. It’s a marker of a general human tendency to hold back bad news more than good news.

Bohns advised workers to ask themselves three questions before sharing their honest opinion or feedback. First, is this information helpful? Second, would I want to hear this? And finally, do they want my feedback?

Speaking up tells the other person that you noticed something and felt it mattered enough to mention, according to Bohns.

The question, then, isn’t simply whether your opinion is honest, but if it serves the person hearing it. Will it help them improve or offer insight into themselves?

If your opinion is unkind or about something they can’t change, it might be the better route to keep it to yourself.

If a new colleague repeatedly mispronounces the CEO’s name, gently correcting them now could spare them embarrassment later.

Pointing it out could feel uncomfortable in the moment, but it could end up helping your colleague make a good impression on senior management.

Before holding back with honesty or feedback, consider whose feelings you are protecting. As Bohns writes in her book: “Are you being kind, or are you avoiding your own discomfort?”

Bohns advises against giving advice to someone who hasn’t asked for it. You may end up explaining something they already understand better than you do, she said.

Even with good intentions, deciding what someone needs to hear or how much honesty they can handle can come across as condescending, Bohns writes in her book.

Instead of making that decision for them, ask if they’d welcome your feedback. “Give them the autonomy, then respect their decision, whatever it might be,” she said.

Saying exactly what you think isn’t always the best career move.

“There are times when honesty is the best policy,” Bohns said. “On the other hand, honesty is not the best policy if whatever we say is going to be honest without any instrumental value.”

#5453. Seattle VC firm Ascend closes $17M fund to back ‘Third Act’ startups in physical AI and hardware

by Todd Bishop on Nov 11, 2026 at 7:15 amNovember 11, 2026 at 7:30 am

Venture firm Ascend has closed a $17 million third fund and landed its first institutional investor, in what founder Kirby Winfield calls the toughest fundraising market for small venture firms in 15 years.

The Seattle-based firm invests at the earliest stage, often writing the first check into a startup. It was the first investor in Overland AI, the maker of autonomous military vehicles, and an early backer of subsea geothermal startup Endurance Energy, among others.

Ascend Fund III will back more physical AI startups building robots, energy systems, defense technology and other ventures that blend software and hardware — part of a larger bet on what the Ascend team likes to call Seattle’s “Third Act.”

Winfield said raising a third fund in this market shows that Ascend has “arrived on the national stage,” along with Seattle’s rise as a hub for this new class of startups. He said the firm’s track record puts it in the same league as the country’s top seed investors.

“We are not just some nice guys in the corner of the country helping out our neighbors,” said Winfield, who works closely with Jen Haller, Ascend partner and chief of staff, and Nate Bek, a principal at the firm.

Who’s backing the fund: The new institutional investor is FirstLook Partners, a firm that invests in smaller venture funds. Josh Porter, FirstLook’s co-founder and managing partner, said the firm, which is “very bullish on the Seattle ecosystem,” looked at several startup markets outside San Francisco and New York and met many investors in Seattle, “but all roads kept leading back to Kirby.”

Porter said Winfield has “lived the founder journey” and has “the operational chops to sit across the table from a founder and empathize with what they’re going through.”

The rest of the fund comes from family offices, founders who have sold companies, and more than a dozen founders of Ascend portfolio companies.

A tough market for small funds: Ascend’s raise comes as smaller venture firms struggle to bring in new money. Their investors, mostly wealthy individuals and family offices, are waiting longer for returns from earlier funds.

Just 211 newer venture firms closed at least one fund through the end of September, down from 927 in all of 2022, according to the PitchBook-NVCA Venture Monitor. Established firms took a record 88.2% of the money raised by U.S. venture funds in the first nine months of the year, the report found. Porter said smaller firms have to show “a right to exist and a right to win deals.”

Ascend launched its first fund in 2019 and ultimately raised $15 million. Its second fund closed at $25 million in 2023. The firm generally operates in the $15 million to $25 million range and writes the same size checks regardless of fund size, Winfield said.

“We think Kirby knows his place in the larger ecosystem, knows the value he brings to the table, and has sized his fund accordingly,” Porter said.

The firm has already drawn about 60% of the money committed to Fund III. GeekWire first reported that the firm was raising the fund in April 2025, based on filings at the time. Endurance was one of the firm’s first investments from the new fund, in mid-2025.

Ascend’s track record: Winfield started Ascend after two decades in leadership roles at four startups. He described the first fund as a proof of concept that “stumbled into some unicorns,” including Fabric, an e-commerce software company that was valued at $1.5 billion in 2022. Ascend was in its first round.

With its second fund, Ascend moved away from consumer and marketplace investing to focus on enterprise AI and deep tech. Its most successful investments from that fund, according to Winfield, include Overland AI, Sabi, Yoodli and Zocks.

After Ascend’s first checks, its portfolio companies have gone on to raise more than $1.5 billion from investors including Accel, Benchmark, Bessemer, Founders Fund, Khosla and Lightspeed, according to Ascend.

Ascend’s second and third funds rank in the top 10% of funds of $50 million or less, based on current valuations of their portfolio companies, Winfield said, citing figures Ascend shared with its investors at its annual meeting. The firm didn’t disclose specific returns or how much cash it has returned to its investors.

What Ascend looks for: The firm looks for ideas that seem too difficult, too boring, too confusing or too small for big multistage venture firms to evaluate. Ideally, Winfield said, its founders are doing something that makes Series A investors “a little bit nervous.”

That’s why Ascend hasn’t made many more defense tech investments since backing Overland, he said. Valuations for well-known founders in the sector have soared as more investors have piled in.

“The time to invest in defense tech was when nobody was investing in defense tech,” Winfield said.

Porter said Ascend’s focus on Seattle and physical AI is “really the bet we made with Ascend,” adding that Endurance and Overland have the potential to become “generational, category-defining companies.”

Fund III also backs AI software and infrastructure companies, including Seattle-area startup Govstream.ai, which uses AI to speed city permitting.

Seattle’s economic climate: Winfield is a champion of Seattle’s startup scene, known for Ascend’s annual Founders Bash party in the city and his ever-present ☔🔥☔ emojis on social media, symbolizing hot startups in rainy Seattle.

Ascend’s refreshed website and brand, launched with Fund III, nod to the firm’s Seattle roots with its longstanding Seattle Startup Toolkit and a Spotify playlist of Pacific Northwest indie rock and hip-hop.

But Winfield has also been a vocal critic of state and local policies he sees as hostile to startups, including Washington’s new tax on income over $1 million, which takes effect in 2028 and survived a repeal vote last week. He worries the tax could eventually be extended to people earning $150,000 a year, which would make it harder for startups to recruit employees from places like Texas.

“The chilling effect that’s going to have on the ecosystem is real, and it’s happening,” he said.

About 60% of Ascend’s portfolio companies are based in Seattle, according to the firm.

Bek said hardware companies such as Endurance and Overland still have good reasons to be in Seattle, including testing on Lake Union and in Yakima, access to the sea and University of Washington talent. For Overland, he said, that also means proximity to Joint Base Lewis-McChord.

Combined with the region’s history in aerospace, defense and energy, Winfield noted, those advantages make Seattle one of the country’s key hubs for building physical products. He called it “El Segundo Northwest,” a reference to the Los Angeles-area city that has become a hub for defense and hardware startups.

As Winfield notes, Ascend isn’t the only early-stage firm chasing these companies. Pre-seed firms such as Cantos, Ironspring and Silent Ventures are backing similar founders, and some Seattle firms that historically focused on software are becoming more open to investing in hardware.

Ultimately, he said, Seattle still benefits from a long legacy of technical founders, and Ascend is “betting that those folks are going to continue to create companies that are worth hundreds of billions of dollars.”

#5452. Before Megaspeed, there was Supermicro: The other Nvidia partner tied to China chip smuggling—and to Jensen Huang

Whether she was a spy, a fixer, or just a paramour of Jensen Huang, the name Alice Huang (no relation) has roiled the business world this week following reports that the two were having an affair. The revelation snowballed into Jensen’s shocking resignation Wednesday.

Now come reports that officials are looking into other companies Alice was working with. Bloomberg reported, based on an anonymous source, that the Department of Justice is running multiple probes into Nvidia. One is focused on antitrust issues and two others are focused on Megaspeed—where Alice Huang was a former top executive—and Super Micro Computer. Separately, the U.S. Attorney’s Office in Manhattan is probing whether entities linked to Alice Huang were involved in alleged efforts to smuggle Supermicro hardware laced with Nvidia’s red-hot GPUs into China. It is unclear whether that probe is tied to smuggling cases already brought in the U.S. or Asia. Neither Jensen Huang, Nvidia, nor Supermicro have been formally charged with any wrongdoing.

Supermicro stock tumbled 12% after U.S. markets opened this morning. The company did not immediately respond to Fortune’s request for comment.

Thus far, much of the speculation about Jensen Huang’s catastrophic downfall as the leader of Nvidia has centered on Megaspeed, the Singapore firm that reportedly became one of Nvidia’s largest buyers in Southeast Asia. But Supermicro, the San Jose server maker run by Charles Liang, Jensen Huang’s friend of three decades and an important partner to Nvidia, has been in under the microscope regarding export-control compliance and is being pulled along with Nvidia.

Fortune has reported on the Supermicro case since before federal agents arrested its co-founder in March, and that reporting shows a company with a documented track record of governance and compliance failures. Despite its history, Supermicro has remained in lockstep with Nvidia. Liang and Jensen have shared the stage together at Computex in Taiwan, where Jensen was photographed in 2024 with Alice at a cocktail bar.

In March, federal prosecutors charged Supermicro co-founder Yih-Shyan “Wally” Liaw and two others with allegedly routing about $2.5 billion in servers laced with Nvidia H200 and B200 GPUs to China through a Southeast Asian front company. Bloomberg later reported the front company is OBON, a Bangkok-based AI infrastructure firm, which has not been charged. Supermicro was not charged and has said it was a victim of the scheme.

Liaw, who immediately resigned his executive and board roles at Supermicro following his arrest, has pleaded not guilty. His trial was pushed to March 2027 after Liaw’s lawyers told the judge in his case that subpoenas issued to Supermicro could be material to Liaw’s defense. Nelson Boxer, Liaw’s attorney, declined to comment.

One of Liaw’s co-defendants in the smuggling case, Ting-Wei “Willy” Sun, pleaded guilty in October, including to a charge that he deleted an encrypted messaging app from his phone on the day of the arrests. Sun’s attorneys did not respond to a request for comment, and it’s unclear if Sun has a cooperation agreement with the government.

There is no public evidence so far that the Supermicro and Megaspeed cases are directly connected but there are mounting threads. Thursday, Singapore’s Ministry of Home Affairs issued a statement noting that the Singapore Police Force and Customs had initiated investigations into Megaspeed and Alice Huang and in doing so sought information from Supermicro. Supermicro only offered “limited cooperation,” Singaporean authorities said.

In a July 2025 meeting, Singapore officials raised this with U.S. authorities and asked for their assistance in getting Supermicro’s cooperation and have repeated the request “on several occasions” to the Department of Justice and the FBI.

“Despite these repeated requests, Singapore has to date received limited information or assistance in respect of the company,” the statement reads. Supermicro did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Supermicro’s export-control problems did not start with Liaw’s arrest, Fortune’s reporting has found. In 2006, the company pleaded guilty to illegally exporting computer equipment to Iran through a distributor in Dubai, mirroring the basic scheme prosecutors alleged in the Liaw case.

Liaw himself has been through the crisis wringer before. He left Supermicro in 2018 amid a board-led investigation tied to Supermicro’s Nasdaq delisting and an SEC probe of its accounting, which ended with a $17.5 million settlement in 2020. Liaw returned as a consultant in May 2021, became a full-time employee, and rejoined the board in December 2023.

In 2024, short seller Hindenburg Research accused Supermicro of accounting manipulation and export-control failures and the company denied the allegations. Ernst & Young then resigned as auditor mid-audit, saying it could no longer rely on management’s representations. A special committee recommended in December 2024 that Supermicro replace CFO David Weigand and the company agreed to do so “immediately.” The company didn’t name a successor until October.

As Fortune has reported, the Liaw indictment describes thousands of nonworking dummy servers staged in warehouses to fool auditors, contractors using hair dryers to peel off serial-number labels, and a compliance auditor who was off-site allegedly enjoying “entertainment” paid for by another company during an inspection. It also shows how the alleged scheme fed directly into Nvidia’s supply pipeline. In December 2024, Liaw allegedly told the front company that “the only way” to get Nvidia to commit B200 chip allocations was to create monthly forecasts. Nvidia is not accused of wrongdoing in the Liaw indictment.

After Liaw’s arrest, Supermicro’s board opened its own investigation, overseen by independent director Scott Angel and former audit committee chair Tally Liu (no relation to Liang’s wife and co-founder Sara Liu). In August, Supermicro said that probe found no evidence that current senior management knew about the alleged scheme to diver the chips. The investigation resulted in an unspecified number of terminations in sales, business development, and technical support, Supermicro said at the time, for failure to follow policies or the code of conduct.

Supermicro has also disclosed a grand jury subpoena covering the Liaw case and the company’s compliance program and internal controls, along with subpoenas or inquiries from the SEC, the Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security, and foreign authorities.

Through all that has beleaguered Supermicro, the company’s relationship with Nvidia has appeared to remain steadfast. This will all become a test for Supermicro’s new CFO, Mark Long, a former Western Digital finance chief who took over from Weigand last month and reports to Liang. The two tag-teamed the company’s most recent earnings call, when it reported record fiscal first-quarter revenue of $19.9 billion, well ahead of Wall Street consensus estimates. Supermicro also raised its full-year revenue forecast to $72 billion to $82 billion.

But now, Supermicro—and its CEO Liang—is losing an important champion in Nvidia’s Huang. Liang built much of Supermicro’s AI-era business through the close relationship with Nvidia combined with Supermicro’s almost supernatural ability to get the newest GPUs to market quickly. Liang has also maintained a public friendship with Huang that included joint keynotes in Taipei before adoring crowds.

Nvidia will now be led in the interim by Kress while an outside investigation into the foreign intelligence operation will be run by former acting SDNY U.S. Attorney Joon Kim and powerhouse law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz.

Nvidia is slated to report third-quarter results on November 17, with Kress in place of Huang. House lawmakers have requested a closed-door grilling with Huang the following day. In January, Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) is likely to lead the Senate Banking Committee, and she’ll have subpoena powers. Warren has already sought answers from Nvidia about Supermicro and chip smuggling in June and she re-upped her request this week.

Amanda Gerut is the west coast editor at Fortune, overseeing publicly traded businesses, executive compensation, Securities and Exchange Commission regulations, and investigations.

#5451. I Looked Beyond Silicon Valley and Found a New Playbook For Building Startups

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Founders in small countries can’t rely on abundant capital or elite networks. Here’s what startups in big markets can learn from them.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

Silicon Valley teaches founders to think big. Smaller startup markets teach them how to build when almost nothing is guaranteed.

Over the past year, I have met founders and investors across the Baltics, Georgia and Guatemala through Baltic Fintech Days, a 500 Global Eurasia Demo Day in Tbilisi and Volcano Summit. These ecosystems differ in language, history and access to capital, but the strongest founders shared a common advantage: They could not rely on a large domestic market, abundant venture funding or proximity to the world’s most powerful networks.

That constraint shaped how they built. They thought internationally earlier, stretched resources further and cultivated relationships across borders. As capital becomes more selective and growth at all costs continues to fall out of favor, founders everywhere can learn from companies built in markets that have never had the luxury of excess.

Here are five lessons from some of the world’s smallest startup ecosystems.

A founder in the United States can build a large company without ever leaving the domestic market. Founders in Latvia, Lithuania, Estonia, Georgia or Guatemala rarely have that option.

The entire population of Lithuania is smaller than that of Los Angeles. Latvia has fewer than 2 million residents, while Georgia has fewer than 4 million. Even Guatemala, the largest of the markets I visited, represents only a fraction of the purchasing power available in the United States.

As a result, international expansion is not a distant ambition for many of these founders. It is part of the original business model.

At Baltic Fintech Days, I met entrepreneurs who were thinking about cross-border payments, compliance and market entry well before reaching the scale at which an American startup might begin considering international growth. Their home markets gave them useful places to test, but not enough room to stop there.

This forces founders to ask important questions early: Can the product travel? Can it serve customers across languages, currencies and regulatory systems? Does the problem exist beyond the founder’s immediate network?

Building globally does not mean launching in 10 countries at once. It means avoiding assumptions that make international expansion unnecessarily difficult later. Founders should consider localization, payment infrastructure, regulation and cross-border distribution while the company is still young enough to adapt.

Founders love to talk about resourcefulness, but the concept takes on a different meaning in ecosystems where capital, talent and customers are all more difficult to access.

At 500 Global’s Eurasia Demo Day in Tbilisi, I saw companies working to gain attention far beyond their immediate geography. They could not assume that investors would already understand their markets, recognize their universities or trust their local references. They had to communicate the problem, the opportunity and their credibility with unusual precision.

That constraint can produce better companies.

When capital is scarce, founders have less room for performative hiring, unnecessary tools or growth that cannot be tied to customer demand. They learn to test assumptions quickly, sell before everything is perfect and use partnerships to extend their reach.

Founders in major technology hubs should apply the same discipline even when more resources are available. Ask what the company would prioritize if it had half the budget, half the team and half the time. The answer often reveals which initiatives are truly essential.

Scarcity is painful, but it can also create focus. A company that learns to operate efficiently before raising significant capital may be better prepared to survive market corrections, fundraising delays and unexpected competition.

Smaller markets are often discussed only in terms of what they lack. That framing overlooks what they can offer.

The Baltics have developed deep expertise in fintech, digital infrastructure and cross-border business. Georgia sits at the intersection of Europe and Asia and is developing a generation of founders accustomed to navigating multiple markets. Guatemala offers access to Central America, proximity to the United States and entrepreneurs with firsthand knowledge of industries and consumers that remain poorly understood by many global investors.

At Volcano Summit in Guatemala, the value of the ecosystem was not simply that it brought international investors into the country. It created a place where local and regional founders could build relationships without first relocating to San Francisco, Miami or New York.

Founders should resist the urge to erase where they come from in an attempt to appear more investable. Geography can be a source of differentiated insight.

A founder who understands regional payment behavior, informal commerce, remittances or local regulation may see an opportunity long before an outsider does. The goal is not to build a business that only works locally. It is to turn local knowledge into an advantage that can travel.

The most compelling question is not, “Why would a major company come from this market?” It is, “What can a founder see from this market that others cannot?”

In mature startup hubs, founders can mistake proximity for access. They may attend dozens of events, collect hundreds of contacts and still fail to build relationships that materially help the company.

In smaller ecosystems, relationships often function as infrastructure.

One trusted introduction can connect a founder to a customer, investor or market that would otherwise be difficult to reach. Government agencies, accelerators, diaspora networks and local operators frequently play an outsized role in helping companies cross borders.

I saw versions of this at Baltic Fintech Days, through 500 Global’s network in Georgia and at Volcano Summit. These gatherings mattered because they connected local credibility with international reach. They reduced the distance between founders and people who could help them enter new markets.

Founders should approach relationship-building with the same discipline they apply to product development. Instead of asking how many people they met, they should ask whether they are building trust with the right customers, partners and advocates.

That also means becoming useful before asking for something. Founders can share market intelligence, make introductions and offer thoughtful feedback. In smaller ecosystems, reputations travel quickly. Generosity and reliability compound.

A founder in a well-known ecosystem benefits from familiar signals. Investors recognize the schools, employers, accelerators and other funds around the table. Founders from less visible markets must often establish credibility without those shortcuts.

That makes storytelling a core business capability.

The strongest founders I encountered did not simply explain what their products did. They connected a local problem to a much larger shift. A payments challenge became a story about global commerce. A compliance product became infrastructure for the international workforce. A regional marketplace became evidence of changing consumer behavior across emerging economies.

Founders should not expect investors or customers to do this translation themselves.

A strong pitch should answer four questions: Why does this problem matter? Why is the opportunity larger than it first appears? Why is this team uniquely equipped to solve it? And why is now the right moment?

This is especially important for founders building outside established technology centers. Investors may incorrectly interpret an unfamiliar market as a small opportunity. The founder’s job is to distinguish the company’s starting point from its potential destination.

Talent is distributed far more evenly than capital, attention or access. Some of the world’s most ambitious founders are building in places that receive only a fraction of global venture investment.

The Baltics, Georgia and Guatemala are not interchangeable, nor should they be reduced to a single category of “emerging markets.” Each has its own strengths, challenges and history. What connects them is the resourcefulness required to build beyond the limits of a small domestic ecosystem.

Founders everywhere can learn from that mindset.

Start globally. Use constraints to sharpen your decisions. Turn local knowledge into an advantage. Treat relationships as infrastructure. And make the scale of your ambition impossible to misunderstand.

The next category-defining company may not come from the place investors visit most often. It may come from the market whose founders learned to build without waiting for the world to notice.

Silicon Valley teaches founders to think big. Smaller startup markets teach them how to build when almost nothing is guaranteed.

Over the past year, I have met founders and investors across the Baltics, Georgia and Guatemala through Baltic Fintech Days, a 500 Global Eurasia Demo Day in Tbilisi and Volcano Summit. These ecosystems differ in language, history and access to capital, but the strongest founders shared a common advantage: They could not rely on a large domestic market, abundant venture funding or proximity to the world’s most powerful networks.

That constraint shaped how they built. They thought internationally earlier, stretched resources further and cultivated relationships across borders. As capital becomes more selective and growth at all costs continues to fall out of favor, founders everywhere can learn from companies built in markets that have never had the luxury of excess.

#5450. Canton Coin Gets SEC "Digital Commodity" Label: Here's What the Two Prongs Actually Mean

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

The SEC's Division of Corporation Finance called Canton Coin a digital commodity on November 3. The ruling rests on two representations, including the absence of a "central party."

The most important words in the SEC's Canton Coin letter aren't "digital commodity." They are the ones the staff put in front of that label: the conclusion holds "in reliance on the representations" Canton's lawyers made. The SEC didn't independently prove the network has no central party. It accepted a description and attached a conclusion to it.

On November 3, the Division of Corporation Finance's Office of Chief Counsel answered Canton Network's October 30 request. The response came from Deputy Chief Counsel Jonathan A. Ingram and was addressed to the staff team of Ted Yu, Andrew Schoeffler and Mark Vilardo. The Division said it views Canton Coin as a "digital commodity" as the term is described in the SEC's March interpretation.

It also said it will not recommend enforcement action if Canton Coin is minted programmatically by Super Validators, Validators and application providers, as described in the request. That holds without registration under Section 5 of the Securities Act or Section 12(g) of the Exchange Act, and it applies if the issuer relies on an opinion of counsel. The facts the staff relied on are laid out in the Canton Network's incoming letter.

Early coverage focused on the classification label. The more useful story, though, is how the staff got there.

The staff pointed to two representations. The first is that Canton Coin is intrinsically linked to, and derives its value from, the programmatic operation of the Canton Network, along with supply and demand dynamics. Its value does not come from an expectation of profits from the essential managerial efforts of others.

That phrase echoes the Howey test, the long-standing U.S. framework for investment contracts. The prong asks a simple question: when someone holds this token, are they betting on a team's work, or on a network that runs by itself? On the facts presented, the staff's answer was the network.

This is the more familiar half of the analysis, and most token projects argue some version of it. Because almost every issuer makes the same claim, the first prong carries less weight on its own, which is why the second one deserves a closer look.

The second representation is that the Canton Network has no "central party," as the March interpretation defines that term. In the SEC and CFTC's framework, a digital commodity belongs to a functional crypto system that has no central party overseeing participation or distributing rewards to users.

This prong is the one to watch, because Canton Coin is minted by Super Validators, Validators and application providers. Those are named roles in a structured network, so a skeptic could fairly ask whether the Super Validator tier looks like a central party in practice. The letter's answer rests on the word "programmatically": the minting follows protocol rules rather than anyone's discretion.

Legal commentators reading the March interpretation have also pointed out that it doesn't fully explain how the "central party" concept relates to its separate definition of decentralization. The Canton letter doesn't settle that either. It applies the term to one set of facts and stops there.

A no-action letter is narrower than it sounds. The Division itself says the response states its position on enforcement action only and expresses no legal conclusion on the issues presented. It also says the positions rest on the representations in the request, and that different facts or conditions might lead to different conclusions.

In practice, that comes down to three points. First, the letter is staff-level guidance rather than a Commission vote. Second, it protects reliance on the specific arrangement described, not the token in every future circumstance. Third, if the representations change, the comfort can disappear.

For a company, the letter is still valuable, since a written statement that staff won't recommend enforcement is a strong signal. Even so, it shouldn't be mistaken for a permanent legal classification. It is a snapshot of staff views based on facts someone else supplied.

The framework behind the letter is the Commission's March 17 interpretation, which the CFTC joined. It sorts crypto assets into five categories: digital commodities, digital collectibles, digital tools, stablecoins and digital securities. Four of the five are generally treated as non-securities, and the securities analysis stays fact-specific for the rest.

The two documents do different jobs. The interpretation is a general map: it tells the market how the Commission thinks about categories and which features push an asset one way or the other. The Canton letter is an application. It takes a named token, tests it against the map's digital commodity category, and gives a case-specific enforcement answer.

That sequence matters. The interpretation says what a digital commodity looks like, and the letter says that, if the facts are as represented, Canton Coin looks like one.

The practical lesson is about preparation. Canton's request framed its facts to fit the two prongs, and the staff responded in those terms. Projects hoping for similar treatment will likely follow the same template: document how value arises from network operation, and document why no single party oversees participation or distributes rewards.

The harder test will come from tokens with more visible governance or a more active operating team. Those projects will have to explain why their structure doesn't amount to a central party, and the Canton letter doesn't say where that line sits.

For now, the letter works best as an early data point rather than a final answer. The classification label drew the attention, but the representations behind it are what other projects will study. How the staff handles the next request, especially one with a messier governance story, will show whether the "no central party" prong is a narrow gate or a wide one.

#5449. Tech Moves: Wizards of the Coasts names president; new execs at Skydance, Pulumi, Marchex and Syndio

Tech Moves covers notable hires, promotions and personnel changes in the Pacific NW tech community. Submissions: [email protected]

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 11, 2026 at 10:24 amNovember 11, 2026 at 11:04 am

— Dan Ayoub, the past head of Dungeons & Dragons, has been named president of Wizards of the Coast & Hasbro Digital Games. Ayoub joined the Renton, Wash.-based Wizards of the Coast in 2022 and counts himself among the longtime players of D&D and Magic: The Gathering.

“D&D is 52 years old. Magic is 33. Brands don’t last that long because of any one leader; they last because generations of creators and fans keep choosing them,” Ayoub said. “We owe it to them to protect what makes these worlds special.”

Earlier in his career, Ayoub spent more than a decade at Microsoft, primarily with its 343 Industries video game studio, now called Halo Studios.

— Farah Ali has joined the media company Skydance as vice president of engineering, based at its Bellevue, Wash., office. She previously spent a decade at Electronic Arts over two stints, most recently as vice president of AI transformation and technology.

Ali has also served as an affiliate professor at the University of Washington, teaching courses in software entrepreneurship, and as a technical advisor for Madrona Venture Labs. She was co-founder and chief technology officer of FreightWeb, a Seattle-based logistics technology startup.

Paramount Skydance last month completed its acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery (WBD), with the combined company taking the name Skydance. Shortly after, the company announced the departure of two WBD leaders from the Bellevue site: Avi Saxena and Tyler Whitworth.

— Irene Chang has joined Pulumi as chief revenue officer. The Seattle startup automates cloud infrastructure tasks such as managing networks and databases, optimizing costs and ensuring compliance.

Chang said Pulumi’s culture and product won her over. “We automate deployments so teams can provision resources in seconds and scale from simple apps to enterprise architectures without losing control or compliance,” she wrote on LinkedIn.

Chang was previously Postman’s VP of corporate sales for the Americas and before that held VP roles at Cloudflare.

Pulumi is No. 15 on the GeekWire 200, a ranked index of the Pacific Northwest’s top startups.

— Marchex, the Seattle-based, publicly traded call and conversation analytics company, has named Travis Fairchild as president. The news was disclosed in an SEC filing. Fairchild was previously with Marchex for 18 years in strategy and business development roles.

He left in 2021 to become CEO of Archenia, a Las Vegas-based customer qualification and acquisition company, which Marchex acquired in July.

Troy Hartless, who in September 2025 added president to his role as chief revenue officer, will return to serving solely as CRO.

— General Fusion has named David Janashvili as chief financial officer, effective Nov. 30. The Vancouver, B.C.-based company is developing fusion energy devices and became the first fusion venture to go public, through a SPAC. It trades on Nasdaq as GFUZ.

Janashvili joins from Surami Partners, which provides financial services for clean tech companies, and previously led climate tech investment banking at CIBC Capital Markets. Across numerous roles, he has advised boards and management teams of public and soon-to-be public companies.

— Gravity Payments has appointed CEO Tammi Kroll as chairman of its board of directors while she continues to lead the digital payments company.

“Her appointment as Chairman recognizes more than a decade of leadership at Gravity and her role in helping the company grow while remaining focused on the independent businesses and employees it serves,” the company said.

Kroll joined the company in 2015 as CTO, chief operating officer and chief information officer. She took over as CEO in 2022 after founder Dan Price resigned while facing assault and reckless driving charges. That case and a second were dropped, and Price maintained his innocence.

— Syndio, a Seattle-based pay equity startup, has two more leadership changes following the addition of seven new executives in April:

Syndio is No. 45 on the GeekWire 200, a ranked index of the Pacific Northwest’s top startups.

— Seattle-based real estate brokerage Redfin has named Andy Swanton as general manager of rentals. He returns to the company after a short stint in 2022 as VP of properties. Swanton has also worked for Opendoor and BYD.

— Seattle cybersecurity company ExtraHop has appointed Rupert Clayson as head of sales for Europe, the Middle East and Africa (EMEA). The company reports growth in sectors including financial services and energy, and offers defense against AI-assisted security attacks. Clayson, who is based in London, joined from TeamViewer and was previously with Fortinet.

— POSaBIT Systems, a Seattle-based company providing point-of-sale and payments technology for the cannabis industry, has named Emily Eagon as CFO. Eagon joined POSaBIT last year as vice president of finance and has more than 25 years of experience in finance and accounting roles, including leadership at Verdigris and predictis.

#5448. ‘That Nvidia guarantee is not worth what it was worth a week ago’: What Jensen Huang’s exit means for neoclouds

Jensen Huang’s resignation from Nvidia hits the AI industry’s most indebted borrowers hardest, according to one investor who backs AI infrastructure.

Nvidia said Thursday that Huang resigned as president, CEO and board member, effective immediately. His exit follows his admission of an extramarital affair with a woman U.S. intelligence officials believe to be a Chinese spy, and following a board investigation into the affair. CFO Colette Kress is now interim CEO, and the board named Harvey Jones its first chair.

While Nvidia’s leadership switch-up is sending shockwaves across every industry that relies on its chips to those who simply have stock or their 401Ks resting in company, some say the companies that are most at risk are the so-called neoclouds that rely on Nvidia’s chips.

Nvidia designs the chips that most AI models are trained on, and Taiwan’s TSMC manufactures them, and that’s a problem. So says Joe Kaiser, who started Switchyard Partners at the beginning of this year after serving as CEO of Mercato Partners, which managed about $1.5 billion.

Neoclouds such as CoreWeave and Nebius buy those chips by the hundreds of thousands, fill data centers with them and rent the computing power to AI labs and other companies, competing with Amazon, Google and Microsoft.

But Nvidia does more than sell to them. It invests in them: the company held about $329 million in Nebius shares, for example, at the end of June. Nvidia also guarantees their business. In July, Nvidia began offering to rent back unused GPU capacity from neocloud partners at a fixed rate, a floor meant to make banks more willing to lend. The company later joined a $500 billion financing platform with six institutional partners, of which Nvidia may backstop up to $125 billion. That backstop, Kaiser said, posed an issue for what lenders are pricing.

“The chip isn’t what puts them at risk, but it’s the financial backstop that allows CoreWeave or Nebius to go get those hundreds of millions of dollars of debt from Blackstone and Brookfield,” Kaiser told Fortune. “Why is Blackstone willing to back a CoreWeave project? It’s because they know that there’s an Nvidia backstop, a written backstop, behind it, and so it lowers the risk, and then obviously lowers the interest rate.”

CoreWeave carried $35 billion in debt at the end of June, and lenders had grown wary of businesses that depend wholly on AI demand, well before Huang left.

“If the capital providers now say that Nvidia guarantee is not worth what it was worth a week ago, that puts those neocloud businesses at risk,” Kaiser said. “At the end of the day, this is a heavy-asset, infrastructure-based industry.”

OpenAI and SoftBank’s SB Energy may be the biggest beneficiaries of Nvidia’s backstops, with CoreWeave and Nebius close behind. Kaiser referenced how Nvidia has been in talks over a reported $250 billion backstop to help OpenAI lease an Ohio data center campus that SB Energy is developing.

Following Huang’s resignation, Neocloud stocks fell Thursday: CoreWeave dropped about 9%, giving back part of a 25% rally the day before. Nebius fell 16%, though it also issued weak full-year guidance the same day. Nvidia itself lost about $450 billion in market value in the days after Huang admitted the affair, before Thursday’s drop.

Kaiser doesn’t expect Nvidia to lose its grip on AI training for at least two or three years, because customers built on its CUDA software will find it “really hard” to switch. The fight is over inference, the work of running models once they’re trained, which Kaiser said now takes up more AI compute than training. There, buyers are weighing Nvidia’s general-purpose chips against cheaper ones built for specific jobs: Qualcomm for robotics, Cerebras, Etched, Google’s TPUs and Amazon’s Trainium.

“If Nvidia no longer has Jensen as its rainmaker, did that just tip the scale towards using specialized chips?” Kaiser said.

“The bigger play is actually for the specialty chip makers,” he said, but said AMD and Broadcom will inevitably gain an opening. Google and Amazon could win twice: by pitching their own chips to labs like OpenAI and Anthropic, and by lending their balance sheets. “The Googles and others can step into that Nvidia backstop arrangement,” he said.

TSMC should come through fine, Kaiser said. He estimated about two-thirds of its capacity goes to Nvidia, but said it could shift that to other customers “in pretty short order.”

Kaiser said Huang ran Nvidia on a “hub-and-spoke” model. “The stories are true about Jensen having 60-plus direct reports,” he said, which now leaves “this leadership vacuum and vision vacuum.”

He referenced Intel after Andy Grove stepped down as CEO in 1998. “Andy Grove and Jensen both have just this iron-fist approach to management, very disciplined approach,” he said. Intel kept growing revenue after Grove left, he said, but the company lost margin and “didn’t adapt as well” as chip demand moved toward new uses.

“Intel is the roadmap here to what might be ahead for Nvidia.”

Kaiser also tied Huang’s exit to last week’s midterms, where data centers became a campaign issue. Calling Huang the industry’s “true spokesperson” for data centers, and with that spokesperson now gone, he said, the case for giant single-site data centers weakens further.

“This is just more push for distributed edge compute,” he said, “away from these mega monolithic data centers.”

Catherina covers markets, the economy, energy, tech, and AI.

#5447. Jersey Mike’s Opens Its First UK Shop — And It Has a Sub You Can’t Get in the U.S. Blimey!

About 300 locations are planned for the UK and Ireland, part of a push toward 15,000 restaurants worldwide.

Jersey Shore, meet Oxford Circus. Jersey Mike’s opened its first restaurant in the United Kingdom on Monday, according to Nation’s Restaurant News. It’s the chain’s first international location outside Canada.

The guy running the show is Peter Cancro. He bought the original sub shop in 1975 at age 17, built it into a national powerhouse and sold it to Blackstone in 2024. Now he’s back as master franchisee for the UK and Ireland, where he sees room for about 300 locations. The UK tops the chain’s list of about 14 priority markets, and the company is in talks with potential operators in Mexico, the Middle East, Korea and Continental Europe.

The Jersey Mike’s menu across the pond mostly mirrors the U.S. one — with a few exceptions. It adds a chicken tenders sub, since turkey isn’t as big a draw in Europe, and a hot ham and cheese that isn’t sold in the States. The chain, which recently went public, has some catching up to do with rival Subway, which has more than 2,100 UK shops, down from 2,446 in 2019. Is Mike’s sweating it? Fuhgeddaboudit.

#5446. AWS gives developers a free local stand-in for its cloud, built from scratch by AI agents

by Todd Bishop on Nov 11, 2026 at 10:51 amNovember 11, 2026 at 10:51 am

AWS says its engineers didn’t write or review a single line of code in its newest developer tool, and the company is touting that as a selling point.

AWS Emulator, released Wednesday, simulates AWS services on a developer’s own machine. It’s built from more than 400 API models covering more than 200 AWS services. Developers and AI coding agents can use it to test code without a network connection and without paying for the real cloud.

The tool addresses a problem that coding agents such as Amazon’s Kiro and Anthropic’s Claude Code have made worse. Agents can write code faster than teams can test it against the real cloud. Agents check their work by running the code and reading the results, over and over, and doing that in the cloud adds delays and costs.

The emulator lets them run that loop on a developer’s own machine.

In an ironic or perhaps appropriate twist, AWS used AI agents to build the emulator. Agents also maintain it, testing it against real AWS and fixing the gaps they find.

“The emulator was written entirely by autonomous agents. Our team hasn’t written or reviewed any of the code,” wrote Matt Goldberg, the AWS senior principal engineer behind the project, in a blog post.

Goldberg compared his agents to himself as a kindergartner, too young to hold a crayon properly, who got yelled at by classmates for ruining a group drawing of dinosaurs. The problem wasn’t bad intent, he wrote, just a lack of competence. The answer, for agents, is clearly defined areas to fill in.

“I think agents also need coloring books,” he wrote.

The agents work from AWS’s public API models, which describe how each service should behave, and check their work against the real AWS cloud.

The agents run on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore in three teams. One writes “fidelity tests” — real-world scenarios such as creating a queue, sending a message and deleting the queue — and checks each against real AWS. A second runs those tests against the emulator and files issues for failures, and a third fixes them, one agent per issue.

Every change passes through an automated gate where other agents check coding standards and security. Goldberg wrote that hundreds of agents now fix thousands of issues a day.

The project started as a weekend experiment, inspired by Anthropic’s demonstration earlier this year in which a team of Claude agents built a C compiler. Goldberg gave Kiro a three-step prompt and got a passable first version of Amazon SQS, AWS’s message queuing service, in 15 minutes.

By the end of the weekend, Goldberg wrote, Kiro had built a rough version of the rest of AWS, with obvious gaps, and his team started using it to test its software that Monday.

Swami Sivasubramanian, AWS vice president of agentic AI and emerging tech, tied the project to a lesson he described to GeekWire in June. He spent four nights babysitting Kiro as it tried to rebuild a replication engine he and Allan Vermeulen built by hand nearly 20 years ago.

Once he gave the agent a spec and a way to test its work, the job took about two hours.

“When agents write the code and check their own work, the engineer’s job is to give them room to work on their own and to build the specs, tests, and merge gates that decide when that work is correct,” Sivasubramanian wrote in a guest post on CTO Werner Vogels’ blog.

It’s the same idea behind Amazon’s recent move to rewrite its engineering playbook for an era when AI writes the code.

The emulator has limits. Devin Pratt, an IDC analyst, told InfoWorld that it doesn’t yet simulate throttling, outages or differences in which services and features are available by region, and that it doesn’t sandbox the code it runs. The agents’ backlog of known gaps is public, in a GitHub folder called “things-that-do-not-work.”

Other AWS emulators exist, most notably LocalStack, which this year put its free version behind an account requirement and limited it to noncommercial use. AWS released its emulator for free under CC0, a public domain dedication, with the full commit history on GitHub.

The company says it will share more at its upcoming re:Invent conference.

#5445. This Remake of a Classic ’90s Video Game Sold 5.2 Million Copies in 4 Days: ‘So Freaking Wild’

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Nintendo’s update of the classic got off to a faster start than any other Switch 2 game the company has published.

Gamers are going zany for Zelda. The line outside Best Buy’s Union Square store in New York wrapped around the corner. The first fans had been waiting since 7 a.m. for the midnight launch. Some came in costume. One couple brought their newborn in a stroller, The Drum reports.

They were there for The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, a Switch 2 remake of the 1998 Nintendo 64 classic. It sold more than 5.2 million copies worldwide in its first four days, including 810,000 in Japan, according to Nintendo. The company says no other Switch 2 game it has published has had a bigger four-day start.

“It was so freaking wild,” Lisa Valentino, Best Buy’s chief ads and media officer, tells The Drum. She says gaming cuts across every demographic. “It is culture, and it is this phenomenon.”

The original game is often ranked among the greatest video games ever made. The Ocarina of Time remake has reimagined visuals but keeps the time-jumping gameplay, where Link switches between his child and adult selves.

Gamers are going zany for Zelda. The line outside Best Buy’s Union Square store in New York wrapped around the corner. The first fans had been waiting since 7 a.m. for the midnight launch. Some came in costume. One couple brought their newborn in a stroller, The Drum reports.

They were there for The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, a Switch 2 remake of the 1998 Nintendo 64 classic. It sold more than 5.2 million copies worldwide in its first four days, including 810,000 in Japan, according to Nintendo. The company says no other Switch 2 game it has published has had a bigger four-day start.

#5444. AI industry execs brace for future without leading hype man, Nvidia’s Jensen Huang

Tech industry insiders awoke Thursday morning with an unfamiliar, and somewhat alarming notion to contemplate: life without Jensen Huang.

Huang’s abrupt resignation as CEO leaves one of the world’s most valuable companies without the leader who has steered it for the past 33 years; the person who almost singlehandedly transformed Nvidia from a small maker of video game graphics chips into the driving force of the AI boom.

“NVIDIA’s leadership crisis is a stress test for the AI boom,” Stephanie Balaouras, Forrester’s VP, group research director, told Fortune.

The importance of Nvidia, and of Huang, to the AI industry extends well beyond the company’s own P&L statement. In addition to being the leading maker of the GPU chips powering AI services like ChatGPT and Claude, Nvidia has become the AI industry’s “central bank” financing scores of other companies. And then there’s Huang’s unique standing as AI’s senior statesman and cheerleader on everything from AI regulation to industrial policy.

Whether the AI industry turns out to have lost its most famous champion with the ignominious exit of Huang and his famous black leather coat, or a more crucial, Jenga-like piece may be the most important economic question to be answered in the coming weeks and months.

“Obviously Nvidia is more than Jensen Huang, but he kind of championed a whole range of investments,” a VC investor focused on early-stage companies told Fortune.

“There is a question around whether the pace of investment in AI and the size of the amounts of capital going into companies can be continued. Because by any stretch of the imagination, it’s been quite extreme,” the investor said.

In the immediate aftermath of the news, the stock market appears to be keeping its composure. While shares of Nvidia were down 6.3% in midday trading on Thursday, and certain AI-linked stocks took a hit, the broader market reaction was relatively muted, with the Nasdaq down only 95 points.

But with spending on AI and data centers so important to the broader U.S. economy, the extent of the potential fallout from the Nvidia shakeup is difficult to overstate.

Looming largest on the horizon is Anthropic’s widely anticipated initial public offering, scheduled to occur next week. The Anthropic IPO (along with OpenAI’s IPO expected in 2027) represent make-or-break moments for the AI industry—closely watched events that will serve as proxies for the health, and momentum, of the AI business.

If nothing else, one startup founder told Fortune, the Nvidia drama raises the stakes for Anthropic’s upcoming IPO: “If the Anthropic IPO doesn’t go well and if the OpenAI IPO [down the line] doesn’t go well, there’s a question of: Is there a path to profitability for any players in the AI space?”

Antropic is seeking to raise upwards of $60 billion in the offering slated for November 18, giving the five-year old AI company a valuation that could exceed $1.4 trillion when it makes its expected Wall Street debut next week.

Karl Alomar, a partner at venture firm M13, argued that investors will recognize the strength in Anthropic’s business, regardless of the Nvidia shakeup.

“From where I stand, Anthropic is still in as good, as strong and as good a position as it was before this news came out,” Alomar said.

“I’m not sure it’ll have a massive impact on them. Anthropic’s numbers are fantastic, and they’ve clearly shown that they have excess capacity for what they need,” he said.

Anthropic’s business prospects are closely intertwined with those of the cloud providers, which provide the data centers and compute capacity to train and run AI models like Claude. (According to Anthropic’s S-1 filing, it has roughly $900 billion in compute spending commitments over the next several decades.)

While the tech giants like Alphabet, Amazon, and Microsoft have the wherewithal to ride out whatever turbulence is caused by the changes at Nvidia, the situation may be trickier for the smaller “neo-cloud” companies—many financed by Nvidia—that buy Nvidia chips in bulk and rent out the computing power.

Huang has championed these neo-cloud companies because it was good for business and the company’s influence, Jay Goldberg, an analyst at Seaport Research Partners and one of the few on Wall Street with a sell rating on Nvidia’s stock. “He’d rather have 300 small customers who are dependent on him than three massive ones who you can’t negotiate with,” he said.

With Nvidia CFO Coleen Kress now serving as interim CEO, the company’s attitude towards neo-clouds could shift. According to a report in The Information on Thursday, Kress has occasionally pushed back against Huang’s deals in the AI ecosystem, including a deal to backstop $250 billion in credit for an OpenAI datacenter project.

The “Nvidia money train” that has kept parts of the market that propped up could come to an end, said one venture capital partner invested in numerous AI startups. “ The idea that they could count on Nvidia for future financing is unlikely.”

Shares of CoreWeave one of the leading neocloud providers were down 7.5% on Thursday, while Nebius Group, another neo-cloud company which gave a lighter-than-expected sales forecast during its quarterly earnings on Thursday, were down 18%.

Investors are likely to look harder at the numbers Huang used to justify the complex web of investments. Jason Schloetzer, an associate professor at Georgetown University’s McDonough School of Business, expects investors and policymakers alike may start re-examining “Jensen math.”

U.S. policy towards data centers could also come in for harsher treatment, particularly after last week’s midterm elections in which voters overwhelmingly registered their opposition to having the facilities built in their communities.

Huang gave much of the industry credibility, even amid the backlash to datacenters. He was well-liked and not seen as a polarizing political figure, said Goldberg, of Seaport Research. But with Huang gone, the data center industry becomes “much more vulnerable to political pressure,” he said Goldberg.

Similarly, lawmakers advocating stricter regulation of AI technology, both the large language models as well as the chips that power the models, now have a much stronger hand. Huang was an outspoken proponent of loose regulations for AI. But his affair with a woman alleged to be a Chinese spy has destroyed his credibility on the regulatory issues.

“This guarantees new export controls,” Ed Mills, policy analyst at investment firm Raymond James, said of the spy scandal that contributed to Huang’s downfall. “It was extremely likely before the scandal and this is the accelerant to push it over the finish line.” Three bills proposing new export controls on AI chips and advanced semiconductor equipment are currently attached to the defense authorization bill awaiting passage on Capitol Hill.

It is also possible that Washington will enact licensing requirements or restrictions on open-source AI models. Huang had been a leading voice opposing such measures. Because the best open source models on the market have been created by Chinese AI labs, “open source equals China” in the minds of many lawmakers, particularly China hawks, Mills said. “If Washington is serious about trying to win the AI race against China we need to see regulations on open source,” he said.Brad Carson, the former Democratic Congressman who is now president of Americans for Responsible Innovation, a lobby group that supports AI regulation, said he was less certain of the threat Huang’s removal as CEO poses to open source AI. Even after Huang’s downfall, such licensing requirements are unlikely given the support open-source AI has among certain factions in Congress and the technical difficulty of designing effective rules for these models, he said.

The AI policy push will happen against the backdrop of a widening investigative effort, with Nvidia’s relationship with companies such as Megaspeed and Super Micro under the microscope.

“What’s happened at Nvidia is for Nvidia to address,” said Tony Ball, CEO of Entrust, a digital security company. “But in terms of the way AI is going to continue to add value to organizations and productivity, this was an inevitable structural challenge, and governance and policy issue that the world was going to have to wrestle to the ground.”

Beatrice Nolan is a tech reporter on Fortune’s AI team, covering artificial intelligence and emerging technologies and their impact on work, industry, and culture. She's based in Fortune's London office and holds a bachelor’s degree in English from the University of York. You can reach her securely via Signal at beatricenolan.08

Allie Garfinkle is a senior writer and editor at Fortune, where she runs Term Sheet; leads coverage of private capital, investors, and startups; and co-chairs the Brainstorm conference series.

Jeremy Kahn is the AI editor at Fortune, spearheading the publication's coverage of artificial intelligence. He also co-authors Eye on AI, Fortune’s flagship AI newsletter.

#5443. Rand Fishkin’s Seattle game studio serves up first trailer for ‘The Snackbar at the End of the World’

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 11, 2026 at 11:21 amNovember 11, 2026 at 11:21 am

If the eventual release of “The Snackbar at the End of the World” is a full-on meal for video game fans, news this week of the game’s first trailer should at least suffice as an appetizer.

Seattle-based Snackbar Studio, co-founded by SparkToro founder Rand Fishkin and his wife, writer Geraldine DeRuiter, unveiled its debut title and Steam page on Tuesday. The hand-drawn narrative adventure RPG puts players in the role of a chef trying to save a struggling family restaurant in a magical version of 1960s Italy.

The studio now plans to launch the game late next year, after originally targeting the second half of 2026. Snackbar raised $2.15 million from 38 angel investors two years ago, and the project began four years ago, according to Fishkin. The team includes five co-founders (Fishkin, DeRuiter, game designer Nicolas Kraj, lead programmer Miriam Cabrera and art director Francesco Mazza) plus about 10 contractors.

In the studio’s description on Steam, players forage for ingredients in the “forbidden wilds” outside town, battling explosive tomatoes, chaotic zucchini and vendetta-driven poultry. They then cook dishes back at the restaurant before a tyrannical mayor known as the Sindaco can shut it down. The game mixes combat and stealth with cooking mini-games based on real-world recipes.

The trailer is set to “’O surdato ’nnammurato,” a classic Neapolitan song performed by professional musicians recruited by the studio’s music director. Fishkin said he and DeRuiter both cried the first time they heard it.

Fishkin is best known in Seattle tech circles as co-founder of SEO software company Moz and audience research startup SparkToro, and he more recently launched Alertmouse, a tool for tracking online mentions. DeRuiter, a writer and author, is Snackbar’s head writer.

In a LinkedIn post this week, Fishkin recalled telling DeRuiter during the COVID lockdown that he wanted to fulfill a childhood dream of making a video game. Her reply: “Don’t wait. Do it now. I’ll do it with you.”

In the same post, he said the game’s themes include found family and fighting fascism “even when there’s no hope you’ll win.” He called it a love letter to DeRuiter’s small family village in the mountains outside Naples, to that era of Italy, to video games, and to the many people both of their families have lost in recent years.

Moments like hearing that song come often in the work, Fishkin said, such as when a new feature clicks or a new animation brings DeRuiter’s characters to life. He has always loved art without being good at any form of it. “I may not be able to create art, but I can enable it,” he said. “What a wonderful feeling.”

There have been lows, too. The team spent its initial 18 months on the project with a contract agency that didn’t work out, losing money with nothing to show for it. Fishkin is glad they kept going, “even when it felt financially irresponsible.”

The game is entirely human-made, and Snackbar’s no-AI stance is firm. “Geraldine hates AI with the fury of a thousand suns,” Fishkin said. He once suggested, just once, that she use Google’s AI Mode to find a synonym, and she was mad at him for the rest of a six-hour flight home from Philadelphia. Even if players, the rest of the team and the games media were fine with AI (and they’re not), DeRuiter alone would make it a no-go, he said.

Still ahead are 10 to 12 months of finishing the game’s content, playtesting, bug fixing, marketing and launch prep. Fishkin called it daunting, but said team members have done it many times before, “even though it’s our first rodeo.”

Fishkin is still juggling Snackbar with SparkToro and Alertmouse, and describes his role at the studio as mostly oversight and management. SparkToro is growing again, and Alertmouse recently hit a big milestone in annual renewals with high retention. He and his Alertmouse co-founders are putting more money into the company to fund growth.

Balancing the three roles is a challenge, he said, but only rarely completely overwhelming. “Like this week.”
