#5442. She Started a Small Gathering to Celebrate Women in Sports. Eight Years Later, The Sports Power Awards Are Sponsored by ESPN Films

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

After launching the Sports Power Brunch in 2019, sports publicist LaTonya Story has grown it into the Sports Power Awards, attracting major sponsors including the NFL, Prime Video, Visa and ESPN Films.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

Ironically, the more connected we become online, the more valuable in-person experiences are. It’s classic scarcity theory, and sports publicist and entrepreneur LaTonya Story understands it as well as anyone. That insight helped inspire her to launch the Sports Power Brunch, an event celebrating the most influential women in sports.

Now, after seven years as The Sports Power Brunch: Celebrating the Most Powerful Women in Sports®, the event is entering a new era as The Sports Power Awards™. The rebrand will debut at the eighth annual celebration on Feb. 10, 2027, at The Beverly Hills Hotel during Super Bowl LXI Week in Los Angeles.

Story spoke with Entrepreneur about building the event from the ground up, the thinking behind the rebrand, and the keys to its enduring success.

The Sports Power Brunch wasn’t Story’s first foray into event planning. It grew out of something she was already doing in Atlanta: Ladies Pigskin Sundays, weekly gatherings for women who love football.

Through her connections in the sports industry, Story grew the events to include DJs, giveaways, and even NFL-provided swag bags. So when the Super Bowl came to Atlanta in 2019, she was already well positioned to host a bigger celebration.

“I wanted to do an event that honored and celebrated women in sports who I personally admired,” she says. Guided by the belief that “a closed mouth don’t get fed” and “if you have not, because you ask not,”

Story took the initiative to reach out to women she admired, many of whom she had never met, and launched the inaugural Sports Power Brunch in her hometown.

“I live by the philosophy: ‘If you build it, they will come,’” she says. “Ultimately, my end goal is to have an actual sports awards show for either streaming or linear television.”

Of course, bringing influential people together doesn’t automatically make for a great event. Story is conscious of that, which is part of the reason behind this year’s format changes.

“One thing I noticed with our previous format, which included panel discussions, is that people were so excited to meet, greet, and talk to one another,” Story says. “Sometimes you lose that excitement when you transition from the awards into a panel discussion.”

Not wanting to lose that momentum, Story decided to have guests go straight from the awards show into the post-event networking mixer, with panel discussions moved to the second day.

“The true value of a live event isn’t measured solely by bringing people together in a room, although I love doing that,” Story says. “For me, it’s really about longevity and impact, giving sponsors a memorable experience that keeps them coming back, and building a brand that invests in the real success of people.”

Story estimates that roughly 90% of the brunch’s revenue comes from sponsors, with the remaining 10% generated by ticket sales. Her emphasis on relationship building has helped keep sponsors coming back year after year. The NFL has been a legacy sponsor since 2019, Prime Video has supported the event for four to five years, and Delta Air Lines is returning for its third year.

Still, Story is always looking to bring on new sponsors, often through connections made at the events themselves. This year, Visa joins the lineup, thanks in part to a relationship Story built with a former Moët Hennessy executive who previously sponsored one of her events in Las Vegas.

“She remembered me and spoke my name behind closed doors at her new company,” Story says. “That’s a testament to what we’ve created and continue to build.”

Equally important to the networking is the women being honored, something Story takes immense pride in. “About 95% of the women we honor are really behind the scenes,” she explains. “They’re senior executives in sports. Some are front-facing, and some are not.”

Story points to Clutch Sports Group COO Farah Leah and Detroit Pistons President Melanie Harris as examples. “They may not be household names, but they’re doing the true work in the industry,” she says.

For more recognizable figures, Story presents the Trailblazer Award, which will go to WNBA legend Nneka Ogwumike this year.

The selection process also involves strategic considerations. Story makes a point of honoring someone from the Super Bowl host city, which this year will be Rams EVP Molly Higgins. She also selects someone from the NFL office to recognize the league’s role as a partner. This year, that honor goes to SVP Tracy Pearlman.

On the surface, a curated awards show might seem like a superficial way to bring people together. But the business logic is sound: It gives invitees, especially honorees, a compelling reason to attend while reinforcing Story’s authority as a connector and tastemaker in the industry.

“You know, I’ve never had someone say they couldn’t come,” Story laughs. “So that is a great point.”

Ultimately, a host can only control so much. Guests’ experience is up to them, but Story does what she can to make everyone feel welcome.

“I’ve had people email me who came solo and said, ‘I’m an introvert, but I just really felt I needed to be in that room,’” Story shares. “They tend to open up once they get in the room.”

Part of that secret sauce is thoughtful table curation. While sponsors can choose their own seating, Story strategically places ticketed guests near people who could be valuable connections.

“I try to make sure that I’m putting people at tables where they can get to know each other and where there could be some synergy,” she says. “One woman who was attending told me, ‘Oh, no! I already know them. Place me somewhere with someone I don’t know, where I can do business.’ Things like that are really important.”

Story also makes a point of giving guests time to connect, allowing an hour and a half for networking after the awards.

“What’s so funny about the event is that people may not see each other every day or may only know each other through social media,” she says. “It’s so fun to see people running across the room, hugging and catching up. Business deals are being made in that room, too. People are looking at the tables to see which sponsors are represented or which executives are there, and then taking that next step to forge relationships that last long after my event.”

The same year Story hosted the inaugural Sports Power Brunch, her 30-year-old son, Sterling, passed away from cancer just two days before Christmas after being misdiagnosed. Rather than letting the tragedy derail her work, Story turned her grief into a mission, establishing the Sterling Legacy Fund to support health-related causes and organizations such as the American Cancer Society.

Still, Story wanted the foundation to feel more personally connected to her son. Sterling was a devoted basketball fan who still had an Allen Iverson Fathead on his wall when he died.

“My day job is as a sports publicist, and my first opportunity to work in sports was volunteering for the Allen Iverson Celebrity Summer Classic in Hampton, Virginia,” Story says.

Sterling’s love of basketball inspired the fund’s signature initiative, Sterling Courts, which renovates basketball courts in his memory. The initiative has brought lasting improvements to communities hosting the Sports Power Brunch, including an outdoor half court at the Downtown Boys & Girls Club in Las Vegas and a full-size indoor court in New Orleans during Super Bowl LIX in 2025. Both projects were completed in partnership with Prime Video, while Microsoft helped renovate computer labs, teen centers, and gaming centers at both locations.

“You never really get through grieving,” Story shares. “But as I processed my grief, I just knew there was something I could do with the platform I have, even if my son wasn’t a household name.”

Story’s, well, story, is proof that you don’t need to reinvent the wheel to find success. By making the most of the resources and relationships you already have, you can simplify the process.

“I always tell people to bloom where they are planted,” Story says. “My very first event was at Davio’s restaurant in Atlanta. I just reached out to people in my network at the time. Most people ask, ‘How do I reach this big organization or that company?’ But you can start by working with people in your immediate circle.”

That approach may simplify the process, but it doesn’t make building an event easy. Securing sponsorships is difficult, and retaining them can be even harder.

“Start small, and then you can grow from there,” Story says. “If you build it, they will come, but sometimes you have to hit the pavement. Never stop pitching, never stop selling, and find people who believe in you.”

She knows firsthand how much that support matters. “At my first event, I couldn’t even pay the entire bill, so my friends put their credit cards down to help cover it. To see where I am now is such a blessing. I believed in myself first, and the people around me believed in me, too. They poured into me and helped grow what is now the event you see today.”

Ironically, the more connected we become online, the more valuable in-person experiences are. It’s classic scarcity theory, and sports publicist and entrepreneur LaTonya Story understands it as well as anyone. That insight helped inspire her to launch the Sports Power Brunch, an event celebrating the most influential women in sports.

Now, after seven years as The Sports Power Brunch: Celebrating the Most Powerful Women in Sports®, the event is entering a new era as The Sports Power Awards™. The rebrand will debut at the eighth annual celebration on Feb. 10, 2027, at The Beverly Hills Hotel during Super Bowl LXI Week in Los Angeles.

Story spoke with Entrepreneur about building the event from the ground up, the thinking behind the rebrand, and the keys to its enduring success.

#5441. Nvidia’s new chairman Harvey Jones is a ‘charming elder statesman’ set to lead the search for the next CEO. But did he enable the current crisis?

In the wake of former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s stunning departure from the company, employees received an email from someone most of them had probably never heard of before, even though he’d been affiliated with the company and its board for decades. His name is Harvey Jones, and he was writing to tell them that he’d just been appointed the company’s first-ever Chair of the Board, and that Nvidia CFO Colette Kress would serve as interim CEO.

“I’m writing to share an important update,” Jones’ note began, according to leaked screenshots of the email. He then tried to reassure employees no doubt left shaken by the past weeks’ revelations and the sudden departure of Jensen Huang, a man who co-founded the company and, until today, had been synonymous with its success. “The Board takes seriously our duty as steward of this great company,” Jones said.

That sense of calm and confidence is something Jones is known for, according to two longtime friends and former coworkers. Although Jones, 73, may not be a household name, he has worked in the technology industry, and in semiconductors, for over 30 years, according to his biography on the Nvidia website. He founded two companies, served as CEO of another, and since 2004 has been managing partner of investment firm Square Wave Ventures. He’s been on Nvidia’s board since 1993, the year Huang founded the company.

Jones comes from a successful Connecticut family—his full name is Harvey Jones III—with an “old school, conservative” way about him, Penny Herscher, who has known Jones since 1984 and used to work for him, tells Fortune. His father was a U.S. Army Colonel and church-goer, who then became a vice president at the Walt Disney World Company. Jones himself is a billionaire, which Forbes says is “almost entirely due to his Nvidia director’s compensation” and the fact that he owns 0.03% of the company.

“Harvey has a deep sense of history,” Chris Rowen, who cofounded the semiconductor processor company Tensilica with Jones in 1997, tells Fortune. He has a house on Nantucket and enjoys sailing classic yachts and fine art. “He has a smooth polish,” Rowen said. But Rowen also said that, despite outward appearances, there’s nothing effete about Jones. “He is such a gentleman, so articulate, and so well-sanded on the outside that you might worry there isn’t a deep fierceness and technical insight inside, but beneath that smooth exterior is a really bright, insightful, aggressive guy.”

At a time of great turbulence, Jones can offer Nvidia a “steady pair of hands” to “sort out” its next chapter, Herscher said. She described him as a “charming elder statesman” who at this point in his career is likely “very hard to ruffle.”

Jones and Rowen played distinct roles while leading the team at Tensilica. While Rowen played the role of technical leader and mentor, Jones was a skilled manager who helped keep the team on track. “His experience was such that he exuded this confidence and experience,” Rowan said. “If he thought we were on the right track, people were instantly comforted. He really communicated a sense of the larger picture and gave people a great deal of confidence that the wider world needed and approved of what we were doing.”

“He’s very strategic,” Herscher said. “I’m sure he’s right now figuring out the right strategy and steps going forward. He’s always looking around corners.”

Jones’ experience and board tenure also begs the question of how he failed to identify the enormous reputational risk of Huang’s affairs, three of which are known as of this writing. Huang also notoriously had many reports, up to 60 at one point, and no clear successor or succession planning.

“Jones may be the right person to steady the ship, but his longevity is both his greatest qualification and the strongest reason to scrutinize his leadership,” Jonathan Tower, managing partner at the VC firm Catapult tells Fortune. “The board cannot simply present itself as the solution without examining its role in creating the problem.”

Case in point: Huang’s affair with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia’s vice president of health care, was known inside the company, and appears to violate its code of conduct, The New York Times reported. The code of conduct instructs all employees to “avoid situations where our actions create conflict” including “personal relationships.” The board promises to promptly investigate all reports of misconduct. What happened?

Jones will likely lead the process to select Nvidia’s next CEO, Herscher said, though she had not spoken to him about it directly, and Nvidia did not respond to Fortune’s request for comment. But that’s typically how the process would work in a situation like this, Herscher said, drawing on her knowledge from sitting on three public boards, and being the co-founder of The Chairs Circle, which runs educational programs for board chairs.  The fact that Jones also sits on Nvidia’s Nominating and Corporate Governance Committee makes it even more likely that he will lead this process, she said, as usually that committee is involved in the process.

The search will likely take at least a few months, Herscher said. The board will likely hire a recruiter to identify candidates—something Bloomberg reported this week that Nvidia has already done. That firm will likely do the first outreach, Herscher said, and then Jones will speak to the most promising candidates, along with the rest of the internal search committee.

All signs point to Jones being an effective recruiter, with a wide net of contacts in the industry, Herscher said.

Longtime technology executive Chi-Foo Chan described Jones as “a very persuasive guy” in a 2019 oral history interview with the Computer History Museum, referring to the conversations the two had when Jones convinced Chan to join Synopsys, the electronics company Jones led from 1987 to 1998.

Nvidia shareholders are hoping those skills can wrangle a big fish to come in as Nvidia’s next CEO. Potential successors may include Rene Hass, who is currently the CEO of the chipmaker Arm.  President Trump, who allegedly did not act on reports of Huang’s affair with a suspected Chinese spy, suggested former Apple CEO Tim Cook might be a good pick.

Whoever it is, they’ll need the right operational and product development chops to keep the GPUs flowing.

#5440. Lila Bio lands $3.65M grant to fight pulmonary hypertension with AI-designed proteins

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 11, 2026 at 2:31 pmNovember 11, 2026 at 2:31 pm

Lila Bio, a startup spun out of Nobel laureate David Baker’s lab at the University of Washington, has received a $3.65 million grant from the National Institutes of Health to develop a treatment for pulmonary hypertension.

The condition causes high blood pressure in the arteries that carry blood from the heart to the lungs. It forces the heart to work harder and can lead to heart failure.

The Small Business Innovation Research fast-track award supports Lila’s efforts to develop a protein-based treatment for pulmonary hypertension that could be given by injection a few times a year.

“Most approved therapies only manage symptoms, such as vasodilators,” Lila CEO Jake Kraft said in a LinkedIn post, referring to drugs that widen blood vessels. “Lila Bio is pursuing clinically-validated, disease-modifying mechanisms that treat the underlying disease.”

The funding comes from the NIH’s National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute and is divided into two phases. The initial $605,981 will support early testing in mice, rats and non-human primates. The second phase, totaling $3,049,462, will support further animal testing and studies using lung tissue from patients.

Kraft and chief scientist Anindya Roy co-founded Lila in 2023. Both worked as postdoctoral fellows at UW’s Institute for Protein Design, which Baker directs. Lila raised $10 million in seed funding the year it was founded. Last year, it announced a collaboration with pharmaceutical giant Eli Lilly to develop treatments for solid tumors.

The startup uses AI and machine learning to design therapeutic proteins through two platforms. One supports the pulmonary hypertension project, creating long-acting injectable drugs designed to remain active in the body for weeks or months. The other focuses on targeted radiotherapy, using proteins to deliver radioactive isotopes to tumors.

“We want to bring medicines to patients,” Kraft told GeekWire in an earlier interview. “We don’t want to just say we’ve designed a protein, but we actually want to be able to say we’ve saved lives.”

#5438. AI voice company WellSaid retools for agents while keeping its commitment to human actors

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Todd Bishop on Nov 11, 2026 at 2:56 pmNovember 11, 2026 at 3:19 pm

WellSaid, the AI voice company that spun out of Seattle’s Allen Institute for Artificial Intelligence in 2019, is reinventing itself for the era of AI agents.

The company this week launched WellSaid Producer, which connects its voiceover direction tools directly to AI assistants such as Claude and Microsoft Copilot.

Instead of logging into WellSaid’s app, corporate users can ask the AI assistant for a voiceover to accompany a training or marketing video, for example. The assistant then sends the script to WellSaid, which generates the audio using its licensed voices.

It’s part of a broader overhaul and refocusing of WellSaid’s business. The company has spent the past two years moving away from individual users to focus on businesses. It now has about 30 employees, down from more than 70 in late 2024.

Along the way, WellSaid has turned profitable, CEO Benjamin Dorr told GeekWire.

“We’ve been calling this adventure Act II, so I guess Producer is Scene I,” Dorr said. Extending the metaphor, he acknowledged that “the cast is a lot smaller,” and noted that many of the company’s leaders are new, recruited from his own network.

Dorr joined WellSaid as CFO in 2024 and became CEO in spring 2025. He was previously chief operating officer of Cordial, a San Diego marketing software company, and earlier worked in tech investing and banking at The Carlyle Group, Morgan Stanley and Citi.

He succeeded Brian Cook, the former Nintex CEO who led WellSaid for about 16 months. Co-founder Matt Hocking, who was CEO until early 2024, remains on WellSaid’s board and is now chief product officer at Type, an AI startup for creative writers.

Dorr’s leadership team includes three executives who also worked at Cordial and joined WellSaid since last fall: Natalia Holts, senior vice president of finance and accounting; Jeni Bishop, vice president of marketing; and Bryan Keefer, vice president of product.

Chris Johnson, the chief product and technology officer, and co-founder Mixail Petrochuk, the chief technology officer, remain from the earlier leadership team.

The company is maintaining its longstanding practice of building its AI voices from recordings of professional voice actors, who are paid royalties when businesses use their voices to narrate training courses, marketing and other videos.

WellSaid drew widespread attention in 2023 when it created a spot-on synthetic version of former NPR “Planet Money” host Robert Smith’s voice, with his permission, as part of a special series by the popular radio show and podcast.

Its customers include nearly half of the Fortune 100, according to WellSaid. The company’s licensing approach stands out in a sector that remains a wild west, with models trained on audio scraped from the internet and tools used to fake the voices of public figures.

“We view [Model Context Protocol], and agents in general, to be as disruptive to software as the Web once was twenty years ago.”

How it works: Producer uses Model Context Protocol, or MCP, a standard way for AI assistants to connect to other software. It works with Claude, ChatGPT, Copilot and Atlassian’s Rovo, and Dorr said AI agents that work on their own will be able to use it by the end of the year.

Companies using WellSaid Producer can set up style guides so brand names, acronyms and technical terms are pronounced the same way in every file. When a product name or script changes, Producer can update every affected voiceover in one pass, and each finished file carries a record of its license.

WellSaid also says it’s the first voiceover platform to generate audio natively at 48 kHz, the standard for film and video. WellSaid will continue to offer its Studio app for customers who want to work there directly.

Producer is sold as a platform, with customers committing to buy credits for minutes of finished, licensed audio. WellSaid’s licenses today are mostly one-time buyouts, but Dorr said the company wants to price more like the traditional voiceover industry, where an ad voiceover is priced by its length, reach and how long it runs.

The strategy: Dorr said voiceover is just one step in a larger production process, and many creative tools now include basic AI speech that is sometimes good enough. He sees AI agents letting companies combine specialized tools from vendors they trust, instead of settling for one all-in-one app.

“We view MCP, and agents in general, to be as disruptive to software as the Web once was twenty years ago,” he said.

Voice actors: Actors’ revenue share rates won’t change when their voices are used through AI assistants, Dorr said. One of his first moves as CEO was to open the company’s stock option pool to its top 20 voice actors, and WellSaid is building a voice actor advisory board, with more details expected to be released in December. Dorr said WellSaid plans to add custom royalty structures, “potentially all the way up to union rate cards.”

Customers will also be able to use voice models from other companies alongside WellSaid’s own, for features its models lack, such as one voice speaking several languages. The voices still come from WellSaid’s actors under its licensing terms. “We’re not moving from our position on commercial licensing,” Dorr said.

The business: WellSaid has about 1,000 business customers, and its top 25 customers each spend more than $100,000 a year, Dorr said. Moving away from individual users “did flatten our growth compared to a lot of AI companies growing at astronomical rates,” he said.

By comparison, rival ElevenLabs, which has offered voice generation through Claude since 2025, was valued at $22 billion in a recent employee tender offer.

WellSaid raised venture debt from Multiplier Capital in March but didn’t disclose the amount. Its most recent disclosed equity funding was a $10 million Series A round in 2021 that valued the company at $65 million, according to PitchBook.

Dorr said debt was a better fit than equity for a “modestly growing and, now, profitable company,” at a time when investors’ growth expectations “have become extreme.” He said WellSaid will consider other financing in 2027 “if our ambitions outstrip our ability to reinvest.”

#5437. These 10 Side Hustles Are Making People the Most Money Right Now, According to Fiverr

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

From book design to podcast production, these opportunities go beyond the usual freelance gigs.

Your skills could be worth more than you think. From producing podcasts to building apps, recent Fiverr data highlights lucrative side hustles that could monetize your spare time.

The data has a receptive audience. A survey of 1,370 Americans released earlier this year by email and text messaging marketing platform Omnisend found that 28% currently have a side hustle. The majority of that group (80%) said they started their side business for financial reasons, not for fun. Respondents also indicated that side hustles are more about meeting financial necessity than about pursuing interesting passion projects.

Among those with side hustles, over 50% started their ventures with the goal of making extra money to pay the bills or other essentials. Meanwhile, 27% were drawn to side hustles to pay off debt, add to their income or save for a life goal, like owning a home or preparing for retirement.

Side hustles often bring in less income than a full-time job, but people seem to be satisfied with the supplemental cash anyway. The same survey indicated that 51% of respondents earned $500 or less every month from their side gig. However, 76% were still happy with their additional income.

So, looking to launch a side hustle of your own? Fiverr data points to specialized services, from website development to brand style guides, that could turn your expertise into extra income.

Read on to see the 10 most lucrative side hustles right now, according to the platform.

Cybersecurity is a side hustle for people who can spot weaknesses and explain how to fix them. Fiverr’s offerings include consultations, compliance services and security management. Those are distinct specialties, so it makes sense to offer a focused service instead of advertising a promise to secure every aspect of a business.

An app idea is only the starting point. Turning a spark into something usable takes design and coding skills. Mobile app development projects focus on apps for platforms such as iOS and Android. On Fiverr, freelancers sell a defined piece of the app-building process, like a prototype or a specific feature. For example, they could offer to build a booking tool for a local business.

Sometimes it is easier to understand what a product does when a person demonstrates it. Live action explainers use videos to introduce a service or show a product in action. They can also walk viewers through a problem and its solution. Fiverr freelancers could offer packages that combine filming and editing, and even include scripting.

Search engine marketing (SEM) is a paid digital marketing approach designed to increase a website’s visibility on search engine results pages. Businesses use SEM to present targeted ads at the top or bottom of search results. They use paid advertising to make their products or services more visible. Fiverr’s SEM categories include setup and strategy consultations, campaign management, shopping ads and ad review.

Website building includes tasks like building online stores. For side hustles, it can be useful to specialize in one aspect of the building process. For example, freelancers can offer portfolio websites for photographers or sites that emphasize bookings for service-based businesses. Specialization can make the work easier to price and describe.

Many AI projects often involve organizing and labeling information. Fiverr has a data annotation marketplace that covers tasks like image annotation. Freelancers carry out various responsibilities, including identifying objects in images. In order to make this side hustle lucrative, it helps to be specific about services offered. For example, are you more focused on tagging, labeling or annotating data?

A style guide explains how a brand’s visual identity should work across different materials. Fiverr’s brand-design offerings include color palettes, typography guidelines and usage parameters. Those decisions should be part of a well-documented system. For freelancers, the opportunity is to develop a useful guide that specifies elements like logo placement and color choices.

Generative engine optimization (GEO) focuses on making content easier for AI-powered systems to understand and reference. It is different from simply pursuing a position in a traditional list of search results. Freelancers who select this area could offer services like reviewing a company’s key pages or clarifying product descriptions. They could also document how AI systems currently describe the brand.

It is not enough to simply record a podcast conversation. Podcast production is the work required to bring a podcast to life. Freelancers are tasked with delivering a finished episode, including editing the recording and putting the audio together. A sample podcast production offer could cover an episode, an intro and outro and one revision round.

A finished book manuscript still needs visuals and formatting that suit the book. Fiverr’s design marketplace differentiates between book design and book covers: the cover and interior formatting are two separate things. A freelancer might specialize in either one or offer a clearly defined combination. An interior design package could tackle chapter layouts and page numbers, while book covers refer to the visuals at the front of the book.

#5436. ‘I Just Cannot Get Ahead’: Why Americans Are Under Extreme Financial Pressure, According to a New Report

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

One 73-year-old borrower described owing nearly $40,000 across 19 credit cards.

Why does getting ahead feel so out of reach? A new analysis from the Urban Institute offers a look at the financial strain Americans are facing.

The report, which drew from U.S. Census Bureau data, revealed that 23.5% of Americans with a credit history have debt in collections. They owe a median amount of $2,913.

As grocery bills and other essentials take a bigger toll on household budgets, some Americans are relying on credit cards to bridge the gap. However, steep interest charges can turn that short-term relief into debt that is difficult to pay off, even for borrowers who are making payments.

Susan Cannon described that cycle to Business Insider earlier this year. The 73-year-old owes nearly $40,000 across 19 credit cards, with interest rates ranging from roughly 12% to 35%. She lives in a mobile home in rural Texas. Despite paying more than the minimum balance on her credit cards, she struggles to reduce her balances while continuing to charge necessities such as groceries and gas to her credit cards.

“I can’t get the balance down because I am still having to use credit cards at the end of the month to get groceries and gas,” Cannon told the publication. “I pay my bills, but because of the interest rates, it keeps going up — I feel like I’m being gouged.”

Despite Cannon’s best attempts to build a savings account, her monthly payments are all going towards interest payments on her credit cards.

“I just cannot get ahead,” Cannon told Business Insider.

Where Americans live can make a noticeable difference in how heavily overdue their bills are. For example, in rural Jim Hogg County in South Texas, more than half of residents with a credit history have debt in collections, according to the report. Nationwide, the share is 23.5%, making the county’s rate more than twice the national figure.

How quickly an unpaid bill reaches collections depends on the type of debt. Credit card accounts typically enter collections four to six months after a missed payment, while unpaid medical bills generally take three to six months. The balances also differ: The analysis put the median delinquent credit card debt at $680, compared with $1,492 for medical debt.

Student loans follow a different path, with the rules varying between federal and private lenders. Federal loans generally fall into default after 270 days without payment. Borrowers can then pursue options such as loan rehabilitation to resolve the default and restore their loans to good standing.

The New York Federal Reserve determined that Americans collectively owe $18.8 trillion in debt as of the second quarter of the year.

#5435. Ex-Seattle startup DeltaGen acquired by new AI company backed by Veeam co-founder

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 12, 2026 at 5:51 amNovember 12, 2026 at 5:51 am

DeltaGen, an AI startup that got its start in Seattle before moving to San Francisco this year, has been acquired by Worker.ai, a new small-business software company backed by Veeam founder Ratmir Timashev.

Worker, which launched Thursday, acquired all of DeltaGen for an undisclosed price that included a substantial cash component and equity in Worker, DeltaGen co-founder and CEO Rene Bystron told GeekWire.

Bystron joins Worker as co-founder and COO, and nine other DeltaGen employees are coming with him, including co-founders Michal Studnicka and Matus Ondreicka.

Worker, led by co-founder and CEO John Roberts, a former private equity operator based in Raleigh, N.C., is building software that lets small businesses hand off recurring work to AI agents. DeltaGen’s voice technology captures decisions made in conversations and turns them into assigned tasks.

Roberts had been a DeltaGen customer before Worker needed voice technology, Bystron said. “We could have raised another round and kept building independently, but this gave us the capital and experience to move faster with people we trusted,” he said.

Launched in 2024, DeltaGen raised a $1.2 million pre-seed round in early 2025 to build generative AI tools for financial professionals, with a focus on streamlining mergers and acquisitions. The company relocated from Seattle to San Francisco earlier this year.

“I still love Seattle and miss it like crazy,” said Bystron, who is keeping his apartment in Belltown. “But being closer to the AI founders, customers and investors in San Francisco makes a real difference at this stage. It also didn’t help that Washington has been chipping away at its tax advantage.”

Timashev, who co-founded data backup giant Veeam, is backing Worker to help small businesses such as manufacturers, service companies and family businesses grow.

“AI can now give small businesses more capacity without asking already stretched owners to work longer days,” he said in a statement. “Worker is my bet on that shift.” The size of his investment was not disclosed.

DeltaGen’s current product is an AI voice platform, which will continue as it’s integrated into Worker. DeltaGen’s AI voice platform will continue as it’s integrated into Worker, which is opening access gradually through a waitlist.

#5434. What Changing College Enrollment Trends Reveal About the Future of Work

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Here is what’s driving changes in student preferences and how universities can adapt academic programs and align curricula with workforce needs to help students make better career choices.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

College enrollment in the United States is growing, but the programs attracting students are changing. While some academic disciplines are experiencing renewed demand, others are seeing enrollment decline, raising important questions about how student preferences are evolving and whether universities are adapting quickly enough.

Recent findings from the National Student Clearinghouse Research Center reveal that enrollment growth is not evenly distributed across academic fields. Health professions, certain STEM disciplines and career-oriented credentials are gaining momentum, while computer science enrollment has declined in some degree categories.

For university leaders, these changes present a challenge that goes beyond attracting more students. They must understand where academic demand is shifting, what these patterns suggest about the future workforce and how their institutions should respond.

Healthcare-related education is emerging as one of the stronger areas of enrollment growth. According to the National Student Clearinghouse, enrollment in health professions programs at two-year institutions increased by 7.7% in fall 2025 compared with the previous year. Biological sciences enrollment at four-year institutions also increased by 3.7%.

Interest in newer technology disciplines is another notable development. Nearly 80,000 students were enrolled in data science and data analytics programs nationwide in fall 2025, reflecting the growing presence of these specialized fields in higher education.

However, not all technology-related programs are following the same trajectory. Graduate enrollment in computer science declined by approximately 14% in fall 2025. This contrast illustrates why universities cannot treat broad categories such as technology or STEM as having uniform enrollment demand.

Community colleges are also seeing greater interest in shorter academic pathways. Between fall 2021 and fall 2025, undergraduate certificate enrollment at community colleges increased by 28.3%.

Together, these patterns suggest that students are exploring a wider range of educational options, including specialized degrees and shorter credentials that may offer more direct connections to particular occupations.

Changing enrollment patterns may reflect a broader reassessment of the relationship between education and employment.

Students making decisions about higher education must consider tuition costs, the time required to complete a program and the employment opportunities available after graduation. Programs with recognizable occupational pathways may therefore appear particularly attractive.

Healthcare offers a useful example. Many occupations require specific qualifications, certifications, or clinical training, making the connection between education and employment relatively clear. Continued demand for healthcare workers may also influence how prospective students evaluate these programs.

Technology presents a more complicated picture. Artificial intelligence is changing how some technical tasks are performed, potentially influencing perceptions of traditional computer science careers while creating interest in more specialized fields such as data analytics.

However, enrollment trends alone cannot establish why students are changing their academic choices. Demographic changes, institutional capacity, tuition costs, immigration patterns and labor market expectations can all influence enrollment.

The important lesson for universities is that student demand is not static. Understanding the factors behind changing preferences is becoming essential to academic planning.

For decades, universities have made academic planning decisions based on established program portfolios, historical enrollment, faculty resources and institutional priorities. These considerations remain important, but changing student demand requires a more responsive approach.

Institutions should regularly evaluate which programs are attracting students, how enrollment patterns compare with regional and national workforce needs, and whether graduates are finding opportunities related to their education.

This does not mean expanding every program experiencing short-term growth or discontinuing those facing temporary declines. Enrollment trends can fluctuate, and some disciplines provide substantial educational and societal value even when they do not lead directly to a specific occupation.

Instead, universities need to combine enrollment data with employment projections, graduate outcomes and employer feedback.

For example, growing interest in healthcare programs may justify additional clinical partnerships or training capacity where workforce demand supports expansion. Similarly, changing interest across technology disciplines may create opportunities to update curricula, introduce interdisciplinary programs, or integrate emerging technical skills into existing degrees.

Employer collaboration can also help institutions identify gaps between academic preparation and workplace expectations. By involving industry partners in curriculum discussions and experiential learning opportunities, universities can make their programs more responsive without sacrificing academic standards.

Ultimately, effective program planning requires institutions to anticipate change rather than respond only after enrollment patterns become difficult to ignore.

Universities also have a responsibility to help students understand the implications of their academic decisions.

A growing program is not necessarily the right choice for every student, just as declining enrollment does not automatically mean a discipline offers limited career opportunities.

Prospective students need accessible information about program requirements, potential career pathways, graduate earnings and opportunities for further education.

Academic and career advising can play a more proactive role by helping students connect their interests and abilities with realistic educational and professional goals.

Technology can support this process by making program information easier to access and helping advisors provide more personalized guidance. However, meaningful advising must consider individual aspirations rather than relying solely on enrollment trends or projected salaries.

For institutions, providing this transparency can help students make informed choices while strengthening the connection between academic offerings and long-term outcomes.

The current enrollment shifts should serve as a reminder that academic demand will continue to evolve alongside technology, industry requirements and student expectations.

Universities that rely exclusively on historical enrollment patterns risk overlooking emerging opportunities and changing student needs. Yet reacting to every short-term trend can be equally problematic.

The institutions best positioned for the future will be those that consistently evaluate their programs, strengthen relationships with employers and use evidence to guide academic decisions.

The goal is not simply to offer the most popular degrees. It is to build an academic portfolio that remains relevant, adaptable and capable of preparing students for a workforce that will look different from the one universities serve today.

#5433. I’ve Worked With 131,201 Entrepreneurs — and 95% of Them Make These 2 Mistakes

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

After helping more than 131,000 business owners, I’ve learned that sustainable growth usually comes down to avoiding two surprisingly common mistakes.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

After nearly 30 years of working with small business owners, you start noticing patterns.

It doesn’t matter whether someone owns a dental practice, a restaurant, a home services company or an ecommerce business. It doesn’t even matter how smart or talented the entrepreneur is. Certain mistakes show up again and again.

I understand why. Running a business means making dozens of decisions every day. The urgent stuff screams for your attention. New ideas are exciting. Cutting expenses feels responsible. And the latest marketing or technology trend can make you wonder whether you’re falling behind.

Meanwhile, the boring fundamentals that actually drive growth are easy to neglect.

I’ve learned that firsthand. I built PostcardMania from scratch starting in 1998, without investors or outside funding, and I’ve made plenty of mistakes along the way — including one that nearly cost me my company.

After working with 131,201 entrepreneurs, though, two mistakes stand out. I see some version of them in roughly 95% of the small business owners I interact with.

Too many entrepreneurs view marketing primarily as an expense to control. I look at it differently: Marketing is the engine that brings customers into your business.

That doesn’t mean spending recklessly. It means knowing your numbers. How much does it cost you to acquire a customer? What is that customer worth over time? Which campaigns consistently generate profitable business?

Once you know those answers, cutting marketing simply because it looks expensive can actually be one of the riskiest things you do.

I learned that during the 2008-09 housing crash and subsequent financial crisis. At the time, 46% of PostcardMania’s clientele was tied to real estate and mortgages. When those industries collapsed, we lost thousands of customers. Revenue dropped, and eventually I began wondering whether we could make payroll.

I refused to lay people off, so advisers suggested cutting our postcard marketing. I reluctantly agreed. It backfired.

Fewer postcards meant fewer leads. Fewer leads meant even less revenue. In 2009, revenue fell 15%. Eventually, I realized that if I wanted revenue to recover, I needed to restore the flow of leads. I brought our marketing budget back to its previous level, and the business recovered.

That experience changed how I think about marketing forever.

So when Covid hit in 2020, and our weekly revenue plunged more than 40%, I did the opposite of 2008: I kept marketing steady. Within five weeks, our weekly revenue had fully recovered and was back above $1 million. Leads rose 9.24% over the next six months without increasing budget. And since then, our revenue has nearly doubled from $60 million annually to nearly $120 million.

Big companies understand that growth requires marketing investment. In August, Kraft Heinz announced they were investing an additional $100 million in its turnaround plan, with most of those funds going toward marketing. The company said it was already seeing stronger performance where those investments were being made.

The lesson for entrepreneurs is simple: If you need more revenue, you need more marketing. Growth requires feeding what works.

Identify your top marketing tactics by measuring revenue and return on investment. From there, ask yourself, “How much more can I responsibly put behind this?”

Entrepreneurs love a shortcut. I do, too. The problem is when the shortcut becomes the strategy.

A new platform appears. An algorithm changes. AI explodes. A marketing hack goes viral. Suddenly everyone feels like they’re falling behind if they aren’t jumping on the bandwagon. But businesses aren’t usually built through a collection of hacks. They’re built by finding things that work and getting exceptionally good at repeating them.

Chili’s is a useful example. The restaurant chain experimented with flashy technology, including robot servers that quickly expanded to 61 locations. The results were disappointing — just a few months later, Chili’s announced it was pulling the plug on its robot initiative.

Instead, they pivoted to a much less “exciting” strategy: fundamentals.

Over the past two years, Chili’s parent company invested in stronger Wi-Fi, updated payment systems and ordering technology for restaurant staff. Its CIO has said every technology initiative now has to contribute to better food service and guest experience.

Meanwhile, Chili’s stock had risen more than 500% between June 2022 and July 2026, with 20 consecutive quarters of same-store sales growth. Of course, those results reflect a turnaround that isn’t just “ditch the robots,” but the philosophy is worth paying attention to: Fix the fundamentals before betting big on flashy tech.

We’ve taken a similar approach at PostcardMania. I’ve watched countless new marketing channels and technologies arrive over the last 28 years, but I’ve never abandoned a strategy simply because something newer came along. Direct mail has essentially built us up into a $120 million company, and it remains a core part of our marketing today. What we’ve done instead is layer newer tools — digital advertising, tracking, automation and programmatic technology — around what was already proven to work.

And the numbers keep validating that decision. We analyzed 117,857 leads in 2025 — every single direct mail and digital lead generated that year — and discovered that we made $416.04 per direct mail lead and only $38.59 per digital lead, a 978% difference.

That doesn’t mean digital is bad. We invest heavily in digital, too. It means you shouldn’t confuse “new” with “better.” It also means you should figure out how new technology can make proven tactics even stronger.

After nearly three decades in business, I’ve become much less impressed by what’s new and much more interested in what works.

Track your marketing. Invest in what produces profitable customers. Keep improving it. Test new ideas without abandoning proven ones. Those principles aren’t flashy, but they’re the bedrock of success.

After nearly 30 years of working with small business owners, you start noticing patterns.

It doesn’t matter whether someone owns a dental practice, a restaurant, a home services company or an ecommerce business. It doesn’t even matter how smart or talented the entrepreneur is. Certain mistakes show up again and again.

I understand why. Running a business means making dozens of decisions every day. The urgent stuff screams for your attention. New ideas are exciting. Cutting expenses feels responsible. And the latest marketing or technology trend can make you wonder whether you’re falling behind.

#5432. Seattle’s Allen Institute helps create a ‘Rosetta Stone’ for brain cells to unlock clues to disease

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 12, 2026 at 8:00 amNovember 11, 2026 at 5:15 pm

A coalition of 56 institutions across nine countries is publishing groundbreaking research today on the basal ganglia — a group of brain structures that help control movement, emotions, motivation and habits. The region is linked to psychiatric and degenerative disorders, including schizophrenia, bipolar disorder and Parkinson’s disease.

The scientist have produced a biological Rosetta Stone that creates a shared system for naming and describing cells in the basal ganglia across species. The goal is to help researchers compare findings, collaborate and accelerate their understanding of this essential brain region.

“This is groundwork that is necessary to really make progress,” said Michael Hawrylycz, principal investigator with the Seattle-based Allen Institute who helped organize the consortium.

The project, called the BRAIN Initiative Cell Atlas Network, or BICAN, produced a basal ganglia atlas that is publicly available for basic researchers, clinicians and others to use.

The research is being presented in a package of 26 articles in a special issue of the journal Cell. The data comes from humans, macaques, marmoset and mice. One of the benefits of comparing the basal ganglia between species is understanding which components are uniquely human, providing potential insights into neurological diseases.

Despite the critical and wide-ranging roles, the basal ganglia is relatively small — it’s about 2% of the brain with a volume roughly the size of a large gumball.

For the project, the researchers pulled information from 25.5 million brain cells, including 21 million human cells. They used a variety of techniques to tease out insights, including RNA sequencing to identify gene activity from single cells in precise locations; epigenomic studies revealing where genes are switched on or off; and measurements of electrical activity combined with cell shape and genetic information.

It’s a lot of data to stitch together and make sense of, Hawrylycz said. “AI is a perfect tool” for the job, he said, because it excels at finding patterns.

The findings could help guide future treatments, but the work remains basic research rather than clinical research, Hawrylycz said.

The new research is the first major installment of the third phase of a brain-mapping effort that began in 2014. The first phase demonstrated that scientists could analyze individual cells on a large scale. The second produced an atlas of the mouse brain.

BICAN aims to create a standardized atlas describing cells throughout the brains of humans and other primates. Hawrylycz said the work is expected to take another two or three years.

#5431. ZetaChain's 55M ZETA Burn Isn't a One-Time Event: What Proposal 2 Really Does

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

ZetaChain's Governance Proposal 2 would halt its L1 around Dec 9, mint ZETA 1:1 on Solana and burn about 55M ZETA in monthly installments. Voting closes Nov 7.

Headlines are calling it a 55 million ZETA burn. Read the proposal's own schedule, though, and nothing close to 55 million disappears on the day the chain halts. The figure is real, but it arrives in twelve installments over 2027.

ZetaChain published Governance Proposal 2 on November 4, and its announcement post lays out the mechanics. About 55 million ZETA of undistributed validator emissions will be burned monthly through 2027, following the schedule on which they would have been emitted. The roadmap in the same post puts the pace at twelve monthly burns of roughly 4.6 million ZETA each, from January to December 2027.

That detail changes how the number should be read. Most of the early flash coverage collapsed it into a single burn, which implies an immediate supply shock. The staged schedule tells a different story. These tokens were never going to circulate, because they are validator rewards for an L1 that is about to stop. Burning them on the original emission timetable keeps the published release schedule intact and introduces no new mechanism, as ZetaChain's FAQ puts it.

Governance Proposal 2 builds on Proposal 68, which approved the move to Solana in September with 99.4% in favor. Proposal 2 supplies the mechanics. Voting runs 72 hours and closes on November 7, and ZetaChain says nothing moves unless it passes.

If it does pass, every ZETA balance is recorded at snapshot block 20,755,000, expected around December 9. The ZetaChain L1 halts at that same height and isn't restarted. Claims open the same day through the ZetaHub migration portal, and ZetaChain's new private AI app, ZetaLabs, launches alongside it.

The proposal also pairs the migration with a new whitepaper, which ZetaChain calls the document of record for the token after the move.

The snapshot goes well beyond a simple wallet count. It records liquid, staked, unbonding and unclaimed-reward balances. Staked ZETA is credited automatically, so nobody has to unstake, and exchange balances convert without any action from holders. Staking rewards stop at the snapshot height.

Holders who want to claim directly face a short process. They connect the wallet that held ZETA, sign a message naming a Solana wallet, and receive the full balance shortly afterward. The claim costs no fee and requires no SOL. According to the post, the portal asks only for a signature, never for a transaction or a seed phrase. A minimum of 10 ZETA at the snapshot is needed to claim.

Two edge cases deserve attention. First, ZETA wrapped or sitting in pools and contracts can't be claimed by a key, so holders need to unwrap and exit before the snapshot. Second, assets still held as ZRC-20 tokens at the snapshot can be claimed back on their original chain through a separate bridged-assets page, with a $5 minimum per token. Both are the kind of detail that catches people out when a deadline arrives.

On Solana, ZETA becomes a native SPL token under the same ticker, with 9 decimals and no freeze authority. The full snapshot total is minted before the portal opens, and then the mint authority is revoked, so no one can ever mint more. No third-party bridge is involved.

That sequence is the strongest holder protection in the plan, and it is also the part that can be checked in public. The supply stays capped at 2.1 billion less whatever has been burned, and ZetaChain says it will publish the SPL mint address and the migration program address before December 9. Once those exist, anyone can compare the minted total against the snapshot and confirm that the authority was actually revoked. That confirmation deserves the most scrutiny.

Meanwhile, the portal and its program are under independent review by Hacken, and ZetaChain says the portal opens only after the review is complete and the report is published. The ERC-20 version of ZETA on Ethereum is unaffected by the proposal. Purchaser and core contributor vesting completes on January 1, 2027, and ZetaChain says no newly released ZETA will be sold in 2027.

The biggest practical risk is inattention. Most holders don't need to do anything until December 9, but exchange users depend on each exchange's own conversion window, and anyone holding ZETA through a contract or pool has homework to do beforehand.

Scams add another layer of risk. Any migration with a claim portal invites imitators, and ZetaChain tells holders to trust only its official domains and social accounts. A simple rule of thumb helps here: a site that asks for a seed phrase should be closed immediately, since the legitimate flow only needs a message signature.

On the technical side, claims are checked against the published snapshot rather than the live chain, so they continue to work after the halt. ZetaChain says it will announce any change to the process in advance.

The vote decides the terms, not the direction. If Proposal 2 fails, the direction approved in Proposal 68 stands and ZetaChain returns with a revised proposal. Nothing moves on these terms.

If it passes, the sequence is clear. The security report, mint address and migration program address arrive before December 9. The snapshot, halt, mint and portal opening follow on the day, and the monthly burns run through 2027. ZetaLabs then adds a Premium tier in the first quarter of 2027, with ZETA as the token for access and payment.

Taken together, this looks more like a retirement plan for an L1 than a dramatic supply event. The burn is gradual, the mint is capped, and the claim process is simple on paper. Execution is what will matter most: the audit report, the published addresses and the clean revocation of mint authority. Those are the items to watch between now and December 9.

The breakdown puts a major psychological level in view, with traders watching if bulls can reclaim $1,000 before another wave of selling hits. Zcash is also approaching its 0.5 Fibonacci retracement level, an area that could attract buyers looking for a potential relief rally.

Its investment campaign and development funding have failed to reverse the selling pressure. A technical bounce will depend heavily on Bitcoin stabilizing after its own recent weakness. #5429. ‘We’re still here’: Technology Access Foundation keeps opening doors for students of color, 30 years later

by Todd Bishop on Nov 12, 2026 at 8:11 amNovember 12, 2026 at 11:17 am

Editor’s note: Microsoft, which underwrites GeekWire’s Impact Series, is a longtime TAF supporter. The company was not involved in this story.

Back in the fall of 2002, then-Microsoft CEO Steve Ballmer wrapped up a luncheon speech at Seattle’s Rainier Club by asking a question that few people in the room expected — least of all the college freshman he directed it to.

“So you want an internship this summer?” he asked Miya McClain, as she remembers it.

She was Miya Sneed then, 18 and homesick at Mills College in Oakland, Calif. She had come home to speak for Technology Access Foundation, the Seattle nonprofit where she had gone from knowing nothing about computers to building software and leading a team of student interns. Earlier in the luncheon program, she had shown the crowd a scheduling system she built for TAF.

Microsoft had planned the offer in advance and already had her resume, but she had no idea what was coming. A Seattle Times photographer caught the look of shock on her face, and the photo ran the next day on the front of the newspaper’s business section.

That internship, the first of two, led to a full-time job at Microsoft after college. She spent eight years there before moving into product leadership roles at Nordstrom, Cisco and Smartsheet. Today McClain is senior vice president of product management at SumerSports, a sports analytics company.

“Most of my jobs came through connections with TAF,” she said, crediting the organization for repeatedly “opening doors I didn’t even know could be opened.”

That’s the path Trish Millines Dziko had in mind when she left Microsoft 30 years ago to start TAF with her partner, Jill Hull Dziko: teach kids of color to work with technology, and get them hired by tech companies.

But about eight years in, she saw a problem. TAF’s interns were thriving, she said, but many couldn’t get into college computer science or engineering courses because their high schools had already steered them into lower-level math and science.

To change that, TAF would need to reach students by sixth grade, inside the schools.

So TAF went into public education. The organization, which marked its 30th anniversary Oct. 1, now co-manages a public middle and high school in Federal Way, Wash., and coaches teachers in other public schools.

“No matter what our kids do, we teach them to use STEM skills. They have to critically think. They have to solve problems. … They have to communicate. They have to lead.”

Executive director, Technology Access Foundation

Working with entire schools, rather than kids who signed up for a tech program, changed the goal, too. The focus now is on skills students can use in any field, whether or not it’s tech.

Students learn science, technology, engineering and math through projects that combine subjects and put classroom lessons to use. In 2020, for example, two students at TAF’s Federal Way school turned a gardening robot into a model 3D printer using a cake-frosting syringe, a threaded rod and a motor, as GeekWire reported at the time.

“What we want to make sure is, no matter what our kids do, we teach them to use STEM skills,” Millines Dziko said. “They have to critically think. They have to solve problems. … They have to communicate. They have to lead.”

The shift has cost TAF money. The organization has missed out on larger funding opportunities, Millines Dziko said, because it isn’t focused solely on tech and isn’t growing as fast as some funders would like. In the early 2010s, as education philanthropy flowed to charter schools, TAF couldn’t raise enough to open the additional schools it had planned.

“But we stuck with what was true, and what works for our kids,” she said, “and we’re still here.”

Millines Dziko grew up in New Jersey, raised by a single mother who cleaned floors for a living. She told the Seattle P-I in 1995 that she believed she’d been placed in a lower-level math class because of her race. She took summer-school classes to work her way into honors.

She studied computer science at Monmouth College on a basketball scholarship and began working at Microsoft in 1988 as the first tester on SQL Server. “She was always a force to be reckoned with,” said Bob Muglia, the longtime Microsoft executive who hired her, speaking with GeekWire at the organization’s 30th anniversary party in October. His foundation now supports TAF.

She later moved into a diversity role and took over Microsoft’s high school internship program, making it technical and filling it almost entirely with Seattle kids of color. When she pushed the company to reach students earlier, she said, “the attitude was, it’s not broken, so let’s not fix it.”

Then her partner, Jill Hull Dziko, a social worker in Seattle Public Schools’ behavior-disorder classrooms, brought seven or eight middle schoolers to campus. They were rowdy on the shuttle ride over and went silent when they walked into a room of high school interns testing a new handheld computer.

On the way back, Millines Dziko recalled, they were saying, “I want to be an engineer. I want to do what they did.”

She left Microsoft in August 1996 and put $150,000 of her own money into TAF. If she didn’t help others, she told the P-I the next year, her late mother “would want me to have my butt kicked.”

TAF set up in a Columbia City storefront next to a Taco del Mar. When they first opened the door, she said, they could see the basement through the subfloor, and the staff wired the network themselves. The first students started after-school classes in 1997, training for paid summer internships.

McClain joined the second class as she entered ninth grade, along with her older sister. Millines Dziko taught them to take apart a computer and write their first programs. “She’s encouraging, but she’s also very strict,” McClain said. “We all got jobs that summer, so obviously she taught us something.”

In 2000, TAF started a program for younger students called TechStart. At the anniversary party in October, Sherry Williams, TAF’s executive director of operations, who joined in 1997 as its fourth employee, told the crowd about a young girl who was afraid of math. The girl’s mother brought her every afternoon, and the girl kept working at it.

One day she walked in wearing a T-shirt that said “I love math.”

“Although her school wasn’t serving her, in our after-school program, she was being served,” Williams said. “And she knew she could do anything after that.”

TAF opened a public school, TAF Academy, with Federal Way Public Schools in 2008. Mike Miles, one of its first ninth-graders, went reluctantly. The school looked way too small, he told the Federal Way Mirror the following year. “I didn’t want to have six kids in my class, but my parents made me go anyway.”

He was ahead in math, and the new school couldn’t offer the class he needed, so he spent his first year in the back of the room teaching himself from a textbook.

The next year, TAF arranged for him to take math at another public school down the street. Looking back as a parent, he said in a recent interview, he appreciates that the school was willing to “swallow your pride a little” and acknowledge that it couldn’t give him what he needed. He got the math education there, and where he is today, he said, is “better than what I ever could have expected.”

Miles, now 32, graduated in 2012 with TAF Academy’s first class, earned a business degree at Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute and leads data teams at a cybersecurity startup in the Washington, D.C., area.

He remembers sitting in a circle in social studies, discussing the 2012 killing of Trayvon Martin, an unarmed Black teenager in Florida, and learning to keep disagreements from turning into “a shouting match,” a skill he relies on in his work now.

Federal Way wasn’t the original plan. TAF spent two years designing a school for Seattle Public Schools, and in 2006 it proposed one for Rainier Beach High School, first as a replacement for the school and then as an academy inside the building.

Many students and teachers saw it as a takeover. Teachers worried the academy would drain resources from the existing school, and families objected that the district had discussed the proposal for a year without telling them. At a packed community meeting that November, there was shouting, and the PTSA president walked out with dozens of students, The Seattle Times reported.

“It was just the dumbest and the most frustrating thing I had ever been through,” Millines Dziko said in a recent interview. “I said we’re done, no more.”

Federal Way Superintendent Tom Murphy read about it, called her and came up to Seattle to meet. After a couple of hours, she said, he told her, “You belong in Federal Way.” TAF is now working with its fifth superintendent there, she said.

The lowest point, she said, came around 2012, when TAF had to lay off staff for the second time. Education philanthropy was pouring into charter schools, a planned expansion into Renton had stalled for lack of money, she said, and TAF had just moved into a new building.

She recalled seeing reports that only a small share of major philanthropic funding went to nonprofits led by people of color, and she started asking herself a question. “Is me being a leader of this organization gonna hold us back from getting funding? Would it be better if we had someone who was white to lead the organization?”

She talked it over with Williams and Zithri Saleem, two of her top leaders, and “we almost went down that road,” she said. But she reconsidered. “That’s not the answer either,” she said. Instead, TAF had to “get out there and show them,” and find other people interested in its work.

Seattle came back around after Denise Juneau became superintendent. In 2020, the school board approved a TAF partnership at Washington Middle School in the Central District. Three years later, facing a budget shortfall, the district cut it, as GeekWire reported at the time. “It’s solely about money,” Millines Dziko told The Seattle Times then.

Asked whether she could see herself working with Seattle Public Schools again, she said, “No.” The district has “way too many problems,” she said, and dealing with them “takes our energy away from places where we could be having impact.”

In 2024, TAF was among the nonprofits chosen in MacKenzie Scott’s open call, after a process that included peer review. TAF expected $1 million and got $2 million. “It wasn’t the money; it was the belief in our work,” Millines Dziko said.

TAF used $500,000 for operating needs it had been saving for and put the rest in a certificate of deposit, she said.

TAF reported about $4 million in revenue and $5 million in expenses in its Form 990 for the fiscal year that ended June 30, 2025, and ended the year with about $11.4 million in net assets. Millines Dziko said the organization’s annual budget is now close to $7 million, and its fundraising team raises about 93% of it, mostly through grants.

TAF Academy had been recognized for test-score gains. It was named a School of Distinction in 2012 for improvement in middle-school reading and math. In 2016, the district cited three consecutive years of recognition as one reason for merging it with Saghalie Middle School. The combined school, TAF@Saghalie, opened in 2017, and TAF co-manages it with the district.

TAF@Saghalie’s four-year graduation rate for the class of 2025 was above 88.5%, compared with 82.6% statewide, according to state data. On state tests in 2024-25, 17% of the school’s low-income students who took the tests in grades 6–8 and 10 met the English language arts standard and 11% met the math standard, compared with 30% and 15% for low-income students in the same grades across Federal Way Public Schools.

Millines Dziko argues that standardized tests don’t measure what matters. They assume every student had a teacher who covered everything on the exam, she said, and “they demean kids,” charting their academic course as early as third grade.

TAF trains teachers to track each student’s growth and is building its own way to document it. Teachers score students from 1 to 4 against standards, backed by photos of projects and samples of student work. The data lives in the modern version of SQL Server, the Microsoft database Millines Dziko was hired to test in 1988.

The system is in the third year of a pilot. Only selected teachers are participating, and TAF is still working out how much time teachers can spend documenting students’ work while teaching, she said. TAF is bringing in an evaluator from the University of Washington Bothell to review the pilot, she said.

Millines Dziko’s goal is for every district in the country to use it, and for standardized tests to “go out the window,” with the money states spend on them going to teacher training instead. “I believe it will,” she said.

Miles liked the project-based learning but said he found gaps in his preparation when he got to college. “I took physics at TAF Academy, took physics in college, and I was not prepared,” he said. What he got in return, he said, was “a different way of thinking.”

TAF looked like a program for teaching technical skills, he said, but “they taught kids how to be people.” He tries to pass that on to his son, he said, including putting others first and using his gifts to help others.

TransformED, TAF’s teacher-coaching program, places a full-time coach in a partner school for five years. It works with five schools now and plans to add 10 more over five years, at about $200,000 per school per year, Millines Dziko said. In September, TAF hired a former Atlanta principal, Donya Loyd Kemp, to lead it, as GeekWire reported.

Millines Dziko is wary of the rush to bring AI into classrooms. Students can use it to find sources, she said, but then they have to investigate those sources themselves. “It should be used as a tool to gather quickly, so I can now use most of my time doing the thinking.”

Millines Dziko said the region’s tech companies should invest in public schools as a way to attract and keep families here, not just with donated products and the occasional volunteer day. “That’s performative,” she said.

What she wants are lasting relationships, like the ones TAF has with smaller companies that come back to its schools every year to give students real problems to solve. As for the big tech companies, “I need them to be more about pouring into instead of extracting out of,” she said.

Millines Dziko turns 70 in July. For the past year and a half, she said, Williams and Joshua Halsey, TAF’s executive director of education, have taken on more of the leadership, freeing her to spend more time raising money and building relationships.

She doesn’t expect to stop working, she said, predicting that she’ll never retire.

At the 30th anniversary party, she hugged about three-quarters of the room, by her count. Looking around at her former students, many with kids of their own, it hit her.

“This is 30 years, man, and look at y’all,” she said, recalling the moment later. “Y’all are good.”
